look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for a reel or portfolio that shows wireframes, UV layouts and texture maps, not just final renders. Clean topology, sensible polycounts and tidy UVs show real skill. Polished renders alone can hide messy geometry or purchased assets.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the parts of the pipeline you need, such as hard surface or organic modeling, retopology, UV unwrapping, PBR texturing and lighting. Check they can deliver in your file formats and engine, and stay within a set polycount and texture budget.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state or federal license is required to work as a 3D artist. Software vendor certifications exist but are optional. Verify past work instead. Call references, confirm credits on shipped projects and ask exactly which parts of a team piece they made.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolio pieces that match common tutorial projects or store-bought models, no breakdowns or source files, and vague answers about their role on team work. Also note confusion about game-ready versus render-only assets, or ignoring scale and naming rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through one piece from blockout to final render. Ask how they handled a polycount cut, how they bake normal maps and how they respond to art direction notes. Strong artists explain their tradeoffs clearly and simply.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a 3D artist?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio that matches your style and medium, with breakdowns showing wireframes, UVs and textures. Check they know your software and engine, can work within technical budgets and take feedback well. No license is required, so references and confirmed project credits matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a 3D artist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid test that mirrors real work, such as modeling and texturing one prop from a concept sheet within a set polycount and texture size. Ask for the source file, wireframe and texture maps, not just a render. Review topology, UVs, accuracy to the brief and how they handled your notes.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test discovery questioning, objection handling, clear written follow-up and honest forecasting. A strong account executive listens more than they talk, finds the buyer’s real problem, and knows who signs the contract before they send a proposal.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe past deals in concrete detail: the buyer’s role, the typical deal size, the length of the sales cycle, and why each deal was won or lost. Their account of quota results stays consistent across interviews, and they can explain how they built their own pipeline.

look.label: Licenses that may apply
look.text: Most account executive roles need no license. Some regulated products do, for example insurance, securities, real estate or mortgage loans. Requirements vary by state and by product, so confirm what your field needs and verify any license through the regulator’s public lookup.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague or shifting numbers, blaming others for every lost deal, and no clear idea of how buyers decide. Other warning signs are talking over the prospect in a role-play and sending no follow-up after the interview, the very task they would own in the job.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a deal they lost and what they would change. Ask how they revived a stalled deal, how they handled a price objection, and how they decided which deals to drop from their forecast.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an account executive?
qa.a: Look for someone who can explain past deals in detail, from first meeting to signed contract. Strong candidates ask sharp questions, handle objections calmly, follow up in writing, and forecast honestly. Check that their quota results stay consistent. If you sell a regulated product, such as insurance or securities, confirm any license your state and product require.

qa.q: How do I test an account executive before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role-play discovery call where you play a buyer with a hidden concern and a tight budget. Score how well they uncover the problem, handle objections and agree on a next step. Then ask for a written follow-up email within a day. This shows listening, persistence and clear writing.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they run a renewal conversation, spot an upsell the customer actually needs, and handle a pricing objection without discounting too fast. Check written follow-up too. Clear recap emails and organized notes in a CRM matter as much as phone skills.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about retention and customer outcomes, not just quota. They can describe a specific account they saved or grew, what the customer’s problem was, and how they knew more product would help. They ask about your churn reasons and how accounts are handed off.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who treats every call as a sales pitch, blames customers for churn, or can’t name the metrics they owned. Vague answers about renewal rates or account size, or bad-mouthing past clients, suggest they may not protect your relationships.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how many accounts they managed and at what size. Ask them to walk through a renewal that almost failed. Ask how they decide when to upsell and when to hold back. Ask how they keep track of contract dates and open issues.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for general account management in the US. Verify past employers, titles and dates. If the role involves selling insurance or securities, the person needs the matching state license or industry registration, and rules vary by state.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an account manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who keeps customers, not just closes deals. Strong account managers know their renewal and expansion numbers, listen before they pitch, and stay organized across many accounts. They write clear follow-ups and handle complaints calmly. Ask for specific stories about accounts they saved or grew, and check references from past managers.

qa.q: How do I test an account manager before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role-play. Give them a mock customer whose renewal is due, who has a complaint and a small budget. See whether they ask questions, address the problem, and suggest an add-on only if it fits. Then have them write the recap email. This shows listening, judgment and written follow-through.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Each state board of accountancy issues CPA licenses, which are needed to sign audit opinions but not to keep a company’s books. Requirements vary by state. Verify any CPA license on the state board’s website. Management accounting certifications are optional.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test journal entries, accruals, account reconciliations, the month-end close and basic revenue recognition under US GAAP. Check spreadsheet skills, your accounting software, payroll and sales tax basics, which vary by state, and controls such as separating who approves and who pays.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates close on a set schedule, reconcile every balance sheet account, document entries and explain variances in plain words. They spot errors early, keep clean audit trails and can show a close checklist or process they improved.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for plugging differences to make accounts balance, confusion between cash and accrual accounting, weak reconciliation habits, and comfort with one person controlling the whole payment process. Be careful with anyone vague about audit findings on their past work.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your month-end close. A bank reconciliation is off by a small amount. What do you do? How do you record a customer who prepays for a year of service? Strong answers follow clear steps and correct entries.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an accountant?
qa.a: Look for solid accrual accounting, careful reconciliations and a reliable month-end close, plus strong spreadsheet and software skills and respect for internal controls. A CPA license is needed only for some work, such as audits, and requirements vary by state, so verify it on the state board website when it matters.

qa.q: How do I test an accountant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid test with sample transactions: record journal entries, reconcile a bank statement with planted errors and prepare a simple trial balance. Include a prepaid expense and an accrual. Review accuracy, how they found and explained differences, and whether another accountant could follow their work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to run a three-way match of purchase order, receiving record and invoice. Have them code invoices to the right expense accounts, catch a duplicate or altered invoice, and work fast and accurately in your accounting software or spreadsheets.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No US state license is required for this work. Optional accounts payable certifications from professional associations exist, and bookkeeping or accounting coursework helps. Verify past employers and references. Any background check must follow federal FCRA rules and state or local fair chance laws, which vary.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe how they prevent duplicate payments and verify vendor bank changes by calling a known number. They understand payment terms, early-pay discounts, W-9 collection and year-end 1099 reporting, and they keep clear records for month-end close and audits.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who pays invoices without approval or a matching purchase order, changes vendor bank details from an email alone, or sees no problem with one person setting up vendors and releasing payments. Vague answers about fixing past errors are also a warning.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you find and recover a duplicate payment? What do you do when an invoice does not match the purchase order? How do you handle a vendor’s request to change bank details? Walk me through your month-end steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an accounts payable specialist?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, steady attention to detail and solid internal control habits. A good candidate knows three-way matching, invoice coding, vendor setup with W-9s, 1099 reporting basics and fraud checks such as verifying bank changes by phone. Experience with your type of accounting software is a plus, and references should confirm reliability with payment deadlines.

qa.q: How do I test an accounts payable specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid or timed exercise with sample invoices, purchase orders and receiving records. Include one duplicate invoice, one price mismatch and one suspicious bank change request. Ask the candidate to decide what to pay, code each invoice and explain what they would flag. Their reasoning matters as much as speed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check cash application first. A strong specialist matches payments to open invoices, handles short pays and lump-sum checks, clears unapplied cash and reads an aging report. Test spreadsheet skills such as lookups, filters and pivot tables, and ask which accounting or billing systems they have used.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for in-house accounts receivable work. Optional credit and collections certifications exist, so confirm any listed. Verify past roles and systems with references. If you run a background check, get written consent first and follow federal rules plus any state or local limits, which vary.

look.label: Collection rules they should know
look.text: If they will collect from consumers, they should know fair collection practices. The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act mainly covers third-party collectors, but some states apply similar rules to businesses collecting their own debts. Ask how they handle disputes, call times and written records.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a steady follow-up routine: reminders before due dates, calls at set intervals and clear escalation steps. They log every contact, resolve billing errors fast and talk about lowering past-due balances or days sales outstanding. They stay firm but polite and protect the customer relationship.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about reconciling accounts, no example of resolving a payment dispute, or pride in threatening customers. Be wary if they blame customers for every late payment, skip notes on calls, or cannot explain how they handle credits, refunds and write-off requests.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an accounts receivable and collections specialist?
qa.a: Look for accurate invoicing, solid cash application and a calm, persistent collection style. They should read aging reports, match payments to invoices and fix discrepancies quickly. Good record keeping matters, since every call and promise to pay should be logged. If they will contact consumers, they should understand fair collection practices and the rules that apply in your state.

qa.q: How do I test an accounts receivable and collections specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short exercise with sample invoices, a bank deposit list and a few partial payments. Ask them to apply the cash, flag mismatches and list which accounts to call first. Then role-play a call with a customer who is upset about a billing error. Watch for accuracy, clear notes and a respectful but firm tone.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: For credentialed roles, confirm designations such as ASA, FSA, ACAS or FCAS in the Society of Actuaries or Casualty Actuarial Society member directory. For exam progress, ask for official pass records the candidate can share. Some work on US retirement plans requires an Enrolled Actuary credential.

look.label: Signing authority
look.text: If the role signs statements of actuarial opinion, such as reserve opinions filed with state insurance regulators, check that the candidate meets the American Academy of Actuaries qualification standards for that work. Ask how they keep up the required continuing education.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give a small claims data set and ask for a reserve estimate or a rate indication. Watch their skill with tools like Excel, SQL, R or Python, and how they clean data, state assumptions and check results.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain results in plain words to underwriters, finance staff or plan sponsors. They name the limits of their data and assumptions, document work so a peer could rerun it, and question numbers that look too good.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Exam claims they cannot back with official pass records, models they cannot explain step by step, no habit of checking data quality, or answers that give one exact number and hide the real range of outcomes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an actuary?
qa.a: Look for exam progress or a designation that fits your field, such as life, health, pension or property and casualty. Check sound skill with data tools, clear reasoning about assumptions, and the ability to explain results to people who are not actuaries. For roles that sign opinions, confirm they meet the required qualification standards.

qa.q: How do I test an actuary before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task with sample data, such as estimating claim reserves or pricing a simple policy. Ask them to list assumptions, show checks on the data and explain the answer in plain words. Then ask how the result would change if a key assumption moved. Their reasoning matters more than one exact number.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for additive manufacturing work, and industry certificates are optional. For aerospace, medical or rocket parts, ask about experience with process qualification and quality systems. Verify parts they built, build reports and inspection records, and references who saw their work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test design for additive manufacturing, build orientation and supports, process parameters, and the processes you use, such as powder bed fusion, directed energy deposition or polymer printing. Check post-processing like stress relief, heat treatment and machining, inspection with CT scanning, and safe metal powder handling.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain why a build failed using data and fix it with design or parameter changes. They control powder lots and machine logs, plan post-processing from the start, and can show a part that went from prototype to qualified production.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for printing without tracking powder, parameters or build records, careless handling of metal powders that can burn or explode, and no grasp of residual stress or porosity. Be wary of anyone who only knows desktop printers for a production metal role.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a build that failed and how you found the cause. How do you choose orientation and supports for a part with thin walls? How do you control powder reuse? Strong answers name specific data, settings and inspection results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an additive manufacturing engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with your printers and materials, parts that reached real use, and strong records of powder, parameters and inspection. Check design for additive skills, post-processing knowledge and powder safety habits. No license is required, so build records, part samples and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an additive manufacturing engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise, such as redesigning a sample part for printing and planning its orientation, supports, post-processing and inspection. Or share a failed build with photos and logs and ask for the cause and fix. Review technical judgment, safety awareness and how clearly they document their reasoning.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as an administrative assistant. Professional administrative certifications are optional. Verify skills through references from managers they supported, and ask what they managed directly, such as calendars, travel, expense reports or supply orders.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test calendar management across time zones, travel booking, expense reports, document formatting and spreadsheet basics. Check clear, error-free email writing, file organization in shared drives, and how they prioritize requests from different people with competing deadlines.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong assistants anticipate needs, such as booking a room before anyone asks, and confirm details instead of assuming. They keep tidy records, protect confidential information and handle last-minute changes calmly. Managers they supported describe them as reliable and discreet.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for double bookings, typos in sample work, or vague answers about how they track tasks. Be wary of anyone who discusses past employers’ confidential matters freely or who cannot name the tools they used every day.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you plan a multi-city trip on short notice. How do you handle two executives who want the same time slot? Tell me about a mistake you caught before it caused trouble. Strong answers show systems, checks and clear priorities.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an administrative assistant?
qa.a: Look for strong organization, accuracy and discretion, plus skills in calendars, travel, expense reports, documents and spreadsheets. Check how they juggle requests from several people and keep track of deadlines. No license is required, so references from managers they supported and a short practical task matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an administrative assistant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: a set of meeting requests across time zones, a trip with changing details and a messy document to format. Ask them to build the calendar, draft the itinerary and clean up the document. Review accuracy, prioritization, clear communication and whether they flag conflicts or missing information.

look.label: Proof of past campaigns
look.text: Ask for two or three campaigns they ran. Look for the goal, the rough budget size, the channels used, the results and what they did themselves versus the team. Strong candidates can show dashboards or reports with private client details removed.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license for advertising work. Free certifications from major ad platforms and analytics tools show basic product knowledge, but they expire and are easy to pass. Confirm they are current, and weigh real results far more heavily.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can build a campaign structure, choose audiences, write ad copy, set up conversion tracking and read a performance report. They should explain cost per click, cost per acquisition and return on ad spend. For ad systems roles, test tagging, ad server setup and basic data queries.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about testing ideas, cutting what does not work and moving budget to what does. They know platform ad policies and FTC rules on truthful ads and endorsement disclosures. They understand that privacy laws on tracking and data use vary by state.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of anyone who promises guaranteed results, reports only clicks and impressions, or cannot explain why a campaign failed. Another warning sign is wanting to run your ads in accounts they own, so you lose your data and history if they leave.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an advertising specialist?
qa.a: Look for real campaign results tied to business goals, not just clicks. They should explain budgets, targeting, tracking and key metrics in plain terms. Check that they know ad platform policies, FTC truth in advertising rules and privacy laws, which vary by state. No license is required, so past work matters most.

qa.q: How do I test an advertising specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short sample report from a past campaign with the names removed. Ask what is working, what they would cut and where they would move the budget. You can also ask them to outline a small campaign for one of your products, with audiences, ad ideas and how they would measure success.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check for a bachelor’s degree in aerospace, mechanical or a related engineering field, ideally from an ABET-accredited program. A PE license is rarely required in industry roles, and licensing rules vary by state. For certification work, ask whether they have served as or worked with an FAA Designated Engineering Representative.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the core of your role, such as stress analysis, aerodynamics, propulsion, controls or orbital mechanics. Confirm hands-on use of CAD, finite element analysis and computational fluid dynamics tools, plus scripting for data analysis. Ask them to check a software result with a quick hand calculation.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain design trade-offs in weight, cost, safety margin and schedule. They know the standards your work follows, such as AS9100 quality systems or DO-178C for flight software. They document carefully and can describe a test, failure or review where their analysis changed a decision.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about which part of a project they actually owned. Trusting software output without checking units, loads or boundary conditions. Treating design reviews, documentation or test data as paperwork. Claiming certification or flight test experience they can’t describe in concrete terms.

look.label: Clearance and export rules
look.text: Defense and space roles may need a security clearance or fall under ITAR or EAR export rules. State these requirements in the posting and verify them through the proper lawful process, with legal guidance. Don’t ask about birthplace, ancestry or other protected traits.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an aerospace engineer?
qa.a: Look for an engineering degree, often from an ABET-accredited program, and depth in the area you need, such as structures, propulsion, avionics or guidance. Strong candidates explain trade-offs, check their own analysis and know your industry’s standards. A PE license is seldom required in aerospace industry roles, and licensing rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test an aerospace engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short problem tied to your work, such as sizing a bracket for a given load, estimating climb performance or finding errors in a flawed analysis. Ask them to show assumptions, units and safety margins. Then have a senior engineer walk through their reasoning with them in a technical interview.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Ask for program results they can share, examples of partner recruiting and policy documents they wrote, and call references. Confirm they know the FTC expects affiliates to disclose their commission clearly and expects the brand to monitor this.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they design commission structures, recruit and vet partners, and read network or tracking platform reports. Check fraud detection, such as cookie stuffing, fake leads and brand keyword bidding, and how they measure whether affiliate sales are truly new customers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates focus on profit, not just affiliate revenue. They know which partners bring new customers and which only claim sales that would happen anyway, such as some coupon sites. They write clear program terms and enforce them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for growth driven by coupon and cashback sites with no check on whether the sales are new, no fraud controls, and loose approval of partners. Be wary of anyone who ignores disclosure rules or cannot explain how commissions are tracked and reversed for returns.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you find and stop affiliate fraud? How do you set commission rates for different partner types? Tell me about a partner you removed and why. Strong answers mention specific fraud signals, attribution rules and margin math.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an affiliate marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has grown an affiliate program profitably, recruits quality partners, and spots fraud and low-value traffic. They should know tracking platforms, commission design, attribution and FTC disclosure rules. No license is required, so program results, partner references and clear answers about margin matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an affiliate marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a sample partner report. Ask them to flag likely fraud, rank partners by real value, suggest commission changes and name new partners to recruit. Judge whether they think about profit and new customers, not just total affiliate sales.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: There is no US license for AI engineers, and degrees vary widely. Verify the work instead. Ask for links to shipped products, code repositories or writeups, and confirm their exact role in each project with a past manager or teammate.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test retrieval over documents (chunking, embeddings, ranking), prompt design, tool calling for agents and evaluation. Strong candidates also handle latency, cost per request, rate limits and model provider failures, and they write solid code in the language your team uses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about evaluation sets and how they measured quality before and after a change. They can explain how they reduced made-up answers, guarded against prompt injection, and kept private data out of prompts and logs where it did not belong.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Demos that only work on a few hand-picked examples, no way to measure whether answers are correct, and vague claims of building agents without details. Be wary of anyone who sends customer data to outside models without checking contracts or privacy rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask what broke when their assistant met real users and how they fixed it. Ask how they would choose between a larger model, a smaller one, or better retrieval for a task, and how they would prove the change helped.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an AI engineer?
qa.a: Look for shipped products built on language models, not just demos. Good AI engineers combine solid software skills with retrieval, prompt design, agent tool use and careful evaluation. They can explain tradeoffs in quality, speed and cost, and they take security and privacy seriously. No license is required, so judge them on real work and references.

qa.q: How do I test an AI engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small paid task: build a simple question answering tool over a few sample documents you provide, with no confidential data. Ask for a short set of test questions and a note on how they measured accuracy. Then review the code together and ask what they would change before real users touch it.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to turn a vague user problem into an AI feature spec. Strong candidates define the task, the data it needs, the success metrics, and what happens when the model is wrong. They should also know when a simple rule beats a model.

look.label: Evaluation know-how
look.text: This person decides how good is good enough. Look for someone who builds test sets, sets a quality bar before launch, picks fitting measures such as accuracy or human ratings, and plans checks for quality drops after release.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this role. Courses and vendor certificates show interest, not skill. Verify past roles and shipped products through references, and ask what they personally decided versus what the team decided.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about cost, speed and failure cases, not just demos. They plan for bias, privacy and safety reviews with legal and security teams. They can explain model limits to customers and executives in plain words.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Promising a model will be right every time. No metrics from past launches. Treating evaluation as only the engineers’ job. Vague answers about what data was used and whether the company had the right to use it.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an AI product manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has shipped AI features, not just prototypes. They should define clear success metrics, set a quality bar before launch, plan for errors and misuse, and work well with engineers, data scientists and legal. Ask about specific launches and the tradeoffs they made.

qa.q: How do I test an AI product manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Describe a feature idea, such as summarizing support tickets, and ask for a one page plan covering the user need, data, success metrics, launch quality bar, failure handling and rollout. Then ask how they would decide to delay launch if quality fell short.

look.label: No license to check
look.text: There is no US license or required certification for AI safety work. Verify skill through published papers, open-source code, evaluation reports or red-teaming findings the candidate can walk you through step by step.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Designing evaluations that measure a specific model behavior, writing Python to run them at scale, and reading results with statistical care. They should spot when a benchmark is contaminated or a metric is being gamed, and explain how they confirmed a failure was real.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They separate what a model can do from what it does by default and report uncertainty plainly. They know common failures such as jailbreaks, prompt injection, reward hacking, sycophancy and hallucination, and they propose fixes, not just problems.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Big claims with no reproducible evidence, results based on a single prompt, and no baseline or control. Be wary of vague talk about alignment with no concrete methods, or of anyone who shares dangerous details carelessly or dismisses responsible disclosure.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they would tell whether a model is being honest or just agreeing with the user. Ask how they kept test data out of training data, and what they did the last time a result surprised them.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an AI safety specialist?
qa.a: Look for proof of hands-on work, such as evaluations they built, red-teaming findings, or papers and code you can review. Strong candidates pair solid Python and machine learning skills with careful experiment design and honest reporting of limits. No US license exists for this role, so judge them on work samples and how clearly they explain their reasoning.

qa.q: How do I test an AI safety specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-limited task. Provide access to a small model or API and ask them to find and document failure modes, such as jailbreaks or false answers, then suggest a mitigation. Score the method, reproducibility and clarity of the write-up. Keep the task free of truly harmful content and don’t use it as unpaid production work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test careful reading, clear writing and fact-checking. Strong AI trainers follow long labeling guidelines exactly, spot subtle errors in model answers, and explain their ratings in plain words. If you need domain work such as coding, math or medicine, test that knowledge directly with real sample tasks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for consistent ratings across similar examples, short but precise written justifications, and questions about edge cases instead of guesses. Good candidates notice when guidelines conflict and flag it. They keep steady quality over a long batch, not just the first few items.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or certification is required for AI training work. Verify what matters for your project instead: degrees or work history for expert domains, writing samples, and past annotation or content review experience. Confirm the person can sign and follow confidentiality terms for your data.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for answers that look pasted from an AI tool, rushing through tasks with uniform scores, ignoring the guidelines you provided, or vague claims of expertise they cannot show in a test. Reluctance to accept quality checks or confidentiality terms is also a warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handle an item the guidelines do not cover, how they stay consistent over hundreds of tasks, and how they judge whether a model answer is factually correct. Ask for an example of feedback that changed how they rated or labeled.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an AI trainer?
qa.a: Look for close attention to detail, strong writing, and the ability to follow detailed guidelines without drifting. For specialized projects, confirm real subject knowledge. Good trainers explain their judgments clearly, flag unclear cases, and keep quality steady across long batches. Since the work is often remote contract work, reliability and data confidentiality matter too.

qa.q: How do I test an AI trainer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid sample using your real guidelines. Include a few model answers with hidden errors, some ambiguous items and one or two repeats. Check accuracy against your answer key, consistency on the repeats, and the quality of written explanations. Compare results across candidates on the same set for a fair review.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No federal or state license is required for this role. Voluntary certifications such as CAMS or CFE show formal training, so confirm them with the issuing body. Check past roles at banks, credit unions, money services businesses, fintechs or broker-dealers with references.

look.label: Knowledge to check
look.text: Ask them to explain the Bank Secrecy Act, customer due diligence, beneficial ownership checks, OFAC sanctions screening, and when a Suspicious Activity Report or Currency Transaction Report is filed. Strong candidates explain each in plain words and link it to real work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give them a sample customer file and transaction history. Watch how they spot structuring, rapid movement of funds, activity that doesn’t fit the business or a possible sanctions match. See if they clear false positives and write a short, factual case narrative.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They document every decision, ask for more information before closing an alert, and know when to escalate. They stay accurate with high alert volumes, are comfortable with screening and case management tools, and learn your risk policy quickly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful if they would tell a customer about a suspicious activity report, which federal law prohibits. Other warning signs are sharing past case details freely, clearing alerts without notes, vague answers about screening lists, or treating compliance as box-ticking.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an AML and KYC analyst?
qa.a: Look for solid knowledge of the Bank Secrecy Act, customer due diligence, sanctions screening and suspicious activity reporting. Good analysts are detail-minded, write clear case notes and know when to escalate. No license is required, but a voluntary certification such as CAMS can show training. Experience in your type of business, such as banking or payments, is a plus.

qa.q: How do I test an AML and KYC analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a fictional customer profile with a few months of transactions and some screening alerts. Ask them to flag risks, clear or escalate each alert, and write a short case narrative. Then talk through their reasoning. Never use real customer data in the test, since it is confidential.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for analog or mixed-signal design. Verify work instead: chips taped out and working in silicon, characterization reports, patents or papers, and references who can confirm which blocks the candidate owned. Degrees help, but silicon results matter most.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test transistor-level design and simulation across process, voltage and temperature corners, with Monte Carlo runs for mismatch. Check the blocks you need, such as amplifiers, data converters, PLLs, regulators or high-speed links, plus layout awareness, noise analysis and lab characterization.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain tradeoffs in noise, power, area and speed, and know what changed between simulation and silicon. They work closely with layout, write clear specs and test plans, and can describe a silicon bug they found and fixed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who only ran typical-corner simulations, cannot explain parasitics or matching, or have never seen their circuits measured. Be wary of vague credit for team chips, and of anyone who blames layout or test teams for every silicon miss.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a block you designed from spec to silicon. What corner or mismatch case nearly broke it? Tell me about a silicon result that surprised you and how you debugged it. Strong answers name measurements, simulations and specific design changes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an analog and mixed-signal engineer?
qa.a: Look for chips taped out and proven in silicon, deep knowledge of the blocks you need, and careful verification across corners and mismatch. Check lab skills and how they work with layout and test teams. No license is required, so silicon results, design reviews and references matter more than titles.

qa.q: How do I test an analog and mixed-signal engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise, such as designing an amplifier or regulator to a short spec, with hand analysis and a plan for corner and Monte Carlo checks. Or share a schematic and measured data with a hidden flaw and ask for a diagnosis. Review reasoning, tradeoffs and how they verify their own work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for analytics engineers, and tool certificates are optional. Verify real work: ask for SQL models or a shared repository, documentation they wrote, and references from analysts who relied on their tables.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test advanced SQL, dimensional modeling, version control with Git, and SQL transformation tools that support tests and documentation. Check they write tests for nulls, duplicates and relationships, follow naming rules and define each business metric once.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates build small, well-named models in layers, document the columns that matter and agree on metric definitions with finance and analysts. They review code, catch broken numbers before dashboards do and remove unused tables.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for one giant query nobody can read, the same metric defined differently in several places, no tests, and tables named after people or dates. Be careful with anyone who edits production data by hand to make a report match.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How would you define active customers so every dashboard agrees? Tell me about a broken number you traced back to its source. How do you change a table many reports use without breaking them? Strong answers mention tests, reviews and communication.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an analytics engineer?
qa.a: Look for strong SQL, clean data modeling, version control and a habit of testing and documenting every model. Good candidates agree on metric definitions with the business and keep names consistent. No license is required, so code samples and references from analysts who used their tables matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an analytics engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a few messy raw tables and ask them to build clean, tested models and one agreed metric, such as monthly revenue. Ask for code in Git, tests and short documentation. Review correctness, naming, structure and how clearly they explain their choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to build Android apps, and no Android certification is commonly required. Verify real work instead: apps they helped publish on the Play Store, code samples, and references who confirm the candidate’s own features and fixes.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test Kotlin, Jetpack Compose and the older View system, activity and fragment lifecycles, coroutines, ViewModel and Room. Check Gradle builds, runtime permissions, background work limits, testing, and support for many screen sizes, device makers and Android versions.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have shipped and updated apps through store review, kept up with yearly target API requirements and fixed crashes found in real user reports. They handle configuration changes and process death, test on low-end devices and follow accessibility basics.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for slow work on the main thread, leaked contexts, state lost on screen rotation and every permission requested at launch. Be careful with candidates who test on one device only or cannot explain the activity lifecycle.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you keep state when the system kills the app in the background? Tell me about a crash you found from production reports. How do you schedule reliable background work under battery limits? How did you move a screen to Compose? Strong answers are specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an Android developer?
qa.a: Look for apps they shipped and maintained, with Kotlin code they can explain. Check Jetpack Compose, lifecycle handling, coroutines, testing, accessibility and support for many devices. Experience with store policy and target API updates matters too. No license is required in the US, so published apps and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an Android developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your app, such as a Compose screen that loads a list from a sample API, survives rotation and shows loading and error states, with a few tests. Review Kotlin style, coroutine use, lifecycle handling, accessibility and how it behaves on a small screen.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as an Angular or Vue developer. Course certificates exist but are optional. Verify real work instead: live apps, code samples and references who confirm which features, upgrades or components the candidate built personally.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: For Angular, test TypeScript, components, dependency injection, RxJS, signals, routing and reactive forms. For Vue, test the Composition API, reactivity, Pinia, Vue Router and single-file components. In both, check testing, accessibility, responsive layouts and handling of API errors.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know the version you run and have upgraded apps across major versions. They explain change detection or reactivity in plain words, split screens into clear components, and keep business logic in services or composables rather than templates.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for subscriptions that are never cleaned up, logic piled into templates, and state changed from many places. Be careful with anyone whose experience is mostly AngularJS or Vue 2 with no recent work on current versions, since both have reached end of support.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an upgrade across major versions and what broke. How do you avoid memory leaks from observables or watchers? How do you share state between distant components? How do you make a custom form control accessible? Strong answers name specific steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an Angular and Vue developer?
qa.a: Look for real apps built in the framework you use, Angular or Vue, on a current version, with code they can explain. Check TypeScript, state handling, testing, accessibility and upgrade experience. Skills carry over between the two, but switching takes time. No license is required in the US, so real work matters most.

qa.q: How do I test an Angular and Vue developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task in your framework, such as a form with validation that loads and saves data through a sample API, with loading and error states. Ask them to use Git and add tests. Review component structure, reactivity or RxJS use, cleanup of subscriptions, accessibility and code readability.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask the candidate to design a small REST or GraphQL endpoint with clear naming, error codes and pagination. Then have them wrap it in a simple client library. Watch how they handle versioning, authentication and retries.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about the developers who will use their work. They write clear docs and sample code, keep changes backward compatible, and publish SDKs through standard package managers with semantic versioning and changelogs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they retired an old API version without breaking customers. Ask how they set rate limits, or how they kept an SDK consistent across two or more languages. Real stories include trade-offs and mistakes.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for breaking changes shipped without notice, no automated tests, or secrets hard-coded in sample code. Be careful with candidates who skip documentation, ignore security basics like input validation and OAuth scopes, or can’t explain status codes.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Instead, review public code samples, published packages or API docs they wrote. Cloud or security certifications can help but are optional, and they never replace a hands-on review.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an API and SDK developer?
qa.a: Look for solid API design skills, experience with REST or GraphQL, and comfort writing client libraries in the languages your users need. Good candidates write clear documentation, plan for versioning and backward compatibility, and take security seriously. Ask for samples of APIs or SDKs they built or helped maintain.

qa.q: How do I test an API and SDK developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Have them design a small endpoint with error handling and authentication, then write a client function, tests and a short README. Review the code together. Ask them to explain their naming, how they would version the API and how a new developer would get started.

look.label: Credentials worth checking
look.text: No US state license exists for this work. Certifications such as OSWE, GWAPT or CSSLP show focused study, but they are optional. Confirm any listed cert through the issuer’s online lookup. Give more weight to real findings, such as published CVEs or credited bug reports.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give them a short code sample with planted flaws, such as SQL injection, broken access control or unsafe deserialization. A strong candidate finds the bug, explains how an attacker would use it and writes a fix your developers would accept.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They read code well in your main languages and know the OWASP Top 10 beyond the names. They push for threat modeling early in design. They explain risk in plain terms and work alongside developers instead of just filing tickets.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Relies on scanner output without confirming findings. Can explain the bug but not the fix. Talks about testing systems they had no permission to touch. Marks every issue as critical, which teaches developers to ignore real problems.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a serious flaw they caught close to release and how they got it fixed. Ask how they would add security checks to a CI pipeline without slowing builds. Listen for specific tools, tradeoffs and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an application security engineer?
qa.a: Look for someone who reads code in your languages, understands common flaws like injection and broken access control, and can write practical fixes. They should know secure design and CI security tooling. No state license is required, so judge real work, such as code reviews, disclosed bugs or past projects, over certificates alone.

qa.q: How do I test an application security engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-boxed exercise using a small app or code sample with planted vulnerabilities. Ask them to find the flaws, rank them by risk and propose fixes. Then have them walk you through their reasoning. Never ask them to test live systems you don’t own.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for AI adoption work. Vendor AI certificates are optional. Verify past projects instead: ask for case studies with measured before-and-after results, and ask client references what was actually adopted and is still in use.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they find good use cases, estimate value, design prompts and workflows, build simple evaluation sets and train staff. Check they understand data privacy, confidentiality and copyright questions, and that rules on AI and personal data differ by state and industry.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates start with a real business process, pick a small pilot, measure time or quality gains, and keep a human review step where errors are costly. They can describe projects they stopped because AI was the wrong tool.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for promises of large savings with no measurement plan, confidential data pasted into public tools, no thought about errors or bias, and demos that never reached daily use. Be careful with anyone who dismisses staff concerns or training.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an AI rollout that people stopped using, and why. How do you check whether answers are accurate? How do you decide which tasks to automate first? Strong answers include specific measures, risks and how they trained the team.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an applied AI specialist?
qa.a: Look for real projects with measured results, a habit of starting small and testing, and strong attention to privacy, accuracy and training. Good candidates can explain where AI did not help. No license is required, so case studies and client references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an applied AI specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task, such as reviewing one of your workflows and proposing where AI could help, with a pilot plan, risks and a way to measure success. Ask them to demo one step with sample data, never real customer data. Review practicality, honesty about limits and clarity.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for a portfolio that shows finished campaigns, games or publications they led, not just pieces they made. Look for a clear visual idea carried across many formats. Ask what they decided, what the team made and what the brief required.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they turn a brief into a direction. Look for mood boards, type and color choices, layout systems and clear notes for designers. They should know the main design tools well enough to judge files, even if they no longer make every asset.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong art directors explain the why behind each choice and tie it to the audience and goal. They give feedback that is specific and kind. They meet deadlines, keep a style consistent across a team and can show results such as a relaunch or a shipped game.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolios with no clear credit for their own role, work that all looks the same whatever the client, or vague talk about results. Be wary of anyone who dismisses budgets, brand rules or feedback, or who cannot explain how they handle image rights and licensing.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a project where the client rejected their direction and what they did next. Ask how they brief a new illustrator or photographer. Ask how they handled a missed deadline on their team. Real leaders give concrete steps, names of roles and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an art director?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio of work they led, not just made, with a strong idea carried across formats. Check that they can explain choices in terms of audience and goals, guide designers with clear feedback and work within budgets, brand rules and deadlines. No state license is required for this work, so references and past results matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an art director before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic brief and ask for a direction, not finished art. A mood board, type and color choices and a few rough layouts are enough. Then ask them to critique a sample design as if briefing a junior designer. Keep the task small, use made-up material and consider paying for the time.

look.label: Match the design stage
look.text: Chip work splits into front end and back end. Front-end engineers write RTL and verify it. Back-end engineers handle synthesis, floorplanning, place and route, timing closure and signoff. Decide which stage you need before you screen, since few people are deep in both.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: For front end, test Verilog or SystemVerilog RTL, clock domain crossing, and testbench or UVM skills. For back end, test static timing analysis, timing constraints, power planning and DRC or LVS cleanup. Ask how they balance power, performance and area.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to design chips, and no state licenses this work. Most hires hold an electrical or computer engineering degree. Verify past roles, and confirm the person has worked on designs that went to tape-out if your role needs it.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can describe a block they owned from spec to silicon. They explain a timing or functional bug they found and how they fixed it. They speak clearly about tradeoffs and know where their part fit in the full chip flow.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for people who cannot explain their own role on a team project, who only list tool names without depth, or who freely share a past employer’s confidential design details. That last habit suggests they may treat your designs the same way.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an ASIC and chip design engineer?
qa.a: Look for proven work at the stage you need, front-end RTL and verification or back-end physical design. Check that they can explain timing, clock domain crossing and power, performance and area tradeoffs. Experience with designs that reached tape-out is a strong plus. No license is required, so focus on skills and verified past roles.

qa.q: How do I test an ASIC and chip design engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, focused task. A front-end candidate might write a small FIFO with a clock domain crossing and a basic testbench. A back-end candidate might review a timing report and propose fixes. Keep it to a few hours, never ask for proprietary work, and review the reasoning with them afterward.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for product managers. Optional product courses and certificates exist, but they do not prove skill. If a degree matters for the role, confirm it through the school’s registrar or a degree-verification service, with the candidate’s written consent.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can turn a user complaint into a clear problem statement, pick one metric to watch, and write a short spec. They should explain trade-offs between scope, quality and time in plain words, and read a simple chart without guessing.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about users before features. They ask how engineers and designers work, admit what they do not know, and can describe a class project, internship or side project where they changed a decision because of evidence or feedback.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who jump to building features without asking who the user is. Be wary of anyone who takes sole credit for team work, cannot say how they would know a change worked, or gives vague answers about past projects.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a product they use every day and one change they would make. Ask about a time they had to say no to someone. Ask how they would rank three requests with only one week of engineering time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an associate product manager?
qa.a: Look for clear thinking about users, comfort with basic data, and good written and spoken communication. They should work well with engineers and designers without needing to be in charge. Past product titles matter less than evidence they learn fast, take feedback, and can explain why they made a choice.

qa.q: How do I test an associate product manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short written case about a small product area. Ask for a one-page plan naming the user, the problem, one success metric and a first step. Then discuss it for about 30 minutes and push back on one choice. Keep the task to a few hours so it stays fair.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for a reel with links to the finished game, video or track. Ask which parts they recorded, designed, mixed or implemented themselves. Credits are often shared, so request raw files or before and after clips to see their own work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required for audio engineering work. Optional vendor certifications for audio editing software or game audio tools exist and show training, but a portfolio and references matter more. Call past clients to confirm the credits they list.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test recording clean dialogue or foley, editing out noise and clicks, and mixing to a stated loudness target. For games, check that they can loop sounds without seams, set up variations and implement audio in a game engine or audio middleware.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong engineers keep tidy sessions with clear file names, versions and backups. They ask about delivery formats, sample rates and loudness specs before starting. They know US broadcast follows ATSC A/85 and that streaming and game platforms set their own targets. They work well with designers and programmers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for samples, music or plugins they cannot show a license for. Be wary if they cannot explain their role on listed credits, skip backups, or deliver files without clear names. Mixes that sound loud but clip or distort are another warning sign.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an audio engineer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio that matches your medium, whether games, video or music. Confirm what they personally did on each credit. Check clean recording, careful editing, balanced mixes and correct delivery specs. For games, look for implementation skills in an engine or audio middleware. Ask how they license sound libraries and plugins, and check references from past clients.

qa.q: How do I test an audio engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task that mirrors real work. Send raw dialogue or effects with some noise, and ask for a cleaned, mixed file at a stated loudness and format. For game roles, add a looping sound with a few variations. Review the result, the session files and naming, and how well they followed your brief.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as an internal auditor. Many hold the Certified Internal Auditor (CIA) designation, a CPA license or, for IT audit, the CISA. Check each one through the issuer’s online lookup. CPA licenses come from state boards, so rules and lookups vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them walk through a process such as purchasing or payroll and name the risks and the controls that should catch errors or fraud. Test sampling, workpaper documentation, spreadsheet or data analysis, and writing a clear finding with cause, effect and a practical fix.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain findings in plain language, stay objective without being hostile, and follow up until fixes are in place. For public companies, hands-on Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX) control testing is a plus. They ask how the audit plan is set and who the audit team reports to.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about what they personally tested versus what the team did. Treating audit as box-checking. Willingness to soften a finding because a manager pushed back. Sharing confidential details from a past employer’s audits. A claimed credential that does not show up in the issuer’s lookup.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a control they found was not working. How did they test it, what did they report, and what changed? Also ask how they handled a manager who disagreed with a finding, and how they decide sample sizes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an internal auditor?
qa.a: Look for sound judgment about risk, comfort testing controls, clear writing, and the independence to report bad news. Credentials like the CIA, CPA or CISA help but are not legally required. Match experience to your needs, such as SOX testing for a public company or IT audit for system-heavy work. Verify any credential directly with the issuer.

qa.q: How do I test an internal auditor before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case with a process description, a few sample transactions and a list of controls. Ask them to spot the weak controls, choose what to test, and write one finding with cause, effect and a recommendation. Judge how they reason, not just the answer. Use made-up data and give every candidate the same task.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to connect two APIs: read records from one, transform the data, and write it to the other. Watch how they handle authentication, pagination, rate limits and failed calls. Strong candidates read API docs quickly and write clear, testable code or workflows.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask what happens when a step fails and who owns the process. They build in logging, alerts and retries, and they make sure a rerun does not create duplicate records. They map the manual process before automating it and document what they built.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work in the US. Vendor certifications for integration platforms, cloud services or workflow tools exist and show some study, but they do not prove skill. Check code samples, a portfolio of past integrations and references from people who used their work.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Stores passwords or API keys in plain text, scripts or shared spreadsheets. Automates a messy process without understanding it first. Cannot describe an integration that broke and how they fixed it. Knows only one tool and treats every problem as a fit for it.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through an integration they built from start to finish. Ask how they handled duplicate or missing records, how they managed access and secrets, and how they measured the time saved. Listen for specific systems, data volumes and real tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an integration and automation engineer?
qa.a: Look for someone who can work with APIs, webhooks and data formats like JSON and CSV, and who writes scripts or builds workflows that are easy to maintain. They should plan for failures with logging, alerts and retries, protect credentials, and document their work. Ask for examples of processes they automated and how they measured the result.

qa.q: How do I test an integration and automation engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task using test accounts or sample data, never live systems. For example, pull records from one API, clean them, and load them into another system or file. Review how they handle errors, duplicates and secrets, and ask them to explain their choices. A clear write-up matters as much as working code.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles call for a bachelor’s degree in mechanical, electrical or automotive engineering, ideally from an ABET-accredited program. A Professional Engineer license exists in every state but is rarely required for vehicle design work, since many states exempt manufacturers’ in-house engineers. Rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check 3D CAD modeling, reading and applying GD&T on drawings, DFMEA, simulation such as finite element analysis, and test planning with data analysis. For safety or software roles, confirm working knowledge of the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and ISO 26262 functional safety.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can explain a part or system they worked on from requirement to validation, including what failed in testing and how they fixed it. They weigh cost, mass, manufacturability and supplier input, not just the model. For juniors, student race car or off-road vehicle teams count.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about their own role on team projects. No grasp of tolerances or how parts are actually made. Brushing off test failures. Claiming sole ownership of a whole vehicle system. Offering to share confidential drawings or data from a former employer.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: walk me through a design change you made after a failed test. How did you set tolerances on two mating parts? Which DFMEA items did you rate highest and why? Listen for specific loads, materials, test methods and numbers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an automotive engineer?
qa.a: Look for an engineering degree that fits the role, hands-on CAD and analysis skills, and real experience taking a design through testing. Strong candidates discuss cost, weight, manufacturing and safety standards, not just the model. A PE license is rarely required in this field, and rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test an automotive engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or clearly scoped exercise. For example, share a simple bracket drawing with a load case and ask them to spot tolerance problems, suggest a material and outline a validation test. Then have them walk you through their reasoning. Never ask for free production work you plan to use.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Some states require car salespeople to hold a salesperson license or registration from the state motor vehicle agency, and others do not, so check your state. They need a valid driver’s license to move cars and join test drives. Verify past sales with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test product knowledge, greeting and qualifying a shopper, running a test drive and handling trade-in and price questions. Check CRM use, follow-up by phone, text and email, and knowledge of rules like the FTC Used Car Rule’s Buyers Guide window sticker.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates sell steadily month after month and earn repeat and referral customers. They follow up without pressure, know the inventory and features well and get strong customer survey scores. References describe honest, organized and calm work.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for stories of bait-and-switch pricing, add-ons hidden in the monthly payment, promised financing approval or a misstated vehicle history. Be wary of a trail of short jobs or customer complaints, and of anyone who talks down to shoppers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a sale from greeting to delivery. How do you follow up with a shopper who left without buying? How do you explain a price or trade-in value someone disputes? Strong answers sound honest, organized and specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an automotive sales consultant?
qa.a: Look for a steady sales history, strong follow-up, real product knowledge and honest, low-pressure manners. They need a valid driver’s license, and some states also require a car salesperson license or registration. They should know consumer rules such as the FTC Used Car Rule and keep clean CRM records.

qa.q: How do I test an automotive sales consultant before hiring?
qa.a: Run a role-play on the lot or in the showroom. Have them greet a shopper, ask questions, present a car, handle a trade-in objection and set a follow-up. Ask them to write the follow-up text or email. Judge listening, product knowledge, honesty and whether they stay respectful when pushed.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Verify a valid driver’s license, and a commercial driver’s license of the right class for heavy trucks. Run a driving record check with written consent. States that allow autonomous vehicle testing set their own rules, often requiring company permits and trained operators, so requirements vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test defensive driving, steady attention during long, uneventful drives, and fast, safe takeovers. Check clear event notes that engineers can use, following test plans and routes exactly, and comfort with laptops, tablets and remote monitoring screens. Remote roles also need judgment about when to intervene.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates take over early when unsure rather than late, describe system behavior precisely, and keep logs complete. They follow procedures through boredom and pressure, keep phones away, and can explain the difference between a planned test event and a real safety risk.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a poor driving record, stories of phone use or distraction, and vague or missing event notes. Be wary of anyone who trusts the system too much, treats takeovers as failures, or bends test procedures to finish a route faster.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Describe a time you had to take over or brake suddenly. What did you note afterward? How do you stay focused on a long, quiet shift? What would you report if the vehicle hesitated at a light? Strong answers show calm judgment and precise notes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an autonomous vehicle operator?
qa.a: Look for a clean driving record, the right license class for your vehicles, steady focus and quick, calm takeovers. Check they write clear, accurate event notes and follow test plans exactly. Autonomous vehicle testing rules vary by state, so confirm what your state permit requires of operators.

qa.q: How do I test an autonomous vehicle operator before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid evaluation with a trained safety lead on a closed course or in a simulator. Include routine driving, a planned takeover and a surprise event, then ask for written event notes. Review takeover timing, smoothness, attention, procedure use and whether their notes would help engineers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Dispatchers at airlines flying under Part 121 domestic or flag rules need an FAA Aircraft Dispatcher certificate. Ramp and ground staff need no license, but airports require a badge with a fingerprint-based background check. Check dangerous goods and deicing training records, plus references from operations managers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test flight planning, weight and balance, weather and NOTAM reading, and crew duty and rest limits. Check minimum equipment list deferrals, fuel planning and delay recovery. For ramp roles, check marshaling signals, towing, fueling safety, loading to load plans and foreign object debris checks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know the federal rules for your type of operation, use the safety reporting system freely and stay calm during irregular operations. They communicate clearly with crews, maintenance and air traffic control, and they document every decision that affects a flight.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for casual talk about stretching duty limits, ignoring weather minimums or skipping walkarounds. Be careful with anyone who hides mistakes instead of reporting them, cannot explain a load sheet, or treats ramp safety rules as optional.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A flight has a deferred item and forecast icing. Walk me through your release decision. How do you recover a schedule after a ground stop? What do you check before an aircraft pushes back? Strong answers cite rules and put safety first.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an aviation operations specialist?
qa.a: Look for the right FAA certificate for dispatch roles, solid knowledge of the rules for your operation, and training records for dangerous goods, deicing or ramp work. Strong candidates use safety reporting systems and stay calm during disruptions. References from operations managers confirm their judgment.

qa.q: How do I test an aviation operations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid tabletop scenario with sample weather, NOTAMs and a maintenance deferral, and ask for a go or no-go decision with reasons. For ramp roles, run a supervised skills check on signals and walkarounds. Judge rule knowledge, safety thinking and clear communication.

look.label: Standards they should know
look.text: Ask which certification standards they have worked under. For civil aircraft, look for DO-178C for software, DO-254 for complex hardware, DO-160 for environmental testing, and ARP4754 for system development. Rocket and defense programs often use military or customer standards instead. Have them explain one standard in their own words.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Look for a degree in electrical, computer or aerospace engineering. The FAA does not license avionics design engineers. A state Professional Engineer license exists but is rarely required in aerospace, and rules vary by state. An FAA Designated Engineering Representative appointment is a strong plus for certification work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the skills the job actually uses. Examples include schematic and board review, signal integrity, power design, EMI control, and data buses such as ARINC 429, MIL-STD-1553 or CAN. Other examples include embedded C, sensor interfacing, and writing requirements that can be traced to tests.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about requirements, failure modes and test evidence, not just circuits. They have taken a board or unit through qualification testing such as vibration, thermal or EMI. They can explain a failure they found, how they traced the root cause, and what they changed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who cannot say what they personally did on a team project. Another warning sign is treating documentation and traceability as busywork. Be wary of vagueness about safety assessments or design assurance levels. So is claiming certification experience without naming the standard or the review they supported.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an avionics engineer?
qa.a: Look for an engineering degree and hands-on work with flight hardware or software. They should know the standards your program follows, such as DO-178C, DO-254 or DO-160.
