They should also know data buses like ARINC 429 or MIL-STD-1553. The best candidates explain design choices in terms of safety, testing and traceability.

qa.q: How do I test an avionics engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short design review task. One option is a schematic or block diagram with a few planted errors, plus a set of requirements. Ask them to find the problems, rank them by safety impact, and propose verification tests. You can also ask them to walk through a past qualification test they ran.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses backend engineers, and many roles do not require a degree. Verify work history, review code samples or public repositories, and treat cloud certifications as a bonus, not proof of skill. Run background checks only with written consent, following federal and state rules.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to design a small API, model the data behind it, and write tests. Check their SQL, indexing, error handling, retries, authentication, and how they keep secrets out of code. Watch how they reason about load and failure, not just whether the code runs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask about data volume, users and uptime needs before picking tools. They can walk through a past outage, its cause and what changed after. They add logging and monitoring without being asked, and explain trade-offs in plain words.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Pushing one favorite framework for every problem. No tests in sample work. Storing passwords in plain text or building SQL from raw user input. Blaming others for every past failure. Vague answers about what they personally built versus what the team built.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about a slow endpoint you fixed. How did you find the cause?” Ask how they changed a database schema without downtime. Ask what they would check first if a service suddenly started returning errors in the middle of the night.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a backend engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid skill in at least one server language, databases and API design, plus habits that keep systems safe and running: tests, logging and careful handling of user data. Strong candidates explain trade-offs clearly and own past mistakes. No license is required, so judge proof of work: code samples, past projects and a practical test.

qa.q: How do I test a backend engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-boxed task that matches your real work, such as building a small API with a database and tests. Keep it to a few hours, or pay for longer work. Then review it together. Ask why they chose that structure, how it would handle more traffic, and what they would change with more time.

look.label: Background to verify
look.text: Run the background check your bank requires. Federal law bars people convicted of certain crimes of dishonesty or money laundering from working at an insured bank without the FDIC’s consent, or at an insured credit union without the NCUA’s, so check this before an offer is final.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test counting cash and making change, balancing a short mock drawer, and spotting an altered check or a fake bill. A short role play shows how they explain a hold or refer a customer to a banker.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates are accurate and calm when the line is long, follow procedures every time, speak warmly with customers and report a mistake right away. Cashier experience with balanced drawers is a good sign.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for careless counting, impatience with rules, pushing customers hard to buy, or suggesting ways around identification or cash reporting rules. Any dishonesty in the application should end the process.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Your drawer is short at the end of the day. What do you do? A customer wants to deposit cash in pieces to stay under $10,000. What do you do? How do you spot a counterfeit $100 bill? Strong answers follow procedure every time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a bank teller?
qa.a: Look for honesty, accuracy with cash and numbers, and friendly service. Cashier or retail experience with balanced drawers helps. Test counting and balancing, check their judgment on fraud and cash reporting, and make sure they pass the background check banks require, including the federal rule on certain past convictions.

qa.q: How do I test a bank teller before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid skills test: count a mixed set of bills and coins, balance a mock drawer, spot an altered check and a fake bill, and role play a customer whose check is on hold. Score accuracy first, then speed, clarity and how they follow procedure.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for in-house banking operations roles. Payments and anti-money laundering certifications are optional but show study of the rules. Verify experience instead. Call references from past bank partners or fintech teams, and ask exactly which programs, accounts and money flows they ran.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they handle ACH, wires and card settlement, daily reconciliation of bank and ledger balances, returns and exceptions, and partner bank reporting. Check their grasp of Bank Secrecy Act and know-your-customer duties, and how they manage partner bank audits and complaints.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates treat the partner bank as a regulated party with its own risk rules, not a vendor. They document money flows end to end, keep clear runbooks, catch reconciliation breaks the same day, and can explain who owns each compliance task under the program agreement.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about who holds customer funds, unreconciled balances carried forward, or reliance on memory instead of written procedures. Be wary of anyone who sees compliance as the bank’s problem alone or cannot explain how ACH returns and disputes are handled.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a reconciliation break you traced to its cause. How did you prepare for a partner bank audit or exam request? What happens when a wire goes to the wrong account? Strong answers name specific reports, controls and escalation steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a banking operations manager?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with ACH, wires and daily reconciliation, plus working knowledge of Bank Secrecy Act and know-your-customer rules. Check they have managed a partner bank relationship, including audits, reporting and incidents. No license is required, so references from past banks or fintech teams and written procedures they built matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a banking operations manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise using sample bank statements and an internal ledger with a few planted breaks, such as a duplicate transfer or an unposted return. Ask them to reconcile, explain each difference and draft a note to the partner bank. Review accuracy, clarity and how they would stop the error from repeating.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Some states, counties and cities require a food handler card, often within a set number of days after hire. Check your local health department’s rule. Barista certificates from coffee groups are optional. They show interest, but no US law requires them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a shot pulled to your recipe and a drink with steamed milk. Watch dose, tamping, shot timing and milk texture. Notice whether they purge and wipe the steam wand after each use.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They greet people while working, remember orders and keep moving in a rush without skipping steps. They clean as they go, talk about dialing in a grinder and ask about your menu and busy hours.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Leaving dried milk on the steam wand, ignoring sanitizer or mixing up allergen milks are warning signs. Be careful with anyone who blames past coworkers for hard shifts or refuses opening, closing or cleaning tasks.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handle a line out the door, what they change when shots run too fast, how they prevent mix-ups with dairy-free milks and what they do when a customer is unhappy with a drink.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a barista?
qa.a: Look for steady drink quality, friendly service under pressure and clean habits. Espresso machine experience helps, but attitude and reliability matter just as much. Check whether your state or county requires a food handler card. Confirm the candidate can work the shifts you need, such as early openings or weekends.

qa.q: How do I test a barista before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid working interview. Ask them to make a few drinks from your menu, including espresso and a milk drink. Then have them take a mock order and do a cleanup task. Watch speed, consistency, cleanliness and how they talk to customers. Trial work generally must be paid under wage laws.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles call for a degree in chemical, electrical, mechanical or materials engineering, or in chemistry. No US license is required for most battery work. A Professional Engineer license is optional, and its rules vary by state. If they will ship lithium cells, ask for proof of current hazmat shipping training.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can read a cell datasheet, explain capacity fade and impedance growth, and choose between chemistries such as LFP and NMC. Pack and grid roles need battery management system logic, thermal design and cell balancing. Lab roles need hands-on cycler use and clean data analysis.

look.label: Safety and standards knowledge
look.text: Strong candidates can explain thermal runaway, how to stop it from spreading through a pack, and how to handle damaged cells safely. Ask which standards they have designed or tested to, such as UN 38.3 for shipping, UL 2580 for vehicles or UL 9540A for energy storage.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk in numbers: cycle counts, C-rates, temperature limits and failure rates. They can describe a cell or pack that failed, how they found the root cause and what they changed. They link design choices to cost, safety and manufacturing yield.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about their own part in a team project. Treating lithium cells casually or skipping safety steps in a lab story. Claiming expertise in every chemistry with no test data to back it up. No idea how a design moves from prototype to production.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a battery engineer?
qa.a: Match the candidate to your stage of work. Cell roles need deep electrochemistry. Pack roles need electrical, thermal and battery management skills. Manufacturing roles need process and quality control. In every case, look for strong safety habits, knowledge of the standards your product must meet, and clear stories about failures they solved.

qa.q: How do I test a battery engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task that uses sample or public data. For example, share a cell datasheet and ask them to size a pack for a set voltage, energy and power, with notes on cooling. Or share cycling data and ask them to spot degradation and explain likely causes. Then discuss their reasoning in an interview.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for in-house benefits work. Selling or advising on insurance as a broker needs a state insurance license, which varies by state. Benefits certifications are optional. Verify experience through references and ask which plans, carriers and enrollment cycles the candidate ran.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test knowledge of ERISA, COBRA and state continuation laws, Affordable Care Act reporting, retirement plan basics, leave coordination and HIPAA privacy for plan data. Check accuracy with carrier eligibility files, invoice reconciliation, open enrollment setup and clear employee communication.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong specialists explain benefits in plain words, reconcile carrier bills every month and catch enrollment errors before they become denied claims. They meet notice deadlines, protect health information and work well with brokers, payroll and plan administrators.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for confusion about COBRA notices or qualifying life events, sloppy enrollment data, or careless talk about employees’ health information. Be wary of anyone who gives tax or legal advice on plans with false certainty or ignores differences in state law.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your open enrollment process. Tell me about a carrier billing error you found and fixed. How do you handle a mid-year change request after a life event? Strong answers name steps, deadlines, systems and how they kept employees informed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a benefits specialist?
qa.a: Look for working knowledge of ERISA, COBRA, Affordable Care Act reporting, leave and retirement plan basics, plus accuracy with eligibility files and carrier invoices. Check how they protect health information and explain benefits simply. No license is required for in-house work, so references and examples of enrollments they ran matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a benefits specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise: a sample enrollment file, a carrier invoice with a few planted errors and an employee question about a life event change. Ask them to reconcile the invoice, fix the file and draft a reply. Review accuracy, rule knowledge, privacy and clear, friendly writing.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they write solid SQL, build a clean data model such as a star schema, and write calculated measures in DAX or Tableau calculations. Ask them to explain how they would speed up a slow report and keep data refreshes reliable.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license exists for BI developers in the US. Power BI and Tableau both offer optional vendor certifications that show focused study. A portfolio of real dashboards and a degree or experience in data work tell you more than any certificate.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask who will use the dashboard and what decisions it supports before building anything. They define each metric in writing, check totals against the source system, set up access controls such as row-level security, and keep visuals simple and easy to read.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for crowded dashboards full of charts with no clear purpose. Be wary if they cannot explain where a number comes from or how they validated it. Sharing a past employer’s confidential data in a portfolio is also a warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about a time your dashboard didn’t match the finance team’s numbers. How did you find the cause?” Also ask how they handled a report that loaded too slowly, and how they collected feedback from managers after launch.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a BI developer?
qa.a: Look for strong SQL, sound data modeling, and hands-on skill in your tool, such as Power BI or Tableau. Good candidates start by asking what decisions the dashboard should support. They check their numbers against source systems and explain metrics in plain language. A portfolio with sample or anonymized dashboards shows their design sense.

qa.q: How do I test a BI developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a small sample dataset with a few messy fields and a short business question. Ask them to clean the data, build a simple model, and create one dashboard page in a few hours. Then have them walk you through their choices, how they checked totals, and what they would add with more time.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for most billing work. Optional certifications exist, especially in medical billing, where knowledge of claim forms, codes and HIPAA privacy rules matters. Verify past roles with references. Several states and cities limit employer credit checks, so check local rules first.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test invoice accuracy, reconciling billing to contracts and payments, issuing credits and handling disputes. Check spreadsheet skills, the billing or accounting system you use, subscription or usage billing logic, sales tax basics and clear written replies to customers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates catch errors before invoices go out, trace a wrong charge to its root cause and fix the process. They write calm, clear explanations to customers and keep an audit trail for every adjustment.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for careless data entry, credits given without approval or notes, and weak understanding of how billing ties to revenue and collections. Be wary of harsh or threatening language about overdue bills, which collection laws can restrict.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a billing error you found and how you fixed it for good. How do you handle a customer disputing a charge? How do you reconcile billing to payments at month end? Strong answers include clear steps and controls.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a billing specialist?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, strong spreadsheet and billing system skills, and calm, clear communication with customers. They should reconcile invoices to contracts and payments, document every credit and find root causes. No license is required, though medical billing calls for coding and HIPAA knowledge. References on accuracy matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a billing specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with sample contracts, usage data and draft invoices containing a few planted errors. Ask them to find and fix the errors, issue any credits and write a short reply to a customer who disputed a charge. Judge accuracy, notes, controls and tone.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for bioinformatics scientists. Verify degrees with the school and review published papers, preprints and public code repositories, asking which analyses they personally ran. If results reach patients, the lab must follow federal clinical lab rules, so ask about pipeline validation experience.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test Python or R, the Linux command line and the analyses you run, such as sequence alignment, variant calling, RNA-seq differential expression or single-cell clustering. Check statistics, multiple testing correction, workflow managers, containers, version control and running jobs on a cluster or cloud.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write reproducible pipelines with pinned software versions and documented parameters. They check data quality first, spot batch effects, question surprising results before reporting them and explain biology and statistics clearly to bench scientists and leaders.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for running tools with default settings they cannot explain, no quality control steps, results that cannot be reproduced, or trying methods until the answer looks significant. Be wary of anyone who claims team papers without naming their own part.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a result that turned out to be an artifact and how you found it. How do you handle batch effects? How would you confirm a variant call is real? Strong answers name specific tools, checks and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a bioinformatics scientist?
qa.a: Look for coding skill in Python or R, strong statistics, and hands-on experience with your data types, such as genomic, proteomic or single-cell data. Check reproducible pipelines, public code and published work. No license is required, so verified work samples, code and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a bioinformatics scientist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a public dataset, such as running quality control and differential expression on a small RNA-seq set. Ask for code in a repository, a short report and the reasons for each parameter choice. Review reproducibility, statistics, code clarity and biological interpretation.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state issues a license to practice as a biologist, so verify degrees and training instead. Confirm the claimed bachelor’s, master’s or PhD. If the role requires it, ask for proof of lab safety training, such as biosafety, bloodborne pathogens, chemical hygiene or animal care and use courses.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Match the test to your lab’s daily work. That might be sterile technique, accurate pipetting, PCR, cell culture, microscopy or field sampling. Also check data skills: basic statistics, clean spreadsheets and, where needed, analysis in R or Python.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong biologists design experiments with proper controls and can explain why. They keep detailed, dated lab notebooks that someone else could follow. They talk openly about failed experiments and what they changed. They can clearly describe their own part in any paper or poster they list.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who cannot explain their own role in listed projects or who skip over controls and replicates. Be wary of casual talk about safety rules, waste disposal or record keeping. Any hint of adjusting data to fit an expected result is a serious warning.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through an experiment that did not work and how they fixed it. Ask how they would set up controls for a test you describe. Ask how they record and store raw data so results can be checked later.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a biologist?
qa.a: Look for a verified degree, hands-on skill in the techniques your work uses, and careful record keeping. No state license exists for biologists, so rely on transcripts, training records and references. Strong candidates explain their experimental design, including controls, and speak honestly about failed results. Check that they follow safety rules for chemicals, biological materials or animals where the job involves them.

qa.q: How do I test a biologist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task tied to your real work. For lab roles, watch them prepare a dilution series or run a routine technique under supervision. You can also hand them a small data set and ask for a summary with basic statistics. Then ask them to design an experiment with controls to answer a simple question you provide.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state or federal license exists for blockchain engineers. Verify real work instead. Ask for public code repositories, deployed contract addresses you can inspect on a block explorer, and audit reports that cover their code. Private certificates exist, but they prove less than shipped, reviewed code.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can write and test smart contracts in the language your chain uses, such as Solidity or Rust. Probe their grasp of reentrancy, access control mistakes, oracle manipulation and integer issues. Also test their skill with fee optimization, upgrade patterns and node or network setup.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They write thorough unit and fuzz tests before any deployment. They explain what belongs on-chain and what belongs off-chain. They have shipped to a live network, worked through a security audit or reported a bug. They plan for key management, pause switches and safe upgrades.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Deploys contracts without tests or outside review. Can’t explain how well-known exploits worked. Lists past projects you can’t tie to any code or contract address. Stores secrets or private keys in code, or shrugs off how admin keys are protected.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a contract they deployed, what broke or nearly broke, and what they would change today. Ask how they would upgrade a live contract safely, and how they decide when code is ready for real funds.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a blockchain engineer?
qa.a: Look for proven, inspectable work: public code, deployed contracts and audit reports. Strong engineers write careful tests, know common smart contract attacks, and plan for upgrades and key security. There is no US license for this work, so judge them on the code they have shipped and how clearly they explain their design choices.

qa.q: How do I test a blockchain engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task on a test network. Ask them to review a small contract with planted bugs and explain each flaw and fix. Or have them write a simple contract with tests. Score the quality of their tests, their security reasoning and how clearly they document tradeoffs, not just whether the code runs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a bookkeeper, and bookkeeping certifications are optional. Only licensed CPA firms can issue audit opinions, so a bookkeeper should not offer audits. If they will prepare tax returns for pay, they need an IRS preparer tax identification number.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test recording transactions, bank and credit card reconciliations, accounts payable and receivable, and accrual versus cash basis. Check the accounting software you use, payroll entries, a clean chart of accounts, sales tax tracking and year-end 1099 preparation.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates reconcile every account each month, ask about unclear transactions instead of guessing, and keep receipts and notes organized. They close on time and hand the accountant clean, documented books.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for unreconciled accounts, heavy use of a catch-all expense account, and personal and business spending mixed together. Be wary of anyone who wants sole control of payments and bank access with no review, since that invites errors and fraud.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you handle a bank transaction you cannot identify? Walk me through your month-end close. How do you fix an error found in a prior month? Strong answers mention reconciliations, documentation and checking with the owner or accountant.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a bookkeeper?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, monthly reconciliations, solid knowledge of your accounting software and good habits with receipts and notes. They should understand accrual and cash basis, payables, receivables and payroll entries. No license is required, so references and a skills test matter more than certificates. Paid tax preparation needs an IRS preparer number.

qa.q: How do I test a bookkeeper before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a sample bank statement, a few receipts and a partial ledger. Ask them to record the transactions, reconcile the account and flag anything unclear. Judge accuracy, account choices, notes and whether they ask the right questions instead of guessing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most brand ambassador work needs no license. If they will pour alcohol or hand out food samples, check state and local rules, which may require responsible server training, a food handler card or a permit. They also need a valid driver’s license if they will drive.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they open a conversation with a stranger, explain the product in a sentence or two, and accept a ‘no’ politely. Check they can set up a display, follow store or venue rules, track samples and leads, and report results after each shift.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates are reliable, on time and energetic for a full shift. They learn product facts quickly, stay friendly without being pushy, and send clear recaps with photos, sample counts and customer comments. Past event or retail references praise them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for no-shows or lateness in references, exaggerated product claims and pressure tactics. For social media ambassadors, be wary of anyone who will not disclose that they are paid, since the FTC requires clear disclosure of brand partnerships.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a slow event and how you drew people in. How do you answer a question you cannot answer? How do you report a shift’s results? Strong answers are specific about setup, opening lines and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a brand ambassador?
qa.a: Look for reliability, a friendly and confident manner with strangers, and the ability to learn product facts fast and repeat them accurately. Check references from past events or stores. Most roles need no license, but alcohol or food sampling may need state or local training or permits, and social media work needs FTC disclosure.

qa.q: How do I test a brand ambassador before hiring?
qa.a: Hold a short role-play. Give them a product fact sheet, then have them approach you as a shopper, handle a skeptical question and close with a sample or sign-up. You can also pay for a single trial shift. Judge energy, accuracy, respect for a ‘no’ and the quality of their shift recap.

look.label: Portfolio depth to review
look.text: Look for complete identity systems, not just logos. Strong portfolios show color palettes, type choices, brand guidelines and real uses on packaging, websites, signage and social media. Case studies should explain the client’s problem, the options explored and why the final direction was chosen.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check logo construction at small and large sizes, typography pairing and hierarchy, and color systems with readable contrast. They should prepare correct files for print and screen, including vector formats, CMYK and RGB versions, and spot colors where needed.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No US state licenses brand designers. A degree or certificate can help but proves less than the work itself. Verify that portfolio pieces are their own, ask what their role was on team projects, and call references about deadlines, feedback and handoff.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of portfolios built only from mockups or templates, logos that look close to well-known marks, and designers who can’t explain their choices. Also watch for reluctance to hand over source files or to sign a written agreement transferring copyright.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how a brand they built held up a year later. Ask how they handled a client who rejected every early concept. Ask how they write guidelines so staff and outside vendors apply the identity correctly without the designer in the room.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a brand designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio of full identity systems with guidelines and real applications, not just logos. They should explain the reasoning behind each choice, prepare files for print and digital use, and handle feedback calmly. No license is required in the US, so references and verified work matter most. Make sure they will sign a written copyright transfer.

qa.q: How do I test a brand designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small, paid task with a clear time limit. For example, ask them to apply your current logo and colors to a new item, such as a flyer or social post, or to sketch two quick logo directions from a short brief. Judge their questions, reasoning and file quality, not only how polished it looks.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for brand marketing, and degrees and marketing certificates are optional. Ask for campaign case studies showing the brief, the work and the results, and confirm their exact role. Call references from agencies and teams who worked with them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test brand positioning, writing a creative brief, managing agencies and keeping messages consistent across channels. Check they can measure brand health through surveys, search interest and share of voice, and tie campaigns to business results, not just impressions.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can state a brand’s position in one sentence, know the audience well, and keep every channel consistent. They give agencies clear briefs, measure results honestly, and know advertising rules such as the FTC guides on endorsements and influencer disclosures.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolios of attractive ads with no stated goal or result, constant brand changes, or reliance on vanity metrics. Be careful with candidates who ignore disclosure rules for influencers, cannot explain their part in agency work, or chase trends that do not fit the brand.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a campaign that did not work and what you learned. How do you measure brand awareness? How do you brief an agency? Strong answers name the audience, goal, measures and what changed because of the results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a brand marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for campaign case studies with clear goals and measured results, sharp positioning skills, and experience managing agencies and partners. Check they keep messages consistent and follow FTC rules on endorsements and influencers. No license is required, so case studies and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a brand marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: a product and target audience. Ask for a positioning statement, a one-page creative brief and how they would measure success. Review clarity, insight into the audience, fit with your brand and whether the measures go beyond vanity metrics.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Engine work needs strong C++ or Rust. Extensions and in-browser apps need modern JavaScript and TypeScript. Ask them to explain the rendering path: parsing, style, layout, paint and compositing. They should know how to profile dropped frames and memory use with browser developer tools.

look.label: Security knowledge to check
look.text: Browsers run untrusted code all day. Look for a firm grasp of the same-origin policy, CORS, Content Security Policy, process sandboxing and memory bugs like use-after-free. Extension builders should know how to scope permissions and why broad host access worries reviewers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for accepted patches to an open-source browser engine, bug reports with minimal test cases, or published extensions with real users. Strong candidates read web specs. They cite them when browsers behave differently, and they write tests that catch regressions.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who treat cross-browser bugs as random instead of tracing them to a spec or engine difference. Other warning signs are vague answers about debugging a crash or slowdown, extensions that request every permission, and no habit of writing tests.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this work. Verify skill through public code, review history in open-source projects, extension store listings and references from past teammates. Confirm that any code they share is theirs and not covered by a past employer’s confidentiality terms.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a browser engineer?
qa.a: Match the candidate to the layer you need. Engine roles call for C++ or Rust and knowledge of rendering and memory. Extension and web app roles call for JavaScript, browser APIs and careful permission design. In all cases, look for security instincts, a habit of reading specs, profiling skill and public work you can review.

qa.q: How do I test a browser engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-limited task close to your real work. Have them find why a page stutters while scrolling, fix a layout bug that shows up in only one browser, or review an extension manifest for extra permissions. Then ask them to walk through their reasoning, tools and tests. The explanation shows as much as the fix.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No state license is needed to work as a business analyst. Optional certifications such as CBAP or CCBA show study and logged experience, but they are not required. Give more weight to real work samples, such as requirements documents, process maps or dashboards the candidate built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can pull and clean data with spreadsheets or SQL, map a current process step by step, write clear requirements or user stories, and run an interview with staff to find out how work really gets done.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask why a problem matters before proposing fixes. They tie each recommendation to a measurable result, explain trade-offs in plain words to non-technical people, and describe how they checked whether a change actually worked after launch.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who only lists tools, cannot name the outcome of past recommendations, jumps to a solution before understanding the process, treats a correlation as proof of cause, or blames stakeholders when requirements went wrong.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a process they mapped and what changed afterward. Ask about a time the data contradicted what a manager believed, and how they handled two departments that wanted conflicting things.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a business analyst?
qa.a: Look for someone who can work with both numbers and people. They should analyze data, map processes, write clear requirements and explain findings to non-technical staff. Ask for work samples and stories with measurable results. Certifications are optional and no license is required.

qa.q: How do I test a business analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Share a small, anonymized data set and a description of one messy process. Ask for a simple process map, two or three findings backed by the data, and one recommendation with its trade-offs. Then have them present it in ten minutes and answer follow-up questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Business continuity and emergency management certifications are optional, and some states run their own emergency manager certification programs. Federal incident command training is common for emergency roles. Verify through redacted plans, exercise reports and references from leaders who used their plans in a real event.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test business impact analysis, setting recovery time and data loss objectives with business owners, risk assessment, plan writing and tabletop exercise design. Check crisis communication, incident command basics, coordination with IT disaster recovery, and supplier and site continuity planning.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates build plans people can follow under stress, test them through regular exercises and fix the gaps afterward. They get business leaders to own recovery priorities, keep contact lists current and can describe a real outage or disaster they helped manage.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for template plans that were never tested, a focus on IT systems alone, or exercises that end without action items. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a business impact analysis or has no way to keep plans and contact lists up to date.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a business impact analysis you led. Tell me about an exercise that exposed a gap and what changed. What did you do in the first hour of a real incident? Strong answers show specific roles, decisions, timelines and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a business continuity manager?
qa.a: Look for experience leading business impact analyses, writing usable plans and running exercises that produce real fixes. Check crisis communication and incident command skills, and coordination with IT recovery teams. No license is required, though optional certifications and federal incident command training help. Redacted plans and real incident stories matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a business continuity manager before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid tabletop exercise: describe a scenario, such as a regional power outage hitting your main office, and reveal new facts every few minutes. Ask them to lead the response and then outline plan changes. Review priorities, communication, decision speed and the quality of their follow-up actions.

look.label: Proof of closed partnerships
look.text: Ask for two or three partnerships they built from first contact to signed deal. A strong candidate names the partner type, the deal structure, their exact role and what the partnership produced afterward, not just meetings booked.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they size up a possible partner, map who decides on the other side and shape a deal both sides want. Look for clear thinking on revenue share, exclusivity, integration effort and how the partnership will be measured.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about partner incentives as much as your own goals. They know when to walk away from a bad fit. They work smoothly with product, legal and sales teams, and they keep partners active after the contract is signed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague claims like ’I opened doors’ with no outcomes. Credit taken for deals others closed. Promises of instant introductions through personal contacts. Plans to share a former employer’s confidential partner terms or pricing, which may breach agreements they signed.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: ’Tell me about a partnership that stalled. What did you do?’ and ’How did you decide between a reseller deal and an integration?’ Real experience shows in specific tradeoffs, named obstacles and honest lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a business development manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of partnerships they built and closed, with clear details on their role and results. They should understand reseller, integration and co-marketing deals, negotiate terms both sides accept and keep partners engaged after signing. No license is required for this role, so judge them on proven work and references.

qa.q: How do I test a business development manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Name your product and ask them to pick three possible partners, explain why each fits and outline a first deal proposal. Then role-play a negotiation where you push back on revenue share or exclusivity. Watch how they reason, listen and find terms that work for both companies.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for structured problem solving, financial modeling in spreadsheets, and clear written recommendations. A strong hire can break a vague question like “why is growth slowing” into parts, pick the right data, and land on a decision with tradeoffs stated plainly.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe past projects by the decision made and the result measured, not just the slides built. They mention working across sales, finance, product and operations, and they can name a metric they defined and kept tracking after launch.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for answers full of frameworks but no numbers, no owner and no outcome. Be wary of someone who cannot explain what they would stop doing, blames other teams for stalled projects, or has never handed a process off to run without them.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. An MBA, consulting background or project management certificate can help but is not proof of skill. Verify past titles and dates, and ask references about specific projects the candidate led.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through a recommendation leadership rejected. What did you do next?” and “How did you choose the metric for your last big project?” Strong answers include the data used, who disagreed, and what changed afterward.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a strategy and operations manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who turns open-ended problems into clear decisions and measurable plans. They should model numbers comfortably, write concisely, and earn trust across teams they do not manage. Ask for examples where their work changed a decision and a metric moved because of it.

qa.q: How do I test a strategy and operations manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case using a sanitized dataset from your business, such as declining repeat orders. Ask for a one-page recommendation and a simple model within a set time. Then have them present it and push back on their assumptions. Judge their reasoning, prioritization and how they handle challenge, not polish.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work. Vendor certifications for your platform, such as administrator or consultant credentials, show baseline knowledge. Most vendors offer a public lookup, so confirm the credential is current. Treat certifications as a plus, not proof of real-world skill.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for requirements gathering, process mapping, and no-code configuration of workflows, fields, permissions and reports. Add data imports and cleanup, basic SQL, and clear user stories and test cases. Ask how they would change a live system safely, using a sandbox and a release plan.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about business results, not just clicks. They can explain a past rollout or upgrade: who they gathered needs from, what they tested and how they trained users. They document their work, follow change control and know when a request needs a developer or a vendor ticket.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Makes changes straight in production. Can’t explain how they manage user access or protect sensitive data. Blames users for low adoption. Lists many platforms but can’t go deep on any. Has no examples of documentation, testing or rolling back a change that broke something.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through an integration that failed and how you found the cause.” “How do you push back on a department head’s request?” “How do you prepare for the platform’s scheduled updates?” Specific answers naming systems, steps and results point to hands-on work.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a business systems analyst?
qa.a: Look for deep, hands-on experience with your platform or a close match, plus strong skills in gathering requirements and mapping processes. Good candidates test in a sandbox, document changes, protect data access and train users well. Vendor certifications help, but no state license is required. Past rollouts with clear results matter more than a long list of tools.

qa.q: How do I test a business systems analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic exercise using fake data. Share a messy process description and ask them to write requirements, propose a configuration, list test cases and outline a rollout plan. You can add a small data cleanup task in a sample spreadsheet. Then have them walk you through their choices and tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most US purchasing jobs need no license. Voluntary supply management and inventory certifications are a plus, not a must. Some states license dealers or buyers of grain and other farm products, so check your state’s rules if the role covers those goods. Confirm past employers and job titles.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Comparing quotes on total cost, not just unit price, by counting freight, lead time, minimum order and payment terms. Matching a purchase order, receiving record and invoice. Building a clear spreadsheet. Working in an inventory or ordering system.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Gives specific examples of savings or delivery problems they solved. Follows up on open orders before they turn late. Keeps clean supplier records. Knows when to line up a backup supplier. Explains how they negotiated without hurting the supplier relationship.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Judges every deal by the lowest price alone. Cannot explain how they handled a late or wrong shipment. Is vague about approval limits or paperwork. Treats vendor gifts or favors casually. Blames suppliers for every problem and owns none.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through the last set of quotes they compared and why they chose one. Ask what they do when a supplier misses a delivery date. Ask how they decide how much to order and when.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a buyer and purchasing agent?
qa.a: Look for someone who compares total cost, not just price, and who tracks orders until the goods arrive. Strong buyers show organized records, clear follow-up habits and real examples of negotiating price or delivery. Most roles need no license, though some states license buyers of farm products. Watch for loose attitudes about vendor gifts or approval limits.

qa.q: How do I test a buyer and purchasing agent before hiring?
qa.a: Give them three sample supplier quotes with different prices, freight, lead times and minimum orders. Ask them to pick one and explain why. Then hand them a purchase order and an invoice with a mismatch and see if they catch it. Finish with a short role play where a supplier says an order will be two weeks late.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to work as a drafter or CAD designer in the US. Some hold an optional professional drafting certification or a software vendor certification. A degree or certificate in drafting helps, but a portfolio of real drawings they made matters most.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Building a clean 3D model with a logical feature tree. Turning it into a 2D drawing with correct views, dimensions, tolerances, notes and title block. Applying GD&T or construction drawing standards that match your work, and working in your exact software and file formats.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Asks about material, manufacturing process or building method before drawing. Spots missing dimensions or conflicts in an engineer’s markup. Keeps layers, file names and revision blocks tidy. Has done your type of output, such as sheet metal flat patterns, weldments or permit sets.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: A portfolio of only renderings with no dimensioned drawings. Chained dimensions that stack tolerances, or duplicate dimensions. Cannot explain how they control revisions. Treats the engineer’s sketch as final without questions, or blames the shop for every build problem.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: “Tell me about a drawing that came back from the shop or site with a question. What went wrong?” “How do you choose which dimensions to show?” “How do you make sure nobody builds from an old revision?”

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a drafter and CAD designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio of fully dimensioned drawings, not just renderings. Confirm they know your software, your drawing standards and your type of product or building. Strong candidates ask how a part will be made, catch errors in markups and keep revisions organized. No license is required, so judge real work over titles.

qa.q: How do I test a drafter and CAD designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task using a non-sensitive part or plan: a marked-up sketch to model and turn into a finished drawing in your software. Set a time limit and pay for anything longer than a couple of hours. Check views, dimensions, tolerances, title block and whether they flagged unclear or missing information.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most call center roles need no license, though some regulated calls, such as discussing insurance coverage, may need a state license. Verify past work with references and check a typing and accuracy test. If they will handle card or health data, confirm privacy training.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test listening, clear and polite speech, typing while talking, and finding answers in a knowledge base or CRM. Check how they calm an angry caller, follow a script and compliance steps, and write accurate call notes the next agent can use.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates stay calm and warm through repeated calls, solve the problem on the first contact where possible and know when to escalate. References mention good attendance, steady quality scores and willingness to learn new products and systems.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for impatience in a role-play, guessing instead of checking, poor notes and blaming customers. Be wary of anyone careless about verifying a caller’s identity, or who would read card numbers aloud or store them in notes.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about your hardest call and how it ended. What do you do when you do not know the answer? How do you verify a caller? Strong answers show patience, clear steps and respect for privacy rules.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a call center representative?
qa.a: Look for patience, clear communication, accurate typing and solid problem solving under pressure. They should follow scripts and privacy steps, know when to escalate and write useful notes. Most roles need no license, though some regulated calls may. References on attendance and quality matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a call center representative before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short mock call with a frustrated customer and a real problem from your business, using a sample knowledge base. Then ask them to write the call notes. Add a timed typing and data entry check. Judge tone, accuracy, how they verify identity and whether they solve the issue or escalate correctly.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many roles call for an active RN or social work license. You can check it on your state board’s online lookup, and social work license titles and rules vary by state. Voluntary certifications such as Certified Case Manager (CCM) are common. Entry-level coordinator roles may need no license at all.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them work through a prior authorization, explain a claim denial and set up a follow-up plan. Look for comfort with electronic health records and insurance terms like deductibles and referrals. Check for Medicare and Medicaid basics and clear notes that another staff member could pick up.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe closing the loop. That means confirming the patient got to the appointment, the referral was received and the results were reviewed. They explain care in plain language, juggle many cases calmly and know when to bring in a nurse or physician.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about caseload size or follow-up, or stories that name or identify past patients. Be wary of anyone who blames patients for missed care or shows little grasp of HIPAA privacy rules. Also watch for anyone who gives clinical advice beyond their license.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a patient who kept missing appointments and what they did. Ask how they track tasks across a large caseload. Ask them to walk you through an insurance denial they helped appeal. Listen for specific steps, not general statements.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a care coordinator?
qa.a: First check any license the role needs, such as RN or social work, on your state board’s site, since rules vary by state. Then look for insurance know-how and steady organization across a full caseload. Clear documentation, HIPAA awareness and calm, plain communication with patients and families also matter.

qa.q: How do I test a care coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short written case. For example, a patient leaves the hospital with a new prescription, a specialist referral and a plan that needs prior authorization. Ask them to list next steps, draft a case note and script a call to the patient. Use made-up details only, never real patient information.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most casino and sportsbook staff need a gaming license or registration from the state gaming regulator, or from the tribal gaming authority at tribal casinos. Which jobs need one, the background checks and timing all vary by state. Confirm the candidate can qualify before you plan a start date.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: For dealers, test game procedures, chip handling, payout math and game protection. For sportsbook and trading roles, test odds, limits and risk management. For all roles, check anti-money laundering duties under the Bank Secrecy Act, responsible gaming tools, self-exclusion lists and customer identity checks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates follow procedures exactly, spot cheating, advantage play or suspicious betting patterns, and report them calmly. They explain rules clearly to customers, respect responsible gaming limits and know that state rules often bar employees from betting with their own employer.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for sloppy chip or cash handling, shortcuts on game procedures, casual attitudes toward reporting large cash or suspicious activity, or offers to help friends with bonuses or limits. Be wary of anyone vague about past gaming licenses or who bets heavily on markets they would manage.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A player keeps buying in with cash just under reporting thresholds. What do you do? How do you handle a disputed payout? How would you spot a match-fixing pattern in betting data? Strong answers name procedures, escalation and records.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a casino or sports betting professional?
qa.a: Look for exact procedure discipline, strong math for payouts or odds, and solid knowledge of anti-money laundering, responsible gaming and integrity rules. Check that the candidate can get the gaming license or registration your state or tribal regulator requires before starting work. References from past gaming employers are important.

qa.q: How do I test a casino or sports betting professional before hiring?
qa.a: For dealers, hold an audition dealing your games while you watch procedures, chip handling and payout accuracy. For sportsbook roles, give a paid case setting odds and limits on an event with sharp action, plus an anti-money laundering scenario. Review accuracy, rule knowledge and judgment.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most CFO roles don’t legally require a CPA license, but many strong candidates hold one. State boards issue CPA licenses, and rules vary by state, so confirm active status with the issuing board. Also verify degrees, past titles and dates of employment.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for skill in building a 13-week cash flow forecast, reading a balance sheet for risk, and setting a budget with clear owners. They should explain numbers plainly to a board. If you plan to raise money, test how they model dilution and prepare investor materials.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They tie numbers to decisions, not just reports. They can describe a monthly close they sped up, a raise or loan they led, and an audit they managed. Former CEOs, auditors or investors speak well of their judgment under pressure.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about their own results, blaming past teams for missed numbers, or weak grasp of internal controls. At a public company, the CFO must personally certify financial reports under federal law, so be wary of anyone uneasy with that duty.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through the last time cash got tight and what they did. Ask how they prepared for their last audit, and what they changed in their first 90 days at their last job. Strong answers name specific steps and trade-offs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a CFO?
qa.a: Look for experience at a company of your size and stage, solid accounting knowledge, strong cash forecasting, and clear talk with a board and investors. A CPA license helps but is not always required. Check references from CEOs, auditors and investors who worked closely with them.

qa.q: How do I test a CFO before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case using sample or real numbers. Ask them to build a simple cash forecast, flag risks in a balance sheet, and give a brief summary as if to your board. Watch how they ask questions, explain trade-offs and handle pushback. Limit confidential data or use a nondisclosure agreement.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Change management certifications from several training providers show method knowledge but are optional. Verify past programs instead: ask what changed and how adoption was measured, and call references from sponsors and from the teams who had to adopt the change.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test stakeholder analysis, communication and training plans, and ways to measure adoption, such as system usage or process compliance. Check they can spot resistance early, coach leaders to sponsor the change, and adjust the plan when people are not adopting it.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about people and behavior, not just announcements. They involve managers and frontline staff early, measure real adoption after go-live, and keep supporting teams after the launch. They can show a plan that changed based on feedback.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates whose plan is mostly emails and slide decks, who treat training as the whole job, or who stop at go-live. Be careful with anyone who cannot say how they measured adoption or who labels every concern as resistance.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a change people resisted and what you did. How do you know if a new system is really being used? How do you get a busy executive to sponsor a change? Strong answers name actions, measures and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a change and transformation manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of programs where people actually adopted a new system or way of working, with measured results. Check stakeholder planning, communication, training and coaching of leaders. No license is required and certifications are optional, so references from sponsors and affected teams matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a change and transformation manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case: a new system launching to several departments, one of them openly resistant. Ask for a short change plan with stakeholders, messages, training and adoption measures. Review whether it is practical, focuses on people, and continues after go-live.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test partner recruitment, joint business planning and pipeline forecasting. Ask the candidate to build a 90-day plan for a new reseller, including enablement steps, shared targets and how they would track deal registration and partner-sourced revenue.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can name the partners they grew, explain how they split margin and incentives, and show how they handled channel conflict with a direct sales team. They talk about partner revenue, not just personal quota.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they decided which partners to invest in and which to drop. Ask about a partner that stopped selling and what they did. Ask how they ran a co-marketing campaign and measured the results.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who only describes closing deals themselves, cannot explain partner tiers or program rules, or blames partners for every missed number. Vague answers about forecast accuracy or partner pipeline are also a warning sign.

look.label: Tools and know-how to check
look.text: Check comfort with a CRM and a partner relationship management system, deal registration, MDF or co-op funds, and partner training portals. No state license is required for most channel sales roles, so focus on proven results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a channel sales manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of growing revenue through resellers, distributors or consultancies, not only through direct selling. Good candidates explain how they recruited partners, trained them, set shared goals and settled conflicts with direct sales. Ask for specific partner results and how they forecast partner pipeline.

qa.q: How do I test a channel sales manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Describe a mid-size reseller that sells a competitor’s product and ask the candidate to plan how to win them over and get them selling in 90 days. Have them present the plan, then role-play a tough partner meeting about margins or a lost deal.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for chat and email support, so writing samples matter most. Ask for a few real replies with customer details removed, check references on quality and speed, and confirm privacy training if they will see payment or health data.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test clear, friendly writing with correct grammar and spelling, handling several chats at once, using saved replies without sounding robotic and searching a knowledge base. Check ticketing tools, tags and notes, and how they answer an upset customer on social media.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates answer the real question in the first reply, set clear next steps and match the customer’s tone. They edit saved replies to fit, report product bugs with clear details and suggest fixes to help articles.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for typos, long or vague replies, pasted macros that miss the point and blaming the customer. Be wary of anyone who would share account details without verifying identity, or argue with customers in public social media threads.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Show me a reply you are proud of and explain why. How do you handle three chats when one customer is angry? When do you escalate? Strong answers explain how they prioritize, verify identity and close the loop.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a chat and email support agent?
qa.a: Look for clear, warm and correct writing, the ability to solve problems in one reply and steady speed across several chats. They should use ticketing tools, verify identity before sharing account details and escalate well. No license is required, so writing tests and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a chat and email support agent before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid writing test with a few real tickets, including an angry customer, a bug report and a refund request, plus a sample help article. Ask for replies and internal notes. Judge accuracy, tone, grammar, whether they solved the issue in one reply and when they chose to escalate.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many states and counties require a food handler card for cooks, and many also require at least one certified food protection manager on staff. Rules vary by state and county, and some add allergen training. Culinary degrees are optional; references and a paid trial shift matter more.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test knife skills, timing, seasoning and plating to your spec, plus food safety basics: cooking, holding and cooling temperatures, cross-contamination and allergen control. For chef roles, check menu costing, ordering, inventory, kitchen scheduling and training a team.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong cooks keep a clean, organized station, taste constantly, label and date everything and stay calm and consistent during a rush. Strong chefs also cost recipes accurately, control waste and train cooks to produce the same dish every time.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for skipping handwashing or thermometers, messy stations, cutting raw meat and produce on the same board, or brushing off allergen questions. Be wary of anyone who cannot follow a recipe spec or blames others for every past kitchen problem.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you cool a large batch of soup safely? How do you handle an allergy order during a rush? Tell me about a night the kitchen fell behind and what you did. Strong answers name steps, temperatures and teamwork.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a chef or cook?
qa.a: Look for solid technique, speed and consistency, clean work habits and real food safety knowledge, including temperatures and allergens. Check any food handler card or food protection manager certificate your state or county requires. For chef roles, also check costing, ordering and leading a team. References and a trial shift matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a chef or cook before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid trial shift or cooking test: have them prepare two or three of your dishes to spec, then watch station setup, knife work, timing, tasting and cleanup. Ask food safety questions as they work. For chef roles, add a menu costing exercise. Wage laws usually require paying for real work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a general license for chemists, though Puerto Rico does. Verify degrees with the school and review publications, patents or reports. Voluntary professional certifications exist. Work with controlled substances needs a federal registration held by the researcher or site, so ask about that experience.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the techniques the job uses, such as synthesis and purification, HPLC, GC-MS, NMR or infrared spectroscopy, or modeling software for computational roles. Check they can interpret spectra, keep a complete lab notebook and follow good laboratory or manufacturing practice where required.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong chemists plan experiments before running them, record everything as they go, and troubleshoot failed reactions or odd results step by step. They read safety data sheets, follow the chemical hygiene plan without reminders and explain results simply to non-chemists.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for casual attitudes to fume hoods, protective gear or waste handling, gaps in notebook records, or results that look too clean. Be wary of anyone who cannot interpret their own spectra or explain why a method was chosen.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a reaction or method that failed and how you fixed it. How do you confirm a compound’s identity and purity? Describe a safety incident you saw and what changed afterward. Strong answers name instruments, data and specific steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a chemist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on skill with your techniques and instruments, careful records and strong safety habits. Check they can interpret data, troubleshoot and follow good laboratory or manufacturing practice if your work is regulated. No state requires a general chemist license, so verified degrees, publications and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a chemist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid practical or data task close to your work, such as interpreting a set of spectra and chromatograms to identify an unknown, or planning a synthesis route with safety notes. Review accuracy, reasoning, how they record their work, and how they handle hazards and uncertainty.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they turn a messy set of executive priorities into a clear weekly plan. Check written communication, meeting design, follow-up discipline and the ability to run a cross-functional project from kickoff to close without constant direction.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates give concrete examples of decisions they moved forward, conflicts they resolved between leaders and projects they shipped. They talk about the executive’s goals before their own, protect confidentiality naturally and can explain how they earned trust across teams.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about impact, credit taken for every team result, or careless talk about past employers’ private matters. Be wary of someone who wants authority without accountability or sees the role mainly as a stepping stone to power.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they decided what reached the executive’s desk and what didn’t. Ask about a time they told a senior leader something unwelcome. Ask how they tracked commitments from meetings and what happened when an owner missed a deadline.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or certification is required for this role. Verify past titles, scope and reporting lines through references, ideally including a former executive they supported and a peer they worked alongside. Confirm any degrees they list.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a chief of staff?
qa.a: Look for sound judgment, discretion and the ability to drive work through other people without direct authority. They should write clearly, run tight meetings, manage several projects at once and stay calm under pressure. Fit with the executive matters a lot, so test how well they understand your goals and working style.

qa.q: How do I test a chief of staff before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a realistic packet, such as a messy inbox, a list of open projects and notes from a leadership meeting. Ask them to set priorities for the week, draft a meeting agenda and write a short follow-up memo. Then discuss their choices and what they chose not to do.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to serve as a CISO. Senior security certifications, such as CISSP or CISM, are common and can be verified with the issuing body. Check references from executives and board members, and confirm their past scope, team size and the incidents they led.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they build a risk-based security program, set a budget and roadmap, and lead incident response. Check knowledge of frameworks such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, the rules that apply to your industry, and how they report risk to a board in business terms.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have led a real incident and can explain what they told executives, regulators and customers. They tie security spending to business risk, build teams that keep good people, and work with legal on breach notice laws, which vary by state.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who speak only in tools and jargon, promise total security, or blame others for past breaches. Be careful with anyone who cannot describe a budget they managed, how they measured progress, or how they handled a disagreement with the CEO or board.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about the worst incident you led and what you would do differently. How do you report security risk to a board? How do you decide what not to fund? Strong answers are specific, calm and honest about mistakes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a CISO?
qa.a: Look for someone who has built and run a security program, led real incidents, and reported risk to executives and a board. Check they know the laws and frameworks that apply to you, including state breach notice laws and SEC disclosure rules for public companies. No license is required, so references and past results matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a CISO before hiring?
qa.a: Ask for a short presentation on a realistic scenario, such as a ransomware attack at a company like yours, or their plan for the first ninety days. Have executives or board members play their roles and ask hard questions. Review their priorities, plain language, honesty about tradeoffs and how they handle pressure.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: If the role will sign and seal plans, confirm an active Professional Engineer (PE) license on the state board’s online lookup for each state where you build. Licenses are issued state by state. An Engineer in Training (EIT or EI) has passed the FE exam but must work under a PE’s supervision.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short grading and drainage exercise: set spot elevations, size a pipe or swale, and check slopes against local standards. Have them read a geotechnical report and explain what it means for the foundation. Check fluency in the civil design and CAD software your team actually uses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates walk you through a project from survey to final inspection. They name the agencies that reviewed the plans, explain how they answered comments, and describe time on site checking the work. They talk about tradeoffs in cost, schedule and constructability, not just the math.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about their own role on team projects, or software results they cannot explain or check by hand. Be careful with anyone who offers to stamp plans in a state where they hold no license, or who treats permit and stormwater rules as mere paperwork.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Tell me about a plan set that came back with heavy review comments. What did you change?” Or: “How did you handle a field condition that did not match the drawings?” Real experience shows in specific details, numbers they checked and who they called.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a civil engineer?
qa.a: Match the license to the job. Anyone sealing plans needs an active PE license in your state, which you can verify on the state board’s website. Then look for experience in your project type, such as roads, land development or water systems, knowledge of local review agencies, and field time spent checking construction against the plans.

qa.q: How do I test a civil engineer before hiring?
