qa.a: Give a short, realistic task. Hand them a plan sheet with a few planted errors in grades, pipe slopes or callouts, and ask them to find and explain each one. Or ask for a quick drainage or grading calculation. Keep it to an hour or two, use a made-up project, and pay for anything longer.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most states require independent adjusters to hold a license, and many also license staff adjusters employed by insurers. Rules vary by state. Confirm an active license in each state where they will handle claims, using the state insurance department’s lookup, and check for disciplinary actions.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading a policy against a loss: coverage grants, exclusions, deductibles and limits. Check estimating software skills, recorded statements, photo and scene documentation, reserve setting, and clear coverage letters. Ask how they meet their state’s fair claims handling deadlines, which vary by state.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong adjusters keep tidy, dated file notes that a stranger could follow. They explain coverage decisions in plain words, spot fraud indicators without accusing anyone, and know when to involve a supervisor, an engineer or a special investigations unit.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for adjusters who decide coverage before reading the policy, leave long gaps in file notes, miss contact deadlines, or promise payment amounts on scene. Be wary of a lapsed or missing license, or of anyone who treats every claimant as a suspect.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a claim where coverage was unclear and how you decided it. How do you handle a claimant who disputes your estimate? When do you send a reservation of rights letter? Strong answers cite policy language, documentation steps and state rules.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a claims adjuster?
qa.a: Look for an active adjuster license in every state where they will work, since rules vary by state, plus a clean disciplinary record. Check they can read policy language, write accurate estimates and keep clear file notes. Experience in your line of insurance, such as auto, property or workers’ compensation, matters more than general claims experience.

qa.q: How do I test a claims adjuster before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise built from a closed, anonymized claim. Provide the policy, photos and statements, and ask them to decide coverage, set a reserve and write the letter to the policyholder. Review how they cite policy language, document their reasoning and explain the decision in plain words.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: Most client services managers need no license. In regulated fields, ask your compliance team first. Insurance roles that discuss coverage may need a state producer license, which varies by state. At securities firms, staff who take orders or give account advice may need FINRA registration and exams such as the Series 7.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Run a role-play with an upset client whose request you cannot fully meet. Watch whether they listen, restate the problem, explain what they can do and set a clear next step. Also check how they track open requests in a CRM or ticket system.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe specific accounts they kept, renewals they saved or service changes they managed. They talk about clients by need, not by complaint. They know when to escalate, make small promises with dates and write short, clear emails a busy client can act on.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Blaming past clients or coworkers for every problem. Promising whatever a client asks without checking with the team. Vague answers about how many accounts they handled or what they did when a client threatened to leave. Slow or careless replies during your own hiring process.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a client who wanted to cancel and what they did next. Ask how they would sort ten requests due the same day. Ask them to describe a service change that went wrong and how they fixed it with the client.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a client services manager?
qa.a: Look for calm problem solving, clear writing and a record of keeping clients. Ask for examples of accounts they managed, renewals they saved and service changes they handled. Check that they can organize many requests at once and know when to escalate. If your field is regulated, confirm any license or registration the role needs.

qa.q: How do I test a client services manager before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role-play with a frustrated client, then ask for the follow-up email they would send. Add a sorting exercise: a list of open requests with different deadlines and stakes. Judge their tone, accuracy and clear next steps, and whether they promise only what your company can deliver.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: If the role needs a clinician, check the active license on the state board’s lookup; nurses may hold a multistate license. Physicians can earn board certification in the clinical informatics subspecialty, and nurses can earn an informatics certification. EHR vendor certifications vary by system and employer.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test workflow analysis and EHR build, such as order sets, documentation templates and decision support alerts, plus terminologies like SNOMED CT, LOINC and RxNorm. Check they understand HL7 and FHIR interfaces, usability testing, privacy rules and when software may fall under FDA medical device rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates start with how clinicians actually work, measure alert override rates and outcomes after go-live, and retire alerts that do not help. They speak both clinical and technical language, test builds with real users and treat patient safety reviews as routine.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for adding alerts without measuring overrides or fatigue, building without frontline input, skipping testing before go-live, or a lapsed clinical license. Be wary of anyone who blames clinicians for workarounds instead of fixing the workflow that caused them.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an alert you redesigned or removed and what changed. How do you test an order set before go-live? Describe a safety event linked to the EHR and how you responded. Strong answers include data, users and specific build changes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a clinical informatics specialist?
qa.a: Look for real clinical experience combined with EHR build and workflow skills, knowledge of standards like HL7, FHIR and clinical terminologies, and a safety-first mindset. Verify any clinical license on the state board’s lookup and any board certification. Ask for examples where their changes improved care or reduced alert fatigue.

qa.q: How do I test a clinical informatics specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case: share a mock clinical workflow with a problem, such as a high-override alert, and ask them to redesign it, explain how to test it and how to measure results after launch. Review clinical accuracy, user focus, safety thinking and how clearly they explain tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for clinical research associates. Check for current Good Clinical Practice training based on the ICH E6 guideline. Some candidates hold voluntary certifications from professional clinical research associations. Confirm past monitoring roles and therapeutic areas with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for source data verification, close reading of a study protocol, spotting protocol deviations and writing clear monitoring visit reports. They should know FDA rules on informed consent, IRB oversight and investigational drug or device studies. They should also know how adverse events are recorded and escalated.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They name the study phases, therapeutic areas and number of sites they have monitored. They can describe the electronic data capture systems they have used, a site they helped improve, and how they prepared a site for an audit or inspection. They are ready for the travel the role needs.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about what they did on site visits. Be wary if they would correct site data themselves instead of raising a query. Another warning sign is treating consent form errors as minor paperwork. Late or sloppy visit reports in past roles are also a concern.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a monitoring visit from planning to final report. Ask what they did when they found a missing or wrong consent form. Ask how they handled a site that kept missing data entry deadlines or under-reported adverse events.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a clinical research associate?
qa.a: Look for hands-on site monitoring experience, current Good Clinical Practice training and a working knowledge of FDA rules on consent, IRBs and investigational products. Strong candidates write clear visit reports, catch protocol deviations and work well with site staff. No state license is required, though some hold voluntary professional certifications.

qa.q: How do I test a clinical research associate before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short mock protocol excerpt plus a sample case report form and source document that contain a few planted errors. Ask them to find the discrepancies, flag any consent or safety reporting issues and draft a brief follow-up letter to the site. Review their accuracy, judgment and writing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses research coordinators. Ask for current Good Clinical Practice and human subjects protection training, which most sponsors and review boards expect. Voluntary coordinator certifications exist. If they ship specimens, check dangerous goods shipping training; if they draw blood, check state phlebotomy rules, which vary.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the informed consent process, eligibility screening, source documentation, entering data into electronic data capture systems and resolving queries. Check they can report adverse events on time, keep the regulatory binder current, track investigational product and prepare for monitoring visits and audits.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong coordinators know the protocol well enough to spot a deviation before it happens. They keep records that are attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate, explain studies to patients without pressure, and stay calm juggling several studies, sponsors and visit windows.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for anyone who has backdated or rewritten records, obtained consent after study procedures began, or treats protocol deviations as mere paperwork. Be wary of casual handling of patient health information and vague answers about who actually did the work at past sites.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a protocol deviation you caught and how you reported it. How do you explain a study to a patient who seems unsure? What do you do when a lab value is missing at a visit? Strong answers cite the protocol, sponsor and review board.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a clinical research coordinator?
qa.a: Look for hands-on trial experience in your study phase and therapeutic area, current Good Clinical Practice training, and careful, honest documentation habits. Check they can run consent, screening, visits and data entry, and work well with monitors. No state license is required, so training records, references and audit history matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a clinical research coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Use a paid exercise with mock materials: give a short protocol excerpt and a patient file, and ask them to check eligibility, list the visit procedures and fill in a sample case report form. Add a role-play consent conversation. Review accuracy, protocol knowledge and how they handle patient questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for cloud work. Certifications from the major cloud providers are optional but common. They expire after a set period, so check the issue date and confirm each one through the provider’s online verification page or digital badge.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Building infrastructure as code instead of clicking through a console. Setting up access with least privilege. Networking basics like subnets and firewalls. Monitoring and alerts, plus backups that are actually restored in tests. Reading a monthly bill to find waste.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe outages they handled and what they changed afterward. They can explain a cost cut with before and after numbers. They tag resources, write runbooks and design so one failed server or zone does not take the whole service down.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Sharing one admin login across a team, storing secret keys in code, no plan for restoring data, or never having looked at a bill. Be wary of someone who claims mastery of every provider and tool but cannot explain what their own setup costs to run.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: What was your worst outage and how did you find the cause? How would you cut a bill that doubled last month? How do you give a new developer access safely? Specific stories with numbers and tradeoffs beat textbook definitions.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a cloud engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with the provider you use, infrastructure as code, strong security habits around access and secrets, and a record of controlling costs. Certifications help but are optional, and no license is required. Ask for concrete stories about outages, migrations and savings, and check references from teams they supported.

qa.q: How do I test a cloud engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task in a sandbox account with a spending limit. Ask them to deploy a small app with code, lock down access, add monitoring and estimate the monthly cost. Or show a sample bill and diagram and ask what they would fix first. Never hand over production credentials.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work in the US. Certifications are optional but useful, such as the cloud providers’ own security certifications or the vendor-neutral CCSP. Check them through the issuer’s online verification, and weigh proven hands-on work more than paper.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Identity and access management with least privilege, network rules and private connectivity, encryption and key management, logging and alerting, and infrastructure as code. Have them review a sample policy or template and find overly broad permissions, public storage and open ports.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Explains past audit findings or incidents in plain terms. Shows how they automated guardrails instead of fixing settings by hand. Understands the shared responsibility model and works with developers so security checks fit into deployment pipelines without blocking releases.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Relies on one tool’s dashboard without understanding the settings beneath it. Grants admin access just to make something work. Cannot explain how to rotate a leaked access key. Shares confidential details or real credentials from a past employer.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “How would you lock down a brand new cloud account?” “A storage bucket was found public. What are your first three steps?” “A team wants full admin rights. How do you respond?” Listen for specific steps, logging and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a cloud security engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work securing access, network rules, encryption and logging on the cloud platform you use. Strong candidates automate controls with code, explain risks in plain terms and work well with developers. Certifications help but are optional, and no state license is required. Verify any certification with its issuer.

qa.q: How do I test a cloud security engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task in a sandbox account or on a sample template that contains planted problems, such as public storage, open ports and overly broad permissions. Ask them to find the issues, rank them by risk and explain the fixes. Never give a candidate access to your live systems or real credentials.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an active law license and good standing with the state bar where they are admitted. Rules for in-house lawyers vary by state. Many states let out-of-state attorneys work in-house through a registration, so check what your state requires.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them redline a customer or supplier agreement under time pressure. Watch how they handle limitation of liability, indemnity, IP ownership and data terms. Then have them review a product feature for privacy, consumer protection and advertising issues.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They use playbooks and fallback positions, know which points are worth a fight, and keep deals moving. They ask product questions early, write short practical guidance, and say clearly which risks the business can accept and which need a fix before launch.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Marking up every clause with no sense of priority, advice buried in legal jargon, or treating every launch as a no. Be wary of vague answers about past deal work, or claims of privacy or export expertise with no concrete examples.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a hard negotiation they closed and what they gave up to get it. Ask how they reviewed a launch that collected user data and what changed as a result. Ask when they bring in outside counsel.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a commercial and product counsel?
qa.a: Look for an active law license in good standing, and check your state’s rules for in-house lawyers. Look for real experience negotiating customer and vendor contracts and advising product teams on privacy and consumer law. The best candidates give clear, business-friendly answers, set priorities in negotiations, and help launches happen safely instead of blocking them.

qa.q: How do I test a commercial and product counsel before hiring?
qa.a: Use mock documents, not confidential ones. Give a sample agreement and ask for a redline with short notes on the key risks and fallback positions. Add a one-page product spec and ask for a brief memo on legal issues to resolve before launch. Judge their priorities, clarity and practical judgment, not just how many issues they flag.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test clean, fast writing across formats: a press release, an internal staff memo and a short social post on the same news. Check grammar, a consistent style, and whether they adjust tone for reporters, employees and customers without changing the facts.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No US state license is required for communications work. An optional public relations accreditation exists, but many strong candidates do not hold it. Verify past roles with references, and confirm that any media coverage they list actually ran and that they played a real part in it.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for a portfolio of published work they can walk through in detail. They can explain who approved it and what result it had. They know how newsrooms work and keep brand voice consistent. They stay calm and organized when news breaks or plans change.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for samples they cannot explain or that were mostly written by others. Other warning signs are promises of guaranteed press coverage, careless errors in their own application, sharing confidential details from a past employer, or a habit of spinning facts instead of stating them accurately.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a time a story or announcement went wrong and what they did in the first hour. Ask how they get sign-off from leaders and legal. Ask how they decide what staff hear first and how they measure whether a campaign worked.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a communications manager?
qa.a: Look for strong, accurate writing, a portfolio they can explain line by line, and real experience with press, internal announcements and brand voice. Good candidates understand how reporters work, manage approvals smoothly and stay steady during a crisis. No license is required, so rely on work samples, references and a practical writing test.

qa.q: How do I test a communications manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-limited task based on a realistic scenario. For example, ask for a press release, a staff memo and a social post announcing the same change. Then add a sudden complication and ask how they would respond. Judge clarity, accuracy, tone for each audience and speed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for clear, warm writing that stays calm under pressure. Check moderation judgment, setting up channels, roles and bots on Discord or forum software, running events, and turning member feedback into short, useful notes for product and support teams.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can show a community they grew or steadied, with real examples of threads, events or guidelines they wrote. They talk about members by name, know when to step back, and measure health by useful conversation, not just member counts.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of someone who only cites follower numbers, bans or deletes posts to avoid criticism, argues with members in public, or can’t explain how they handled a heated thread. Vague answers about past communities often mean little hands-on time.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a member who kept breaking rules but was well liked. Ask what they did when a product bug angered the community, and how they decided which feedback to pass to the team and which to answer themselves.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for community management. Verify past work instead: ask for links to communities they ran, guidelines or event recaps they wrote, and references from people who worked with them. Respect any confidentiality limits from former employers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a community manager?
qa.a: Look for steady, friendly writing, fair moderation judgment and comfort with tools like Discord, forums and event platforms. Strong candidates show real communities they managed, explain how they handled conflict, and can turn member feedback into clear notes for your product team. Value engaged, useful conversation over raw member counts.

qa.q: How do I test a community manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task. Share a few sample posts, including an angry complaint and a rule-breaking message, and ask how they would reply and moderate each. Ask for a one-page plan for a small online event. Review tone, judgment, clarity and how well they protect both members and your product.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No license is required for compensation work in the US. Some candidates hold voluntary certifications such as the Certified Compensation Professional (CCP) or Certified Employee Benefit Specialist (CEBS). Treat these as a plus, not a must, and confirm them with the issuing body.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for hands-on spreadsheet work: matching jobs to salary survey data, building pay ranges with midpoints, calculating compa-ratios and pricing a merit budget. Strong analysts also know basic statistics for pay equity reviews and can explain results to managers without jargon.

look.label: Legal knowledge that matters
look.text: Look for working knowledge of FLSA exempt and nonexempt rules, the federal Equal Pay Act and Title VII. Pay transparency and salary history laws vary by state and city, so good candidates know to check the rules where your staff work.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask about your pay philosophy and which labor market you compete in before suggesting numbers. They can describe a range they built, a pay gap they found and fixed, and how they kept salary data confidential.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about data sources, setting pay by gut feel, careless handling of salary files, or advice to treat salaried staff as exempt without checking the duties tests. Be wary if they cannot explain how they checked their own math.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a compensation analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong spreadsheet skills, experience with salary surveys and pay ranges, and solid knowledge of wage and equal pay laws. Good analysts explain numbers clearly, keep salary data private and tie pay decisions to a written policy. A voluntary certification such as the CCP helps but is not required.

qa.q: How do I test a compensation analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short exercise with made-up data: a few jobs, market survey figures and current salaries. Ask them to build pay ranges, flag people far below or above range and suggest next steps. Use fake names and numbers only, and judge how they explain their choices as well as their math.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for compiler work. Many compiler engineers hold computer science degrees, often graduate degrees, but strong ones also come straight from industry. Verify with public patches to open-source compilers such as LLVM or GCC, published papers, and references who confirm what they shipped.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test intermediate representations, static single assignment form, optimization passes, instruction selection, register allocation and scheduling. For AI chips, check MLIR, tensor operations, memory layout, tiling and vectorization. Check strong C++, reading assembly, and testing with fuzzing and differential checks against another compiler.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can show a change they made, the benchmark it improved and the bug it nearly caused. They understand the target hardware, read generated code to find problems and treat correctness as more important than speed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who have only written toy parsers but claim backend experience, cannot explain undefined behavior, or tune for one benchmark while ignoring correctness. Be careful with anyone who cannot reduce a failing program to a small test case.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an optimization you added and how you proved it was safe. How do you find which pass caused a miscompile? How would you choose tile sizes for a matrix multiply on a new chip? Strong answers explain tradeoffs and name tools.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a compiler engineer?
qa.a: Look for deep knowledge of compiler internals, such as intermediate representations, optimization passes and code generation, plus strong C++ and an understanding of your target hardware. Public patches to open-source compilers and published papers are strong evidence. No license is required, so verified work and references matter more than credentials alone.

qa.q: How do I test a compiler engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work, such as writing a simple optimization pass on a small intermediate representation, or finding why a test program is miscompiled and reducing it to a minimal case. Review correctness, test coverage, how they reason about safety and how clearly they explain their steps.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a compliance analyst. Optional certifications such as CAMS for anti-money laundering or CRCM for bank regulatory compliance show formal training. Confirm any listed credential directly with the issuing body, and check degrees only if the role truly requires one.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give them a sample customer file or transaction list and ask them to flag what needs a closer look. Strong analysts read a rule, apply it to messy facts, write a clear note explaining why, and know when to escalate instead of deciding alone.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask which regulations they worked under, such as the Bank Secrecy Act, and what their part was. Ask them to walk through an alert from first review to final decision, or explain how they tracked license renewals and reporting deadlines across several states.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They keep careful records, explain findings in plain words, and can show how they keep up with rule changes. They talk about problems they caught and how they improved the process, not just the single case they closed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about which rules applied, or pride in clearing alerts fast without saying how. Be wary of anyone who shares confidential case details from a past employer, since federal law requires suspicious activity reports to stay confidential.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a compliance analyst?
qa.a: Look for someone who knows the rules your business falls under and can apply them to real cases. They should write clear, well-supported notes, keep organized records, and escalate issues at the right time. Certifications like CAMS or CRCM help but are optional. Verify any credential with the body that issued it.

qa.q: How do I test a compliance analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic exercise using made-up data. For example, ask them to review a few customer profiles or transactions, flag anything unusual, and write a brief note on what they would do next. Judge how they cite the rule, explain their reasoning, and decide what to escalate. Never use real customer data in the test.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No general US license exists for compliance officers. Optional certifications include CCEP, CHC for healthcare, CRCM for banking and CAMS for anti-money laundering. Securities firms may need staff with specific industry registrations. Confirm any credential directly with the body that issued it.

look.label: Industry rules they must know
look.text: Match their knowledge to your sector. A clinic needs someone fluent in HIPAA. A bank needs the Bank Secrecy Act. A factory needs OSHA rules. Privacy and employment laws also differ by state, so ask which states they have covered.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for risk assessment, clear policy writing, careful recordkeeping and internal investigations. They should explain a complex rule in plain words to frontline staff and build training people actually finish. Ask for a sample policy or training outline with confidential details removed.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates give specific examples of finding a problem, fixing it and documenting the fix. They stay calm when telling leaders bad news. They know when to bring in legal counsel and when a matter must be reported to a regulator.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who treats compliance as box-checking, gives vague answers about past audits or shares confidential details from a former employer. Be wary if they suggest hiding issues from regulators or cannot describe how they handled a real violation.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a compliance officer?
qa.a: Look for solid knowledge of the laws in your industry and the states where you operate. Check for clear writing, strong records habits and the backbone to raise problems with leadership. Certifications like CCEP or CAMS help but are optional. Verify them with the issuing body and ask for real examples of issues they found and fixed.

qa.q: How do I test a compliance officer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case based on your business, such as an employee complaint or a missed filing. Ask them to list the risks, the rules involved, who to notify and what to document. Then have them draft a one-page policy or a five-minute staff training. Judge accuracy, clarity and sound judgment.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for composites work, and aerospace employers often certify technicians on their own processes. For repairs on certificated aircraft, federal rules require work by or under the supervision of a certificated mechanic or repair station. Verify training records and references who saw their layups.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading ply tables and layup drawings, cutting and laying plies at the right orientation, debulking, vacuum bagging, and running autoclave or oven cures. Check prepreg out-time and freezer tracking, trimming and drilling, bonding, tap tests, and safe handling of resins and fibers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates keep a clean layup area, follow ply tables exactly, and log every cure and material lot. They spot wrinkles, bridging or bag leaks before cure, ask when a drawing is unclear, and can describe parts they built and how they passed inspection.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for skipped debulks, missing ply records, expired prepreg, and contamination from mold release or silicone. Be wary of anyone who hides defects, guesses at ply orientation, or ignores protective equipment and resin safety rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a layup and bagging setup you have done. What do you check before starting a cure? How do you track prepreg out-time? Tell me about a part that failed inspection and what changed. Strong answers name specific checks and records.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a composites technician?
qa.a: Look for hands-on layup and cure experience with your materials, strict records of plies, lots and cure cycles, and care with clean work and safety. Check bagging and trimming skills and how they handle defects. No state license is required, so a practical test, training records and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a composites technician before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid hands-on test. Ask them to lay up a small flat panel from a ply table, bag it and prepare it for cure, recording every step. Inspect ply orientation, bag quality, cleanliness and records. Add a short drawing review to check they ask about anything unclear.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give them a small labeled image set and ask them to train or fine-tune a model. Look for clean train and test splits, sensible augmentation, the right metric such as mean average precision or IoU, and honest notes on where the model fails.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license for this work. Check degrees, past projects and public code instead. For medical scan work, confirm experience with FDA rules for software as a medical device and with HIPAA rules for patient images.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about data first: how images were collected, labeled and checked. They have shipped a model to real hardware, like an edge camera, car or robot. They can explain trade-offs between speed, memory and accuracy in plain terms.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Only notebook demos on well-known benchmark datasets. No plan for night scenes, glare, motion blur or new camera angles. Claims of near-perfect accuracy with no mention of data leakage, class imbalance or how the test set was built.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a model that worked in testing but failed in the field, and what they changed. Ask how they chose between detection and segmentation. Ask how they found and fixed bad labels in a dataset.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a computer vision engineer?
qa.a: Look for shipped work, not just research demos. Strong candidates understand data collection and labeling, pick the right metrics, and have run models on real devices with limits on speed and memory. For medical imaging, look for experience with FDA software rules and HIPAA. No state license applies, so check past projects and code closely.

qa.q: How do I test a computer vision engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task using a small image set from your own kind of work. Ask them to train a model, report results on a held-out test set, and list failure cases with example images. Then review it together. Their explanation of what went wrong and what they would try next tells you more than the score.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Ask for an OSHA 30-hour construction card. Check any Certified Construction Manager (CCM) or PMP credential with the body that issued it. Contractor licensing varies by state and sometimes by city, so confirm whether your project also needs a licensed general contractor or engineer.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them build a short critical path schedule from a scope sheet, spot conflicts in a set of drawings and price a change order. Strong managers can explain float, long-lead equipment and how a delay in one trade affects the others.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about the largest project they ran from start to finish and how they handled a slipping schedule. For factories, data centers or other complex sites, ask how they coordinated power, cooling or process equipment and managed commissioning and turnover.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They speak in specifics: daily logs, three-week lookaheads, RFIs, submittals, inspections and punch lists. They can name a past mistake and what they changed. Owners, superintendents and subcontractors describe them as clear, fair and organized.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about budgets or schedules, blaming every problem on subs or owners, a weak safety record, or credentials they cannot show. Be cautious if they cannot explain how permits and inspections worked on their past jobs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a construction manager?
qa.a: Look for proven experience on projects like yours in size and type, strong scheduling and cost control, and a solid safety record. Verify an OSHA 30-hour card and any CCM or PMP credential. Licensing rules vary by state, so check what your project requires. Call references from owners and subcontractors.

qa.q: How do I test a construction manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short scope and a few drawing sheets. Ask for a basic critical path schedule, a list of conflicts or missing details, and a priced change order. Then walk through how they would run the first weekly meeting. Their reasoning matters more than perfect numbers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most laborers need no license, but some states require OSHA 10 or 30 hour training on public projects. Crane operators need certification under OSHA rules, and some states add a license. Riggers and signal persons must be qualified. Truck drivers need a CDL. Verify cards and call foremen.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the tasks you need, such as reading plans, layout, formwork, concrete placing and finishing, rebar tying or roofing. For operators, check pre-use inspections, grading to stakes, trenching and safe loading. Everyone should know fall protection, trench safety and hand signals.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show up ready, inspect tools and equipment before use and wear protective gear without reminders. They work steadily, keep the site clean and speak up about hazards. Operators run machines smoothly, protect buried utilities and follow spotters and signal persons exactly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for skipped inspections, no fall protection habits, or stories of entering unprotected trenches. Be careful with operators who cannot explain load charts or utility locates, or anyone whose references describe repeated no-shows or damaged equipment.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What do you check before starting an excavator? When does a trench need protection? How do you tie off on a roof? Tell me about a concrete pour that went wrong and what the crew did. Strong answers name real steps and safety checks.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a construction worker or equipment operator?
qa.a: Look for hands-on skill in your trade, safe work habits and any required cards, such as OSHA training where your state requires it or crane certification. Check equipment experience by machine type. References from foremen and superintendents show reliability, effort and safety better than resumes do.

qa.q: How do I test a construction worker or equipment operator before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid, supervised skills check on site, such as setting forms, tying rebar or operating a machine on a short grading or loading task. Start with a pre-use inspection. Judge safety, control, accuracy and how well they follow directions from a foreman or spotter.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Ask for proof of any certification claimed, such as Certified Construction Manager (CCM), PMP or an OSHA 30-hour construction card. None is required by federal law for this role. Contractor licensing rules vary by state, so check what your project needs and verify any license with the state board.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Reading drawings and specs, building a schedule with a clear critical path, tracking costs against the budget and change orders, and writing clear RFIs and meeting notes. Have them spot conflicts in a drawing set or recover a schedule that has slipped.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a project that ran late or over budget and what they did about it. Ask how they handled a failed inspection, a subcontractor who missed dates or a disputed change order. Strong answers include numbers, documents and specific steps.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They have run projects similar in size and type to yours. They know how permits and inspections work in your area, put decisions in writing and keep safety on every meeting agenda. Owners and subcontractors they worked with speak well of them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about budgets or schedules. Blaming every problem on others. No experience with closeout, punch lists or handover documents. Casual talk about skipping permits or inspections. Certifications they claim but cannot show proof of.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a construction project manager?
qa.a: Look for experience on projects like yours in size and type, and solid skills in scheduling, budgeting and contracts. They should know local permit and inspection steps and communicate clearly in writing. Verify any certification they claim, such as CCM, PMP or OSHA 30. Check references from owners and subcontractors.

qa.q: How do I test a construction project manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task built from a real project: a few drawing sheets, a schedule and a budget with a pending change order. Ask them to find problems, update the schedule and write a brief update for the owner. Then talk through their choices. Follow up with calls to past owners and subcontractors.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for two or three case studies that show the problem, the constraints, the drafts and the final words. Look for before and after screens, error messages and onboarding flows, not only marketing copy or blog posts. No US license exists for this work, so the portfolio carries the weight.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test whether they can write a clear button label, a helpful error message and a short empty state. Check for plain language, a consistent voice, accessible wording for screen readers, and text that fits tight space limits and works when translated.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates ask who the user is and what they are trying to do before writing. They explain why each word was chosen, work closely with designers and engineers, use design tools like Figma, and test their words with real users or research.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for clever or jokey wording that hides the meaning, error messages that blame the user, and drafts with no reasoning behind them. Be careful if they cannot describe pushback from a team or how feedback changed their work.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through an error message they rewrote and what changed after. Ask how they built or followed a style guide, how they handled legal or product disagreements, and how they measured whether their words worked.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a content designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio with real product screens, not just marketing writing. Good content designers write short, clear words that help people finish a task. They can explain their choices, work well with designers and engineers, write with accessibility in mind, and use research or testing to check that their words work.

qa.q: How do I test a content designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task based on a real screen from your product. Ask them to rewrite a confusing error message, label a few buttons and write an empty state. Then ask them to explain their choices and what they would want to learn from users. Their reasoning matters as much as the words.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them edit a messy draft and write a short original piece from a brief. Look for clear structure, accurate facts, consistent style, clean grammar and headlines that match the content. Check that they followed your word count, audience and tone.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for published samples close to your topics, with links where possible. Ask what they wrote and what an editor changed. Much writing is ghostwritten under a client’s name, so a short test tells you more than bylines do.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask who the reader is, what the goal is and which style guide you follow. They cite sources and flag claims they can’t verify. They understand basic SEO without stuffing keywords, and they handle revision requests on time.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for generic samples, test work that is much weaker than the portfolio, unverified facts or copied passages. Be wary if they can’t explain their process. Ask how they use AI tools and make sure their answer fits your policy.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handle conflicting edits from two reviewers. Ask how they research a topic they don’t know and how they turn interview notes into a draft. Ask which style guides they have worked with and how they keep a long piece consistent.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a content writer and editor?
qa.a: Look for clear, accurate writing in your subject area. They should be able to edit other people’s drafts well and adapt tone for articles, newsletters and web pages. No license is required in the US. Review relevant samples, check references, and confirm they can research, cite sources and meet deadlines.

qa.q: How do I test a content writer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to the real work. For example, ask them to edit a rough draft and write a newsletter intro or web section from a brief. Set a deadline and a word count. Score accuracy, structure, grammar, tone and how well they followed instructions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a contract manager. Some candidates hold voluntary certifications from professional contract management associations. Verify any certification directly with the body that issued it. A law degree can help, but most roles do not require one.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have the candidate redline a short supplier agreement. Look for sound handling of indemnity, limitation of liability, payment terms, renewal and termination clauses. Check that they spot conflicts with your standard terms and can explain each change in plain words.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates track obligations, deadlines and renewal dates in a system, not from memory. They know when to bring in legal counsel. For federal contracts, look for working knowledge of the Federal Acquisition Regulation. State and local government contracts follow their own procurement rules.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of candidates who accept every change the other side asks for or cannot explain why a clause matters. Watch for anyone with no experience managing contracts after signing. Also note anyone willing to give legal advice without involving an attorney.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a negotiation that stalled and how they moved it forward. Ask how they caught a missed renewal or an unmet obligation. Ask which clauses they will not concede and why. Concrete, detailed answers show real practice.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a contract manager?
qa.a: Look for clear drafting, steady negotiation and careful tracking after signing. The candidate should understand key clauses like indemnity, liability limits and termination, and know when to involve a lawyer. No license is required, but some hold voluntary certifications you can verify. For federal work, knowledge of the Federal Acquisition Regulation matters; state and local contracts follow their own rules.

qa.q: How do I test a contract manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short sample agreement with a few one-sided or conflicting clauses. Ask the candidate to redline it and write a brief note explaining each change. Then role-play a short negotiation on one disputed term. Finally, ask how they would track the contract’s deadlines and renewal after signing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many controllers hold a CPA license, which each state’s board of accountancy issues and renews. Check the license status on that board’s public lookup. A CPA is not legally required for most private-company controller roles, so decide in advance if you need one. Some candidates hold the voluntary CMA certification instead.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for someone who can run a full month-end close, reconcile every balance sheet account, book accruals and prepaids, and apply US GAAP to revenue recognition. They should build clean financial statements, explain variances against budget, and work fluently in your accounting system and spreadsheets.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong controllers describe a close calendar they built or shortened. They explain controls like segregation of duties, approval limits and bank reconciliation review in plain terms. They have worked through an external audit, and they can explain the numbers clearly to owners and managers who are not accountants.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with candidates who are vague about how long their close took or who prepared versus reviewed the work. Other warning signs include blaming auditors for findings, being unable to walk through a reconciliation, or treating controls as paperwork they skip when busy.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through their last month-end close day by day. Ask about an audit adjustment or finding and how they fixed the root cause. Ask how they would set up controls on a small team where one person handles most tasks.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a financial controller?
qa.a: Look for proven experience running a monthly close, reconciling accounts and producing GAAP financial statements. Check how they design controls and handle audits. A CPA license is common but not always required; if they claim one, verify it with the state board of accountancy. Strong candidates also explain the numbers clearly to non-accountants.

qa.q: How do I test a financial controller before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case with a sample trial balance and bank statement. Ask them to find reconciliation errors, propose adjusting entries and draft a simple income statement and balance sheet. Then ask them to explain one variance to you as if you were the owner. Watch how they spot risks and organize their work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most PLC programming roles need no state license. A Professional Engineer license matters if they will seal engineering drawings, and rules vary by state. Vendor platform certificates are optional. Check electrical safety training, such as arc flash and lockout and tagout, and ask for code samples and commissioning references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test ladder logic and structured text on your PLC platform, HMI and SCADA screens, alarms, and industrial networks such as EtherNet/IP, Modbus or BACnet. Check reading electrical drawings, I/O checkout, PID loop tuning, safety circuits and interlocks, and version control of programs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write clear, commented, structured code that maintenance staff can follow. They test logic in simulation before going live, back up programs and track changes, respect safety circuits, and can describe a commissioning job where they found and fixed a hard fault.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for live edits on running equipment without a backup or change record, bypassed safety interlocks, uncommented code, and no plan for operator training. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain how they troubleshoot with I/O status and electrical drawings.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a line that stopped and how you found the cause. How do you test a program change before it goes live? How do you tune a PID loop that oscillates? Strong answers name specific tools, steps and safety checks.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a controls and PLC engineer?
qa.a: Look for programs and projects on your PLC and HMI platforms, clean and documented code, and commissioning experience in plants or buildings like yours. Check electrical safety habits and change control. Most roles need no license, though a state Professional Engineer license matters for sealed drawings, so code samples and site references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a controls and PLC engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise, such as writing logic for a simple conveyor or pump sequence with interlocks, alarms and a manual mode, in a PLC simulator. Or give a sample program with a planted bug and a fault description. Review structure, comments, safety handling and how quickly and logically they find the problem.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for a COO. Verify past titles, scope and results through references, including former CEOs, board members and direct reports. Confirm degrees with schools if they matter. Run any background check only with written consent under federal rules, and follow state limits.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they build an operating plan, set metrics and budgets, design processes and run a weekly and quarterly review cadence. Check experience leading leaders, managing vendors and overseeing finance, legal, people or supply chain functions, matched to what your company needs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong COOs build systems that work without them, make tradeoffs with clear data and hire leaders stronger than themselves. They fill the CEO’s gaps, deliver bad news early, and can name decisions that failed and what they learned.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague results, credit taken for team wins, only big-company experience when you need hands-on work, or no examples of hard calls such as restructuring a team. Be wary of anyone who wants to replace the CEO’s role rather than support it.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a process you built that still runs without you. How did you split decisions with your last CEO? Describe a quarter when you missed targets and what you changed. Strong answers include metrics, people decisions and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a chief operating officer?
qa.a: Look for a proven record of turning strategy into results at a company of your size and stage, strong operating systems and leaders who grew under them. Check fit with your CEO and culture. No license is required, so thorough references from CEOs, boards and direct reports matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a chief operating officer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case built from your real situation: share an operating problem with data, such as slipping delivery times or rising costs, and ask for a diagnosis and a first ninety-day plan. Have them present to the CEO and key leaders. Review priorities, realism and how they handle challenge.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to serve as a corporate secretary. Many come from law or paralegal backgrounds, and governance certifications are optional. If the candidate is a lawyer, check bar status through the state bar. Otherwise verify through references and redacted samples of minutes and board materials.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test drafting minutes and written consents, preparing board packs, tracking state annual reports and registered agents, and keeping entity records current across states and countries. For public companies, check knowledge of SEC filings, insider reporting and proxy work. Entity management software skills help.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write concise minutes that record decisions, not transcripts. They keep a calendar of every filing deadline, know which actions need board or shareholder approval, and keep subsidiaries in good standing. They handle directors with tact and keep confidential matters private.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for minutes that read like transcripts or omit approvals, missing signatures, or entities that fell out of good standing on their watch. Be wary of candidates who cannot explain bylaws, quorum or written consent rules, or who discuss confidential board matters casually.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you decide what goes into board minutes? Tell me about an entity that lost good standing and how you restored it. How do you track filings across many states? Strong answers describe specific systems, checklists and approval steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a corporate secretary?
qa.a: Look for precise drafting of minutes and consents, strong entity management habits and a firm grasp of bylaws, quorum and approval rules. Check experience with state filings and, for public companies, SEC reporting. No license is required, though many are lawyers or paralegals. References and redacted work samples matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a corporate secretary before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise: share notes from a mock board meeting and a simple entity chart. Ask them to draft minutes, a written consent for one approval and a filing calendar for the entities. Review accuracy, concise wording, correct approval steps and whether they flag missing information.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a corporate trainer. Some hold optional talent development or instructional design certifications. If they will teach regulated topics, such as OSHA Outreach safety courses or CPR, confirm they hold current trainer authorization from the body that issues those cards.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short live teaching sample on a real topic from your workplace. Watch how they set clear goals, check understanding, handle questions and keep the group involved. Also review a lesson plan, slide deck or online module they built themselves.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about results, not just sessions delivered. Look for examples of measuring learning with quizzes, skill checks or follow-up with managers. Strong trainers adapt content for new hires, experienced staff and remote learners, and work comfortably with video meeting tools and a learning management system.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Reading slides word for word, long lectures with no practice, or no way to show that learners improved. Be wary of trainers who can’t explain how they would update content when your process changes, or who blame learners when a session goes poorly.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they turned a subject expert’s notes into a course. Ask how they handled a disengaged or difficult participant, and how they changed a workshop that wasn’t working. Ask what they track after training to see if behavior changed on the job.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a corporate trainer?
qa.a: Look for someone who can both design and deliver training. They should build clear lessons, run engaging classroom and online sessions, and show how they measure results. Ask for work samples like lesson plans or e-learning modules. No license is required, but trainers teaching regulated topics like OSHA Outreach or CPR need current authorization from the issuing body.

qa.q: How do I test a corporate trainer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short process or procedure from your business and ask for a 10 to 15 minute teaching demo, live or on video. Have a few staff act as learners. Score how clearly they explain, how they check understanding and how they handle questions. Then ask how they would measure whether the training worked.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for cost accounting. A state CPA license or the Certified Management Accountant credential shows depth but is optional. Verify any CPA license on the state board of accountancy lookup. For cloud cost work, FinOps experience or certification is a plus.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test standard costing, variance analysis, overhead allocation and inventory valuation under GAAP. Check bills of materials, ERP data, activity-based costing and building a cost model in spreadsheets. For cloud costs, check tagging, allocation by team and reading usage bills.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates walk the factory floor or talk to engineers to understand real costs. They explain variances in plain language, find waste others missed and build models that managers trust and use for pricing and budget decisions.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for allocations nobody can explain, models that are hard to audit, and costs reported without checking source data. Be wary of anyone who cannot reconcile cost records to the general ledger or explain how inventory costs reach the income statement.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a variance you investigated and what you found. How do you allocate shared overhead fairly? How did you reduce the cost of a product or service? Strong answers include the method, the data and the business result.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a cost accountant?
qa.a: Look for strong standard costing, variance analysis and inventory valuation skills, solid spreadsheet and ERP work, and a habit of checking costs against real operations. A CPA license or CMA credential is a plus but not required. For cloud costs, look for allocation and tagging experience.

qa.q: How do I test a cost accountant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with sample production or cloud usage data, standard costs and actual spend. Ask them to calculate unit costs, explain the main variances and suggest where to cut waste. Judge accuracy, how clearly they explain the method and whether the model reconciles to the totals.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check modern C++ (C++17 or later): RAII, smart pointers, move semantics, templates and the standard library. See if they can read a profiler’s output, reason about cache use and spot a hidden copy or allocation in a hot loop.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license exists for C++ developers, and degrees or certificates say little about real skill. Verify past work instead: public code, shipped products, or a reference who saw them fix crashes and speed problems in production.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They reach for sanitizers, debuggers and profilers on their own, write unit tests and know their build system, such as CMake. They can explain undefined behavior, thread safety and why a fix worked, not just that it did.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Raw new and delete everywhere, ignored compiler warnings, or code that only works in one build mode. Be wary of anyone who blames the compiler first, cannot describe a bug they tracked down, or optimizes without measuring.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about the hardest crash they fixed and how they found it. Ask how they would cut latency in a slow loop or fit code into tight memory on a device. Real answers name tools, measurements and trade-offs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a C++ developer?
qa.a: Look for solid modern C++, comfort with memory and performance, and shipped work in a field close to yours, such as games, trading or embedded devices. Check that they test their code, use debugging and profiling tools, and explain their choices clearly. No license is required, so judge real work over titles.

qa.q: How do I test a C++ developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task of a few hours: fix a memory bug in a small program, then speed up a slow function. Ask them to explain what they measured and why the change helped. Walking through code they wrote before also shows depth quickly.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for a portfolio of shipped work, not just concepts. For each piece, have them explain the brief, their exact role, who did the hands-on design, and what changed because of it. A director should show team output they shaped, not only their own craft.

look.label: Leadership to probe
look.text: Ask how they have hired, coached and reviewed designers or writers. Strong candidates describe giving clear feedback, killing weak ideas kindly, and growing junior staff. Ask about a time a team member disagreed and how the final decision got made.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They tie creative choices to business goals and can name results they tracked, such as sales or signups. They treat budgets, deadlines, brand guidelines and legal checks like trademark and image rights as part of the job, not as obstacles.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Taking sole credit for team work, a portfolio of only personal or spec pieces, vague answers about their role, or blaming clients for every failed project. Also watch for no clear approval process, which leads to inconsistent work going out.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or certification is required to be a creative director. Verify past titles and dates with references, ideally a former boss and someone who reported to them. Confirm they had permission to show client work, since some projects are under confidentiality agreements.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a creative and design director?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio of shipped work with a clear account of their role, proof they have led and grown a team, and the ability to link creative decisions to business goals. Check references from both a manager and someone who reported to them. Taste matters, but judgment and leadership matter more at this level.

qa.q: How do I test a creative and design director before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short paid exercise or a live session. Share a real brief and a few rough team drafts, then ask them to critique the work, pick a direction and explain the feedback they would give. You learn how they think, lead and decide. Keep it small and do not use their ideas without paying.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state or federal license is required for most credit analyst roles. A degree in finance, accounting or economics is common. Optional designations such as the Certified Credit and Risk Analyst or Credit Risk Certification show commitment. Verify any claimed credential directly with the issuing body.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for skill in spreading financial statements, figuring ratios like debt service coverage, leverage and liquidity, and analyzing cash flow. Strong spreadsheet skills matter. The candidate should also write a clear credit memo that states the risk, the mitigating factors and a firm recommendation.

look.label: Rules they should know
look.text: Good candidates understand the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and fair lending rules, the Fair Credit Reporting Act on using credit reports, and when adverse action notices are required. They should know to follow your written credit policy and document every exception.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong analysts look past the credit score. They ask about cash flow sources, collateral quality, industry trends and the borrower’s track record. They can explain the five Cs of credit with real examples and defend a decline as clearly as an approval.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of anyone who leans only on scores or software output, cannot explain how they reached a past decision, or makes math errors in ratios. Vague memos, ignoring policy limits, or suggesting factors unrelated to repayment ability are serious warning signs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a credit analyst?
qa.a: Look for solid financial statement and cash flow analysis, accurate ratio work, clear credit memo writing and knowledge of fair lending and credit reporting rules. No license is usually required, but optional credit designations and a finance or accounting background help. The best candidates explain their reasoning and follow your credit policy.

qa.q: How do I test a credit analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a sample loan request with two or three years of financial statements, with personal details removed. Ask the candidate to spread the numbers, calculate debt service coverage and leverage, flag the key risks and write a short memo with a recommendation and terms. Then have them walk you through their reasoning.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to build mobile apps, and no React Native or Flutter certification is commonly required. Verify work instead: apps live in both app stores, code samples, and references who confirm which features the candidate built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test React Native with TypeScript or Flutter with Dart, depending on your stack. Check navigation, state management, networking, offline storage, push notifications and native modules. Make sure they can build, sign and release to both app stores and debug with each platform’s native tools.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know where iPhone and Android differ, such as permissions, back navigation and background work, and handle both on purpose. They can write or fix a small native module when no plugin fits, and keep the app fast on older phones.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for apps that ignore each platform’s conventions, piles of unmaintained plugins and no tests. Be careful with candidates who have never released to both stores or cannot open the native project files when a build breaks.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a bug that appeared on only one platform and how you fixed it. When did you write native code instead of using a plugin? How do you handle framework upgrades? How do you find and fix a slow list? Strong answers are specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a cross-platform mobile developer?
qa.a: Look for apps they shipped to both stores using your framework, React Native or Flutter, with code they can explain. Check state management, performance, native module skills and release experience on both platforms. No license is required in the US, so live apps, code samples and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a cross-platform mobile developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task in your framework, such as a screen that loads a list from a sample API, works offline and shows errors clearly, with a few tests. Ask them to run it on both platforms. Review code structure, performance, handling of platform differences and how clearly they explain their choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a cryptographer. Many roles ask for a graduate degree in mathematics, computer science or a related field. Review their published papers, open source code and security proofs, and ask references which designs or reviews they personally did.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test their grasp of symmetric and public key cryptography, hash functions, signatures and key management, and of standard protocols such as TLS. Check secure coding against side channels, the ability to review a protocol for flaws, and knowledge of the NIST post-quantum standards.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates prefer proven, standard algorithms and well-reviewed libraries over custom designs. They explain threat models clearly, write constant-time code where needed, and welcome outside review. They can tell your engineers in plain words which choices are safe and why.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for anyone who designs their own cipher for production use, treats encoding or hashing as encryption, or dismisses peer review. Be careful with claims of unbreakable systems, outdated algorithm choices, or vague answers about key storage and rotation.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How would you store and rotate keys for this system? What can go wrong when a nonce repeats? How would you plan a move to post-quantum algorithms? Strong answers explain threat models, name standard primitives and admit open questions.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a cryptographer?
qa.a: Look for strong math and computer science training, published work or open source code you can review, and a habit of using standard, well-tested algorithms. Check they can find flaws in protocols and code, and explain risks plainly. No license is required, so peer-reviewed work and references matter more than titles.

qa.q: How do I test a cryptographer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid review task, such as a small protocol design or code sample with planted flaws like nonce reuse or weak key handling. Ask for a written report ranking each issue by risk with a fix. Review what they caught, their reasoning and how clearly engineers could act on it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for this role itself. Firms that hold customer crypto may need state money transmitter licenses, a state trust charter or New York’s BitLicense, so check how the candidate has worked under those rules. Security certifications like CISSP help but are optional. Background checks need written consent under federal law, and some states limit how you use them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for hands-on work with multisig and MPC wallets, hardware security modules, cold and warm storage, and transaction signing policies. Strong candidates can explain key generation ceremonies, backup and recovery, address allowlists, withdrawal approval quorums and how they would rotate keys after a suspected compromise.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They think in terms of threat models and separation of duties. They talk about no single person moving funds alone, logged and reviewed approvals, tested recovery drills and audit evidence such as SOC 2 controls. They can describe a past incident or near miss calmly and explain what they changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Storing seed phrases in cloud notes, email or screenshots. Being proud of holding keys alone. Vague answers about recovery if a signer is unavailable. Dismissing audits, logging or change control as slowing things down. Claiming any setup is unhackable instead of describing layered defenses.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they would design withdrawals for a mix of hot and cold storage. Ask what happens if one key holder leaves the company. Ask how they test a backup without exposing the key. Ask how they would detect and respond to an unauthorized transaction request.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a crypto custody and wallet specialist?
qa.a: Look for real experience securing private keys with multisig, MPC or hardware security modules, plus clear thinking about approvals, recovery and audits. They should insist that no one person can move funds alone. If your firm holds customer assets, they should understand that state licensing or trust rules may apply and that requirements vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test a crypto custody and wallet specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid design task. Ask them to plan a withdrawal flow for a small institution with hot and cold wallets, approval quorums, allowlists and a recovery plan for a lost signer. Then have them review a short signing service snippet for flaws. Never share real keys or production access during testing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Ask for case studies, customer videos, reference programs and customer newsletters they produced. Call references, ideally including a customer they worked with, and confirm they always got written approval before using a customer’s name, logo or quotes.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test interviewing a customer, turning the story into a clear case study, and running a reference program that sales can use without wearing customers out. Check upsell and renewal campaigns, review programs, community events and work with customer success teams.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates build trust with customers and make advocacy easy for them. They track which stories help close deals, rotate references fairly and work closely with customer success. Their case studies show real results in the customer’s own words.

look.label: Red flags
