look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a lesson or module you built, from objective to assessment. How did you know learners understood? Tell me about a lesson that failed and what you changed. How do you make a course work for a learner who uses a screen reader? Strong answers are specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a teacher or instructional designer?
qa.a: Look for teaching samples with clear objectives, practice and assessments that match, plus evidence that learners improved. A state license matters for public K-12 schools and varies by state, while online and corporate roles usually rely on portfolios. Check subject knowledge, accessibility habits and comfort with the tools your courses use.

qa.q: How do I test a teacher or instructional designer before hiring?
qa.a: Ask for a short, paid sample: a mini lesson on a topic from your course, or a module outline with one finished activity and a quiz. For live teaching, watch a short demo lesson. Review whether objectives are clear, practice comes before testing, examples fit your learners and the material is accessible.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for education program managers. Verify past programs with references and examples. If the program serves minors, check state rules on background checks, which vary. Teaching licenses and instructional design certificates help in some programs but are rarely required.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test program planning, budgets, scheduling and partner management, plus learning objectives and assessment design with instructional designers. Check learning platform administration, accessibility, outcome reporting, and privacy rules for student records and for online services aimed at children under thirteen.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong managers measure what learners can do afterward, not just attendance or completion. They use feedback to change content, keep partners and instructors aligned, deliver on time and on budget, and make materials accessible to every learner from the start.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for reporting only sign-ups and completions, no budget ownership, or programs that depend on one instructor’s heroics. Be wary of anyone casual about learner data, accessibility or safeguarding when programs involve children.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a program the data showed was not working and what you changed. How do you measure learning, not just attendance? How do you keep a partner on schedule? Strong answers name metrics, decisions and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an education program manager?
qa.a: Look for experience running learning programs end to end, from content and partners to budgets, schedules and outcome reporting. Check they measure real learning, design for accessibility and protect learner data. No license is usually required, so references, program examples and results matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an education program manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case: describe a program with low completion and mixed feedback, and ask for a diagnosis, a revised plan, a simple budget and the measures they would track. Review whether they use evidence, set clear goals and plan realistic timelines with partners.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No single license covers EHS work, but certifications such as Certified Safety Professional and Certified Industrial Hygienist are respected and can be verified. Some states license asbestos, lead or other specialized work. OSHA outreach training cards show training, not a license.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test hazard assessments, lockout and tagout, confined spaces, hazard communication, OSHA injury and illness recordkeeping and root cause investigation. Check environmental work such as air and water permits, hazardous waste rules and spill plans. Some states run OSHA-approved plans with their own rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates spend time on the floor, train workers in plain language, investigate near misses as well as injuries and fix root causes instead of blaming people. They keep permits, logs and inspection records current and work well with operations managers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for blaming workers for every incident, discouraging injury reports, paperwork without floor presence, and confusion about which injuries must be recorded or reported to OSHA. Be careful with anyone vague about permits or past citations at their sites.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through an incident investigation you led and the fix that followed. How do you decide if an injury is recordable? How would you prepare for an OSHA inspection or an environmental audit? Strong answers cite real rules and specific actions.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an EHS specialist?
qa.a: Look for strong knowledge of OSHA and environmental rules, hands-on inspection and training experience, and investigations that fixed root causes. Certifications such as Certified Safety Professional help, and some states license specialized work or run their own safety plans, so rules vary. References from operations leaders show how they work on the floor.

qa.q: How do I test an EHS specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: a walk-through of a workplace using photos or video, asking them to list hazards, rank risks and propose fixes. Add a sample injury case and ask whether it is recordable. Review accuracy, priorities, knowledge of the rules and how clearly they would train workers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Only a licensed Professional Engineer (PE) can seal drawings, which many permits and public projects require. Each state board issues its own license, so check it in the project’s state through the board’s online lookup. An EIT or EI title means the person passed the FE exam but is not yet licensed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Match the test to your work. Power roles need load, voltage drop, short circuit and arc flash studies. Electronics roles need schematics, board layout and circuit simulation. Battery roles need cell selection, thermal limits and battery management. Radio roles need impedance matching, antennas, link budgets and FCC equipment authorization rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain the trade-offs behind past designs and state their assumptions. They know that states and cities adopt different editions of the National Electrical Code. They bring real drawings or test reports with client details removed. They describe how they tested hardware, not just how they drew it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a claimed PE license that does not show up on the state lookup. Be wary of anyone who offers to seal work they did not design or directly supervise, since state rules forbid it. Vague answers about testing, code checks or failures they caused also signal thin experience.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a design that failed testing and what they changed. Ask how they size a feeder and its overcurrent protection. For product roles, ask how they prepared a radio device for FCC authorization or kept a battery pack from overheating.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an electrical engineer?
qa.a: Look for experience in your exact area, such as power distribution, circuit boards, batteries or radio. If they must seal drawings, confirm an active PE license in your project’s state through the state board. Ask for sample drawings or test reports. Strong candidates explain their design choices, know which code edition applies locally and show how they tested their work.

qa.q: How do I test an electrical engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task that matches the job. A power engineer might size a feeder and breaker for a given load and check voltage drop. An electronics engineer might review a schematic and find errors. A radio engineer might work out a simple link budget. Then ask them to walk you through their reasoning and assumptions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Ask whether the candidate holds IPC J-STD-001 or IPC-A-610 certification for soldering and workmanship, or IPC/WHMA-A-620 for cable and harness work. These are industry certifications, not state licenses, and they expire, so check the date. Bench assembly rarely needs a state electrician license. Building wiring usually does, and those rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them solder through-hole and surface-mount parts, strip and crimp wire to a drawing, and find a planted fault with a multimeter. Watch how they handle tools and whether they follow the schematic and parts list without guessing.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They put on a wrist strap and use a grounded mat without being told. They inspect their own joints under magnification and label wires as they go. They can explain what a cold joint or solder bridge looks like and how to fix it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Too much heat that lifts pads, probing live circuits without a plan, ignoring static precautions, or calling a board done without testing it. Vague answers about which instruments they used and what they measured suggest little real bench time.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through the last assembly that failed test and how they traced the cause. Ask how they rework a fine-pitch part, which workmanship class they built to, and how they record changes on a work order.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an electrical and electronics technician?
qa.a: Look for clean, consistent soldering, comfort reading schematics and wiring drawings, and steady use of a multimeter and oscilloscope. Good static control habits and careful documentation matter too. IPC soldering or harness certification is a plus but not legally required. A state electrician license only matters if the job includes building wiring, and those rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test an electrical and electronics technician before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid bench task that matches the job. Ask them to solder a few through-hole and surface-mount parts, build a small harness from a drawing, and find a fault you planted in a working board. Then inspect the joints under magnification and ask them to explain each step they took.

look.label: License to verify
look.text: Most states license electricians at the journeyman and master levels, but a few leave licensing to cities or counties, and many require apprentices to register. Check the license on your state or local board’s lookup tool and confirm it covers your type of work, such as residential, commercial or industrial.

look.label: Code and safety knowledge
look.text: A strong electrician works to the edition of the National Electrical Code your area has adopted, which differs by state and city. Ask how they handle lockout/tagout, testing for absence of voltage, arc flash protection under NFPA 70E, and permits and inspections.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them read a wiring diagram or panel schedule, size a conductor and breaker for a given load, and trace a fault with a multimeter. For industrial roles, add motor controls, PLC basics or three-phase work. Watch whether they confirm a circuit is dead before touching it.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a hard troubleshooting job: what failed, how they found it and how they proved the fix. Ask about a time their work failed inspection and what they changed. Real answers name specific devices, readings and steps, not general claims.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for offers to skip permits or inspections, a license that is expired or covers a different type of work, and vague answers about past jobs. Be wary of anyone who works on live circuits without a clear reason and proper protective gear.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an electrician?
qa.a: Start with a valid license at the right level for your state or city, since rules vary. Then look for solid knowledge of the locally adopted electrical code, safe habits like lockout/tagout, strong troubleshooting skills, and references from similar residential, commercial or industrial jobs.

qa.q: How do I test an electrician before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short hands-on task on a de-energized training board or mockup. Ask them to wire a three-way switch circuit, read a schematic, or find a planted fault with a meter. Watch whether they test for voltage first, follow code, and explain each step clearly.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test C and C++ written for tight memory and timing limits. Check that they can read a chip datasheet, handle interrupts, and explain common buses like I2C, SPI, UART and CAN. Ask about real-time operating systems and bare-metal code.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have debugged real boards with an oscilloscope, logic analyzer or JTAG debugger. They talk about power budgets, timing and flash space without being asked. They can describe a product they helped ship and what broke in the field.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most embedded roles need no state license. A degree in electrical or computer engineering is common but not required. For safety-critical work, confirm hands-on experience with standards such as ISO 26262 for cars, IEC 62304 for medical devices or DO-178C for aircraft.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who has only worked in simulators, cannot explain the volatile keyword or a watchdog timer, or blames the hardware without proof. Skipping version control, code review or testing on target hardware is also a warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about the hardest bug they traced to hardware and how they found it. Ask how they fit a feature into limited RAM or flash. Ask how they would update firmware in the field without bricking a device.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an embedded engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid C or C++ skills, comfort reading datasheets, and real time spent debugging physical hardware. Good candidates understand interrupts, memory limits, power use and common buses. If your product is safety-critical, look for experience with the standard your industry follows. A shipped product they can explain in detail matters more than a long list of tools.

qa.q: How do I test an embedded engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task on a cheap development board, or a code review of a small driver with planted bugs. Ask them to talk through timing, memory use and failure cases. Watch how they use a debugger or read a datasheet. Keep it under a few hours and focus on reasoning, not trivia.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for this role. Some candidates hold general HR certifications such as SHRM-CP or PHR. These are helpful but optional. Verify past titles, program scope and results with references instead.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test survey design, reading engagement data and turning findings into a short action plan. Check how they plan an onboarding flow for a new hire’s first 90 days. Look for clear writing, budgeting for events and steady coordination with HR, IT and facilities.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates tie programs to results like faster ramp-up, better survey scores or lower early turnover. They protect survey anonymity and plan events that people with disabilities and remote staff can join. They ask employees what they want before launching anything.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who measures success only by event attendance or perks. Be wary of anyone who would share individual survey answers with managers. Vague claims about culture with no examples, metrics or follow-through on feedback are another warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a survey result that surprised them and what changed afterward. Ask how they rebuilt an onboarding program and how they knew it worked. Ask how they handled a program with low participation or a tight budget.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an employee experience manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they improved onboarding, engagement or retention, not just ran events. They should design fair surveys, keep responses confidential and act on results. Good candidates write clearly, manage budgets and work well with HR, IT and facilities. HR certifications can help but are not required by any state.

qa.q: How do I test an employee experience manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or clearly scoped task. Share sample survey results with no real employee data and ask for the top three findings and a 90-day action plan. You can also ask for a first-week onboarding outline for a new hire. Judge their priorities, clarity and how they would measure success.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for employee relations work, though some specialists are lawyers or hold HR certifications. If the candidate is a lawyer, check bar status. Otherwise verify through references and redacted investigation reports, and ask which investigations they led from intake to closure.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test planning and running workplace investigations, interviewing, weighing evidence and credibility, and writing neutral findings. Check knowledge of discrimination, harassment and retaliation laws, accommodation duties, and employees’ federal right to discuss pay and working conditions, plus state laws, which vary.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong specialists stay neutral, act promptly and document every step. They explain decisions to managers in plain words, apply policies consistently and guard against retaliation. They know when to bring in counsel or an outside investigator and share information only on a need-to-know basis.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who decide outcomes before interviewing, promise complainants total confidentiality, or write reports full of opinion. Be wary of anyone who would discipline an employee soon after a complaint without weighing retaliation risk, or who shares case details casually.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through an investigation from complaint to findings. How do you handle conflicting accounts with no witnesses? What do you tell a complainant about confidentiality? Strong answers describe planning, neutral questions, evidence standards and careful documentation.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an employee relations specialist?
qa.a: Look for experience running fair, prompt investigations, neutral report writing and sound knowledge of discrimination, harassment, retaliation and labor law. Check they apply policies consistently and know when to involve counsel. No license is required, so redacted reports, references and how they explain past cases matter most. State laws vary.

qa.q: How do I test an employee relations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case: a written complaint, two conflicting witness statements and a policy. Ask for an investigation plan, interview questions and a brief findings memo. Review neutrality, logic, the evidence standard used, documentation and whether they address retaliation and confidentiality limits correctly.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an active law license in good standing with the state bar, and check its public discipline records. Rules for in-house lawyers vary by state; some let them register without local admission. A few states offer board certification in labor and employment law, which is a plus but not required.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for issue spotting across federal, state and local rules, such as Title VII, the ADA, the FLSA and FMLA, plus state leave, pay and noncompete laws. They should draft clear offer letters, agreements and policies, and explain legal risk to managers in plain words.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have handled terminations, workplace investigations and agency charges from start to finish. For staff abroad, they know at-will employment is rare outside the US, plan for notice periods and works councils, and know when to bring in local counsel instead of guessing.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of someone who treats every state or country the same, gives firm answers before asking for facts, or claims expertise in foreign law they are not qualified in. Sharing a former client’s confidential details during interviews is also a serious warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they would handle a manager who wants to fire someone a week after a harassment complaint. Ask how they would end a contract for an employee in another country. Good answers mention retaliation risk, documentation, local law and who else they would involve.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an employment lawyer?
qa.a: Check for an active bar license in good standing and a clean discipline record. Look for real experience with hiring, contracts, terminations, investigations and discrimination claims. If you have staff in other countries, choose someone who knows the limits of US law abroad and works well with local counsel. Clear, practical advice for managers matters as much as legal knowledge.

qa.q: How do I test an employment lawyer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short written scenario, such as a planned firing after an employee complaint, and ask for a brief memo on risks and next steps. You can also ask them to mark up a sample offer letter with planted errors. Use made-up facts, never real confidential data, and keep the task short or pay for it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work in the US. Vendor certifications for the device management platform you run, or general IT security certifications, show study. Confirm any certificate on the issuer’s verification page, and weigh hands-on results more than paper.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Automated zero-touch enrollment, configuration and compliance policies, app and OS update deployment, disk encryption and passcode rules, and remote lock and wipe. Add scripting in PowerShell, shell or Python. They should handle both company-owned laptops and staff phones.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They test changes on a small pilot group before rolling out to everyone. They store encryption recovery keys safely and write down every policy. They judge their own work by how fast a new hire is productive on day one.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Pushing changes to every device at once with no testing or rollback plan. Setting up each laptop by hand instead of automating it. Vague answers about lost or stolen devices, or about wiping a personal phone without erasing the owner’s own data.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they recovered from an update that broke devices. Ask how they keep work and personal data apart on a bring-your-own phone. Ask how they retire a device when someone leaves. Listen for clear steps, not just tool names.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an endpoint and device management engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with automated enrollment, security policies, app and update rollouts, and remote wipe across laptops and phones. Good candidates test changes on a pilot group first, script repeat tasks and document their setup. No US license is required, so check real results and verify any vendor certificate they list.

qa.q: How do I test an endpoint and device management engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task in a test environment, never your live systems. Ask them to enroll a test laptop and phone, require encryption and a passcode, deploy one app and write a brief rollback plan. Then have them walk you through each choice and what they would do if a device fell out of compliance.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for engagement managers. Project management certifications help but are optional. Verify the engagements they ran, including scope, team size and type of client. Call client and team references to hear how they handled scope changes, budget pressure and difficult conversations.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test scoping a project and writing a statement of work, staffing a team, tracking budget and hours, and managing changes through formal change requests. Check client communication, status reporting, and how they handle an unhappy client without giving away free work.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates protect both the client relationship and the firm’s margin. They spot scope creep early, document changes, and keep the team focused. Clients come back to them for more work, and their teams want to work with them again.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who say yes to every client request without a change order, hide problems until they explode, or burn out their teams. Be careful with anyone who cannot describe a project’s budget or how they handled a client escalation.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a client who wanted more than the contract covered and how you handled it. How do you track project health each week? Tell me about an engagement you saved. Strong answers name actions, tradeoffs and the result.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an engagement manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of running client projects that finished on scope, on time and on budget, with clients who came back. Check scoping, change control, budget tracking and calm client communication. No license is required, so client and team references and real engagement results matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an engagement manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid scenario: a client asks for extra features midway through a fixed-scope project and is unhappy with progress. Ask them to draft a reply to the client and a change request, and explain their next steps. Review tone, firmness, commercial sense and clarity.

look.label: Enrollment to confirm
look.text: If your program requires it, confirm the candidate is enrolled in an engineering or related degree program and will still be a student during the internship term. A school email or unofficial transcript is usually enough. No engineering license is expected at this stage.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the basics their major should cover. Examples include reading a drawing or schematic, writing a short script, working a units problem, or using a CAD or spreadsheet tool your team relies on. Ask them to explain each step aloud so you see how they reason.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for hands-on work outside class, such as a design team, senior project, lab job or personal build. Strong candidates can say what they did themselves, what failed and what they would change. They ask clear questions and take feedback without getting defensive.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague claims about team projects with no personal role, no curiosity about your products, or skipping safety steps when describing lab or shop work. Be careful with candidates who will not admit what they do not know, since interns learn through guidance from engineers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a project where something did not work and how they found the cause. Ask what tool or method they learned on their own, and how they split work with teammates. Concrete details beat polished but general answers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an engineering intern?
qa.a: Look for solid course basics in the right discipline, hands-on project or lab experience, and clear communication. Grades matter less than how a student reasons through a problem and responds to feedback. Confirm enrollment and work authorization the same way for every candidate. No engineering license is needed for an intern.

qa.q: How do I test an engineering intern before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic task that fits their year in school, such as a calculation, a simple design sketch, a debugging exercise or a data cleanup. Keep it under an hour. Have them explain their approach aloud. Judge reasoning and clarity rather than speed, and use the same task for every candidate.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to manage software engineers. Check past titles, team sizes and dates with references. If the team designs public works or structures, the person who seals drawings needs a Professional Engineer license, issued by each state, so confirm it with that state’s board.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the core of the job: a role-played one-on-one with a struggling engineer, turning a vague goal into a quarter plan, and reviewing a hiring packet to make a fair yes or no call. Add a light technical talk so they can judge design trade-offs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a time they handled an underperformer, a project that slipped, and someone they helped get promoted. Ask how they run one-on-ones and how they say no to stakeholders. Strong answers name what they did, what changed and what they would redo.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about team results, not their own code. They can name people they grew and hires they made. They give credit freely, own mistakes, explain trade-offs in plain words and show a steady habit for planning, feedback and clear priorities.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Blaming past teams or bosses, taking credit for group work, no example of giving hard feedback, vague answers about hiring, or wanting to keep writing most of the code. Also watch for anyone who measures people only by hours or lines of code.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an engineering manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they have led people, not just projects. Good signs are engineers they hired and grew, plans they delivered, and honest stories about hard feedback. They should be technical enough to judge trade-offs and clear enough to explain them to non-engineers. Check references from people who reported to them, not only from their bosses.

qa.q: How do I test an engineering manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or unpaid case they can finish in a few hours. Have them role-play a one-on-one with a struggling engineer, draft a simple quarter plan from a vague goal, and review a sample interview packet. Score each part against your scorecard. Ask them to talk through their choices so you see how they reason.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They have closed large deals with long sales cycles and many buyers. They can name who signed, who blocked, and how procurement, legal and security review shaped the deal. They talk about their numbers clearly and explain both wins and losses.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test deep discovery, mapping a buying committee, finding an executive sponsor, and building a mutual action plan with dates. Also test forecasting judgment and how they hold value when procurement pushes hard on price and terms.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through their largest deal from first meeting to signature. Ask who the economic buyer was, what nearly killed the deal, and how they forecast it each quarter. Real experience shows up in specific names, steps and setbacks.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague numbers, credit taken for team wins, and stories built only on short, single-buyer deals. Be careful if they blame marketing, product or legal for every loss, or cannot explain why a deal slipped.

look.label: Things to verify
look.text: Confirm quota attainment and deal sizes through references from former managers. Many states and cities limit asking about past pay, so do not rely on pay history. Ask about any noncompete or nonsolicit agreement; enforceability varies by state.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an enterprise account executive?
qa.a: Look for a record of closing large, complex deals with long cycles and many decision makers. Strong candidates explain how they found the economic buyer, handled procurement and legal review, and forecast accurately. Check their claims through references from former managers, and favor people who discuss losses honestly.

qa.q: How do I test an enterprise account executive before hiring?
qa.a: Run a mock discovery call where a leader plays a skeptical executive buyer. Then ask for a short deal plan for a sample account, including stakeholders, risks and a mutual action plan with dates. Finally, review a sample pipeline together and ask which deals they would commit and why.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for enterprise architects. Architecture framework certifications, such as TOGAF, and cloud architect certifications show training but are optional. Verify them with the issuer, and ask references which architecture decisions the candidate owned and how those decisions held up over time.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they map business capabilities, applications, data and integrations, then plan a target state with a realistic roadmap. Check they can compare options on cost, risk and fit, write decision records, and explain the plan to both executives and engineers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates tie every diagram to a business goal, such as faster order processing or fewer duplicate systems. They retire systems, not just add them, and work with engineering teams instead of issuing rules from above. Their roadmaps show dependencies, costs and phases.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who show large diagrams but cannot name a decision that changed because of them. Be careful with anyone who pushes one vendor for every problem, ignores data ownership and security, or has never seen a roadmap through to systems actually retired.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about two overlapping systems you consolidated and what it took. How do you decide whether to build, buy or keep a system? How do you get teams to follow standards? Strong answers name tradeoffs, costs and what happened afterward.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an enterprise architect?
qa.a: Look for someone who has mapped a complex company’s systems and led real changes, such as consolidating platforms or moving to the cloud. Check they connect technology choices to business goals and explain tradeoffs clearly. No license is required, so framework certificates are a bonus; references and retired systems matter more.

qa.q: How do I test an enterprise architect before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case study: a simplified list of your systems, owners and pain points. Ask for a current state map, a target state and a phased roadmap with risks. Review whether they ask good questions, make clear tradeoffs, and present it so both leaders and engineers follow.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: If the hire will seal designs or reports, confirm a Professional Engineer (PE) license on the state board’s online lookup. Licenses are issued by each state. Some states also license geologists, which may matter for site work. Field staff on hazardous waste sites need 40-hour HAZWOPER training and a current annual 8-hour refresher.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them read a sample lab report and flag results above regulatory limits. Ask them to outline a stormwater or wastewater discharge permit application. Check that they can explain sampling plans, chain of custody and quality control, and write a clear summary a non-engineer can follow.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They name the specific federal and state rules that applied on past projects, such as Clean Water Act or Clean Air Act permits. They describe their own role and outcomes plainly. They show work samples with client details removed and mention dealing with regulators directly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about who actually signed or wrote a report. Claiming a license that does not show on the state lookup. Treating permit deadlines or sampling procedures as loose. Suggesting ways to avoid reporting a spill, an exceedance or a permit violation.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a site assessment from records review to final report. Ask what they did when sample results came back over a limit. Ask how they handled a permit renewal or an agency inspection, and what they would do differently.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an environmental engineer and scientist?
qa.a: Match the hire to your work. For sealed designs, look for a PE license valid in your state. For hazardous site work, require current HAZWOPER training. Then look for hands-on experience with the permits, studies or clean-up methods your project needs, clear technical writing, and comfort working with regulators.

qa.q: How do I test an environmental engineer and scientist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task based on your real work, with client details removed. For example, have them review lab data and summarize which results exceed limits, or draft a section of a permit application. Judge accuracy, the rules they cite, and how clearly they explain next steps.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for ERP work. Vendor certifications, such as NetSuite Administrator, NetSuite SuiteFoundation or Oracle Cloud ERP implementation credentials, are optional but show real study. Ask for the credential ID or verification link, and weigh hands-on system work more heavily than any badge.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can build saved searches and reports, set up roles and permissions, create workflows, and run clean CSV imports. For technical roles, test scripting such as SuiteScript or PL/SQL and integrations with other tools. Confirm they can explain order-to-cash, procure-to-pay and month-end close steps.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know basic accounting, like debits, credits and inventory costing, not just menus. They test changes in a sandbox before production, write down what they changed and why, and ask finance and warehouse staff how they actually work before building anything.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with someone who edits production directly without testing, hands out full admin access freely, or can’t separate what they built from what an outside consultant did. Vague answers about data cleanup, backups or audit trails are also warning signs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a month-end close problem they fixed. Ask how they handled a failed data import or a twice-yearly release that broke a workflow. Ask which reports they built that leaders used every week, and why.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an ERP specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience in your system, such as NetSuite or Oracle, plus a working grasp of accounting, orders and inventory. Good candidates manage roles and permissions carefully, test changes in a sandbox and document their work. Vendor certifications help but are optional, and no state license is required.

qa.q: How do I test an ERP specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task in a sandbox or demo account. Ask them to build a saved search or report, fix a broken workflow, or plan a data import with sample records. Then have them explain each step, what could go wrong, and how they would check the numbers with finance.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test calm de-escalation on a live call and a clear written complaint reply. Check that they can turn a messy case history into facts, a timeline and a plan. See whether they know what they can offer within policy and what needs a manager’s approval.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through one complaint they owned from start to close. What did the customer want? What did the records show? Who did they pull in? What did they offer, and how did they confirm the fix held? Vague answers suggest they only passed cases along.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They stay steady under abuse without sounding cold. Their case notes are clear enough for a stranger to follow. They own follow-ups by date and look for root causes. They report repeat problems back to the team, and they can say no while still offering a path forward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for stories that blame customers or coworkers every time. Be wary of promises of refunds or outcomes they had no authority to give. Other warning signs are sloppy or missing notes, defensiveness when questioned, treating fast closure as the only goal, and sharing private customer details as anecdotes.

look.label: Rules in regulated fields
look.text: No license is required for this role in general. In banking, insurance, healthcare or telecom, complaint handling may fall under federal or state rules on record keeping, response times and privacy. These rules vary by industry and state, so ask what rules they have worked under before.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an escalations and complaints specialist?
qa.a: Look for someone who stays calm with upset customers and writes clearly. They should keep careful case notes and follow cases through to a real fix. Ask for specific examples of complaints they owned from start to close. Strong candidates explain the root cause, what they offered within policy, and how they confirmed the customer was satisfied.

qa.q: How do I test an escalations and complaints specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role-play with an angry customer whose problem has no easy answer. Then give them a sample case file and ask for a written reply and an internal summary. Check their tone and accuracy, and see whether they stay within policy. Also look at whether they set clear next steps with dates.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is needed to work as a cost estimator. Optional certifications from estimating and cost engineering associations show study of methods. Verify past work instead: ask for sample estimates with prices removed, bid results and references from project managers who used their numbers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test quantity takeoff from drawings and specifications, unit pricing, labor productivity and subcontractor bid leveling. For project controls, check critical path scheduling, earned value, change order pricing and cost reports. Check the estimating and scheduling software and spreadsheets your team uses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write down every assumption, exclusion and allowance. They compare final costs to their estimates and learn from the gaps. They spot scope missing from drawings, ask subcontractors sharp questions and explain contingency clearly to owners and managers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for estimates built only from old totals without checking current scope, no written assumptions, or hidden padding. In project controls, beware of anyone who adjusts schedules to look good, cannot explain earned value or ignores change orders until the end.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How close was your last estimate to the final cost, and why? How do you level three subcontractor bids with different scopes? How do you show a project is slipping before a deadline is missed? Their method matters more than any single number.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a cost estimator?
qa.a: Look for accurate takeoffs, written assumptions and clear bid leveling, plus experience in your trade or project type. For project controls, look for scheduling and earned value skills. No license is required, so sample estimates, bid history and references from project managers matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a cost estimator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid takeoff from a small set of drawings, or ask them to level sample subcontractor bids and flag scope gaps. For project controls, share a mock schedule and cost report and ask what is going wrong. Review accuracy, assumptions and how clearly they explain risk.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Installers need a state or local electrical license, and rules vary by state. Some states and federally funded projects require an EV charger installer certification or registered apprenticeship training. Check licenses on the state board site. Designers may need a PE license to seal plans, depending on the job.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test load calculations, conductor and breaker sizing, grounding and the electrical code article on EV charging. Check Level 2 and DC fast charger commissioning, network setup, open charging protocols and troubleshooting failed sessions. Ask about utility service requests, permits and accessible parking layouts.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates pull permits, pass inspections the first time and leave labeled, documented installs. They know load management for sites where the panel is short on capacity. They keep chargers online, read error logs and work well with utilities, inspectors and charger makers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for installers who skip permits, oversize breakers to stop nuisance trips, or ignore load calculations. Be careful with anyone who cannot explain ground faults, has no experience with networked chargers, or blames every outage on the charger maker without testing.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: The panel cannot support four new chargers. What are your options? How do you troubleshoot a charger that starts a session and then stops? Walk me through commissioning a DC fast charger. Strong answers mention testing, code and records.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an EV charging specialist?
qa.a: Look for a valid electrical license where your state requires one, EV charger training, and experience with the charger types you use. Check load calculation and permitting skills, plus networking and troubleshooting ability for chargers already in service. References from site owners and inspectors show quality.

qa.q: How do I test an EV charging specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid task such as a load calculation and charger layout for a sample parking lot, or a supervised troubleshooting session on a faulty charger. Ask them to explain each step. Review code compliance, safety habits, accuracy and clear notes for the owner.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No US state requires a license to plan events. Some managers hold the voluntary Certified Meeting Professional (CMP) credential, which requires work experience and a passed exam. Treat it as a plus, not a must, and confirm it with the issuing body.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for budget building and tracking, venue and vendor contract review, run-of-show scheduling, and registration tools. For trade shows, check they know exhibitor manuals, booth shipping deadlines, drayage, and the labor rules some convention centers enforce.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They bring past timelines, budgets or run sheets with private details removed. They can explain attrition and cancellation clauses in hotel contracts. They talk in numbers like headcount, cost per attendee and leads captured, and describe a day something broke and how they fixed it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about budgets they owned. Blaming vendors for every problem. Never having read a venue contract. No backup plans for no-show speakers, bad weather or failed tech. Not knowing what they measured after an event ended.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through the timeline for a 300-person conference from booking to wrap-up. Ask which hotel contract clauses they negotiate first, how they handle attendee accessibility requests, and what goes on their trade-show shipping checklist.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an events manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they have owned events from start to finish. That means budgets, contracts, vendor schedules and on-site staff. Ask for sample run sheets or timelines. Check they can read venue contracts and plan for things going wrong. A CMP credential is a plus, but no state license is required.

qa.q: How do I test an events manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Ask for a plan for a small meetup with a fixed budget, a venue shortlist, a timeline and a run of show. Add a live scenario, such as a keynote speaker canceling two hours before start. You can also hand them a sample venue contract and ask them to flag the risks.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Individuals need no license, but US exchanges must register with FinCEN as money services businesses and usually hold state money transmitter licenses; New York has its own virtual currency license. Rules are changing, so check current guidance. Anti-money laundering certifications are optional. Verify past roles with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test deposit and withdrawal handling, including confirmations, stuck transactions and wrong-network deposits, plus wallet reconciliation and hot and cold wallet procedures. Check token listing due diligence, trade surveillance for wash trading and spoofing, customer identity checks, sanctions screening and suspicious activity escalation.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates follow written runbooks, double-check addresses and amounts, and treat every incident as a chance to improve controls. They understand blockchain basics across several networks, keep clear audit trails and escalate suspicious activity quickly instead of fixing it quietly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for casual handling of private keys or approvals, shortcuts around identity checks, treating token listings as pure marketing, or trading on knowledge of upcoming listings. Be wary of anyone who cannot describe a past incident and what changed afterward.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A customer sent tokens on the wrong network. Walk me through what you do. How would you spot wash trading in a new market? What checks do you run before listing a token? Strong answers name steps, tools, approvals and records.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a crypto exchange operations specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with deposits, withdrawals, wallets and reconciliation, plus knowledge of token listing reviews, trade surveillance and anti-money laundering rules. Check strict security habits and clear incident records. Individuals need no license, but your exchange’s federal and state obligations shape the job. References and scenario answers matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a crypto exchange operations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case with mock data: a withdrawal queue with one suspicious request, a reconciliation gap and a token listing request. Ask how they would handle each, who they would escalate to and what records they would keep. Review security, accuracy, compliance knowledge and calm judgment.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No license is required to work as an executive assistant in the US. Optional administrative certifications exist and show commitment, but a track record matters more. If the role includes notarizing documents, notary commissions are issued by each state, and the rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test calendar management across time zones, booking travel within a budget or policy, and drafting clear, polite emails. Check spreadsheet and document formatting skills. Ask them to use the scheduling, video meeting and file-sharing tools your team already relies on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong assistants anticipate needs before being asked. They confirm details, keep a written record of decisions and follow up without reminders. They speak about past executives with discretion. They give concrete examples of handling a crowded calendar, a last-minute trip change or a tight deadline.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for typos or sloppy formatting in the application, since written work is central to this job. Be wary of anyone who shares confidential details about a former boss. Vague answers about daily tasks, or missed details when you scheduled the interview, are also warning signs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a day when their executive was double-booked. Ask about a trip that went wrong and what they did next. Ask how they decide which requests reach the executive and which they handle themselves. Real experience shows in specific, step-by-step answers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an administrative and executive assistant?
qa.a: Look for strong organization, clear writing and sound judgment about what is urgent. They should handle confidential information with discretion and stay calm when plans change. No license is required, so focus on proven experience with calendars, travel and documents, and on how well they know the tools your team uses. References from past managers help confirm reliability.

qa.q: How do I test an administrative and executive assistant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic task. For example, share a messy week of meeting requests across time zones and ask them to build a clean calendar, flag conflicts and draft one email declining a meeting politely. You could add a simple travel plan within a budget. Judge accuracy, clarity and the questions they ask.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No federal license is needed to recruit. Some states and cities regulate employment or placement agencies, so check local rules if you hire an outside firm. Voluntary recruiter certifications exist, but a confirmed record of filled senior roles and solid references matter more.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for sourcing of passive candidates, sharp outreach writing, structured interviewing of leaders, and offer negotiation. They should also know hiring rules that vary by state and city, such as salary history bans, pay transparency laws and fair chance rules on background checks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They name specific roles they filled, how long searches took and how long hires stayed. They explain their search process step by step. They speak the language of the teams they serve, like sales quotas, finance controls or legal practice areas.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about past placements. Bragging about a huge network without explaining how they source. Sharing confidential details about past clients or candidates. Any hint of screening people on age, family plans or other protected traits, or using “culture fit” as a cover for bias.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a senior search that nearly failed and how they saved it. Ask how they built a diverse, qualified slate for a finance leader. Ask how they handle a top finalist who gets a counteroffer.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an executive and business recruiter?
qa.a: Look for a proven record of filling senior and business roles you can confirm with references. Strong recruiters source passive candidates, assess leaders with structured interviews and close offers well. They know state and local hiring rules, protect confidential information and understand the sales, finance or legal teams they hire for.

qa.q: How do I test an executive and business recruiter before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a real or sample job brief, such as a sales director role. Ask for a search plan, a short outreach message to a passive candidate and three interview questions. Then role play a finalist weighing a counteroffer. Judge their clarity, judgment and how well they respect confidentiality and fair hiring rules.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this work. Course certificates in statistics or testing tools vary widely in rigor. Ask for anonymized test write-ups that show the hypothesis, the planned sample size, the result and the decision, and check references from past teams.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can set a sample size and test length from a power calculation, pick one primary metric before launch, read confidence intervals, and pull and check the data themselves using SQL or a tool like Python or R.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk openly about flat or losing tests. They explain why a win might not last, such as novelty effects, seasonality or users in both groups. They check for sample ratio mismatch before trusting any number and write the plan down first.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Stopping a test the moment it looks significant. Slicing the data by segment until something wins. Calling a before-and-after comparison proof of cause. Sharing only wins, or not being able to say what would make them doubt a result.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Your 50/50 split came back 53/47. What do you do?” Ask: “When would you not run an A/B test?” Ask: “Tell me about a result you later found was wrong.” Strong answers are concrete and calm about uncertainty.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an experimentation specialist?
qa.a: Look for someone who plans tests before launch, sets sample size with a power calculation, and picks one main metric up front. They should catch broken splits, avoid stopping tests early, and admit when results are unclear. No license is required in the US, so judge them on past test write-ups, a practical exercise and references.

qa.q: How do I test an experimentation specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a small anonymized dataset from a past test with a planted problem, such as an uneven traffic split or a metric that changed mid-test. Ask them to decide whether the change worked and explain why. Then ask them to plan a new test: hypothesis, metric, sample size and how long to run it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No general state license covers fabrication work. If the job includes welding, ask for welder qualification records that list the process, position and code, such as a structural steel code. Some cities and states require certified welders for structural or building work, so check your local rules.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading shop drawings and weld symbols, layout and measuring with tape, square and calipers, and setting up shears, saws or a press brake. Check that fit-up holds tolerance and that finished edges are deburred and clean.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates measure twice before cutting, account for kerf and bend allowance, and tack parts in a planned order to control warping. They can explain how they caught or fixed an out-of-tolerance part and keep a clean, organized station.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for skipped safety glasses, gloves or hearing protection, guards left off machines, or no clear way to read a drawing. Be wary of resumes that only list machines without describing parts built, and of people who blame others for scrap.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a part they built from a drawing. Ask how they figure a bend allowance, how they keep a weldment square and flat, and what tolerances their last shop held.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fabrication technician?
qa.a: Look for someone who reads shop drawings accurately, measures carefully and runs your cutting, bending and joining equipment safely. If the role includes welding, ask for qualification records showing the process and position. Some cities and states require certified welders for structural work, so check local rules. Steady habits and clean finished parts matter as much as speed.

qa.q: How do I test a fabrication technician before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task using your own equipment. Hand them a simple drawing and ask them to lay out, cut, bend and join a small part. Then check the dimensions, squareness and finish against the drawing. Watch their safety habits, how they plan the steps and whether they check their work before handing it in.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state licenses facilities managers as a role. Credentials such as Certified Facility Manager or Facility Management Professional are optional but verifiable. Trade work they oversee, such as electrical, HVAC or boiler operation, may need licensed people, and those rules vary by state and city.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they plan preventive maintenance in a computerized maintenance management system, scope and compare contractor bids, read utility bills to find energy waste, and plan a move or fit-out. Check they know OSHA basics, fire and life safety inspections, and ADA access rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know their buildings’ equipment, ages and weak points, and keep asset lists and service records current. They track work orders to closure, hold contractors to clear scopes, and can show a budget they ran, a project they delivered and a failure they prevented.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for running mostly on emergency repairs, no records of fire, elevator or backflow inspections, and loose control of contractor insurance and permits. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a budget variance or who lets vendors decide the scope of their own work.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your preventive maintenance plan for a rooftop HVAC unit. How did you handle a major leak or power outage after hours? How do you check a contractor before they start work? Strong answers name steps, records and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a facilities manager?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with buildings like yours, a working preventive maintenance program, contractor control and budget results they can explain. No license covers the role itself, though trades they oversee may need state or local licenses. References from building owners or occupants show how they handle emergencies and complaints.

qa.q: How do I test a facilities manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise built on your site, such as a sample work order backlog, an equipment list and a budget. Ask them to set priorities, outline a preventive maintenance plan and draft a scope for one contractor job. Review their judgment on safety, cost and occupant impact, and how clearly they explain choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm any degree, enrollment status or graduation date your program requires, and check references from faculty or past supervisors. Most fellowships need no license. If the role includes licensed work, such as clinical or legal tasks, verify that the license is active, since rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the core skill of the project, such as research design, data analysis, policy writing or community outreach. Also check how the candidate scopes a problem, manages time across a fixed term and turns mentor feedback into a better second draft.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: A strong fellow names a specific project idea tied to your mission and explains what they want to learn. They ask who will mentor them. They have finished earlier time-limited work, like a thesis, capstone or volunteer campaign, with a clear result.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague goals, a plan too large for the term, trouble describing their own part in group work, or impatience with feedback. Also be wary if the candidate sees the fellowship only as a placeholder and shows little interest in the actual project.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a project they finished on a deadline and what changed after feedback. Ask what they would do first in your program. Ask how they would share their results at the end of the term.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fellow?
qa.a: Look for a clear fit between the candidate’s goals and your project, proof they can finish work in a fixed term, and openness to mentoring. Check any required degree or enrollment status, call faculty or supervisor references, and verify a license only if the work truly requires one.

qa.q: How do I test a fellow before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task drawn from the real project, such as summarizing a set of sources, analyzing a small data set or drafting a one-page plan. Then give brief feedback and ask for a quick revision. This shows skill, judgment and how well the candidate learns from a mentor.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Fiber and telecom work usually needs no state license, but some states require a low voltage or telecom contractor license. Tower climbers need documented climbing and rescue training. Optional splicing and cabling certifications from industry associations help. Confirm a valid driver’s license, with a CDL where the trucks require one.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test fusion splicing, cleaning and inspecting connectors, OTDR testing and reading traces, and loss testing with a power meter. Check cable pulling, aerial lashing or underground placement, rack and patch panel work, grounding and labeling. Tower roles need climbing, rigging and RF safety knowledge.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates splice consistently with low loss, clean every connector before mating and keep test results organized by fiber. They follow fiber shard and laser safety rules, respect cable bend radius and leave tidy, labeled racks and enclosures.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for skipping connector inspection, guessing at OTDR events, or messy splice trays. Be careful with tower climbers who are casual about fall protection or RF exposure, or anyone who works near power lines without knowing the clearance rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What causes a high loss event on an OTDR trace, and how do you find it? How do you test a new fiber link end to end? Tell me about a cable fault you located. How do you inspect your climbing gear before use? Strong answers name tools and readings.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fiber and telecom technician?
qa.a: Look for hands-on splicing and testing skill, clean work habits and safety training for your setting, such as climbing and rescue training for tower work. Some states require a low voltage license. Test results, photos of past work and references from crew leads show real quality.

qa.q: How do I test a fiber and telecom technician before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid, supervised bench test: fusion splice several fibers, clean and inspect connectors, then test the link with an OTDR and a power meter. Ask them to read the trace aloud. Judge splice loss, neatness, safety steps and how they document results.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to plan a regional event from budget to follow-up. Look for clear goals, a realistic timeline, vendor and venue logistics, a lead capture method and a plan to hand leads to sales within days, not weeks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about pipeline and revenue, not just attendance. They can name how they tracked leads from an event or local campaign, worked with sales reps on target accounts and changed tactics when results fell short.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about an event that went wrong and what they did on the day. Ask how they chose which local markets or accounts to focus on, and how they agreed on lead quality with the sales team.

look.label: Tools and data habits
look.text: Check comfort with a CRM, marketing automation and event or registration platforms. Strong candidates clean and upload lead lists fast, tag campaigns correctly and can explain a simple report on cost per lead or meetings booked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about results, credit taken for work a whole team did, or no mention of sales. Be careful with candidates who focus only on swag and booth design, or who cannot describe a budget they managed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a field marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has run events and local campaigns that fed the sales pipeline. They should manage budgets and vendors, use a CRM well and work closely with sales reps. Ask for examples with results they can explain, such as leads, meetings or deals influenced. Travel readiness and calm problem solving on event days also matter.

qa.q: How do I test a field marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short take-home task: plan one regional event or local campaign for a set budget and audience. Ask for goals, a timeline, promotion, lead capture and sales follow-up. Then have them present it to you and a sales leader. Watch how they handle questions, defend their choices and adjust the plan.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check for a valid driver’s license. If the job involves driving, run a motor vehicle record check with the candidate’s written consent, as the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires. Door-to-door sellers may need a local solicitor permit, which varies by city and county. Selling insurance requires a state license.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they open a conversation with a stranger, ask questions before pitching, handle objections about price or timing, and ask for the order. Also check that they can plan an efficient route and log every visit and next step in your CRM the same day.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about specific accounts, visit routines and results they can explain. They describe a lost deal and what they changed afterward. They stay calm after rejection, follow up without being pushy, and know the products and customers in a territory they have worked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about results, blaming the territory or product for every miss, and high-pressure habits like rushing buyers to sign. For in-home sales, a candidate who does not know about the federal Cooling-Off Rule and buyers’ right to cancel many home sales may create legal risk.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a typical day of visits. Ask how they got past a front desk or gatekeeper. Ask how they decide which accounts to visit first, and how they turned a one-time buyer into a repeat customer.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a field sales representative?
qa.a: Look for someone who starts conversations easily, listens before pitching and handles rejection well. They should explain past results clearly and organize their own day and route. Confirm a valid driver’s license and, with consent, a driving record if they will drive for work. Check whether your area requires a solicitor permit for door-to-door selling.

qa.q: How do I test a field sales representative before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role-play. You play a busy store owner or homeowner with a real objection, such as price or bad timing. Watch how they open, ask questions, respond and ask for a next step. Then ask them to plan a day of visits from a list of addresses and explain their order.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Ask which licenses your equipment requires. Handling refrigerants needs EPA Section 608 certification. Electrical, plumbing or boiler work often needs a state or local license, and rules vary by state. Confirm a valid driver’s license if the job uses a company vehicle, and get written consent before pulling a driving record.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give a real fault to trace, such as a unit that won’t start or shows an error code. Watch how they read a schematic, use a multimeter, follow lockout/tagout and isolate the cause before swapping parts. Check that they can explain the fix and complete a service report.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They name specific equipment they have installed and started up, not just repaired. They talk about confirming the root cause, testing after the repair and leaving the site clean. They explain problems calmly to customers and know when to escalate to engineering or the manufacturer.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about which machines they worked on. Skipping lockout/tagout or other safety steps when describing a job. Blaming customers for every failure. Replacing parts without diagnosing the problem first. No habit of recording work done, parts used and time on site.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through their hardest start-up: what they checked before powering on, what went wrong and how they fixed it. Ask how they handle a repair they cannot finish in one visit, and how they keep a frustrated customer informed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a field service technician?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with your type of equipment, a clear troubleshooting method and strong safety habits. Verify any license the work requires, such as EPA Section 608 for refrigerants or an electrical license, which varies by state. Customer communication and complete service reports matter as much as technical skill, since they often work alone at customer sites.

qa.q: How do I test a field service technician before hiring?
qa.a: Set up a short hands-on exercise with a real or simulated fault on equipment like yours. Watch them follow lockout/tagout, use meters and schematics, find the root cause and explain it as they would to a customer. Ask for a brief written service report. A role-play with an upset customer shows how they handle site visits.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a finance manager. A CPA license, issued by each state under its own rules, or another finance certification is a plus but optional. Verify degrees and past titles, and ask references which budgets and forecasts the candidate actually owned.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test budgeting, rolling forecasts, budget-to-actual variance analysis and cash flow planning. Check spreadsheet models that link the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow, comfort with your accounting system, accrual accounting, month-end close basics and clear reporting to non-finance managers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain why numbers moved, not just how much. They build models others can follow and audit, push back on unrealistic plans with evidence, and work well with department heads. They tighten spending controls without slowing the business and keep forecasts honest.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for models full of hard-coded numbers, no stated assumptions, or forecasts never compared with results. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain the difference between profit and cash, blames others for misses, or treats internal controls and approval limits as mere paperwork.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a forecast that missed and what you changed. How did you cut spending without hurting results? How do you explain a variance to a manager who is not a finance person? Strong answers include specific drivers, decisions and outcomes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a finance manager?
qa.a: Look for hands-on budgeting, forecasting and variance analysis, clean spreadsheet models and clear reporting to non-finance leaders. Check they understand accrual accounting, cash flow and internal controls. No license is required, though a CPA or other finance credential is a plus. References who saw their forecasts against real results matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a finance manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case using simple sample financials and a draft budget. Ask them to build a forecast, explain the biggest variances and recommend spending changes in a one-page memo. Review whether the model is clear and auditable, the logic is sound and the writing is easy for managers to act on.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for FP&A work. A degree in finance, accounting or economics is common. If a candidate lists a CFA charter, an FP&A certification or a CPA license, which each state issues, confirm it through the issuing body’s public lookup.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Spreadsheet modeling with clean, traceable formulas, lookups, pivot tables and scenario toggles. Budget versus actual variance analysis. Linking the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow. Driver-based forecasting tied to volume, price and headcount. Clear charts and short summaries that a manager can act on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain numbers in plain words and tie every forecast to a business driver. They write down their assumptions, check their own totals and flag risks early. They have worked with department heads to build budgets, not just filled in templates handed to them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Hardcoded numbers buried inside formulas. Blaming every variance on “timing” without digging deeper. Confusing a forecast with the monthly accounting close. Vague claims about software or models they cannot walk you through step by step. No questions about how the business actually makes money.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Tell me about a forecast that missed badly. What drove it, and what did you change? How did you get a manager to own their budget? Walk me through how you would model a price increase and its effect on volume and cash.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a financial analyst (FP&A)?
qa.a: Look for strong spreadsheet modeling, budget versus actual variance analysis and forecasts built on real business drivers. A finance or accounting background is common, but no license is required.
