The best candidates explain numbers in plain language, document their assumptions and have partnered with managers on budgets. Verify any listed CFA, FP&A or CPA credential with the issuing body.

qa.q: How do I test a financial analyst (FP&A) before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short take-home or live task using made-up data. Ask them to build a simple twelve-month forecast, compare it to actual results and explain the three biggest variances. Then have them present a one-page summary. Judge formula clarity, stated assumptions, accuracy and how well they explain the story behind the numbers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many reporting roles prefer or require a CPA license. Each state’s board of accountancy issues it, and rules vary by state. Check active status through the board’s public lookup. A CPA is not legally required for most in-house reporting jobs, so weigh hands-on experience too.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they apply US GAAP to real facts, such as revenue under ASC 606 or leases under ASC 842. Check that they can draft footnotes, build consolidations, tie statements to the trial balance and write a short technical accounting memo.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates cite the relevant Codification topic, explain their judgment in plain words and document it clearly. For public companies, look for hands-on work on Form 10-K and 10-Q filings, SOX controls and steady working relationships with external auditors.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who rolls forward last year’s workbook without asking why, cannot explain the reasoning behind a treatment, or stays vague about their own role in past filings. Treating audit requests or internal controls as a nuisance is another warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a new or unusual deal they accounted for, which guidance they used and what they concluded. Ask how they settled a disagreement with auditors and which disclosures they personally drafted.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a financial reporting accountant?
qa.a: Look for solid US GAAP knowledge, clear technical writing and experience preparing full financial statements with footnotes. A CPA license helps, and rules vary by state. For public companies, look for SEC filing and SOX experience. The best candidates can explain why they chose an accounting treatment, not just how they booked it.

qa.q: How do I test a financial reporting accountant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case, such as a customer contract or a new lease, with made-up figures. Ask for the journal entries, the related footnote language and a one-page memo citing the guidance they relied on. Review whether their reasoning is sound, their numbers tie out and their writing is clear enough for auditors.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Rules vary by state and role. Firefighters usually hold state or accredited Firefighter I and II certification, and EMTs need state EMT certification. Sprinkler and alarm inspectors often need a national technician certification or a state or local license. Check every card with the issuing agency.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test inspection, testing and maintenance of alarms, sprinklers, fire pumps and extinguishers under the fire codes your area adopts. For response roles, check fire suppression, CPR, first aid, hazardous materials awareness and incident command basics. Ask them to read an alarm panel or a sprinkler drawing.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates keep clear inspection records, tag deficiencies properly and explain them to building managers. Response staff drill often, keep certifications current and stay calm. They know impairment procedures, such as a fire watch when a system is down, and report hazards before they cause harm.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for lapsed certifications, inspection reports filled in without real testing, or casual talk about bypassing alarms or closing valves without notice. Be careful with anyone who cannot explain when a system must be taken out of service, or who skips confined space and respirator rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What do you do when a sprinkler system must be shut down for repairs? Walk me through your last emergency call. How do you test a fire alarm without sending a false alarm? Strong answers name steps, notifications and records.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fire protection and emergency response specialist?
qa.a: Look for current certifications that match the role, such as firefighter, EMT or alarm and sprinkler inspection credentials, which vary by state. Check knowledge of the fire codes your area uses, solid inspection records and calm, practiced emergency skills. References from fire marshals or safety managers carry weight.

qa.q: How do I test a fire protection and emergency response specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid, supervised walkthrough of a site where they inspect alarm and sprinkler parts and write up what they find. For response roles, use a tabletop scenario or a skills check of CPR and equipment. Judge accuracy, safety steps and how clearly they report problems.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to write firmware. Most hires hold a degree in electrical engineering, computer engineering or computer science, but shipped products matter more. For regulated products, ask about work under standards such as IEC 62304 for medical devices or ISO 26262 for vehicles.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for strong C, and often C++, on small microcontrollers. They should read datasheets and schematics, write interrupt handlers and drivers for buses like I2C, SPI and UART, and work within tight memory and power limits. RTOS and bootloader experience is a plus.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates debug at the bench with a JTAG or SWD debugger, logic analyzer and oscilloscope. They can explain a hard bug they traced to timing or hardware. They talk about safe firmware updates, watchdogs and how the device recovers when something fails.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with candidates who have only written app or web code and call it embedded. Other warning signs are vague answers about volatile, race conditions or stack use, never having touched real hardware, and blaming the hardware team for every bug.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you share data safely between an interrupt and the main loop? How would you design an update so a power cut cannot brick the device? Walk me through bringing up a new board for the first time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a firmware engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid C on microcontrollers, comfort reading datasheets and schematics, and real bench debugging with a debugger, logic analyzer and oscilloscope. Ask about products they helped ship. If your device is regulated, such as medical or automotive, look for experience with the matching safety standards. No license is required.

qa.q: How do I test a firmware engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid or take-home task, such as writing a driver for a sensor from its datasheet or fixing a buggy interrupt routine. Then review the code together. Ask them to explain timing, memory use and how they would debug it on real hardware. A board on the desk makes the talk concrete.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to manage a fleet. Optional industry certifications, such as Certified Automotive Fleet Manager (CAFM), show formal training. If the job includes driving, confirm a valid driver’s license and, with written consent, review the motor vehicle record. Verify past fleet roles with references.

look.label: Compliance knowledge to test
look.text: If you run commercial motor vehicles, the candidate should know federal FMCSA rules on driver qualification files, hours of service, electronic logging devices, vehicle inspections, and drug and alcohol testing for CDL drivers, including Clearinghouse queries. Rules for vehicles used only within one state vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to work out cost per mile and total cost of ownership from sample data. Ask them to decide whether to repair or replace an aging vehicle. They should also read telematics and fuel card reports and build a preventive maintenance schedule.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates describe concrete results, such as less vehicle downtime, fewer accidents, or lower fuel spending. They also explain how they measured those results. They can talk about negotiating with dealers and repair shops, coaching drivers on safety, and keeping records ready for an audit.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about costs, or no clear process for accidents, recalls or out-of-service vehicles. Be careful with candidates who blame drivers for every problem or treat paperwork as optional. Another warning sign is someone who has never used fleet software or spreadsheets to track the fleet.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fleet manager?
qa.a: Look for proven experience running vehicles, maintenance and drivers, with results they can measure. They should be strong with cost tracking and fleet software. If you operate commercial vehicles, they need solid knowledge of federal safety rules. Certifications like CAFM are a plus but not required. Check references and ask how they handled a serious accident or a budget cut.

qa.q: How do I test a fleet manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short case with sample data, such as fuel, repair and mileage records for a few vehicles. Ask them to find the costliest vehicles, recommend repair or replacement, and draft a maintenance plan. For commercial fleets, add a compliance scenario, such as a missing driver file or an overdue inspection, and ask how they would fix it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required to write flight software. Verify claimed degrees and past projects instead. For aircraft work, ask what DO-178C design assurance levels they worked under. For space work, ask which mission assurance or software standards they followed, such as NASA’s software engineering requirements.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test embedded C or C++ under real constraints: fixed memory, no dynamic allocation after startup, and hard timing deadlines. Check that they understand interrupts, a real-time operating system, scheduling, watchdog timers, and serial or bus protocols that talk to sensors and actuators.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about fault protection before features. They describe hardware-in-the-loop testing, requirements traceability, code reviews, and coding standards like MISRA C. They can explain a bug they caught before flight, how they found it, and what process change kept it from coming back.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who has only written app or web code and treats crashes as restartable. Other warnings: no habit of unit or integration testing, vague answers about timing and memory limits, blaming hardware for every failure, and no curiosity about what happens when a sensor lies.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What happens in your code if a sensor stops responding mid-flight? How did you prove your task deadlines were met? How did you handle a bit flip or a reset in flight? Walk me through tracing one requirement to its test.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a flight software engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid embedded C or C++, real-time and timing skills, and a safety-first mindset. They should know hardware-in-the-loop testing, fault handling and requirements traceability. For aircraft, DO-178C experience matters. For spacecraft, look for work under formal mission assurance standards. Ask for concrete stories of failures they prevented or fixed.

qa.q: How do I test a flight software engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short embedded task, such as a sensor-reading loop with a deadline, a watchdog and a failure case. Have them explain how they would test it on real or simulated hardware. Then review a small piece of flawed code together and see which timing, memory and fault-handling bugs they catch.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many states and counties require food service workers to earn a food handler card within a set time after hire; rules vary by place. No other license is usually needed. Confirm any card they already hold and check references for reliability and food safety habits.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test handwashing and glove use, safe holding temperatures, cleaning and sanitizing with test strips, and allergen awareness. Check speed on a serving line, portion control, cash or card handling, dish machine operation and polite service to customers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong workers clean as they go, keep hot food hot and cold food cold without reminders, follow portion guides and ask when unsure about an allergen. They show up on schedule, help teammates during rushes and stay friendly with customers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for skipping handwashing between tasks, guessing about allergens, using the same cloth for raw and ready-to-eat areas, or careless cash handling. Be wary of anyone who brushes off supervisor instructions or safety rules from past jobs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What do you do if a customer asks whether a dish contains nuts? How do you know a sanitizer is strong enough? Tell me about a busy shift and how you kept up. Strong answers name specific steps, not just good intentions.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a food service worker?
qa.a: Look for reliability, basic food safety knowledge, clean work habits and friendly service. Check whether your state or county requires a food handler card and when it must be earned. Previous kitchen or cafeteria work helps, but a willing learner with good references and safe habits can train quickly.

qa.q: How do I test a food service worker before hiring?
qa.a: Hold a short, paid working trial or a practical walkthrough: ask them to set up a serving station, portion a dish, check food temperatures and sanitize a surface. Ask simple allergen and handwashing questions. Watch speed, cleanliness, attention to instructions and how they treat customers and teammates.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for someone who can write production-quality code fast, query and clean messy customer data, and connect your product to the systems a client already runs. Test debugging inside an unfamiliar codebase, API and data integration work, and the ability to explain a technical tradeoff to a nontechnical stakeholder.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about the customer’s problem before the code. They describe shipping a working fix in days, not months, then turning that one-off into something reusable for the core product team. They stay calm when requirements change mid-meeting and push back politely when a request would hurt the customer.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of candidates who only want clean, well-specified tickets, who blame customers for confusing requirements, or who cannot name a case where they said no to a client. Another warning sign is building custom hacks with no notes, tests or handoff plan for the team that inherits them.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a time they joined a customer team with little context. What did they learn in week one? What did they ship first, and why? How did they feed what they learned back to product? Vague answers usually mean they have not done this work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or certification is required for this role. Verify past work instead: call references from former customers or account leads, review code samples or public projects, and confirm any security clearance or cloud certification only if the job truly requires it.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a forward deployed engineer?
qa.a: Look for a solid software engineer who also handles people well. They should code quickly in unfamiliar systems, work with messy data, and explain choices to customers in plain language. Strong candidates show judgment about when to build a quick fix and when to push a request back to the product team. References from past customer work are often the best proof.

qa.q: How do I test a forward deployed engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-boxed exercise that mirrors a real customer visit. Hand over a small messy dataset and a vague business request, then ask them to clarify the goal, build a working solution, and present it to a mock stakeholder. Score the questions they ask, the quality of the code, and how clearly they explain tradeoffs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for someone who has owned messy projects end to end, not just supported them. Strong candidates describe what they shipped, what they cut, and how they kept a busy founder informed without needing constant direction.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test structured thinking, clear writing and basic financial modeling. Ask for a one-page plan, a short memo to the founder, or a simple spreadsheet. Judge how fast they find the real problem and how cleanly they explain tradeoffs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a project that changed direction halfway through. Ask how they decided what to drop when priorities clashed. Ask them to walk through a launch, hire or investor update they ran, step by step, with real numbers where they can share them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of vague answers that only say “we” and never “I.” Watch for candidates who need detailed instructions, avoid hard conversations, or treat confidential company details loosely. A generalist title alone does not prove they can execute.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license or certification is required for this role. Verify past work through references who saw the candidate operate under pressure, ideally a former manager or founder. A project management certification can help but is not a substitute for proven results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a special projects manager?
qa.a: Look for proven ownership of projects from start to finish, sharp written communication, and comfort with ambiguity. They should switch between launches, hiring and fundraising support without losing track of details. Check references from people who worked closely with them, and confirm they handle confidential information with care.

qa.q: How do I test a special projects manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-boxed task based on a real priority. For example, ask for a one-page plan to launch a product or fill a key role, with timeline, owners and risks. Then discuss it live to see how they defend choices, take feedback and adjust.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they write clean, synthesizable RTL in VHDL, Verilog or SystemVerilog and build self-checking testbenches. Hand them a timing report and ask them to explain the worst failing path and how they would close timing.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a clock domain crossing, or a design that passed simulation but failed on the board. Strong candidates name the actual bug, the tools they used to find it, such as an on-chip logic analyzer, and the fix.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for FPGA design. Most hires hold an electrical or computer engineering degree, which you can verify. Vendor training certificates are optional. Some defense and space roles need a federal security clearance, so state that in the posting.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They treat verification as seriously as design, script their builds, use version control and know their resource budget of logic, DSP blocks and block RAM. They match your field: low latency for trading, signal processing for radios, fault tolerance for satellites.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who writes RTL like software, ignores timing warnings, cannot explain their reset or clocking strategy, or has only ever run designs in simulation and never debugged real hardware.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an FPGA engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid RTL skills in VHDL, Verilog or SystemVerilog, strong verification habits and real experience closing timing and debugging on hardware. Ask for examples of clock domain crossings and board-level bugs they solved. Experience in your field, such as radios, satellites or trading, shortens their ramp-up.

qa.q: How do I test an FPGA engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task: design a small block, such as a FIFO or UART, with a self-checking testbench. Then review a buggy snippet or timing report together and ask them to find the problem. Watch how they reason, not just whether they reach the answer.

look.label: Credentials worth noting
look.text: No state license is required for fraud analyst work. The Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential is common and can be checked with the issuing body. Anti-money laundering certificates help in payments or banking roles. Treat these as a plus, not a must.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Pulling data with SQL or spreadsheets. Linking accounts by device, IP address, email or shipping address. Reading chargeback reason codes. Writing a rule that catches a fraud ring without blocking good customers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Treats false positives as a real cost, not just a side note. Explains how fraudsters adapt after a new rule goes live. Writes clear case notes that a manager, a dispute team or law enforcement could follow.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Wants to block every risky order with no thought for lost sales. Cannot walk through a case they worked from start to finish. Shares confidential details or customer data from a past employer to impress you.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a fraud pattern they caught, what data showed it, what they changed and how they measured the result. Ask how they handle promo abuse versus stolen card use. Real analysts give specific steps from their own work.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fraud analyst?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with transaction or account data, sound judgment on when to block or approve, and clear writing. SQL or strong spreadsheet skills matter. A CFE credential is a plus but not required. Many employers run background checks for roles with financial data. Follow the federal FCRA and your state and local rules, which vary.

qa.q: How do I test a fraud analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small, made-up dataset of orders or sign-ups with a few planted patterns, such as shared devices, card testing or repeat promo codes. Ask the candidate to find them, propose rules and estimate how many good customers each rule would block. Judge their reasoning and notes, not just the answer. Never share real customer data.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this role. Optional certifications such as Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE), Financial Risk Manager (FRM) or Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialist (CAMS) show serious study. Confirm any listed credential directly with the issuing body before you make an offer.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can pull and join transaction data with SQL, spot an unusual pattern and turn it into a clear rule. Strong analysts weigh fraud caught against good customers blocked, and they can explain false positives, chargebacks and account takeover in plain words.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk in dollars saved and good customers kept, not just alerts raised. They describe fixing a rule that misfired, write down their logic, and work well with operations, compliance and product teams who must live with the rules.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with someone who wants to block every risky transaction, can’t explain why a model flagged a case, or handles customer data loosely. Vague answers about past losses or results they personally drove also need follow-up.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about a fraud pattern you caught early. What data showed it?” and “A rule cut fraud but doubled declines. What did you do?” Listen for specific signals, thresholds, testing and how they measured the result.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fraud and risk analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong data skills, especially SQL, plus sound judgment about tradeoffs. A good analyst stops losses without driving away honest customers. Ask for examples of rules they built, how they tested them and what changed. Certifications like CFE or FRM are a plus but not required, so verify them if listed.

qa.q: How do I test a fraud and risk analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a small, made-up transaction dataset with some hidden fraud. Ask them to find the suspicious activity, write one or two rules, and estimate how many good customers each rule would block. Never share real customer data. Then have them walk you through their reasoning in plain language.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Ask which licenses the candidate has worked under. Ocean forwarders need a Federal Maritime Commission OTI license, and air forwarders in TSA’s Indirect Air Carrier program must train their staff. A personal CBP customs broker license is a strong plus but not required. If they hold one, ask for the number and confirm it with CBP.

look.label: Training to check
look.text: If you ship hazardous materials, staff who handle them must have DOT hazmat training, repeated at least every three years. Air and ocean dangerous goods rules add their own training. Ask when they last trained and which goods they handled. Lithium batteries make a good test topic.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can explain Incoterms and who pays what under each, read a bill of lading and an air waybill, and work out chargeable weight. Ask how they would find an HS code, and when an Importer Security Filing is due for US ocean imports.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a shipment that went wrong, such as a rolled booking, a customs hold or a missed cutoff. Strong answers name the documents, the people they called, the costs such as demurrage or detention, and what they changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about who filed customs or ISF data, or mixing up demurrage and detention. Other warning signs are quoting without asking weight, dimensions or Incoterm, blaming carriers for every delay, promising transit times no carrier guarantees, and guessing tariff codes instead of checking.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a freight forwarding specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience booking the modes you use, solid knowledge of Incoterms and shipping documents, and calm problem solving when cargo is delayed or held. Check any customs broker license with CBP, and confirm hazmat training if you ship dangerous goods. Clear, prompt communication with shippers, carriers and customs brokers matters as much as technical skill.

qa.q: How do I test a freight forwarding specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Share a commercial invoice, packing list and Incoterm, then ask them to list the needed documents, work out chargeable weight, and outline a door-to-door plan with key deadlines. Add a problem, such as a customs exam or a rolled booking, and see how they respond and explain the next steps to the client.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check solid HTML, CSS and JavaScript before any framework. Ask them to build a small responsive page, handle a form with validation, and fetch data from an API. Watch how they structure components and manage state.

look.label: Accessibility and performance
look.text: Strong candidates use semantic HTML, keyboard navigation, alt text and proper contrast without being asked. They know how to spot slow pages, shrink large images and bundles, and test across browsers and screen sizes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for a portfolio or code samples with clear, readable code, sensible file structure and some tests. Good engineers explain trade-offs in plain words, use version control well and ask questions about users and design intent.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of someone who only knows one framework and can’t explain the basics under it. Other warning signs: no interest in accessibility, copy-pasted code they can’t explain, ignoring mobile layouts, or dismissing code review feedback.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for frontend engineering. Certificates and degrees are optional and vary widely in value. Verify work instead: review shipped projects, public code, and references from past teams who saw their work firsthand.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a frontend engineer?
qa.a: Look for strong HTML, CSS and JavaScript fundamentals, experience with the framework your team uses, and care for accessibility and performance. Review real projects they built. Strong candidates write readable code, test on many devices and explain their choices clearly to designers and other engineers.

qa.q: How do I test a frontend engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-limited task close to your real work, such as building a small responsive component from a design that pulls data from an API. Then review it together. Ask why they made each choice, how they would handle accessibility, and what they would improve with more time.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can build a feature end to end. That means a working page, an API endpoint, a database change and a test. Ask them to explain how data moves from a form click to a saved record and back to the screen.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about trade-offs, not just tools. They can explain why they picked a framework, how they handled slow queries, and how they kept the interface fast and accessible. They read error logs calmly and write code others can maintain.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who only knows one side and calls themselves full-stack. Other warning signs are vague answers about security, no habit of writing tests, and portfolios built entirely from tutorial projects they cannot extend or explain.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Cloud or security certifications can show effort but are optional. Verify past work instead: review a code sample or public repository, confirm they wrote it, and check references from teammates or managers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a production bug they fixed and how they found it. Ask how they would protect user passwords and stop common attacks like SQL injection. Ask how they deployed code and rolled back a bad release.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a full-stack engineer?
qa.a: Look for proof they can ship a complete feature, from the screen people use to the server and database behind it. Check their grasp of security basics, testing and deployment. Good communication matters too, since they often work with designers and product owners. A real code sample tells you more than a list of frameworks.

qa.q: How do I test a full-stack engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small, paid or time-boxed task that touches both sides, such as a simple form that saves data through an API and shows it on a page. Then review it together. Ask why they made each choice and how they would scale or secure it. Their reasoning matters as much as the finished code.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a fund accountant. A state CPA license is a plus, especially for senior roles, and can be checked on the state board of accountancy lookup. Verify past work with references, including the fund types they supported.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test net asset value calculation, accruals, pricing and corporate actions, and reconciling to custodian and broker records. For private funds, check capital calls, distributions, partner capital accounts, fee and carried interest calculations, and investor allocations.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates meet tight daily or monthly deadlines without errors, investigate breaks fully and document every adjustment. They understand the fund’s documents, explain how each investor’s share moved and support audits smoothly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for breaks left open or forced to match, weak knowledge of fund documents and fee terms, and heavy reliance on others to review simple entries. Be wary of anyone vague about controls around pricing and investor allocations.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you strike a NAV. How do you handle a pricing break or a late trade? How was the management fee or carried interest calculated in a fund you supported? Strong answers are precise and step by step.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fund accountant?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with the fund types you run, accurate net asset value work, strong reconciliations and solid knowledge of fund documents and fee terms. They should meet tight deadlines and support audits. No license is required, though a CPA license is a plus for senior roles.

qa.q: How do I test a fund accountant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a sample trial balance, positions, prices and a few capital activities. Ask them to calculate net asset value and each investor’s share, find planted breaks and calculate a management fee. Judge accuracy, the reconciliation steps and how clearly they document their work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a fundraiser or grants professional. Certified Fund Raising Executive and Grant Professional Certified are optional credentials. Many states require charities to register before soliciting, and some require outside paid solicitors to register, so rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test grant writing to a funder’s guidelines, budgets that match the narrative, and clear outcome measures. For donor work, check prospect research, gift acknowledgment rules, donor database care and stewardship plans. For grantmaking roles, test due diligence and how they judge a grantee’s impact.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can show proposals they wrote and say which were funded and why others were not. They treat donors and funders as relationships, report outcomes honestly, track restricted gifts correctly and keep every deadline in a clear calendar.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for claims of raising large sums with no detail on their own role, padded impact numbers, misuse of restricted gifts, and casual handling of donor data. Be wary of anyone asking to be paid a percentage of money raised, which professional fundraising ethics codes reject.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a grant you won from first contact to final report. Tell me about a proposal that was declined and what you learned. How do you handle a gift with restrictions you cannot meet? Strong answers show honesty, process and follow-through.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a fundraising and grants professional?
qa.a: Look for a record of funded proposals or donor gifts they can explain in detail, clear writing, and honest outcome reporting. Check they understand restricted gifts, acknowledgment rules and donor privacy. Credentials such as Certified Fund Raising Executive are optional, so writing samples and references from funders or executive directors matter more.

qa.q: How do I test a fundraising and grants professional before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise, such as a two-page letter of inquiry for one of your programs, written to a sample funder’s guidelines with a matching budget. For donor roles, ask for a stewardship plan for one major donor. Review fit to guidelines, clear outcomes, accurate numbers and persuasive, plain writing.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: No US license or certification exists for this work, so the portfolio is the main proof. Look for finished characters, environments and props in a consistent style, plus sketches, thumbnails and turnarounds that show how the artist gets from idea to final piece.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test anatomy, perspective, color and lighting with a short paid brief. Check that the artist can produce several quick silhouette options, then refine one into a clean, readable design that fits your game’s style and technical limits.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong artists explain their design choices, take feedback without losing quality, and can match an existing style. Experience delivering files in the formats and sizes your engine or team needs, with organized layers and clear naming, is a big plus.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolios with only polished final images and no process work, art that closely copies known franchises, or unclear use of AI image tools. Hesitation to explain which parts of team projects they made themselves is also a warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through one piece from brief to final, how they handled art direction changes, and how they kept a character consistent across many poses. Ask how they set up files to hand art off to modelers or animators.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a game and concept artist?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio that matches your game’s style and shows process, not just final images. Check fundamentals like anatomy, perspective and color, plus the ability to take direction and hit deadlines. No license is required in the US, so references from past art leads and a written agreement covering who owns the art matter more.

qa.q: How do I test a game and concept artist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid test based on a real but non-critical need, such as three silhouette options for a character and one refined sketch. Set a clear time limit, reference sheet and file format. Judge readability, fit with your style, and how well they respond to one round of feedback.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for shipped games, mods, jam entries or playable prototypes, plus design documents. Play them yourself. Look for clear rules, sensible difficulty curves and levels that teach the player without long tutorials. No US license or required certification exists for game designers, so the work itself is the main proof.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can write a clear design document, balance numbers in a spreadsheet, and build or script a simple prototype in a common game engine. For economy work, see if they can model currencies, rewards and pacing. For story work, read their branching dialogue or quest outlines.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong designers explain why each rule exists and what player behavior it should create. They talk about playtesting, data and iteration, not just ideas. They can name a feature they cut and why. They know the limits of art, code and budget and design within them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a portfolio of pitches with nothing playable, vague answers about their own role on team projects, or dismissing playtest feedback. Be wary of designers who blame other departments for every problem, or who cannot describe how they measured whether a change made the game better.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through one level or system they designed from first sketch to final version. Ask what playtesters did that surprised them, how they handled a balance problem after launch, and how they worked with artists, programmers and producers to settle a disagreement.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a game designer?
qa.a: Look for playable work, not just ideas. Review their shipped games, prototypes and design documents, and play them. Check that they can explain the purpose of each rule, balance a system with numbers, and improve a design through playtesting. Ask exactly what they did on team projects. There is no required license, so judge skills and results.

qa.q: How do I test a game designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task that fits your game. For example, ask them to design one level, a reward loop or a small quest, with a one page document and rough balance numbers. Then have them present it and respond to your feedback. Watch how they reason, prioritize and revise, not just the final idea.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for playable builds, not just screenshots or videos. A game jam entry, a shipped title or a polished prototype shows how the candidate handles controls, pacing and bugs. Ask which parts they built themselves and which came from a team or an asset store.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check their skill in the engine and language you use, such as C++, C# or a visual scripting tool. Also look at version control habits, debugging, performance profiling and how they structure code so others can extend it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to develop games in the US. Degrees and engine vendor certifications can help, but shipped work and code samples matter more. Confirm employment history and any credits listed on released titles.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong developers talk about player feel, scope cuts and tradeoffs, not just features. They finish projects, write clear notes and accept playtest feedback without getting defensive. They can explain why a mechanic was changed or removed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolios built only from tutorials, vague answers about who did what on team projects, or no finished work at all. Be careful with candidates who share code or assets from a past employer, since that may break confidentiality agreements.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a game developer?
qa.a: Look for finished, playable work in the engine and language you use. Check that they can explain their own role on team projects, debug problems calmly and cut scope to meet a deadline. Good communication with artists, designers and testers matters as much as coding skill.

qa.q: How do I test a game developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task that fits your project, such as building a small mechanic or fixing bugs in a sample scene. Set a clear time limit. Then review the build and code together, asking why they made each choice and what they would improve with more time.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check fluency in the language your project uses, often C++ or C#. Test core math for games, such as vectors and collision checks. Ask them to profile and fix a slow frame. Debugging under real constraints shows more than writing fresh code.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for shipped games, game jam entries or playable demos you can run yourself. Strong candidates explain why they chose a design, talk about frame budgets and memory, and describe working closely with designers and artists.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about the hardest bug they fixed in a shipped build. Ask how they kept a game loop stable at the target frame rate. Ask how they handled network lag or desync in multiplayer. Vague answers suggest limited hands-on work.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of portfolios with only tutorial projects, code samples they can’t walk through line by line, or no use of version control. Watch for candidates who blame artists or designers for every problem, or who dismiss testing and code reviews.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to program games. Degrees and engine certificates can help but are optional. Verify past roles through references, confirm credits on shipped titles, and make sure any code samples are theirs and free of a former employer’s confidentiality limits.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a game programmer?
qa.a: Look for strong skills in your engine and language, solid game math, and a habit of profiling and debugging. A playable portfolio or shipped titles matter more than a resume. Pick someone who fits your focus, such as gameplay, engine, tools or online services, and who works well with designers and artists.

qa.q: How do I test a game programmer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid take-home task or a live session in your engine. Examples include building a small mechanic, fixing a bug in existing code, or speeding up a slow scene. Then have them walk you through their choices. Keep the task small so it respects their time and stays fair to all candidates.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an active law license in good standing using the state bar’s public lookup, and check for any discipline. If they will work in a state where they are not admitted, review that state’s in-house counsel registration rules, which vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test business judgment on legal risk, clear advice to non-lawyers, and contract negotiation. Also test how they manage outside counsel and budgets, run compliance programs, and brief a board on governance matters in plain language.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for in-house experience at a company of similar size, stage or industry. Strong candidates have built or led a legal team, handled board work, and can describe deals, disputes or regulatory issues they owned from start to finish.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of someone who only lists risks and never offers a path forward. Other warning signs are vague answers about their own role in deals, no sense of legal spend, or confusion about the fact that their client is the company, not any one executive.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a time they advised leadership against a plan and what happened next. Ask how they chose and managed outside firms, how they cut legal costs, and how they raised a serious issue with the board.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a general counsel?
qa.a: Look for an attorney with an active license in good standing, solid in-house experience, and a record of advising executives and a board. The best candidates turn legal risk into clear business choices, manage outside counsel well, and understand that their duty runs to the company. Check bar status through the state bar’s public lookup.

qa.q: How do I test a general counsel before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case exercise using made-up facts, such as a data breach or a key contract dispute. Ask for a one-page memo to the CEO with a recommendation, then a brief verbal summary as if speaking to the board. Judge clarity, judgment, and how they weigh legal risk against business goals.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to be a general manager, and an MBA is optional. Verify results instead through owners, boards or regional leaders who saw their profit and loss. Some regulated businesses, such as those holding liquor licenses, may need state approval of the manager, which varies by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they read a profit and loss statement, build a budget and forecast, and choose which costs to cut or protect. Check they can hire and lead managers, set clear targets, manage cash and key customers, and keep the site compliant with safety and employment rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain the drivers behind past results, good and bad, without hiding behind market conditions. They build leaders below them, review numbers weekly, decide with incomplete data, and can show a turnaround or growth plan they carried out, not just wrote.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague claims of growth with no numbers they can explain, credit taken for team or market wins, high turnover among their direct reports, and cost cutting that hurt safety or customers. Be wary of anyone who blames prior owners for every problem.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a profit and loss statement you owned and the two levers that moved it most. Tell me about a manager you had to replace. What did you cut in a bad quarter and why? Strong answers are specific and honest about mistakes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a general manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of running a unit like yours with full profit and loss responsibility, results they can explain line by line, and strong leaders they developed. Check how they handle cash, customers, safety and compliance. References from owners, boards and former direct reports matter more than degrees or titles.

qa.q: How do I test a general manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case using a sample profit and loss statement and a brief on your business. Ask for a plan for their first months, the top risks and the levers they would pull. Review their grasp of the numbers, priorities and tradeoffs. Then have senior leaders probe the plan live.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many states require a Professional Geologist license for geology work offered to the public, and rules vary by state. Mining engineers may need a state PE license to seal plans. Anyone working at a mine site needs federal mine safety training. Check licenses on state board sites.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test core logging, geologic mapping, sampling and QA/QC of assay data, GIS and 3D modeling. For mining engineers, check mine planning, slope and ground stability, blast design, ventilation and haul road layout. For water or site work, check groundwater and soil testing.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show clean field notes, maps and logs, and keep sample chain of custody. They separate data from interpretation and state uncertainty clearly. For public company work, they understand qualified person reporting rules and never stretch a resource estimate.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for overstated resource claims, missing QA/QC, or maps with no data behind them. Be careful with anyone who downplays ground control or safety training, or who cannot explain the models in their own reports.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you catch a bad assay batch? Walk me through a geologic model you built and its weak points. Tell me about a ground stability problem you found. How did you decide on drill hole spacing? Strong answers show both data and judgment.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a geologist or mining engineer?
qa.a: Look for field skills, clean data habits and the specialty you need, from exploration to mine planning or groundwater. Check a Professional Geologist or PE license where your state or project requires one, and confirm mine safety training. References from project leads confirm real field results.

qa.q: How do I test a geologist or mining engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid exercise with sample drill logs or assay data and ask for a simple cross section and interpretation, or pose a mine design question that needs a short written memo. Review data handling, QA/QC checks, clarity about uncertainty and safety thinking.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: The GISP certification is voluntary, but it shows tested knowledge and work history. Legal boundary surveys require a state land surveyor license, and rules for photogrammetry and mapping vary by state. Anyone flying drones for paid mapping needs an FAA Part 107 remote pilot certificate.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check work with coordinate systems and projections, cleaning messy location data, spatial joins, buffers and geocoding. For logistics or self-driving roles, also test Python scripting, spatial SQL, routing on road networks, and handling large point cloud or sensor data.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: A portfolio of real maps with data sources and methods noted. They explain why they chose a projection, how they checked accuracy, and how they kept metadata current. They start with the business question, not the software.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Polished maps that mix coordinate systems, lack legends or sources, or show layers that don’t line up. Be wary of anyone who can’t explain how they handled missing or wrong data, or who promises survey-grade accuracy without survey equipment or a license.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about a time two datasets didn’t line up. What caused it and how did you fix it?” Or, “How would you set delivery zones for three warehouses?” Good answers name clear steps, accuracy checks and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a GIS and mapping specialist?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio of real projects, solid knowledge of coordinate systems and data cleaning, and the scripting or database skills your work needs. A GISP certification is a plus but not required. If the job involves legal boundaries or paid drone flights, confirm the state license or FAA Part 107 certificate.

qa.q: How do I test a GIS and mapping specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task. Hand over two small datasets in different coordinate systems with a few errors. Ask them to fix the data, join the layers, make one clear map and write brief notes on their steps. Pay for any task longer than an hour or two.

look.label: Core skills to test
look.text: Look for real depth in state estimation and control. A strong candidate can explain Kalman filters and their extended or unscented forms, sensor fusion of IMU and GPS data, attitude math with quaternions, and control design such as PID, LQR or model predictive control, plus stability margins.

look.label: Tools and code
look.text: Most GNC work runs in MATLAB and Simulink, with flight code in C or C++ and analysis in Python. Ask what they have built in 6-DOF simulation, Monte Carlo runs and hardware-in-the-loop testing, and whether their code ever ran on a real vehicle.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for most GNC roles. Verify degrees in aerospace, mechanical or electrical engineering by contacting the school. A PE license exists and varies by state but is rarely needed here. For defense or export-controlled work, state any clearance requirement in the posting and confirm it through the official process.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a filter that diverged, a vehicle that oscillated in testing, or a sensor that failed mid-flight. Ask which coordinate frames they used and how they checked them. People with real experience give specific causes, fixes and lessons, not textbook definitions.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with candidates who tune gains only by trial and error, cannot explain why a design is stable, mix up reference frames, or skip verification. Vague answers about their own part in a team project and no habit of documenting assumptions are also warning signs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a guidance, navigation and control engineer?
qa.a: Look for strong math in estimation and control, hands-on use of Kalman filters and controller design, and solid MATLAB, Simulink and C or C++ skills. Value experience with simulation, Monte Carlo analysis and hardware testing. The best candidates explain clearly why their designs work and how they proved it before flight.

qa.q: How do I test a guidance, navigation and control engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task. Share a noisy IMU and GPS dataset and ask for a simple filter that estimates position, or give a plant model and ask them to design and tune a controller. Then have them walk you through their choices, stability margins and how they would verify the result.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for software developers, and there is no single official Go certification. Verify skill through public code, past work samples and references. Cloud certifications can show platform knowledge, but they do not prove someone writes good Go.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check concurrency with goroutines, channels and mutexes. Check context for timeouts and cancellation, explicit error handling, small interfaces and the standard library, including net/http. Ask them to write table-driven tests and run the race detector.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They write plain, idiomatic Go that passes gofmt and go vet. They keep packages small and clear and manage dependencies with Go modules. They profile with pprof before optimizing. They can explain tradeoffs in simple words.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for ignored errors, panics used for normal failures, goroutines that never stop, and no tests. Be wary of heavy patterns copied from other languages. It is also a concern if they cannot say when to use a channel instead of a mutex.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a race condition or goroutine leak they found and how they fixed it. Ask how they pass a deadline through a request to the database. Ask how they would shut down a server gracefully without dropping requests.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Go developer?
qa.a: Look for clean, idiomatic Go and safe use of goroutines and channels. They should handle errors explicitly and use context for timeouts. Good tests and real experience running networked services in production also matter. No license is required in the US, so judge them by their code samples, references and a short practical task.

qa.q: How do I test a Go developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-boxed task. For example, ask them to build a small HTTP service with a timeout, one concurrent job and table-driven tests. Run go test with the race flag and go vet. Then have them walk you through their choices. Consider paying for longer tasks, and give every candidate the same task.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Contract management certifications are optional, and federal acquisition certifications mainly apply to government staff. Verify experience through references and redacted proposals or contract files. If the work needs a security clearance, ask whether they hold one, since only the government grants clearances.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test knowledge of the Federal Acquisition Regulation and agency supplements, contract types, clause flow-downs to subcontractors, modifications, and proposal compliance matrices. Check cost and pricing basics, small business rules and federal contractor registration. State and local contracts follow their own rules, which vary.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates read a solicitation clause by clause, flag risky terms early, and keep clean records for audits. They understand cost accounting, cybersecurity and reporting duties, work smoothly with contracting officers, and know how government contract terms differ from commercial ones.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for anyone who treats government contracts like commercial ones, misses required flow-downs, or is casual about certifications and representations. Be wary of vague answers on False Claims Act risk, ethics rules on gifts and hiring former officials, or handling of competitor information.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you review a new solicitation. Tell me about a contract modification you negotiated. Which clauses do you flow down to subcontractors and why? How did you prepare for an audit? Strong answers name specific clauses, steps and records.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a government contracts specialist?
qa.a: Look for working knowledge of the Federal Acquisition Regulation, contract types, flow-downs and compliance duties, plus careful records for audits. Check they understand False Claims Act risk and ethics rules. No license is required, so redacted contract files, proposals and references matter most. State and local contracting rules vary by jurisdiction.

qa.q: How do I test a government contracts specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise using sections of a public solicitation. Ask them to build a compliance matrix, flag risky clauses, list required flow-downs for a subcontractor and draft questions for the contracting officer. Review accuracy against the solicitation, risk judgment and clear writing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this work. Vendor training certificates are optional and prove little on their own. Verify skill through code samples, open-source contributions, written benchmark reports and references from people who saw the speedups ship.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for hands-on GPU programming with CUDA or a similar model, plus memory coalescing, shared memory, occupancy and kernel fusion. They should profile with real tools, reason with a roofline model, use mixed precision safely and tune multi-GPU communication for training and inference.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They measure before changing anything and set a clean baseline. They can say whether code is limited by memory bandwidth, compute or launch overhead. They check numerical accuracy after every change, show before and after numbers, and know when a library call beats a custom kernel.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for big speedup claims with no baseline, hardware details or method. Other warning signs are benchmarks that skip warmup runs or GPU synchronization, ignoring accuracy loss from lower precision, and only tweaking framework flags without being able to explain why they helped.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a slowdown they tracked down and what the profiler showed. Ask how they decide if a kernel is memory bound. Ask what broke when they moved a model to lower precision and how they caught it.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a GPU and performance engineer?
qa.a: Look for proven GPU programming and profiling skill, not just familiarity with AI frameworks. Strong candidates set baselines, explain where time and memory go, protect numerical accuracy, and document results others can repeat. No license is required, so judge them on code samples, benchmark write-ups and references who saw their work ship.

qa.q: How do I test a GPU and performance engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a slow but correct piece of GPU or model code and a fixed test. Ask them to profile it, explain the main bottleneck, speed it up and prove the output still matches. Review their method and written reasoning as closely as the final speedup.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for a portfolio with five to ten finished pieces close to your needs, such as logos, ads, slides or web pages. Look for range, clean typography and consistent brand systems, not just pretty single images.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check skill with standard design software for vector, layout and photo work. Test typography, color, grid layout and file preparation for both print and screen, including correct color modes, bleed and export formats.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong designers explain the reasoning behind each choice and show early sketches, not just final files. They ask about your audience and goals, build style guides, and keep files organized with named layers and editable sources.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolio work the person cannot explain, heavy reliance on stock templates, or pieces that look copied from others. Be careful if they cannot describe their exact role on team projects or resist feedback and revisions.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through one brand project from brief to delivery. Ask how they handled a client who disliked the first round, how they keep a logo readable at small sizes, and how they make sure fonts and images are properly licensed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a graphic and brand designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio that matches your needs, clear reasoning behind design choices, and solid typography and layout skills. Good designers ask about your audience, deliver organized editable files, and understand print and web output. No state license is required for this work, so the portfolio and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a graphic and brand designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid test task, such as a social media ad or one slide using your existing brand colors and fonts. Set a clear brief and deadline. Judge the result on clarity, brand fit, file setup and how well they explain their choices and respond to feedback.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this work. Verify skill through a portfolio, shipped products, code samples, demos, and any talks or papers. For team projects, ask which systems they personally built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for strong C++, solid linear algebra, and shader writing in HLSL or GLSL. They should know at least one modern GPU API, such as Vulkan, DirectX 12 or Metal, and use a GPU frame debugger and profiler to find bugs and bottlenecks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain tradeoffs in plain terms, like forward versus deferred rendering or image quality versus frame time. They think in milliseconds per frame and memory budgets. They show demos running on real target hardware, not just screenshots.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: A portfolio built only from engine presets or tutorials with no custom work. Can’t explain the math behind a lighting model they used. Has never profiled on target hardware, or blames the driver for every bug without evidence.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about the hardest rendering bug they tracked down and how. Ask how they met a frame time target on weak hardware. Ask how they handled shadow artifacts, depth precision problems or motion-to-photon latency in VR.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a graphics and rendering engineer?
qa.a: Look for strong C++, linear algebra and shader skills, plus hands-on work with a modern GPU API. A good portfolio shows custom rendering work, not just engine presets. Strong candidates explain performance tradeoffs clearly and can describe how they profiled and fixed real problems. No US license is required, so judge by work samples.

qa.q: How do I test a graphics and rendering engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task that fits your stack. For example, fix a broken shader, add a simple lighting effect, or find why a scene drops frames using a profiler. Then ask them to walk you through their choices. Their reasoning about math, performance and debugging tells you more than the final image.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Some states and counties require a food handler card for deli, bakery or meat counter work, and the rules vary. Alcohol seller training is required in some states and voluntary in others. Check your state and local rules before the first shift.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to face a shelf, rotate stock first in, first out, and spot an expired date. Have them read a shelf tag and find a misplaced item. Watch whether they work steadily and keep the aisle clear for shoppers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Greets shoppers without being prompted and walks them to an item instead of pointing. Knows when to call a manager. Can explain how they lift and stack cases safely. Mentions checking dates and IDs as a normal part of the job.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treats stocking as a race and skips date rotation. Shrugs off ID checks for alcohol or tobacco. Talks about customers with impatience. Stays vague about past attendance or cannot say what they did when a product ran out.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “How do you rotate dairy when a new delivery arrives?” “A customer wants an item that is out of stock. What do you do?” “An ID for a beer sale looks off. How do you handle it?” Listen for concrete steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a grocery store associate?
qa.a: Look for steady work habits, care with expiration dates and stock rotation, and a friendly way with shoppers. Check that they take ID rules for alcohol and tobacco seriously. If they will work a deli or other food counter, confirm whether your state or county requires a food handler card.

qa.q: How do I test a grocery store associate before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short hands-on task. Ask them to face a shelf section, pull expired items and rotate stock. Then role-play a shopper asking for an item that is out of stock. If the trial is real work on your floor, pay for the time, since wage laws usually require it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license or degree is required for product management, and product or agile certificates are optional. Verify outcomes instead: products shipped, metrics moved and teams led. Call references from engineering, design and the product managers they managed to hear how they set direction and coached others.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test product strategy, prioritization across several teams, and the ability to turn company goals into a clear roadmap. Check how they coach product managers, review specs, use data and customer research, and settle conflicts between teams competing for the same engineers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can name products they shaped and the results, including failures. They grow other product managers, write clear strategy documents, and say no to good ideas that do not fit. Engineers and designers who worked with them describe them as clear and fair.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who take credit for team results without naming others, cannot explain why a product failed, or manage by feature lists instead of outcomes. Be careful with anyone who has never hired, coached or given hard feedback to a product manager.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a strategy you set that changed after customer data came in. How do you decide between two teams’ priorities? How do you coach a struggling product manager? Strong answers name metrics, tradeoffs and specific people decisions.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a group product manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of shipping products that moved real metrics, setting strategy across several teams, and growing other product managers. Check they use data and customer research, make clear tradeoffs and earn trust from engineering and design. No license is required, so references and real outcomes matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a group product manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case: a product area with conflicting goals, limited engineers and some customer data. Ask for a short strategy, a ranked roadmap and how they would split work across product managers. Review clarity, use of evidence, tradeoffs and how they handle tough follow-up questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for growth engineering. Analytics or marketing certificates are optional. Verify with experiments they ran, features they shipped, and references from product or marketing partners who confirm the results and the candidate’s share of the work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test full-stack coding for sign-up and onboarding flows, feature flags, event tracking and analytics queries in SQL. Check experiment design: one main metric, sample size, run length and no early peeking at results. Ask how they keep email, texts and tracking within federal rules and state privacy laws.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show experiments that lost as well as won and explain what they learned. They check tracking before trusting a result, ship small changes quickly, and care about long-term retention and trust, not just a short-term bump in sign-ups.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for claims of huge wins with no control group, tests stopped the moment results look good, and dark patterns such as hidden cancel buttons or fake urgency. Be careful with anyone casual about consent for emails and texts, or about referral fraud.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an experiment that failed and what you did next. How do you decide how long to run a test? How did you find out that tracking was broken? How do you stop abuse of a referral program? Strong answers name data and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a growth engineer?
qa.a: Look for shipped growth work, such as sign-up flows, onboarding or referral programs, backed by experiments they can explain, including ones that failed. Check full-stack coding, analytics, SQL and sound experiment design. They should respect federal consent rules for email and texts and privacy laws that vary by state. No license is required.

qa.q: How do I test a growth engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your product: review a sample sign-up funnel with data, propose one experiment with a clear metric and sample size plan, and build a small version behind a feature flag with tracking. Review their reasoning, tracking quality, code and how honestly they describe risks.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can design a clean experiment. They should be able to write a clear hypothesis, pick one primary metric, estimate the sample size needed and explain when a test is done. Ask them to read a funnel and spot the biggest drop-off.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about the tests that failed as readily as the wins. They explain what they learned, why they chose each test and how they ranked ideas by likely impact and effort. They can pull their own numbers with SQL or analytics tools.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of someone who credits every gain to themselves, quotes big percentage lifts without baselines or sample sizes, or calls tests early. Another warning sign is growth bought through spam, dark patterns or ignoring privacy and email consent rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through one experiment from idea to result. What was the hypothesis, how long did it run, how did they know the result was real, and what happened next? Ask how they handled a test that hurt a key metric.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for this role in the US. Optional analytics or ad platform certificates show tool familiarity but not judgment. Verify past results instead by checking references and asking for work samples with confidential details removed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a growth manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who runs disciplined experiments, not just campaigns. They should explain hypotheses, metrics and sample sizes in plain words, work comfortably with data, and show results from past tests, including failures. Good candidates also respect privacy and consent rules and work well with product, marketing and engineering teams.

qa.q: How do I test a growth manager before hiring?
qa.a: Share a simple funnel with real or made-up numbers and ask for a short growth plan. They should find the weakest step, list three test ideas ranked by impact and effort, and describe how they would measure one of them. Then discuss their reasoning in a follow-up conversation.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for growth marketers. Ad platform certifications are optional. Verify results instead: ask for campaign reports with private figures removed, and confirm with references what they ran and how the results were measured.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test experiment design, paid ads, email, landing pages, analytics and attribution. Check they know federal rules, such as an unsubscribe link and a postal address in marketing email and consent before marketing texts, plus state privacy laws, which vary.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates measure incremental results with holdout tests, not only clicks, track customer quality after signup and cut channels that do not pay back. They explain both wins and failed tests and keep clean notes on every experiment.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for credit taken for growth without a control group, bought email lists, misleading ads, and channels judged on vanity metrics. Be careful with anyone who dismisses privacy rules or cannot explain how their tracking and attribution worked.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you know a channel brought new customers rather than people who would have bought anyway? Tell me about a test that failed. How do you split a budget across channels? Strong answers describe methods and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a growth marketer?
qa.a: Look for measured results across ads, email and experiments, with proof that growth was incremental rather than just clicks. Check analytics skills, budget judgment and knowledge of email, text and privacy rules, some of which vary by state. No license is required, so campaign reports and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a growth marketer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with sample campaign data, and ask where they would move budget and what experiment they would run next. Ask for a short test plan with a hypothesis, success measure and control group. Review reasoning, measurement method and honesty about uncertainty.

look.label: Skills to test
