look.text: Check that they can design a clean A/B test. They should pick one primary metric, set guardrail metrics, estimate sample size and runtime, and explain statistical significance in plain words. Ask them to read a funnel and point to the biggest drop-off worth fixing first.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about experiments that failed as openly as wins and explain what they learned. They tie work to revenue or retention, not just clicks. They know SQL or can pull their own data, and they write short, clear experiment briefs that engineers and designers can act on.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with candidates who claim big lifts without baselines, sample sizes or timeframes. Watch for anyone who stops tests early when results look good, ignores long-term retention, or leans on dark patterns like hidden cancel buttons. Those can harm users and may break consumer protection rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through one experiment end to end: the hypothesis, the setup, the result and the decision. Ask how they chose between acquisition, activation and retention work. Ask about a time a test win did not hold up after launch, and why.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Product or analytics certificates are optional and vary widely in quality. Verify past results through references from engineering or design partners, and ask for redacted experiment docs or dashboards that show how they actually worked.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a growth product manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who runs disciplined experiments and ties them to paying users, not vanity metrics. They should read funnels, write clear hypotheses, understand sample size and significance, and pull data themselves. Good candidates share failed tests openly, protect long-term retention and user trust, and work smoothly with engineers, designers and marketers.

qa.q: How do I test a growth product manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a sample funnel with conversion numbers by step and ask for a short plan. They should name the biggest opportunity, write two or three test hypotheses, pick primary and guardrail metrics, and estimate how long each test needs. Then discuss their reasoning live. Keep it small, and pay for any task longer than a few hours.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check the candidate’s cosmetology or hair license on your state board’s website, including the expiration date. Stylists licensed in another state may need a license in yours before they can work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a working interview or model: a consultation, a haircut and a blowout, and color if the role includes it. Look at their portfolio and ask about recent color formulas and corrections.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates run a real consultation, explain upkeep and price honestly, keep a clean station and rebook clients naturally. Their portfolio shows a range of hair types and steady recent work.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for an expired license, poor sanitation, promising results the hair cannot take, rushing the consultation and talking badly about past salons or clients. A stylist who cannot explain a color formula needs more training.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A client with box dye wants platinum today. What do you say? When do you do a patch test? How do you get clients to rebook? How do you cut curly hair? Strong answers are honest about what the hair can take.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a hair stylist?
qa.a: Look for a current state license, solid cutting and color skills shown in a working interview, a recent portfolio and good habits with sanitation. Listen to how they run a consultation and talk about rebooking and retail. If they bring clients, ask how many visit regularly.

qa.q: How do I test a hair stylist before hiring?
qa.a: Book a paid working interview on a model: a full consultation, a cut and blowout, and color if needed. Watch sanitation, time management and how they talk with the client. Ask the model afterward how the stylist made them feel.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles expect a degree in electrical or computer engineering, or equivalent hands-on experience. A PE license is rarely required for product design work, since many states exempt industry employees, but rules vary by state. For board layout roles, the IPC Certified Interconnect Designer credential is a useful plus.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Match the test to the role. Board designers should read and critique a schematic and a PCB layout, covering power, grounding and signal integrity. Chip or FPGA designers should write and debug Verilog or VHDL. Everyone should show bench skills with an oscilloscope and logic analyzer.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can walk you through a design they took from concept to production. They explain trade-offs in part choice, cost, heat and noise. They mention design for manufacturing and testing, reading datasheets closely, and planning for FCC emissions testing early rather than at the end.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who has only simulated designs and never brought up real hardware on a bench. Other warnings are vague answers about their own part in team projects, no clear way of tracking down faults, or offering to share a former employer’s confidential schematics.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a board that failed at first power-up and how they found the fault. Ask how they choose decoupling capacitors, what changed between prototype and production, and how they handled a part that went out of stock mid-project.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a hardware engineer?
qa.a: Look for a relevant engineering degree or equal experience, and skills that match your work, such as PCB layout, Verilog or VHDL, or analog design. Strong candidates have taken real products to production, debug confidently in the lab, and explain trade-offs clearly. A PE license is seldom needed for product work, though rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test a hardware engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short review task. Share a schematic or layout with a few planted errors and ask them to find and explain the problems. For chip or FPGA roles, ask for a small Verilog or VHDL module with a testbench. Follow up by asking how they would debug a board that will not power up.

look.label: Experience to confirm
look.text: Ask which products they took from prototype through EVT, DVT and PVT builds into mass production. Find out what they owned at each gate, the build volumes, and whether they worked on site with contract manufacturers. Titles vary a lot, so focus on what actually shipped.

look.label: Credentials worth noting
look.text: No US license is required for this role. A PMP certification or an engineering degree can help, but neither proves hardware skill. For medical devices or other regulated products, experience with design controls and ISO 13485 quality systems is a real plus.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for skill in building schedules around long-lead parts, reading a bill of materials, running build readiness reviews, tracking yield and failure analysis, and managing cost targets. They should also plan around FCC and safety certification timelines, which often drive launch dates.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates speak in specifics: a yield problem they helped fix, a part shortage they worked around, a schedule slip they caught early. They explain tradeoffs between cost, schedule and quality clearly to both engineers and executives.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for software-only project experience presented as hardware work, fuzzy answers about build phases, or blaming suppliers and factories for every delay. Be careful if they cannot name a risk they escalated early or say who made key decisions.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a hardware program manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has taken real products through prototype, validation and production builds with contract manufacturers. They should know bills of materials, supplier lead times, yield tracking and certification timelines. Strong candidates give concrete examples of problems they solved and communicate tradeoffs clearly to engineering, operations and leadership.

qa.q: How do I test a hardware program manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short scenario: a key part has a sudden long lead time weeks before a production build. Ask them to outline a revised schedule, the risks, who they would contact, and how they would update leadership. You can also have them review a sample build plan or bill of materials and point out gaps.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for harness design or assembly. Many employers expect training in the IPC/WHMA-A-620 workmanship standard, and aerospace work may add customer standards. Verify certificates with the trainer and check they are current. For engineers, ask for drawings and wire lists they produced.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: For technicians, test stripping, crimping with the right tool and die, pull tests, soldering, splicing, labeling and reading formboard drawings. For engineers, test wire sizing for current and voltage drop, connector and terminal selection, shielding, routing, strain relief, and clear drawings and wire lists.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates check tools and crimp quality before production, build exactly to the drawing and flag drawing errors instead of guessing. Engineers walk the vehicle or machine to plan routing, design for easy assembly and service, and fix field failures at the root.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for crimps made with the wrong tool, soldered crimps where the spec forbids them, nicked conductors, and no labels or test records. Be wary of engineers who size wire without checking temperature or bundle effects, or who never visit the build floor.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you know a crimp is good? Walk me through a harness you designed from wire list to first build. Tell me about a field failure caused by a harness and how you fixed it. Strong answers name standards, tests and specific changes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a wire harness engineer or technician?
qa.a: Look for hands-on harness experience in your industry, workmanship training to the IPC/WHMA-A-620 standard, and care with crimps, labels and test records. For engineers, check wire sizing, connector selection, routing and clear documentation. No license is required, so work samples, test results and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a wire harness engineer or technician before hiring?
qa.a: For technicians, run a short, paid bench test: build a small harness from a drawing, with crimps, a splice and labels, then continuity test it. For engineers, ask them to draft a wire list and routing plan for a simple system. Review workmanship, accuracy to the drawing and how they document their work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to lead marketing in the US, and degrees or certificates are optional. Verify results instead. Call past CEOs and sales leaders, confirm the budgets and teams they really owned, and ask which outcomes they drove and which they inherited.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they build a marketing plan from company goals, set and defend a budget, and tie spend to pipeline or revenue. Check attribution, positioning, input on pricing, hiring and managing agencies, and reporting to a board in plain terms.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong leaders talk about customers and revenue before channels. They show plans that changed once the data came in, name campaigns that failed and why, and have built teams whose members were promoted or went on to lead.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vanity metrics like impressions with no link to sales, credit taken for a whole company’s growth, constant tool or agency changes, and no clear view of how marketing and sales split the funnel. Also beware of plans copied from their last company.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you set last year’s budget, and what did you cut mid-year? Which metric did your CEO judge you on? Tell me about a launch that missed. Strong answers include the numbers they tracked and what they changed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a head of marketing?
qa.a: Look for someone who has owned a budget and a revenue target in a company like yours, in stage and sales motion. They should link marketing spend to pipeline, build and lead a team, and work well with sales and finance. No license is required, so references from past CEOs and sales leaders matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a head of marketing before hiring?
qa.a: Share real, non-confidential data and ask for a short plan for the first quarter: priorities, budget split, team needs and the metrics they would report. Have them present it to your leadership team. Judge their questions, how they tie spend to revenue and how they handle pushback.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short product strategy built from public information about your market. Look for a clear customer problem, a reason to act now, choices about what not to build, and how they would measure success. Strong candidates tie each bet to a business goal.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about outcomes, not features shipped. They can name a product they killed or delayed and explain why. They describe hiring, coaching and letting go of product managers. They explain how they kept engineering, design and sales aligned on one roadmap.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Product management certificates exist but are optional and vary widely in rigor. Verify past titles, team size and results through reference checks with former managers, engineering peers and people who reported to them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Every success is told as “I” with no team credit. They cannot say how a launch was measured or what happened after it. Watch for a roadmap that is a long feature list with no priorities, or blame on engineering and sales for every miss.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a time data and a senior executive disagreed on what to build, and how they decided. Ask how they set goals for their product managers. Ask them to walk through a roadmap they changed midyear and what that change cost.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a head of product?
qa.a: Look for proof they have led product managers, not just done the job themselves. They should connect product choices to revenue, retention or other business goals. They should be able to say no to good ideas and work well with engineering, design and sales. Check references from people who reported to them and from peers.

qa.q: How do I test a head of product before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, clearly limited exercise using public information, such as a one-page strategy for one customer segment. Then have them present it to the leaders they would work with. Watch how they handle pushback, trade-offs and questions they cannot answer. Avoid asking for unpaid work on your real roadmap.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Dietitians hold a national registered dietitian credential, and most states also license or certify them, so rules vary by state. Health coaches need no license, though an optional national board certification exists. In many states only licensed dietitians may provide medical nutrition therapy. Verify credentials online.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: For coaches, test motivational interviewing, goal setting and habit change methods. For dietitians, check nutrition assessment, medical nutrition therapy for diabetes, heart or kidney disease, meal planning and reading lab values. Both need clear documentation and comfort with telehealth if you offer it.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates listen more than they lecture, set small realistic goals and track progress. They stay within their scope and refer clients to doctors or dietitians when needed. They base advice on current evidence and adapt to each client’s food culture and budget.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for promises of fast weight loss, selling supplements to clients, or extreme diets. Be careful with coaches who give medical nutrition advice beyond their scope, or anyone who cannot explain the evidence behind their recommendations.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you help a client who keeps missing goals? Walk me through a first session. When do you refer a client to a doctor? For dietitians: how would you plan meals for a client with diabetes and kidney disease? Strong answers stay within scope and evidence.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a health coach or dietitian?
qa.a: Look for the right credential for the role: a dietitian credential and state license where required for medical nutrition therapy, or coaching training and certification for health coaches. Check motivational interviewing skills, evidence-based advice and respect for scope. References confirm real client results.

qa.q: How do I test a health coach or dietitian before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid role-play coaching session with a staff member acting as a client, then ask for a short plan and progress note. For dietitians, add a de-identified case that calls for a nutrition care plan. Judge listening, scope awareness, accuracy and clear writing.

look.label: Licenses to verify
look.text: Clinical roles need an active license, such as RN, NP, PA or MD, issued by a state board. Rules vary by state. For telehealth, the clinician usually must be licensed where the patient is located. Some nurses hold a multistate compact license. Check status and any discipline on the board’s online lookup.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test clear charting, patient privacy under HIPAA and safe triage. Ask them to document a mock visit or flag an urgent symptom in a patient message. For clinical research roles, check their grasp of informed consent and Good Clinical Practice.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Hands-on patient care paired with comfort in electronic health records and telehealth tools. Strong candidates explain clearly when they escalate to a physician, know the limits of their scope of practice in each state, and give useful feedback on product workflows.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: A license that is expired, restricted or held only in states where your patients are not. Vague answers about past duties or scope of practice. Casual talk about sharing patient data. Certifications the issuing body cannot confirm.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a time a patient’s condition got worse and what they did next. Ask how they handle a request outside their scope. Ask which records systems they have used and how they protected patient privacy.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a healthcare worker?
qa.a: Start with an active, unrestricted license that fits the role and the states where your patients are. Verify it on the state board’s website. Then look for real patient care experience, solid HIPAA knowledge, clear documentation and comfort with digital tools. For research or support roles, look for Good Clinical Practice training and sound judgment about when to escalate.

qa.q: How do I test a healthcare worker before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short, realistic scenario. Give a mock patient message or case and ask them to triage it, write a brief note and say when they would escalate. Never use real patient data. For research roles, ask them to review a sample consent form for problems. Pair the task with a license check and reference calls.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Nursing home administrators need a state license in every state, and many states license assisted living administrators too. Clinic and practice managers need no license, though optional healthcare management certifications exist. Verify licenses on state board sites, and check references from physicians, boards or owners.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test budgeting, staffing and scheduling, revenue cycle basics and reading financial reports. Check knowledge of health privacy and security rules, workplace safety rules, Medicare and Medicaid requirements, credentialing, and accreditation or state surveys. Ask them to analyze a sample report and propose fixes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates track clear measures, such as wait times, claim denials and staff turnover, and explain what they changed to improve them. They prepare for surveys year round, communicate well with clinicians and handle complaints and compliance issues quickly and fairly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague results with no measures, blaming staff for every problem, or weak knowledge of privacy and billing compliance. Be careful with poor survey histories they cannot explain, or anyone who suggests cutting corners on staffing rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a time you reduced claim denials or wait times. How do you prepare for a state survey or accreditation visit? How do you handle a privacy breach? How do you build a budget when payer rates are uncertain? Strong answers include measures and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a healthcare administrator?
qa.a: Look for the license your setting requires, such as a nursing home administrator license, plus proven results in budgeting, staffing, revenue and compliance. Check knowledge of privacy, Medicare, Medicaid and survey rules. References from physicians, owners or boards confirm leadership and fairness.

qa.q: How do I test a healthcare administrator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case study with a sample budget, staffing schedule and denial report, and ask for a short plan to fix the biggest problems. Add a compliance scenario, such as a privacy breach. Judge priorities, accuracy, legal knowledge and clear communication.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for help desk work. Entry-level IT support certifications show basic knowledge but are optional. Verify past support roles with references, and ask which systems, devices and ticket tools they supported and how many users they served.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test password resets and account lockouts in your directory service, laptop setup, printer and network basics, and common office software. Check they log clear tickets, follow a knowledge base, and know when to escalate rather than guess.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates stay calm and polite with frustrated users, ask short questions to narrow the problem, and confirm the fix works before closing the ticket. They write notes another technician can follow, verify identity before resets, and suggest knowledge base updates.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who skip identity checks before password resets, close tickets without confirming the fix, use jargon with nontechnical users, or blame users. Be careful with anyone who installs unapproved software or shares admin passwords to save time.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A user cannot print and says it worked yesterday; what do you check first? How do you confirm someone is who they say before a reset? Tell me about a ticket you escalated and why. Strong answers follow a clear order.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a help desk technician?
qa.a: Look for clear, patient communication, solid basics in accounts, laptops, printers, networks and office software, and good ticket notes. Check they follow security steps such as verifying identity. No license is required, so references, past support work and how they handle a mock call matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a help desk technician before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role play of a real support call, such as a locked account or a laptop that will not join Wi-Fi. Then ask them to write the ticket notes. Review how they ask questions, verify the user, explain steps simply, and know when to escalate.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check that the aide completed training that meets federal rules for Medicare- or Medicaid-certified agencies, at least 75 hours including 16 of supervised practice, or passed a competency evaluation. Check the state registry or certificate where your state keeps one.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Watch a candidate do a bed-to-chair transfer with a gait belt, a partial bed bath on a manikin and a set of vital signs. Ask them to write a visit note, and check they can use your visit verification app.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates are reliable, patient and respectful of a client’s home and choices. They know what to report to the nurse, stay within their tasks and speak kindly about past clients without sharing private details.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for missed shifts in past jobs, unsafe lifting, offering medical advice, carelessness with clients’ money or belongings, and talking about past clients by name. Be careful with anyone who dismisses abuse reporting.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Your client is more confused than usual and has not eaten. What do you do? How do you move a client from bed to wheelchair? A client with dementia refuses a bath. What do you try? Strong answers put safety first and bring in the nurse.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a home health aide?
qa.a: Look for training that meets federal and state rules, a clean background check, reliability and real kindness. Watch them do a transfer and a bath, and check they report changes to the nurse and respect the client’s home, money and privacy. References from past nurses or families say a lot.

qa.q: How do I test a home health aide before hiring?
qa.a: Run a skills check with your nurse: a bed-to-chair transfer with a gait belt, a partial bed bath on a manikin, vital signs and a written visit note. Then ask how they would handle a fall, a refusal and a sudden change, and listen for safe, calm steps.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many states and some counties require a food handler card soon after hire, and rules vary by state. Kitchen leads may need a food protection manager certificate. Anyone pouring alcohol may need state responsible beverage server training. Check what your location requires and ask for current cards.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Watch for safe knife work, correct holding temperatures, and timing several orders at once. For service roles, check order accuracy, clear speech with guests, and calm handling of a complaint. Everyone should clean as they go and know how to prevent cross-contact.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They label and date food without being told. They bring up allergens on their own. They stay friendly and steady when a rush hits. They can explain how they set up a station, and past shift leads speak well of them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers on handwashing, food temperatures or allergens. Blaming guests or coworkers for every problem. No clear story about a busy shift. Arriving late or unprepared to the trial shift. Letting a dropped utensil or spill sit while serving.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through their busiest shift. Ask what they do when a guest reports a nut allergy. Ask how they keep cold food cold on a catering or travel job. Real experience shows in specific, step by step answers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a hospitality worker?
qa.a: Look for solid food safety habits, a calm and friendly manner with guests, and the speed to handle a rush. Confirm any food handler card or alcohol server training your state or county requires. Strong candidates clean as they go, know allergen basics and give specific examples from past shifts.

qa.q: How do I test a hospitality worker before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short paid trial shift or working interview. Under federal and most state wage laws, productive work must be paid. Have cooks prep and plate a simple dish, and have servers take and deliver an order. Watch hygiene, timing, accuracy and how they treat guests and coworkers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for front desk or guest services work. Some states require hotel staff to complete human trafficking awareness training, and staff who serve alcohol may need state server training. Hospitality certifications are optional; references and service examples matter more.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test check-in and checkout on a property management system, reservations, room moves, payments and passing guest requests to other departments. Check calm complaint handling, upselling without pressure, key card security and protecting guest privacy, such as never saying room numbers aloud.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong agents greet guests warmly, solve problems without passing them along, and follow up to confirm the fix worked. They know the hotel and local area well, keep accurate notes for the next shift and stay polite with difficult guests.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for giving out room numbers or keys without verifying identity, arguing with guests, careless handling of card data, or blaming other departments. Be wary of anyone who cannot describe how they recovered a bad guest experience.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A guest arrives late, the hotel is full and their room is not ready. What do you do? How do you verify someone asking for a room key? Tell me about an upset guest you turned around. Strong answers show clear steps and judgment.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a hotel guest services agent?
qa.a: Look for warm, calm service, accuracy with reservations and payments, and good judgment on guest safety and privacy. Check experience with property management systems and complaint handling. No license is required, though some states require trafficking awareness or alcohol server training. References and a role-play reveal more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a hotel guest services agent before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short role-play of real situations: a check-in with a payment problem, an angry guest with a noisy room and a caller asking for another guest’s room number. If possible, add a paid trial shift. Review warmth, accuracy, privacy, problem solving and follow-up.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license for HR work. Many strong candidates hold a SHRM-CP, SHRM-SCP, PHR or SPHR certification, which you can confirm through the issuing body’s online lookup. Treat it as a plus, not a substitute for real experience advising leaders.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Coaching a manager through a performance problem, reading headcount and turnover data, and building a case for a pay change. Look for working knowledge of federal laws like FLSA, FMLA, Title VII and the ADA. They should also know that leave, pay transparency and final pay rules vary by state.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about the department’s goals, not just HR process. They can name a time they changed a leader’s decision with data or a clear risk argument. They push back with tact and keep confidential details out of their stories.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Sharing names or private details about past employees. Always siding with whichever leader is most senior. Advising a firing without documentation or skipping an investigation. Vague answers about results, or stories where every problem was someone else’s fault.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a reorganization they supported and how they told affected staff. Ask about a time a leader wanted to fire someone and they disagreed. Ask how they handled a pay gap they found between people in similar roles.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an HR business partner?
qa.a: Look for someone who understands how the department makes money or delivers its work, not just HR rules. They should coach managers, use data on turnover and pay, and handle hard cases calmly. Check that they know federal employment law and know where state rules differ. Certification helps, but proven advice to leaders matters more.

qa.q: How do I test an HR business partner before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. For example, a manager wants to cut two roles and fire a low performer in the same month. Ask the candidate how they would advise the manager, what documents they need, how they would check legal risk and how they would communicate it. Then role-play the conversation with a skeptical leader.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required, and this is often a first HR job. Entry-level HR certifications are optional. Verify reliability and accuracy through references, past administrative work, internships or HR coursework. Ask what systems and tasks they handled, such as onboarding, records or scheduling.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test accuracy in data entry and HR systems, onboarding checklists, timely Form I-9 completion, offer letters from templates, and organized employee files. Check spreadsheet basics, clear email writing and scheduling across several calendars. Discretion with personal data is essential.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong coordinators keep checklists, follow up before deadlines and catch errors in their own work. They protect personal information, ask when unsure instead of guessing, and give new hires a warm, organized first day. They stay calm when many requests arrive at once.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for careless typos in documents, missed follow-ups, or casual talk about employee information. Be wary of anyone who would request specific I-9 documents from new hires, store personal data in unsafe places, or guess at policy answers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you track many onboarding tasks at once? Tell me about an error you caught in a file or system. What would you do if a manager asked to see a coworker’s file? Strong answers show organization, checking habits and respect for privacy.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an HR coordinator?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, organization, discretion with personal data and clear writing. Check comfort with HR systems, spreadsheets and onboarding steps, including timely Form I-9 completion. No license is required and this is often a first HR job, so references, internships and a short practical task tell you more than credentials.

qa.q: How do I test an HR coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: a sample new hire record with a few planted errors, an onboarding checklist to complete and a welcome email to draft. Review how many errors they catch, how organized and polite the email is, and whether they flag missing items or privacy concerns.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as an HR director or manager. Optional certifications such as SHRM-CP, SHRM-SCP, PHR or SPHR show tested HR knowledge. Verify them with the issuing body. Confirm past titles, team size and scope with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask the candidate to sketch a hiring plan for a growing team, outline a fair pay structure, and walk through a harassment complaint investigation. Strong answers cover documentation, consistent treatment and when to call employment counsel.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They know federal rules like FLSA overtime, FMLA, Title VII and the ADA. They also note that state laws vary on paid leave, pay transparency and final paychecks. They describe results such as lower turnover or faster hiring, and tie HR work to business goals.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about who they managed or what changed under them. Sharing confidential details about past employees. Treating policies as paperwork instead of practice. Suggesting interview questions about age, family plans, health, religion or other traits the law protects.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a layoff or restructuring you led. How did you handle a manager who kept ignoring policy? What HR system or process did you build, and what did it fix? Listen for clear steps, legal awareness and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an HR director?
qa.a: Look for proven leadership of an HR team, solid knowledge of federal employment law, and awareness that state rules vary. Check for experience with hiring plans, pay structures, policies and investigations. Certifications like SHRM-CP or PHR help but are optional. Strong candidates show measurable results and link HR decisions to business goals.

qa.q: How do I test an HR manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give every candidate the same short case. For example, ask them to review a sample policy, respond to a written employee complaint, or present a 90-day plan for your company. Score how they handle facts, fairness, documentation and legal risk. Follow up with reference checks that confirm their scope and results.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work in HR. Professional HR certifications are optional but show study of employment law and practice. Verify experience through references, and ask which policies, leave cases and onboarding processes the candidate owned, and in which states.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test knowledge of federal and state leave laws, wage and hour rules including exempt and nonexempt classification, Form I-9 verification, accommodation requests and benefits enrollment. Check HR system skills, clear policy writing and handling of confidential employee data. State and local rules vary widely.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong generalists know when an issue needs legal counsel, keep accurate records, and give managers practical, consistent answers. They track rule changes in every state where you have staff, handle sensitive conversations calmly and treat employees fairly and confidentially.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for confident answers that ignore state differences, careless handling of medical or personal records, or advice to skip documentation. Be wary of anyone who asks new hires for specific I-9 documents or treats accommodation requests as optional.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a leave request that overlapped with an accommodation request. How do you classify a role as exempt or nonexempt? How do you keep up with state law changes? Strong answers name steps, documents and when they involved counsel.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an HR generalist?
qa.a: Look for working knowledge of leave, wage and hour, I-9 and accommodation rules, plus accurate records and calm handling of sensitive issues. Check experience in the states where you employ people, since rules vary. No license is required, so references and examples of policies or processes they built matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an HR generalist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise with a few realistic scenarios, such as a leave request, a pay classification question and a manager’s complaint. Ask for written responses and next steps. Review legal accuracy, consistency, confidentiality, tone and whether they know when to involve counsel or a benefits provider.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required for this work. Software vendors offer certifications for their HRIS platforms, and some are only available through partner programs. So ask which systems they have configured, not just used. General HR certifications help, but they don’t prove technical or data skills.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for the ability to clean messy exports, match HRIS records to payroll data, and use spreadsheet formulas or SQL. They should calculate headcount, FTE, time to fill and voluntary turnover correctly. They should also define each metric the same way every time.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask how you define a metric before building the report. They document fields, workflows and access roles. They understand effective dates and why history matters. They can explain a pay or turnover trend to managers in plain language, including its limits.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who show real employee data from a past employer as a work sample. Other warning signs are giving broad system access for convenience, skipping checks against payroll, or sharing small-group breakdowns that could identify individual employees.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a system rollout or upgrade they worked on and what went wrong. Ask how they set up role-based security. Ask how they fixed a report that didn’t match payroll. Ask how they supported compliance reporting, such as EEO-1 if your company files it.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an HRIS and people analytics specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on setup experience with an HRIS, not just daily use. They need strong spreadsheet or SQL skills and clear definitions for headcount and turnover. Careful handling of sensitive employee data is a must. No license is required. Vendor certifications can show platform knowledge. Clear writing for managers matters as much as technical skill.

qa.q: How do I test an HRIS and people analytics specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a small, made-up employee dataset with planted errors, such as duplicates, missing dates and mismatched job codes. Ask them to clean it and calculate headcount, turnover and time to fill. Then ask for a one-page summary for leaders. Never use real employee data. Review their logic, their checks and how they protect privacy.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses HR specialists, so no license is required. Voluntary certifications such as the aPHR, PHR or SHRM-CP show tested knowledge. Verify any certification with the issuing body. Also confirm past HR roles, the size of workforces they supported and whether they worked in your state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them classify sample jobs as exempt or nonexempt under federal wage rules. Ask them to explain how Form I-9 is completed and to draft a short policy in plain language. Check that they know leave, final pay and many hiring rules vary by state.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They document conversations and investigations carefully and keep employee records confidential. They apply written policies the same way to everyone. They know when to involve an employment lawyer. They describe disputes they settled by hearing both sides before acting.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for casual talk about sharing employee files, promises of certain legal outcomes, or advice to ask applicants about age, family plans, health or religion. Be wary of anyone who always sides with managers or cannot explain how they kept an investigation fair.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a harassment complaint about a senior manager, rolled out a new policy, or prepared for a termination meeting. Strong answers give concrete steps, the records they kept, who they told and what they would do differently next time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an HR specialist?
qa.a: Look for solid knowledge of federal employment law, such as wage and hour rules, anti-discrimination law and Form I-9, plus awareness that many rules vary by state. They should handle confidential records with care, write clear policies, document everything and stay fair in disputes. Certifications like the PHR or SHRM-CP help but are optional.

qa.q: How do I test an HR specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case: an employee complaint, a few facts and a policy excerpt. Ask how they would investigate, what they would document and when they would involve a lawyer. Add a task to rewrite a confusing policy in plain language. Judge their fairness, accuracy and attention to confidentiality.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Anyone who handles refrigerant must hold EPA Section 608 certification, a federal rule. Ask which type. Type II covers most rooftop and split systems, Type III covers low-pressure chillers, and Universal covers all. HVAC licensing varies by state and sometimes by city, so check local rules and verify any license with the issuing board.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give a fault scenario on a rooftop unit or split system and ask how they would diagnose it. Watch them read a wiring diagram, use a multimeter and gauges, and calculate superheat or subcooling. For larger sites, ask about chillers, boilers, building automation controls or precision cooling in data centers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain the cause of a failure, not just the part they swapped. They recover refrigerant properly, follow lockout/tagout, and write clear work orders. They talk calmly with building staff and know when a job needs a second tech or a specialist.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treating refrigerant recovery as optional or joking about venting. Vague answers about which certification they hold. Replacing parts without testing first. Skipping lockout/tagout, ladder or roof safety. Pushback on keeping service records, which many commercial clients and data centers expect.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about the hardest no-heat or no-cool call they solved and how they found the cause. Ask which system types they have worked on most. Ask how they handle a client who wants a quick fix the equipment cannot safely support.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an HVAC technician?
qa.a: Start with EPA Section 608 certification if the job involves refrigerant, plus any license your state or city requires. Then look for hands-on experience with your type of equipment, from rooftop units to chillers or data center cooling. Strong techs diagnose before replacing parts, work safely, and keep clear service records.

qa.q: How do I test an HVAC technician before hiring?
qa.a: Use a paid working interview or a supervised hands-on test on a training unit. Ask them to find a planted fault, read a wiring diagram and take pressure and temperature readings. Have them explain the findings as they would to a client. Then check their certification card and call references from past employers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license for IAM work. Helpful certifications include CISSP, Security+ and vendor certifications for the identity platform you run. Confirm each one through the issuer’s online verification tool, and weigh them below proven hands-on experience.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them set up single sign-on for a sample app using SAML or OpenID Connect, require multi-factor login, and automate account creation and removal with SCIM or a script. Watch how they troubleshoot failed logins and expiring certificates.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They think in least privilege and role-based access. They can explain joiner, mover and leaver processes, have run regular access reviews, and document every change. They talk about protecting admin accounts and emergency access, not just switching features on.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Handing out broad admin rights to save time, relying on shared accounts, having no plan to remove access when people leave, or giving vague answers about how SAML or OAuth tokens work. Be wary of anyone who tests changes in production first.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they would roll out single sign-on without locking everyone out, how they found and removed stale accounts, and what they did after a login outage or suspicious sign-in. Real answers include clear steps, tools used and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an IAM engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with single sign-on, multi-factor login, directory services and automated account setup and removal. Strong candidates apply least privilege, run access reviews and document changes. Certifications such as CISSP or vendor credentials help, but no state license is required. Proven experience with your identity platform matters most.

qa.q: How do I test an IAM engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid practical task in a test environment. Ask them to connect a sample app through SAML or OpenID Connect, enforce multi-factor login, and write a simple script that removes access for a departing user. Then have them walk you through their choices, risks and how they would roll it out safely.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work. If a candidate lists vendor certifications for software platforms or a project management certification, confirm them through the issuer’s online lookup. Treat certifications as a plus, not proof. Use references to confirm real go-live work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for data mapping and cleanup in spreadsheets, basic SQL, reading API documentation, configuring integrations, and running a training session. Have them map messy sample data to your import template and explain what they would flag for the customer.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about go-live dates they hit, scope they protected, and customers who kept using the product afterward. They write clear project plans, document decisions, and know when to escalate a technical blocker to engineering instead of guessing.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about their own role on past projects and blaming every delay on the customer. Other warnings are skipping backups or sandbox testing before a migration and careless handling of customer personal data or passwords.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a migration that went wrong and how they recovered. Ask how they handle a customer who keeps adding requests mid-project. Ask how they confirm migrated data is complete and accurate before sign-off.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an implementation consultant?
qa.a: Look for a mix of technical and people skills. They should handle data mapping, integrations and testing. They should also explain the setup to non-technical staff and train them well. Ask for examples of projects they took from kickoff to go-live. Check references from managers or customers who saw that work.

qa.q: How do I test an implementation consultant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short exercise that uses fake data. Ask them to clean and map a sample file to your import format. Have them outline a project plan with milestones and deliver a ten-minute training on one feature. Score accuracy, clarity and the questions they ask. Never share real customer data.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: A CPA license is common, and state boards set the rules, so check it with the issuing state. Some specialists are attorneys or IRS Enrolled Agents. Ask whether they hold a sales tax or transfer pricing certification from a professional tax association, and confirm it is current.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for sales and use tax nexus analysis, including economic nexus thresholds that vary by state, product taxability, exemption certificates and use tax accruals. On the transfer pricing side, look for arm’s length analysis under IRC Section 482, choice of method, benchmarking with comparables and intercompany agreements.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain clearly how US sales tax differs from VAT and GST. They have set up or cleaned up a tax engine or taxability matrix. They have written transfer pricing documentation that someone else could defend in an audit, and they keep tidy workpapers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treating every state the same, or claiming one national sales tax rule. Not knowing that documentation must be in place when the return is filed to help avoid IRS penalties. Vague answers about past audits, or blaming every problem on software or other teams.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they would decide whether to register in a new state after sales grow there. Ask how they picked the tested party and method in a recent study. Ask them to describe a sales tax or transfer pricing audit they handled and how it was resolved.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an indirect tax and transfer pricing specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with state sales and use tax, including nexus, taxability and exemption certificates, plus transfer pricing under IRC Section 482 and arm’s length rules. A CPA, attorney or Enrolled Agent credential helps, and state rules vary. Strong candidates have prepared documentation, handled audits and can explain complex rules in plain words.

qa.q: How do I test an indirect tax and transfer pricing specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Share a list of products, states where you sell and sales by state, and ask where you may need to register and why. Then describe a simple intercompany sale and ask which method they would use, which party they would test and what documentation they would prepare. Review their reasoning, not just the answer.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for industrial designers. Most hold a bachelor’s degree in industrial design, but the portfolio matters far more. Ask for process work such as sketches, models and prototypes, confirm credits on shipped products, and call references about their part in team projects.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test sketching, 3D CAD modeling for surfaces and parts, rendering and physical prototyping. Check knowledge of materials and manufacturing methods such as injection molding, plus ergonomics and cost. Ask them to explain how a design changed to meet engineering or factory limits.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show research with real users, many early ideas, and how designs changed through testing. They work closely with mechanical engineers, know how parts are made, and design for assembly and cost. Their portfolios include products that actually shipped.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolios with only polished renders and no process, designs that cannot be made at a reasonable cost, or vague answers about their role on team products. Be careful with designers who ignore materials, ergonomics, safety or feedback from engineering.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a product from first sketch to production. What changed after talking with the factory? How did you choose the material and finish? Strong answers name constraints, tradeoffs, testing and what shipped.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an industrial designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio that shows process, from research and sketches to models and shipped products, not just renders. Check CAD skills, knowledge of materials and manufacturing, and close work with engineers. No license is required, so confirmed credits on shipped products and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an industrial designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid brief close to your products, such as redesigning a handle or small housing for comfort and lower cost. Ask for sketches, a simple CAD model and notes on material and process. Review creativity, manufacturability and how they explain their choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license applies to this work. A facility security officer must hold a personnel clearance at the level of the facility’s clearance and complete required government training. Confirm clearance status through the government’s clearance system, never from a résumé alone, and verify training certificates.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test their knowledge of the NISPOM, now federal regulation 32 CFR Part 117, including reporting duties, visits, insider threat program basics and safeguarding classified material. Check they can process clearance requests in government systems, run self-inspections, and prepare for government security reviews.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates keep records ready for review, report events on time, and train employees so they understand their reporting duties. They work well with government security staff, explain rules in plain words, and know when a matter must be reported rather than handled quietly inside the company.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who discuss classified details from past jobs, claim a clearance that does not show in the government system, or treat reporting as optional. Be careful with sloppy records, missed reporting deadlines or weak answers about handling a possible security violation.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: An employee reports classified data on an unclassified system; what do you do? How do you prepare for a government security review? How do you run insider threat training? Strong answers follow required steps without revealing classified details.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an industrial security and clearance specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work under the federal rules for cleared contractors, experience in the government clearance systems, and good results from past security reviews. They must be able to hold a clearance at your facility’s level, so confirm status through official channels. Judgment, discretion and accurate records matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an industrial security and clearance specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Use realistic, unclassified scenarios, such as a reported security violation, a cleared employee’s foreign travel, or a visit request from another contractor. Ask them to explain the required steps, reports and timelines. Review accuracy against current rules, their judgment, and whether they keep classified details out of the discussion.

look.label: Industry knowledge to probe
look.text: Ask how buyers in your target industry decide, who signs off, and what rules shape their choices, such as compliance review at banks. A strong candidate explains the buying group, its pain points and its words without reading from notes.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test messaging, positioning and content for one vertical. Ask for a short solution brief or landing page draft aimed at a specific buyer. Check whether they turn product features into business outcomes that audience already cares about.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They tie past campaigns to pipeline or revenue, not just clicks. They describe working with sales, product and customer success, and interviewing customers. They can name the kinds of events, publications and communities where their audience spends time.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Generic messaging that could fit any industry, jargon they can’t explain plainly, or bold claims on regulated topics with no plan for legal review. Be wary if they can’t describe a past result or credit every success only to themselves.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for this role in the US. Optional marketing certificates exist but prove little alone. Review work samples, confirm results with references, and make sure portfolio pieces don’t reveal a past employer’s confidential data.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an industry and solutions marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for real knowledge of your target industry, sharp positioning and writing skills, and proof of close work with sales. Strong candidates show campaigns that moved pipeline and can explain buyer roles, objections and buying cycles in the audience’s own language. Ask for samples and confirm results with references.

qa.q: How do I test an industry and solutions marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-limited task, paid if it takes real effort. Share a product overview and a target segment, then ask for a one-page positioning statement, three key messages and a launch plan outline. Score how well they understand the buyer, pick channels and tie the work to measurable goals.

look.label: Real industry depth
look.text: Look for years spent working inside the target industry or technology, not just selling to it. Strong candidates have built, run or bought the systems your customers use. They can explain the rules, budgets and daily pain points of that field without notes.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them lead a mock discovery call with a senior buyer. Then ask them to whiteboard how your product fits that buyer’s systems or workflow. Watch whether they ask sharp questions, handle hard objections honestly and turn technical detail into business outcomes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They speak, write or present on the topic and keep ties with people who do the work. They can name deals they helped win by changing a customer’s thinking. They admit what a product cannot do and know when to bring in engineers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Industry or technical certifications, such as in security or cloud platforms, can support a résumé but are not standard. Confirm any listed certification with the issuing body and check past results through references from sales leaders.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for buzzwords without specifics, no hands-on history in the field, or deal wins they cannot explain step by step. Be wary of candidates who overpromise features, attack competitors without facts, or cannot simplify a complex idea for a nontechnical executive.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an industry specialist?
qa.a: Look for someone who has worked in the industry or technology your customers live in, so buyers treat them as a peer. They should explain complex topics simply, ask strong discovery questions and support the sales team without taking over. Check references from past sales leaders and customers to confirm real impact on deals.

qa.q: How do I test an industry specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Run a role play where they lead a discovery call with a skeptical senior buyer from your target industry. Follow with a short presentation on a real trend in that field and how your product addresses it. Score their questions, accuracy, honesty about limits and ability to speak to both technical and business listeners.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check hands-on work with GPU profiling, request batching, KV cache management, quantization to lower precision, and speculative decoding. Strong candidates can read a profiler trace, find whether a model is limited by memory or by compute, and write or tune low-level code when the serving framework is not enough.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk in measurements: latency at the median and the 99th percentile, tokens per second, GPU utilization and cost per request. They explain trade-offs between speed, cost and answer quality, and they rerun quality evaluations after every optimization instead of assuming nothing broke.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who only talks about training models or writing prompts, claims big speedups without a baseline or a test setup, ignores quality loss after quantization, or has never handled production problems like out-of-memory crashes, slow cold starts or traffic spikes.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, ’Walk me through the last time you cut latency or cost. What was the bottleneck, how did you find it, and what did you measure before and after?’ Then ask how they pick a batch size when they must meet a strict latency target.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for this work, and cloud or vendor certificates are optional. Verify skill through code samples, open-source contributions, published benchmarks they ran, and references from past teams who saw their systems handle real production traffic.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an inference engineer?
qa.a: Look for proven work making real models faster and cheaper in production. They should know batching, caching, quantization and GPU profiling, and back every claim with before and after numbers. Good candidates also guard answer quality, plan for traffic spikes, and can explain their trade-offs clearly to people outside the team.

qa.q: How do I test an inference engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small open model, a basic serving setup and a target, such as halving latency at the same quality. Ask them to profile it, find the bottleneck, apply fixes and report measured results with a quality check. Review their reasoning and notes as closely as the final speed numbers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Verify past campaigns instead. Ask for campaign briefs, creator contracts with names removed and results reports, and call creators or brands they worked with. Confirm they know the FTC Endorsement Guides, which require clear disclosure of paid or gifted posts.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they find creators who fit the audience, check for fake followers and bought engagement, and agree fees, deliverables, usage rights and exclusivity. Check briefing, content review, tracking links or codes, and reporting results against the goal.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates pick creators by audience fit and past results, not follower count. They write clear contracts, give creators room to sound like themselves, insist on proper disclosure and can show which campaigns drove sales or sign-ups.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for anyone who skips disclosure or tells creators to hide it, cannot explain usage rights, judges creators only by reach, or has no reporting beyond likes. Be wary of vague answers about payments, missed posts or brand safety checks.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you spot fake engagement? What goes into a creator contract? Tell me about a creator who missed a deadline or posted something off-brief. Strong answers name specific checks, contract terms and how they fixed the problem.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an influencer marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for proof of campaigns that drove real results, a sharp eye for creator fit and fake engagement, and solid knowledge of contracts, usage rights and FTC disclosure rules. They should build lasting creator relationships and report clearly. No license is required, so case studies and references from creators and brands matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an influencer marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: pick a handful of creators for a sample product, explain why each fits, flag any risks and outline the brief, deliverables, disclosure and how results will be measured. Judge their research, their checks for fake followers and whether the plan ties to a business goal.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work. Common certifications include Security+, CISSP, CISM and GIAC credentials. Most issuers offer online verification, so confirm the name, number and current status. Federal contract roles may require a security clearance, which only the government can grant.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can read alerts and logs from security monitoring tools, triage a suspicious email, and rank risks by business impact. They should map controls to a framework such as NIST CSF or ISO 27001, write a clear policy, and explain findings to non-technical managers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through an incident they handled. How was it detected? Who did they notify? What did they contain first? What changed afterward? Strong answers name specific tools and steps and admit what went wrong.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They know the rules that fit your industry, such as HIPAA for health data or PCI DSS for card payments. They know that breach notification laws vary by state. They document carefully, keep evidence intact and keep their skills current.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for many certifications with no hands-on examples, or blaming users for every incident. Be wary of vague answers about handling evidence, and of any willingness to bypass approvals. Sharing confidential details about a past employer’s breaches is also a warning sign.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an information security analyst?
qa.a: Look for hands-on incident experience, not just certifications. Verify credentials such as Security+ or CISSP with the issuer. Check that they know frameworks like NIST CSF and the rules for your industry. They should write clear policies and explain risk in plain language. Good judgment and discretion with confidential information matter as much as technical skill.

qa.q: How do I test an information security analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic exercise. Share a sample phishing email or a few log entries and ask what happened, how serious it is and what they would do first. You can also ask them to draft a one-page policy, such as password or access rules. Never use your live systems or real company data for the test.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test live phone skills, not just interview polish. Watch how they open a cold call, ask discovery questions, handle a price objection and ask for a next step. Also check that they can write a short, clear follow-up email and log notes cleanly in a CRM.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong reps talk about their past work in numbers: daily calls or emails, meetings booked, conversion rates and quota attainment. They explain how they qualify leads and when they drop a weak one. They ask sharp questions about your product, buyers and sales cycle.

look.label: Rules and licenses to check
look.text: Most inside sales roles need no license. Selling insurance requires a state license, and selling securities requires FINRA registration. Reps calling consumers should know Do Not Call and TCPA basics. Some states require telemarketer registration or set extra calling rules, so this varies by state.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about results, blaming leads or managers for every missed target, and talking over you during a mock call. Other warning signs are reading a pitch word for word, giving up after the first no, or never following up after the interview.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a typical day of calls and emails. Ask about a deal they lost and what they changed afterward. Ask how they get past a gatekeeper and how they decide which leads to call first.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an inside sales representative?
qa.a: Look for clear speaking, steady follow-up and comfort with rejection. Good candidates can share real numbers from past roles, such as calls made, meetings booked and quota reached. They should know how to use a CRM and write tight emails. If they will call consumers, check that they understand Do Not Call and TCPA rules.

qa.q: How do I test an inside sales representative before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role play. Give them a one-page product summary, then play a busy buyer with a common objection. Score how they open, ask questions, handle pushback and close for a next step. Then ask them to write the follow-up email within a set time. This shows real skill better than a resume.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as an instructional designer. Degrees and certificates in instructional design are optional. Verify skill through a portfolio with real courses, storyboards and assessments, and ask references what results the training achieved and which parts the candidate built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test writing measurable learning objectives, sequencing content, building practice and assessments that match the objectives, and storyboarding. Check authoring tool and learning platform skills, accessibility for people with disabilities, and evaluation that shows whether behavior changed on the job, not just course completion.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong designers start with the performance problem and the audience, not the slides. They work well with subject experts, cut content that does not serve the objective, test drafts with learners, and show evidence that people can do the task after training.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolios of polished slides with no objectives, practice or assessment, or courses that only measure completion. Be wary of anyone who ignores accessibility, cannot explain their design choices, or shows client work they were not allowed to share.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a course from needs analysis to evaluation. How did you handle a subject expert who wanted to include everything? How did you know learners could do the task afterward? Strong answers show process, tradeoffs and evidence.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an instructional designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio with measurable objectives, realistic practice, matched assessments and evidence of results. Check authoring and learning platform skills, accessibility habits and how they work with subject experts. No license is required, so portfolio work, references and their design reasoning matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an instructional designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise: share a brief process document and describe the target audience. Ask for learning objectives, an outline, one storyboarded lesson and a few assessment questions. Review whether objectives are measurable, practice fits the job, assessments match the objectives and the material is accessible.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many states require claims adjusters to hold a license, and the rules vary by state and by adjuster type. Confirm license status and lines of authority on the state insurance department’s lookup. Underwriters usually need no state license, but designations such as CPCU or AIC show formal training.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how well they read policy language, apply exclusions and limits, and do the math on deductibles, premiums and settlement amounts. Check that they can weigh risk factors, write clear file notes and explain a decision in plain words a policyholder can follow.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates cite the exact policy section behind each decision. They know that fair claims handling rules and response deadlines differ by state. They document every step, ask for missing facts before deciding, and stay calm and polite with upset claimants.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with anyone vague about their license status, who guesses at coverage instead of checking the policy, or who talks about paying or denying claims to hit a target. Careless handling of personal or medical records is another warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a claim they denied and how they explained it. Ask about a risk they declined or priced higher and why. Ask how they track state deadlines and what they do when facts in a file conflict.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an insurance specialist?
qa.a: Look for a valid state license if the role adjusts claims, since many states require one and rules vary. Then check that they read policies closely, price risk with sound reasoning, keep clean file notes and explain decisions clearly. Training designations help, but real case examples show more.

qa.q: How do I test an insurance specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a sample policy and a short claim file or application. Ask them to decide coverage or price the risk, show their math, and write the note they would send the customer. Score accuracy, the policy sections they cite, and how clear and fair the explanation is.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Every state requires an insurance producer license for each line sold, such as life and health or property and casualty, plus a nonresident license for clients in other states. Check status on the state insurance department’s lookup. Selling variable products also needs securities registration.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they assess a client’s risks, compare policy options and explain deductibles, limits and exclusions in plain words. Check quoting and agency management systems, careful paperwork, follow-up on renewals and claims, and knowledge of rules for replacing existing policies.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates put the client’s needs first, document what they recommended and why, and keep their continuing education current. They keep clients for years, earn referrals and can explain any product they sell without reading the brochure.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a lapsed license, complaints or discipline on record, pushing the highest-commission product, and promises about coverage the policy does not give. Be wary of anyone who suggests replacing policies without a clear benefit to the client.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you decide how much coverage a client needs? Tell me about a claim a client thought was covered but was not. How do you handle a policy replacement? Strong answers show care, documentation and clear explanations.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an insurance agent?
qa.a: Look for an active state producer license in the lines you sell, nonresident licenses where you have clients, and a clean record with the state insurance department.
