They should explain coverage clearly, recommend what fits the client and keep careful records. License and continuing education rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test an insurance agent before hiring?
qa.a: Run a role-play with a sample client, such as a family or a small business. Ask them to gather needs, recommend coverage and explain exclusions and deductibles in plain words. Then ask for a short written summary of the recommendation. Judge accuracy, suitability, honesty and how well they listen.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Anyone preparing and prosecuting patents for others before the USPTO must be a registered patent agent or patent attorney, so check the USPTO’s public roster. Only licensed attorneys can represent others in trademark filings or sue infringers. Bar licenses are issued state by state, so confirm active standing with the state bar.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short claim set or a trademark clearance memo on a sample product. Look at prior art searching, clear claim language, likelihood of confusion analysis, and how they track deadlines for office action responses, maintenance fees and trademark renewals.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask about your technology, market and budget before suggesting a filing. They explain trade-offs, such as a provisional versus a nonprovisional application, in plain words. They keep a reliable docket and can show past work with client details removed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Promises that a patent or trademark will surely be granted. No USPTO registration number when they claim patent work. Vague answers about how they meet response deadlines. Sharing confidential details from other clients, or skipping a conflict check before taking on your matter.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a tough office action they overcame. Ask how they would handle a copycat product sold online, from gathering evidence to a takedown notice or demand letter. Ask when they would advise against filing at all.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an intellectual property and patent specialist?
qa.a: Match the credential to the work. Patent prosecution needs a USPTO registered patent agent or attorney. Trademark filings for others and lawsuits need a licensed attorney, and bar admission is by state. Then look for knowledge of your technical field, careful deadline tracking, clear writing and honest advice about the odds of success.

qa.q: How do I test an intellectual property and patent specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task using non-confidential information, or sign an NDA first. Ask for a draft claim or a prior art summary for a sample invention, or a clearance opinion on a proposed brand name. Judge accuracy, plain language, the risks they flag and whether they note the filing deadlines.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for intelligence analysts. Government and contractor roles often need a security clearance, which you confirm through official channels. Private sector roles may value analytic training, but verify past work instead: ask for unclassified writing samples and call references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test structured analytic techniques, source evaluation, and clear writing with stated confidence levels. Check they can sort reliable from unreliable sources, separate facts from judgments, use open source research tools lawfully, and brief findings in a few minutes to a busy decision maker.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write the bottom line first, explain how confident they are and why, and update judgments when new facts arrive. They protect sources and methods, respect privacy laws, and can say what evidence would change their mind.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who present guesses as facts, rely on one source, or share sensitive details from past roles. Be careful with anyone who suggests collecting personal data illegally, such as pretexting or accessing accounts, or who cannot separate analysis from personal opinion.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an assessment that turned out wrong and what you learned. How do you rate a source you cannot verify? How do you brief a leader who disagrees with you? Strong answers show method, humility and clear reasoning.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an intelligence analyst?
qa.a: Look for clear, short writing, sound source evaluation and the habit of stating confidence and assumptions. Check they collect information lawfully and protect sensitive material. Government work may need a clearance, confirmed through official channels. Otherwise no license is required, so unclassified writing samples and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an intelligence analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a packet of open source material on a realistic threat or event, including some unreliable items. Ask for a one-page assessment with key judgments, confidence levels and gaps. Review whether they spotted weak sources, separated facts from judgments, and wrote for a busy reader.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for proof they finish things: a class project, club role, volunteer work or part-time job held for a season or more. Strong candidates can explain what they did, ask good questions about the work, and show curiosity about how your business runs.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the basics the role will use from day one. That may be writing a clear email, following written steps, using a spreadsheet, or a short task tied to the job. Give every candidate the same task and score it the same way.

look.label: Questions that reveal potential
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a project they finished. Ask what they did when they got stuck, and about feedback they got and what they changed. Ask what they want to learn in this role. Real answers include specific details.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who cannot explain their own listed work, blames teammates for every problem, misses the deadline on a short test task without a word, or shows no interest in learning. Poor follow-up during scheduling often predicts poor follow-up on the job.

look.label: Rules to check before hiring
look.text: Paid interns are employees and need a Form I-9 like any hire. An unpaid internship at a for-profit business must meet the federal Department of Labor’s primary beneficiary test, and some states set stricter rules. If the school grants credit, review its agreement.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an intern or new grad?
qa.a: Look for reliability and a willingness to learn more than long experience. Ask about class projects, part-time jobs or club roles and how they handled problems. Good candidates explain their own work clearly, take feedback well and ask thoughtful questions about the role and your team.

qa.q: How do I test an intern or new grad before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or clearly limited task that matches real work, such as drafting an email, organizing data or summarizing a document. Use the same instructions and deadline for everyone. Score it on accuracy, clarity and whether they followed directions, then discuss their choices in a follow-up conversation.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for internal communications work. Optional communication certifications exist, but writing samples matter more. Ask for real all-staff emails, newsletters, leadership talking points and a change plan, with confidential details removed, and call references from leaders they wrote for.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test clear writing for a mixed audience, editing a leader’s draft without losing their voice, and planning messages for a reorganization or policy change. Check they can run an all-hands, use intranet and email tools, and measure whether staff read and understood.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates ask who must hear news first, such as managers before staff. They keep messages short, plan for questions and feedback, and know when legal or HR must review. They earn trust from leaders and front-line staff alike.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for writing full of jargon, plans that only push news out with no way to listen, and loose talk about a past employer’s confidential matters. Be wary of anyone who would announce layoffs without HR and legal review, since federal and some state laws set notice rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you announced a big change, step by step. How did you prepare managers? How did you know the message landed? Strong answers mention sequencing, manager briefings, FAQs, timing for different shifts or time zones, and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an internal communications manager?
qa.a: Look for clear, plain writing, sound judgment about timing and confidentiality, and experience guiding staff through change. They should work well with leaders, HR and legal, plan messages for every group of employees, and measure whether people understood. No license is required, so writing samples and references from leaders matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an internal communications manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task based on a made-up change, such as a new office policy or a team merger. Ask for a leader’s email, a manager briefing with likely questions and a simple rollout timeline. Judge clarity, tone, the order of messages and how well they anticipate staff concerns.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many strong candidates hold a CPA license, the Certified Internal Auditor (CIA) or, for IT controls work, the CISA. CPA licenses are issued by each state’s board of accountancy and rules vary by state, so check the issuing board’s public lookup. No license is legally required for this role.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to walk through a process such as order-to-cash, map the risks and name the key controls. Look for clear tests of design and operating effectiveness, sensible sample sizes and documentation an external auditor could reperform.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They speak easily about the COSO framework, IT general controls, segregation of duties and management review controls. They can explain how they judged a deficiency as a significant deficiency or a material weakness, and how they helped process owners fix gaps.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treating SOX as a yearly checklist, vague answers about evidence, or no grasp of preventive versus detective controls. Be wary of anyone who can’t explain what makes a control key, or who blames process owners for every failed test.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a control that failed testing and what happened next. Ask how they scoped a SOX program, how they chose in-scope accounts and locations, and how they handled an external auditor’s request for more evidence.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an SOX and internal controls specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience testing controls over financial reporting, not just reading about them. Strong candidates know the COSO framework, IT general controls and segregation of duties. They write clean work papers and explain deficiencies in plain terms. A CPA, CIA or CISA helps, and CPA licenses should be checked with the issuing state board, since rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test an SOX and internal controls specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case: a process narrative, a sample of invoices or journal entries, and one control description. Ask them to find the risks, judge whether the control is designed well, pick a sample and record the results. Check whether their work papers are clear enough for an auditor to reperform.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for inventory work. Optional supply chain certifications show study of methods. If the role uses forklifts, the employer must train and evaluate operators under OSHA rules, so ask about past training. References from warehouse or materials managers matter most.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test cycle counting, reconciling count variances, receiving and putaway, and transactions in your ERP or warehouse management system. Check spreadsheet skills such as lookups and pivot tables, ABC classification, lot and serial tracking, and first in, first out rotation for dated stock.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates find the root cause of a variance before adjusting records. They keep locations clean and labeled, follow transaction rules exactly and spot patterns, such as repeat errors at receiving. They explain shrink and accuracy trends clearly to managers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for anyone who adjusts records to match counts without investigating, skips paperwork for quick moves, or cannot explain how records drift from shelves. Careless data entry in a test and blaming others for every variance are also warning signs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a large count variance and how you found the cause. How would you set up a cycle count program? What do you do when a part shows in stock but cannot be found? Strong answers walk through each step.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an inventory specialist?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, patience and system skills: cycle counting, variance research and clean transactions in your inventory software. Check spreadsheet ability and lot or serial tracking if you need it. No license is required, so references and a short test matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an inventory specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid exercise with a sample stock list, count sheet and transaction history, and ask them to find and explain the variances. Add a short spreadsheet task. Review accuracy, how they trace root causes and whether they suggest fixes, not just adjustments.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most states license private investigators, but rules vary by state. Staff investigators who work only for their own employer are often exempt. If the role needs a license, check it with the state licensing board. A Certified Fraud Examiner credential is a plus for fraud work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a redacted sample report. Look for a clear timeline, facts kept apart from opinion, a source for each finding, and a conclusion the evidence supports. Have them plan interviews with a witness and a subject, and explain how they would preserve documents and digital records.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They stay neutral, keep careful notes and track chain of custody. They know when to bring in legal counsel or HR. They protect confidentiality and know that call recording laws differ by state. They explain findings plainly to managers without overstating them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Talk of pretexting, logging into someone’s personal accounts, or recording calls without checking consent rules. Deciding guilt before gathering evidence. Sharing names or details from past cases. Reports full of opinion or loaded words instead of facts tied to sources.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a case where the evidence pointed away from the first suspicion. Ask how they handled a witness who changed their story. Ask how they kept an inquiry confidential while still working with HR, legal and IT.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an investigations specialist?
qa.a: Look for someone neutral, organized and careful with evidence. They should interview well, document every step, keep chain of custody and write clear reports that separate facts from opinion. Check any required license, since rules vary by state. Fraud work benefits from a Certified Fraud Examiner credential. Strong judgment about when to involve legal counsel matters too.

qa.q: How do I test an investigations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short mock case with a complaint, a few emails and witness statements. Ask for an investigation plan, interview questions and a brief written finding. Check whether they spot gaps, avoid jumping to conclusions and cite evidence for each point. Then discuss their choices to see how they reason and handle confidentiality.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Securities licenses such as the Series 7, 63, 65 or 79 are needed only for certain roles, like brokering, advising clients or banking work. Adviser rules vary by state. Many fund roles need no license. A CFA charter or progress through its exams is a helpful plus, not a legal requirement.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for strong financial modeling: three-statement models, discounted cash flow and, for buyout work, leveraged buyout models. They should read financial statements fast, run due diligence and write a clear investment memo. Clear speaking also matters for investor calls.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They walk you through a past deal or stock pick in plain words. They state the thesis, the key risks and what would prove them wrong. They talk about losing calls as openly as winning ones, and they show what they learned.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a candidate who can’t explain the assumptions behind their own model or who claims returns without context. Be wary if they share confidential details or nonpublic information from a past employer. Dismissing compliance rules is another warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a deal they passed on and why. Ask which number in a model they would stress-test first. Ask how they would explain a bad quarter to an investor. Real experience shows in specific, practical answers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an investment analyst?
qa.a: Look for solid modeling and valuation skills, sound judgment on risk and clear writing. Confirm any securities licenses the role legally needs, since needs vary by role and some adviser rules vary by state. Strong candidates explain past investment calls, including mistakes, and respect confidentiality and compliance rules.

qa.q: How do I test an investment analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a timed case study. Supply public financial statements for a company and ask for a simple valuation model and a one-page investment memo with a buy or pass call. Then have them present it and defend their assumptions while you push back. This shows modeling, judgment and communication at once.

look.label: Licenses to plan for
look.text: Analysts who work on deals at a registered broker-dealer generally need the SIE exam plus the Series 79. Some firms also require the Series 63. Your firm must sponsor the Series 79, so most entry-level hires pass it after joining. For experienced candidates, check past registrations on FINRA BrokerCheck.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test three-statement modeling in Excel, a clean DCF, comparable company and precedent transaction analysis, and basic LBO math. Watch for keyboard speed, consistent formatting and formulas that link correctly. Also check how well they turn numbers into tidy pitch book pages in PowerPoint.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can explain how a change in depreciation flows through all three statements without notes. They catch their own errors. They can discuss a recent deal they followed in the news. They stay accurate and calm under tight deadlines and frequent revisions.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Memorized technical answers that fall apart after one follow-up question. Hardcoded numbers buried in model formulas. Vague claims about deal work they cannot explain step by step. Loose talk about confidential details from a past job, which signals risk with your clients’ nonpublic information.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a model they built and the hardest assumption in it. Ask how they would value a company with negative earnings. Ask what they did when a senior banker changed a deck late at night before a client meeting.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an investment banking analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong accounting and valuation basics, fast and accurate Excel modeling, polished PowerPoint work and close attention to detail. If your firm is a broker-dealer, plan for the SIE and Series 79 registrations. Strong candidates also communicate clearly, keep deal information confidential and stay accurate under tight deadlines.

qa.q: How do I test an investment banking analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a timed modeling test, often one to three hours, using a short set of company financials. Ask for a three-statement model or a simple LBO with a valuation summary. Then have them present the results and defend the key assumptions. Score accuracy, formula structure, formatting and how clearly they explain the numbers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for investor relations. Optional investor relations certificates exist, and finance or accounting training helps. Verify past work with references and public materials they helped write, such as earnings releases. Confirm they know Regulation FD, which bars selective disclosure of material nonpublic information.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test writing an earnings release and call script, preparing executives for analyst questions and building a simple financial model. Check investor targeting, tracking analyst estimates, shareholder data, annual meeting work and coordination with legal, finance and the auditors.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain the business and its numbers clearly, keep the message consistent across every investor meeting and earn trust from analysts. They know what can and cannot be said, and bring market feedback back to leadership honestly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for loose talk about nonpublic results, guidance or deals, and promises to support the stock price. Be wary of anyone who would share information privately with one investor, skip legal review, or cannot read financial statements.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you prepare a CEO for an earnings call? What do you do if an executive shares nonpublic information by mistake? How do you choose which investors to meet? Strong answers mention scripts, Regulation FD steps and targeting data.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an investor relations manager?
qa.a: Look for strong financial literacy, clear writing and calm communication with analysts and shareholders. They should know Regulation FD, insider trading rules and disclosure practices, and work closely with finance and legal. No license is required, so references and public materials they helped prepare matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an investor relations manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with sample quarterly results. Ask for a one-page earnings summary, a short call script and the five toughest analyst questions with answers. Judge clarity, accuracy, consistency with the numbers and whether anything risks selective or misleading disclosure.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to build iOS apps. Course certificates exist, but published apps matter more. Ask for links to apps on the App Store they helped ship, code samples, and references who confirm which features the candidate built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test Swift, SwiftUI and UIKit, Swift concurrency with async and await, networking, local storage and the app lifecycle. Check Xcode debugging and Instruments profiling, accessibility with VoiceOver and Dynamic Type, unit and UI tests, code signing and release through app review.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have shipped and updated apps through app review and can explain a rejection they fixed. They handle offline states, memory and battery use, privacy permission prompts and accessibility, and know when SwiftUI fits and when UIKit is still needed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for force unwrapping everywhere, slow work on the main thread that freezes screens, and no tests. Be careful with candidates who have never shipped an app, cannot explain retain cycles, or ignore privacy rules for data collection and tracking permission.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an app review rejection and how you fixed it. How do you find a memory leak or retain cycle? How do you move work off the main thread safely with Swift concurrency? How do you support Dynamic Type? Strong answers name tools.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an iOS developer?
qa.a: Look for apps they shipped and maintained, with Swift code they can explain. Check SwiftUI and UIKit, concurrency, networking, testing, accessibility and experience with app review and privacy rules. No license is required in the US, so published apps, code samples and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an iOS developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your app, such as a SwiftUI screen that loads a list from a sample API, with loading, error and empty states and a few tests. Review Swift style, concurrency use, memory handling, accessibility with VoiceOver, and how clearly they explain their choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to work as an IT manager in the US. Optional certifications such as ITIL 4 Foundation, CompTIA Security+, PMP or CISSP show focused study. Verify them through each issuer’s online lookup. Confirm past titles, team sizes and budgets with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test budgeting and vendor negotiation, software license tracking, account and access management, and laptop and phone management. Also cover backup and recovery planning and basic network design. Ask them to walk through onboarding and offboarding an employee, from accounts and hardware to removing access.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk in numbers: ticket volumes, uptime, budget size and license costs cut. They keep an asset inventory and written procedures. They explain tradeoffs in plain words to non-technical leaders. They have led a team through an outage or migration and can say what they changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about who actually did the work on past projects. Other warning signs: no habit of testing backups, shared admin passwords, or setups without multi-factor authentication. Be wary if they blame users or vendors for every problem, or have no plan for cutting access when someone leaves.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about their worst outage and what they did in the first hour. Ask how they cut software spending without hurting staff, and how they decide what to hand to an outside IT provider. Listen for concrete steps, dates and results, not buzzwords.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an IT manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has managed both people and systems. They should be able to run a budget and track hardware and software licenses. They should enforce security basics like multi-factor authentication and tested backups, and lead a small team. Certifications help, but no license is required. Clear communication with non-technical staff matters as much as technical depth.

qa.q: How do I test an IT manager before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short case study. Share a mock list of staff, devices and software subscriptions. Ask for a 90-day plan, a ranked list of budget priorities and an offboarding checklist. Then have them present it to a non-technical manager and answer follow-up questions. This shows their judgment, planning and communication.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for IT project management. Certifications such as the PMP and agile certificates show training and can be checked with the issuer. Weigh delivered projects more heavily: ask references about go-lives, budgets and how the candidate handled problems.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test planning a technology rollout from requirements through testing, cutover and go-live. Check scheduling, risk and issue logs, vendor management, budget tracking and change control. Ask how they coordinate data migration, user training and a rollback plan for a system launch.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates understand enough technology to ask hard questions of engineers and vendors. They raise risks early, run focused meetings, and give honest status reports even when news is bad. They plan cutovers in detail and keep users informed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for status reports that stay green until just before go-live, plans with no time for testing or rollback, or candidates who cannot explain the technology they managed. Be careful with anyone who blames vendors or teams for every past delay.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a go-live that went wrong and what you did in the first hours. How do you plan a data migration cutover? How do you handle a vendor missing dates? Strong answers name specific steps, tradeoffs and lessons.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an IT project manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of delivering technology projects to go-live, enough technical knowledge to challenge engineers and vendors, and honest, early risk reporting. Certifications such as the PMP show training but are optional, and no license is required. References about real go-lives matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an IT project manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid scenario, such as a software rollout with a fixed date, a vendor delay and an incomplete test plan. Ask for a revised plan, a risk list and a status update for executives. Review realism, how they protect testing and rollback, and how clearly they communicate.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required for IT support work. Many candidates hold vendor-neutral or vendor-specific certifications in hardware, networking or security. Check them through the issuer’s online verification, and weigh them alongside real troubleshooting experience.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them diagnose a laptop that won’t join Wi-Fi, unlock an account protected by multi-factor authentication, set up a new hire’s device and accounts, and explain a fix to a nontechnical coworker. Watch the order of their steps.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask clarifying questions before touching anything, write down what they fixed, give people only the access they need, and stay calm with frustrated users. Hands-on use of ticketing, device management, backups and password managers is a plus.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Reinstalling or replacing before diagnosing. Sharing or reusing admin passwords. Talking down to users. Vague answers about past setups. No habit of backing up data before making changes.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an outage you handled. What broke, how did you find it, and what did you change afterward? How do you remove a departing employee’s access the same day? Concrete details point to real hands-on work.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an IT support specialist?
qa.a: Look for steady troubleshooting habits, clear communication with nontechnical staff and careful handling of passwords and access. No state license is required, so certifications are optional proof of knowledge. Experience with the systems you already use, such as your email, devices and backups, matters more than a long list of credentials.

qa.q: How do I test an IT support specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic scenario, like a user who can’t sign in or a laptop that won’t print, and ask them to talk through each step. Then have them write a brief ticket note and explain the fix in plain words. Never give a candidate access to live systems or real passwords.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for ITSM work. An ITIL certification shows framework knowledge but is optional, and administrator or implementation certifications for your ticket platform are a useful bonus. Verify certifications with the issuer and ask references what the candidate actually built or changed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they design incident, request, problem and change processes, including priority rules and service level targets. On the platform, check forms, workflows, assignment rules, the service catalog and reports. Ask them to fix a sample process with too many unassigned or reopened tickets.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates start from how people actually work, then set up the tool to fit, not the other way round. They keep workflows simple, track resolution time and backlog, and change rules based on data. They can explain a process to agents and to leaders.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for heavy custom code where standard features would work, which makes upgrades hard. Be careful with candidates who add approvals and fields with no clear reason, cannot show reports that improved, or quote framework terms without examples from real teams.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a process you changed and what happened to resolution times. How do you decide what counts as a major incident? When do you customize the platform and when do you push back? Strong answers name specific changes and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an ITSM specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work running incident, request and change processes, plus admin skills on the ticket platform you use. Check they keep workflows simple and use reports to improve them. No license is required, so ITIL or platform certifications are a bonus; references and before and after results matter more.

qa.q: How do I test an ITSM specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task, such as redesigning a messy incident process from a sample of tickets, or building a simple catalog item with an approval in a test instance. Ask them to explain priorities and assignment rules. Review clarity, simplicity, and whether agents could actually follow it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is needed for most cleaning jobs. Ask for references from past supervisors or clients. Training in chemical safety, bloodborne pathogens or floor care is a plus. When hiring a cleaning company, check its business license where required, its insurance and its bonding.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test chemical dilution and reading safety data sheets, restroom sanitizing, color-coded cloths to stop cross contamination, and floor care such as stripping, waxing and buffing. Check use of auto scrubbers, carpet extractors and vacuums. Hospital and food sites need correct disinfectant contact times.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates follow checklists, notice what others miss and report leaks, broken fixtures or safety hazards. They use wet floor signs every time and store chemicals properly. They work well unsupervised, respect privacy in offices and homes, and handle keys and alarm codes responsibly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for mixing chemicals, such as bleach with ammonia, skipping gloves or signs, or using one cloth for every surface. Be careful with poor references about reliability, missed areas or lost keys, and with vague answers about how they handled a complaint.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you clean a restroom, step by step? What would you do if you found an unknown spill? How do you strip and refinish a floor? What do you do if you break something in a client’s office? Strong answers are specific and safe.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a janitor or cleaner?
qa.a: Look for reliability, attention to detail and safe chemical habits. Check references from past supervisors or clients, and confirm training for your setting, such as disinfection in health care or food areas. For cleaning companies, verify insurance and bonding. No license is required for most cleaning jobs.

qa.q: How do I test a janitor or cleaner before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid trial shift on a real area, such as a restroom and a break room, with a checklist. Watch chemical use, glove use, wet floor signs and thoroughness. Inspect the result, then ask what they would do differently on a busy day.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to work as a Java developer in the US. Vendor certifications for Java exist and show study, but they are optional. Verify real skill through references, code samples and a short practical test instead.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Core Java such as collections, exceptions, generics and concurrency. Building REST APIs with a common framework like Spring Boot, writing SQL for a relational database, unit testing with JUnit, and using Git with Maven or Gradle. Ask them to read a stack trace and find the bug.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain tradeoffs plainly and write tests without being asked. They know how memory leaks and slow garbage collection show up in production. They can describe a real outage they helped fix and what the team changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Can’t explain code in their own portfolio, ignores thread safety, catches exceptions and silently drops them, has never written tests, or blames others for every failed project. Treat unfamiliarity with your exact Java version as a small gap, not a deal breaker.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they would find a slow database query in a live service, how they handled a library upgrade that broke the build, and when they would use a message queue instead of a direct API call. Real experience shows in specific details.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Java developer?
qa.a: Look for solid core Java, experience building APIs with a common framework, comfort with SQL and databases, and a habit of writing tests. Strong candidates explain their choices clearly and have supported code in production. No license is required, so judge them on code samples, references and a practical test.

qa.q: How do I test a Java developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task that matches your work, such as building a small REST endpoint with a database call and unit tests. Keep it to a few hours and consider paying for longer tasks. Then review the code together and ask why they made each choice. A live code review exercise also works well.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to write JavaScript or TypeScript professionally. Degrees, bootcamp certificates and course badges are optional. Verify real work instead: live sites, repositories, packages they publish and references who can confirm the candidate’s own contributions.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test core JavaScript: scope, closures, promises, async and await, the event loop and modules. For TypeScript, check strict mode, generics, union types and narrowing. Test the browser, Node.js or both, as your role needs, along with tests, linting and a modern build setup.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know the language beneath any framework and debug with browser tools and a debugger, not only console logs. They type data where it enters the system, avoid the any type without good reason and write small, tested functions.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for heavy use of any in TypeScript, ignored compiler errors, and confusion about equality, this or the order of asynchronous code. Be careful with candidates who know one framework but not plain JavaScript, or who add a package for every small task.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What happens when a promise rejects with no handler? How do you type an API response you do not control? Tell me about a hard bug caused by asynchronous code. How do you decide when to add a new dependency? Strong answers are concrete.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a TypeScript and JavaScript developer?
qa.a: Look for solid core JavaScript, strong TypeScript habits and real projects they can explain, in the browser, on the server or both. Check async code, testing, debugging and care with dependencies. No license is required in the US, so working code and references count more than certificates or course badges.

qa.q: How do I test a TypeScript and JavaScript developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work, such as typing and fixing a small module that fetches and transforms data, with tests and TypeScript strict mode turned on. Ask them to use Git and explain their choices. Review type safety, async error handling, test quality and how readable the code is.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license for this work, and many roles do not require a degree. Bootcamp and course certificates are optional. Look instead at projects, internships and code they can explain, and call references such as mentors, instructors or past team leads.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test basics, not trivia: reading and changing existing code, writing a small function with tests, using Git, and debugging from an error message. Check one language well, basic data structures, simple SQL and how they ask for help when stuck.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong juniors are curious, ask clear questions and say what they already tried. They read error messages, make small commits and take review comments without defensiveness. Projects they kept improving after a deadline often show more than polished tutorial apps.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for projects copied from tutorials or generated with AI tools that the candidate cannot explain or change. Be careful with anyone who hides being stuck, guesses instead of checking, or dismisses code review. Judge skill and learning, never how recently someone graduated.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a project you built and one thing you would change now. Tell me about a bug that took you a long time to find. What do you do after an hour stuck on a problem? How do you learn a new codebase? Strong answers show a method.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a junior software engineer?
qa.a: Look for working projects or internship code they can explain and change, solid basics in one language, Git habits and calm debugging. Curiosity, clear questions and openness to feedback matter as much as current skill. No license is required and many roles need no degree, so real work and references count most.

qa.q: How do I test a junior software engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task sized for a beginner, such as fixing a small bug and adding a test in a sample repository, or pair with them for a session. Let them search documentation as they would at work. Review how they read code, debug, ask questions and explain what they changed.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for operating systems work. A computer science or computer engineering degree is common but not required. Verify with public kernel patches on mailing lists or code archives, driver or hypervisor work they can explain, and references who confirm what they shipped.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test C, plus Rust where your codebase uses it, and reading assembly. Check memory management, scheduling, interrupts, locking and lock-free techniques, device drivers and virtualization. Ask how they debug a kernel crash from a dump, trace performance problems and test changes on real hardware.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have had patches reviewed and merged in a demanding project and can explain the feedback they got. They reason carefully about concurrency, measure before optimizing and can tell whether a problem lies in hardware, firmware or their own code.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who treat locking casually, cannot explain a race condition they fixed, or blame hardware without evidence. Be careful with anyone who has never debugged a crash on a real system or who skips review and testing for low-level changes.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a race condition you found and how you proved the fix. How would you debug a system that hangs only under heavy load? How is a page fault handled? What review feedback changed one of your patches? Strong answers are precise.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a kernel and operating systems engineer?
qa.a: Look for real work in operating systems, drivers or virtualization, ideally with public patches you can read. Check C, assembly, concurrency, memory management and debugging of crashes and hangs. Careful reasoning and respect for code review matter a lot at this layer. No license is required, so verified work and references count most.

qa.q: How do I test a kernel and operating systems engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work, such as reviewing a small driver or kernel patch with a hidden race condition, or analyzing a crash log to find the cause. Review how they read low-level code, explain concurrency, propose a fix and say how they would test it on real hardware.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for account planning, forecasting and negotiation. A strong key account manager can map a client’s buying committee, spot growth areas, and defend price without giving away margin. Ask them to build a short account plan for a sample customer and walk you through it.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They speak about long client relationships, not one-time deals. They can name the revenue they kept and grew, explain how they handled a renewal at risk, and describe working with operations, finance and support to fix problems before the client noticed.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an account you grew over several years. What was your plan? Who were the decision makers? Describe a time a major client threatened to leave. What did you do, and what happened? Listen for specifics, numbers and their own role.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about results, credit taken for team wins with no detail, or blaming clients for every lost account. Be wary of anyone who only talks about closing new deals and shows little interest in service, follow-through or understanding the customer’s business.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for this work in general. Some industries add their own rules, such as securities or insurance sales, which need specific licenses that vary by product and state. Otherwise, verify past roles and results through references from former managers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a key account manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they kept and grew large accounts over time. Strong candidates plan ahead, negotiate well, forecast accurately and coordinate with other teams. They should explain their results with clear numbers and examples. Check references from former managers, and favor people who show real curiosity about how their clients make money.

qa.q: How do I test a key account manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short case about a fictional major customer, with sales history and a renewal coming up. Ask for a one-page account plan and a brief role-play where you act as a client pushing for a price cut. Judge their questions, priorities and how they protect both the relationship and the margin.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as a Kotlin developer, and no Kotlin certification is commonly required. Verify work instead: published Android apps, server code samples or open-source contributions, and references who can confirm exactly what the candidate built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test null safety, data classes, extension functions, coroutines and Flow. For Android, check Jetpack Compose, app lifecycle and Gradle builds. For services, check Spring Boot or Ktor, Java interoperability, database access and tests. Match the test to the side your team needs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write idiomatic Kotlin rather than Java with new syntax, use coroutines with structured concurrency and handle cancellation correctly. They know when sealed classes help, keep nulls out of core logic and work comfortably in mixed Kotlin and Java codebases.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for the not-null assertion operator used everywhere, coroutines launched in global scope, and blocking calls inside coroutines. Be careful with candidates who cannot explain how Kotlin handles nulls coming from Java code, or who have only followed tutorials.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you cancel coroutines when a screen or request ends? When do you choose Flow over a suspend function? Tell me about a crash caused by a null from Java code. How do you convert a Java class to Kotlin safely? Strong answers are specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Kotlin developer?
qa.a: Look for real Kotlin work on the side you need, Android apps or server services, with code they can explain. Check null safety, coroutines, testing and Java interoperability. For Android, look at Jetpack Compose and published apps. No license is required in the US, so working code and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a Kotlin developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work, such as a Compose screen that loads and shows data, or a small service endpoint with tests. Ask them to handle errors and cancellation with coroutines. Review idiomatic Kotlin, null handling, test quality and how clearly they explain their choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work. Useful certifications include Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA), Certified Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD) and Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS). These are hands-on exams that expire, so check the certificate with the issuer. Treat them as a plus, not as proof of production skill.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them debug a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff or Pending using kubectl describe, logs and events. Check that they can write clean Deployment, Service and Ingress manifests, set resource requests and limits, and explain readiness versus liveness probes. Helm or Kustomize and a CI/CD pipeline are common daily tools.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe real incidents, such as a bad rollout they rolled back, a node that ran out of memory, or an expired certificate. They manage clusters as code with Terraform or GitOps, think about RBAC and secrets, and watch monitoring and cost, not just whether pods start.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Presenting tutorial or single-node lab work as production experience. Running everything as root or with cluster-admin rights. Storing secrets in plain text in Git. Making manual kubectl changes in production with no record. Answering every problem with “add more nodes” instead of finding the cause.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they upgraded a cluster without downtime. Ask what happened the last time a deployment failed and how they found out. Ask how they choose requests and limits, and how they give developers access without giving too much. Vague answers suggest little hands-on time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a container and Kubernetes engineer?
qa.a: Look for production experience running real clusters, not just labs. Strong candidates debug failing pods quickly, write clear manifests, manage infrastructure as code, and take security seriously with RBAC, secrets handling and least privilege. Certifications such as CKA, CKAD or CKS help, but no license is required. Ask for specific incidents they handled and what they changed afterward.

qa.q: How do I test a container and Kubernetes engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task in a sandbox cluster, never your production systems. Include a broken Deployment with a wrong image tag, a failing probe or missing resource limits, and ask them to find and fix the problems while explaining their steps. Then ask how they would roll the change out safely and how they would monitor it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most research labs need no state license. Labs that test patient samples fall under federal CLIA rules, and some states, such as California and New York, also license lab staff. Check the degree, any ASCP certification for clinical work, and AALAS certification if the job involves lab animals.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for accurate pipetting, correct dilution and molarity math, sterile technique, and hands-on use of the instruments you actually run. Ask how they calibrate and maintain equipment. Check that they keep clear, dated records in a paper notebook or electronic lab notebook that someone else could follow.

look.label: Safety habits to check
look.text: A strong candidate reads safety data sheets, picks the right protective gear, labels everything, and knows how to handle chemical and biological waste. Ask about spill response and biosafety levels. You must still give the training OSHA requires, but good habits show they will follow it.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through an experiment that failed and how they found the cause. Ask how they label, store and track samples so nothing gets lost. Ask what they do when a result looks wrong. Real experience shows in specific steps, not general answers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who follows protocols but cannot explain why each step matters. Other warnings: vague claims about instruments, messy or missing records, shrugging off safety rules, or any hint that they would adjust data to make results look better.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a research associate or lab technician?
qa.a: Look for accurate bench skills, careful record keeping and steady safety habits. Check experience with your specific techniques and instruments. Ask how they troubleshoot failed experiments and track samples. If your lab tests patient samples, confirm any state license your state requires. Honesty about data matters as much as technical skill.

qa.q: How do I test a lab technician before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid practical task. Ask them to calculate and prepare a dilution, pipette a set of volumes, and record each step as they would in a notebook. Watch their sterile technique and safety choices. Then ask them to explain a result that looks off. Their reasoning shows real experience.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No individual license covers launch work; the FAA licenses the launch operator, not each person. Verify hazardous operations training, such as cryogenic, high-pressure and propellant handling. Anyone whose role includes explosive materials must be cleared under the employer’s federal explosives license or permit.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test writing and running step-by-step procedures, reading piping and instrumentation diagrams, leak checks, pressurization and propellant loading. Check countdown discipline, go and no-go calls, red-line limits, safe hold and abort steps, test data review, and how they recover and inspect returned hardware.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates follow procedures exactly, stop work when something looks wrong and log every deviation. They know the hardware well enough to spot a bad reading, stay calm on a busy voice net, and can describe an anomaly they helped trace to root cause.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for skipping steps or signing off work they did not see, casual talk about pressure or propellant hazards, and blaming others for test failures. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a red-line limit they worked to or how a hazard area is cleared.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a countdown or test where you called a hold. How do you handle a procedure step that does not match the hardware? Tell me about an anomaly you investigated. Strong answers show procedure discipline, clear communication and safety first.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a launch and test operations specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with test stands, pad operations or hardware integration, strict procedure discipline and a strong safety record. Verify training for cryogenics, high pressure and propellants, and federal explosives clearance where needed. No individual license covers the role, so references from test directors and anomaly reports they wrote matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a launch and test operations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise such as reviewing a sample pressurization procedure and piping diagram with planted errors. Ask them to mark the problems, add holds and red lines, and explain how they would run it. Then walk through a mock countdown with an off-nominal reading. Review safety judgment and clarity.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Sworn officers need state peace officer certification, which varies by state; verify it directly with that state’s standards board. Private security and investigator roles may need a separate state license. Corporate roles that work with police and courts usually need no license, so check investigation experience and references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test report writing, evidence handling and chain of custody, and de-escalation. For corporate roles, check how they handle subpoenas, search warrants and emergency data requests, and how they work with legal counsel. Ask how they keep accurate records that stand up in court.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write clear, factual reports, follow policy and the law under pressure, and know when to involve legal counsel or a supervisor. They de-escalate first, treat people with respect, and keep good working ties with agencies, prosecutors and courts.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a history of misconduct findings or decertification, which you can check through state records where available. Be careful with anyone who shrugs at legal process, would hand over user data without proper legal review, or cannot explain chain of custody.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a time you calmed a tense situation. How do you check whether a police request for user data is valid? Walk me through how you preserve evidence. Strong answers follow clear steps, cite policy and law, and stay factual.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a law enforcement professional?
qa.a: For sworn roles, confirm state peace officer certification, which varies by state, and a clean conduct record. For corporate roles, look for experience handling subpoenas, warrants and evidence, plus close work with legal counsel. In both, strong report writing, sound judgment and de-escalation skills matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a law enforcement professional before hiring?
qa.a: Sworn hiring follows state and agency rules, often including written exams, fitness tests and background investigations. For corporate roles, give a realistic scenario, such as an emergency data request from police, and ask what they would verify, who they would involve and what records they would keep. Review accuracy, judgment and clarity.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm the candidate is admitted to practice law and in good standing in at least one US state. Use the official attorney lookup, run by the state bar in some states and by the state supreme court or its disciplinary agency in others. Check for any public discipline.

look.label: In-house registration rules
look.text: If the candidate is licensed in a different state than where they will work, check that state’s rules. Many states require in-house lawyers licensed elsewhere to register with the court or bar before advising the company. Rules and deadlines vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give them a sample vendor or customer contract and ask them to flag risky clauses and propose edits. Look for clear plain-English summaries, sensible priorities and good judgment about when outside counsel is needed for litigation or specialized areas.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Experience with your industry and its regulators, a habit of explaining legal risk in business terms, and concrete examples of deals closed or disputes resolved. Strong candidates ask how decisions get made, who owns risk and what the budget is for outside firms.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Sharing confidential details about former employers or clients, claiming deep expertise in every area of law, or saying no without offering workable alternatives. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a past matter in general terms or dismisses compliance as paperwork.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a legal counsel?
qa.a: Look for active bar admission in good standing, checked through the official attorney lookup for each state where they are licensed. Then weigh experience with your contracts, products and regulators, sound judgment about risk, and the ability to explain the law in plain business terms. If they will work in a state where they are not licensed, check that state’s in-house registration rules.

qa.q: How do I test a legal counsel before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short, paid or clearly limited exercise built on made-up facts. Ask them to redline a sample contract and write a one-page memo on a regulatory question your business faces. Then discuss their choices. Judge clarity, practical priorities and whether they spot when outside counsel is needed. Do not ask candidates to do real legal work for free.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Law students need no license, but confirm enrollment and good standing with the law school. Some states let supervised students appear in court under student practice rules, which vary by state. New lawyers should be admitted to a state bar or awaiting results, so check the bar’s lookup.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test legal research in primary sources, citation accuracy, issue spotting and clear memo writing. Check they verify every case and quote, especially when using AI tools, and can accurately summarize a contract, a deposition or a statute for a supervising lawyer.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates ask clarifying questions, show their research path and flag what they could not confirm. Their writing is short and organized. They meet deadlines, accept edits well, and treat client information as confidential from day one, including on social media.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for writing samples heavily edited by others, citations that do not exist or say something else, and careless handling of confidential documents. Be wary of candidates who guess instead of researching or who avoid admitting a mistake.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you researched your writing sample. How do you check that a case is still good law? Tell me about feedback that changed how you write. Strong answers describe specific research steps, sources and edits.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a legal intern?
qa.a: Look for strong research and writing, careful citation checking and sound judgment about confidentiality. Confirm law school enrollment or bar admission, since student practice rules vary by state. For-profit employers should also check federal rules on unpaid internships. Writing samples, a short exercise and references matter more than grades alone.

qa.q: How do I test a legal intern before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, timed research exercise on a fictional fact pattern, with a clear question and a page limit. Ask for a brief memo with full citations. Check every authority, then review issue spotting, organization, accuracy and how clearly they state what remains uncertain. Keep the task short or pay for the time.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Under the federal SAFE Act, mortgage loan originators must be state licensed or, at banks and credit unions, registered. Check status and any disciplinary actions in the national NMLS registry. Employee processors and underwriters usually need no license. Rules for other lending vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading tax returns and pay stubs, calculating qualifying income and debt-to-income ratio, reviewing credit reports and appraisals, and meeting disclosure deadlines. Check knowledge of fair lending, ability-to-repay and privacy rules, plus your loan origination or servicing system.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates document every decision, spot inconsistent income or assets, explain loan options plainly and apply the same standards to every applicant under fair lending rules. Clean audit and quality control results on files they handled are good proof.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for pressure to close loans by bending documentation, steering borrowers toward costlier products, careless handling of personal financial data, and disciplinary actions in their license record. Be careful with anyone who treats compliance reviews as obstacles rather than protection.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A self-employed borrower’s income dropped last year. How do you calculate qualifying income? What do you do if a disclosure deadline is about to be missed? How do you help a borrower confused by loan terms? Listen for careful, rule-based steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a loan officer?
qa.a: Look for accurate file work, sound credit and income analysis, and real knowledge of fair lending, disclosure and privacy rules. Mortgage loan originators must be state licensed or registered under federal law, so check the NMLS registry. Rules for other lending vary by state, so confirm what your role requires.

qa.q: How do I test a loan officer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid review of a sample loan file with planted problems, such as income that does not match tax returns or a missing disclosure. Ask them to calculate qualifying income, list conditions and note compliance risks. Review accuracy, documentation and whether they treat the borrower fairly.

look.label: Education and training to verify
look.text: Most research roles ask for a bachelor’s, master’s or PhD in biology, chemistry, physics or a related field. There is no general state license for research scientists. Clinical lab roles may need a state license, but only some states require one. Verify degrees and any biosafety, animal care or GLP training.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask the candidate to plan a simple experiment with proper controls, calculate dilutions and molarity, and follow a written protocol. Have them interpret a real data set or gel image. Check their comfort with the instruments you use, such as PCR machines, chromatography systems or microscopes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Keeps a clear, dated lab notebook. Explains why an experiment failed and what they changed. Talks about controls, replicates and statistics without prompting. Can show posters, papers or reports and describe exactly what their own part in the work was.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about which techniques they ran themselves and which they only watched. No habit of recording data as they work. A casual attitude toward chemical, biological or radiation safety. Claims that every experiment worked the first time.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about an experiment that did not work and how you fixed it.” Ask how they would handle a result that contradicts the expected outcome. Ask what safety steps they follow with a hazardous reagent they used often.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a life scientist?
qa.a: Look for a degree that fits your field, hands-on skill with the methods your lab uses, and careful record keeping. Strong candidates design experiments with controls, explain failed results honestly and follow safety rules without reminders. Ask a former supervisor or principal investigator about their reliability and data integrity.

qa.q: How do I test a life scientist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short practical task tied to your lab. Ask them to calculate a dilution series, plan an experiment with controls, or interpret a sample data set. If it is safe, watch them do a basic bench task such as pipetting or preparing a buffer, and ask them to explain each step.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they segment customers by behavior and lifecycle stage, build a triggered journey across email, push and in-app, and design an A/B test with a clear hypothesis. Basic SQL or spreadsheet skills for pulling cohorts and reading retention curves are a strong plus.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates measure success with holdout groups and incremental lift, not just open or click rates. They know privacy features in some email apps inflate opens. They can show a welcome, onboarding, win-back or replenishment flow they built and explain what changed in retention or repeat purchases.

look.label: Compliance knowledge to check
look.text: No license is required for this role. Check that they know CAN-SPAM basics for commercial email, such as a working unsubscribe and a physical mailing address. They should also know that marketing texts generally need prior express written consent under the TCPA. Privacy laws vary by state, so ask how they keep consent records.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who sends the same campaign to the whole list, cannot explain SPF, DKIM and DMARC or why deliverability drops, ignores frequency caps, or credits all revenue to email without a control group. Vague answers about results often mean they ran sends but did not own strategy.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a journey they built, from trigger to exit rule. Ask what they did when a flow stopped working, how they chose message timing, and how they kept push and email from overlapping. Real experience shows in specific numbers and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a lifecycle and CRM marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they own outcomes like activation, retention and repeat purchases, not just send volume. They should segment by behavior, build triggered journeys across email, push and in-app, test with control groups, and understand deliverability and consent rules such as CAN-SPAM and the TCPA. Ask for examples with real results.

qa.q: How do I test a lifecycle and CRM marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-boxed task using a sample customer dataset. Ask them to define lifecycle stages, pick one drop-off point, and sketch a three to five message journey with triggers, timing, channel choice and draft copy. Have them explain how they would measure lift with a holdout group and what they would test next.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Lawyers must hold an active license from a state bar, and in-house lawyers may need to register in the state where they work, with rules varying by state. Check status and discipline history through each state bar’s lookup. Federal court admission is separate. Paralegals usually need no license.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test early case assessment, litigation holds and e-discovery, review of pleadings and motions, and settlement analysis weighing cost, risk and business goals. For in-house roles, check skill in selecting outside counsel, setting budgets, reviewing invoices and reporting case status clearly to executives.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates give honest assessments of case value and risk, not just optimism. They control legal spend without losing quality, preserve evidence early, and explain options to business leaders in plain words. They know the procedural rules and deadlines of the courts where your cases sit.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for public discipline, missed deadlines or court sanctions, and a habit of escalating every dispute. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a litigation hold, has never managed a budget, or shares details of past clients’ cases in breach of confidentiality.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you decided to settle or fight a case. How do you choose and manage outside counsel and control their bills? Tell me about a discovery dispute you handled. Strong answers weigh cost, risk and business impact with specific steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a litigation attorney?
qa.a: Look for an active bar license in good standing, sound judgment on when to settle, and experience managing discovery, outside counsel and budgets. Check they explain risk to business leaders simply and protect confidential information. Bar rules for in-house lawyers vary by state, so confirm their status where they will work.

qa.q: How do I test a litigation attorney before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise built on a fictional dispute: a complaint, a few key documents and a budget. Ask for an early case assessment memo covering strengths, risks, likely costs, a litigation hold plan and a settlement view. Review legal reasoning, clarity, practicality and whether they flag what they need to learn next.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for this work. Many candidates hold a PhD or master’s in machine learning or a related field, but proven skill matters more. Check published papers, open-source code and model releases they can explain in depth.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them reason through a full training run, including data cleaning, tokenization, scaling choices, distributed training and evaluation. Strong candidates read loss curves, spot data leakage and explain trade-offs between model size, compute budget and data quality.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They design careful experiments with clear baselines and ablations. They admit when results are noisy and rerun them. They can name what failed in past work and why. They care about evaluation, safety testing and reproducible code, not just headline benchmark scores.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Big claimed results with no code, logs or details they can walk through. Prompt writing presented as model training. Vague answers about their own role on team papers. Dismissing evaluation, data licensing or privacy concerns around training data.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, "Tell me about a training run that diverged. How did you find the cause?" or "How would you check whether test data leaked into the training set?" Real practitioners give concrete steps, the metrics they tracked and the tools they used.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an LLM researcher?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience training or fine-tuning language models, not just using them. Review papers, code and project write-ups, and ask what they personally built. Strong researchers run controlled experiments, build solid evaluations and explain trade-offs in plain terms. No license is required, so judge skill through their work and a technical interview.

qa.q: How do I test an LLM researcher before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small, paid task, such as fine-tuning a small open model on a dataset you provide or designing an evaluation for a stated behavior. Ask for code, results and a short write-up of what failed. Then hold a discussion where they critique a paper and propose a follow-up experiment.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for localization work. Some translators hold optional certification from a national translators’ association for specific language pairs. Verify any certificate directly with the issuer. Also check work samples, references and products they helped ship in your target languages.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them localize a short set of interface strings with placeholders, plural forms, dates, numbers and currency. Check that variables stay intact, text fits length limits, the tone matches your brand and every format follows the target locale.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask about context, audience and screenshots before translating. They use translation memory and termbases and can work in file formats like JSON, XLIFF or PO. They also flag issues such as text expansion, right-to-left layouts or hard-coded strings.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for raw machine translation passed off as finished work, broken code placeholders, an ignored glossary or style guide, and claimed fluency that does not hold up in a test. Be wary if they cannot explain why a phrase needs adapting rather than literal translation.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a string with no context, how they keep terminology consistent across releases and how they run language quality checks on a live build. Ask about language skills only as they relate to the job, never about where someone is from.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a localization specialist?
qa.a: Look for proven skill in your language pairs and markets, comfort with translation tools and software file formats, and an eye for cultural fit, not just word accuracy. No license is required in the US, so judge candidates by samples, references and a paid test on your real content.

qa.q: How do I test a localization specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Include a set of interface strings with placeholders and plurals, a marketing paragraph and a screenshot with a layout problem. Have a trusted fluent reviewer score accuracy, tone and terminology. Note whether the candidate asked useful questions and kept every variable and tag intact.

look.label: Credentials to check
