look.text: Most logistics coordinator jobs need no license. If your freight includes hazardous materials, federal DOT rules require hazmat employees to complete training within 90 days of starting and refresh it at least every three years. Ask what training the candidate has had and when. Supply chain certifications are helpful but optional.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for someone who can read and fill out a bill of lading, compare carrier quotes, and spot extra charges like detention or liftgate fees. They should work comfortably in spreadsheets and some kind of shipment tracking or transportation software. For import or export roles, check that they know basic Incoterms.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong coordinators warn customers about a delay before the customer asks. They keep clean notes on every load and check a new carrier’s operating authority and insurance before booking. They can explain how they rerouted a late shipment and what it cost compared with waiting.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with candidates who blame carriers for every problem, cannot describe a shipment they personally fixed, or book carriers without checking authority or insurance. Vague answers about freight claims, paperwork errors, or missed pickups often mean limited hands-on experience.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a load that went wrong from start to finish. Ask how they choose between two carriers with different prices and transit times. Ask how they file a damage claim and what proof they gather first.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a logistics coordinator?
qa.a: Look for someone organized, calm under pressure, and quick to communicate. They should know shipping paperwork, compare carrier rates well, and track loads closely. Ask for real examples of delays they fixed. If you ship hazardous materials, confirm their DOT hazmat training. Experience with the freight type you move, such as LTL, full truckload, or international, matters most.

qa.q: How do I test a logistics coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short scenario. Share a shipment’s details, two carrier quotes, and a sample bill of lading with a few errors. Ask the candidate to pick a carrier and explain why, find the paperwork mistakes, and write a brief message to a customer about a one-day delay. Judge accuracy, reasoning, and how clearly they communicate.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for machine learning engineers, and cloud or vendor certificates are optional. Verify models they put into production: ask for code samples or design write-ups, and ask references how the model performed and was maintained after launch.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test Python, model training and evaluation, serving models with low latency, data and model versioning, and monitoring for drift. For language model work, check prompt design, retrieval, evaluation sets and guardrails. Confirm software basics such as testing and code review.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates measure models against clear baselines, build evaluation sets before shipping, watch production metrics and plan rollbacks. They weigh cost and speed, not only accuracy, and know that some states and cities regulate automated decisions in areas such as hiring and lending.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for experience only in notebooks with nothing shipped, no evaluation beyond a single accuracy number, ignored data leakage, and private customer data sent to outside services without review. Be careful with anyone who cannot explain a model failure they caused.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you know a model in production was getting worse? How do you evaluate a chatbot’s answers? Tell me about a time you made a model faster or cheaper to run. Strong answers include the metrics and tradeoffs they used.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a machine learning engineer?
qa.a: Look for models they shipped and kept running, not only experiments. Check Python, evaluation, serving, monitoring and software engineering habits, plus awareness of privacy and of state and local rules on automated decisions. No license is required, so production stories, code samples and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a machine learning engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task, such as wrapping a trained model in a simple service with tests, or building an evaluation set for a chatbot feature. Ask for code and a short write-up. Review reliability, metric choices, handling of bad inputs and how they explain tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as a machinist. Look instead for a completed registered apprenticeship, a technical college certificate, or national industry credentials in measurement, manual machining or CNC operation and programming. Ask for copies and confirm them with the issuer.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that the candidate can read engineering drawings, including GD&T symbols and tolerances. They should measure accurately with micrometers, calipers, bore gauges and indicators. They should also set tool and work offsets, make basic G-code edits at the control, and pick sensible speeds and feeds for the material.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong machinists name the machines and controls they ran, the materials they cut and the tightest tolerances they held. They talk about first-article inspection, tracking tool wear during a run, and what they changed after a part came out of spec.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who can only load parts and press cycle start but calls themselves a setup machinist. Other warnings are guessing at measurements, skipping inspection or deburring, and loose habits around rotating spindles, guards, chips and coolant.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through setting up a new job on a CNC mill from drawing to first good part. Then ask what they check when a bore measures oversize partway through a run. Detailed, ordered answers show real shop time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a machinist?
qa.a: Look for solid blueprint reading, accurate use of precision measuring tools, and real setup experience on the machines and controls you run. Training through an apprenticeship or technical program helps, but no state license is required. Strong candidates explain the tolerances they held, how they inspect parts, and how they fix problems. They also work safely around moving equipment.

qa.q: How do I test a machinist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid practical test. Hand over a drawing and ask the candidate to explain the tolerances and plan the operations. Have them measure a few finished parts with your gauges. If possible, have them set offsets and run a simple part on your machine while a lead machinist watches. Afterward, check the part against the drawing together.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Ask for EPA Section 608 certification if the job involves HVAC or refrigeration, since federal rules require it to handle refrigerants. Electrical, plumbing and boiler licenses vary by state and city, so check what your location requires for the work you assign. Confirm a driver’s license only if the role needs driving.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have candidates read a wiring or piping diagram, use a multimeter to find a fault, and explain a lockout/tagout sequence step by step. Watch how they troubleshoot. A strong tech checks the simple causes first and works in a logical order.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about preventive maintenance routines, not just emergency fixes. They write clear work order notes, can learn a maintenance software system, and own basic hand tools. They name specific equipment they have serviced, such as rooftop units, pumps, conveyors or boilers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Skipping lockout/tagout or calling it a waste of time. Vague answers about past repairs, or blaming every failure on the equipment. Offering to do licensed electrical or refrigerant work without the required license or certification. No interest in recording what they fixed.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a repair that took more than one try. Ask how they decide what to fix first when three things break at once. Ask what preventive checks they would set up for a pump or air handler. Real experience shows in specific parts, readings and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a maintenance technician?
qa.a: Look for hands-on troubleshooting across electrical, mechanical and plumbing systems, steady safety habits around lockout/tagout, and good records of work done. Check for EPA Section 608 certification if refrigerants are involved, and confirm any state or local trade licenses your work requires. Ask about the specific equipment they have serviced.

qa.q: How do I test a maintenance technician before hiring?
qa.a: Set up a short, paid practical task on safe, de-energized equipment. Ask them to find a planted fault, such as a blown fuse, a bad switch or a leaking fitting, and explain each step aloud. Have them walk through lockout/tagout first. Judge their order of checks, tool use, safety and the work order note they write afterward.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most factory roles need no license. A Professional Engineer license is issued by each state, but industrial exemptions in many states mean in-house engineers rarely need one. Quality certifications such as Certified Quality Engineer or Six Sigma belts are optional; verify them with the issuing body.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading drawings with geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, measuring parts with calipers, gauges or a coordinate measuring machine, and statistical process control. Check they can write work instructions, run a failure mode and effects analysis and lead root cause analysis with methods such as 8D or five whys.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about the scrap, rework and yield they improved, not just tasks they did. They know quality systems such as ISO 9001, or ISO 13485 and FDA rules for medical devices. They spend time on the shop floor and earn trust from operators.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of candidates who blame operators for every defect, cannot explain how a gauge is checked for accuracy, or treat final inspection as the only control. Watch for anyone casual about lockout and tagout, machine guarding or other safety rules, or vague about which improvements were truly theirs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a defect that reached a customer. How did you find the root cause and stop it from coming back? How do you decide inspection sample sizes? How did you bring a new part into production? Strong answers name the data, tools and specific changes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a manufacturing and quality engineer?
qa.a: Look for proof they have launched products into production and cut defects, with results they can explain from their own work. Check drawing reading, measurement, statistical process control and root cause skills. Most roles need no license, so certifications are a bonus. Knowledge of your quality system and industry rules, such as those for medical devices, matters more.

qa.q: How do I test a manufacturing and quality engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise drawn from real work. Share a drawing, a sample of measurement data and a defect report, then ask them to find the likely cause, propose a fix and draft a simple control plan. Review how they use the data, account for measurement error and write steps an operator could follow.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles call for an engineering degree, often mechanical, industrial or manufacturing. Lean or Six Sigma belts are common, but standards vary by issuing body, so ask which projects earned them. A Professional Engineer license is rarely required here. If a role needs one, it is issued by each state’s board.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them read a drawing with GD&T callouts, sketch a process flow, and do a basic time study or line balance. Check their CAD comfort, how they write a PFMEA, and how they would build a control plan for a new part.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe changes they made on a real line, with before and after numbers they measured, such as scrap, cycle time or downtime. They spend time on the floor, listen to operators, and can explain why a fix held over time.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: They use buzzwords like kaizen or 5S but cannot name a concrete result. They blame operators for every defect. They cannot explain a root cause method such as 5 Whys or a fishbone diagram. They skip safety reviews, lockout or guarding when changing a process.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a new product launch they supported, a quality escape they handled, and a changeover they shortened. Listen for the data they gathered, who they involved, and what they would do differently next time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a manufacturing engineer?
qa.a: Look for an engineering degree, hands-on time on a production floor, and proof of measured results like lower scrap or faster cycle times. Strong candidates read drawings well, use root cause tools, write PFMEAs and control plans, and work well with operators and quality staff. Lean or Six Sigma training helps, but real project results matter more.

qa.q: How do I test a manufacturing engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case study. Share a part drawing, the current process steps, cycle times and defect data. Ask them to find the bottleneck, propose changes, and outline a PFMEA and control plan. A guided plant walk where they point out waste and safety risks also shows how they think on the floor.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Traders at securities broker-dealers must be registered and pass qualification exams; check the regulator’s public lookup. Futures roles may need registration too. Crypto market making usually needs no personal license. Verify track records with references and former risk managers, not screenshots.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test quoting logic, spread setting, inventory and hedging, and handling adverse selection when prices move fast. Check coding in Python or a faster language, exchange connectivity, profit and loss attribution, and hard risk controls such as position limits, loss limits and kill switches.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about risk before profit, explain where their past profits came from and size positions to survive bad days. They monitor fills and latency closely, write detailed post-mortems after losses and respect rules against spoofing and wash trading.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for track records with no risk context, no kill switch or loss limits, or offers to inflate volume with self-trades. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a losing period or blames every loss on exchange outages.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your worst trading day and what you changed. How do you adjust quotes when volatility spikes? How do you hedge inventory across venues? Strong answers name limits, data and specific changes, not just results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a market maker?
qa.a: Look for a disciplined approach to risk, clear explanations of past profits and losses, strong quantitative and coding skills, and respect for market manipulation rules. Check any required registration for securities or futures work. Verify track records through references rather than self-reported screenshots or statements.

qa.q: How do I test a market maker before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case with historical order book data: ask them to design a simple quoting strategy, set inventory and loss limits and explain how it behaves in a sharp move. Review risk logic, code quality, realism about fees and latency, and how clearly they explain tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Degrees in marketing, statistics or economics help, and analytics or ad platform certificates show basic tool knowledge. Treat them as a starting point only. Verify past roles and ask for a sample report or dashboard with private data removed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Pulling and cleaning data with SQL or spreadsheets, building a clear dashboard, and reading campaign results. Check that they understand attribution models, conversion funnels, customer acquisition cost, lifetime value and return on ad spend. They should explain basic A/B test ideas like sample size and statistical significance.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They tie every number to a business decision, such as moving budget from one channel to another. They question tracking gaps, duplicate conversions and privacy limits before trusting data. They explain findings in plain words to people who don’t work with data every day.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Reporting clicks, impressions or followers as success without linking them to sales. Treating last-click credit as the full truth. Claiming a campaign caused a lift without a test or control group. Vague answers about which tools they used or what they built versus inherited.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a time their analysis changed where budget went and what happened next. Ask how they handled two platforms reporting different conversion numbers. Ask how they would measure a channel that is hard to track, like podcast ads or word of mouth.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a marketing analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong data skills in SQL or spreadsheets, a solid grasp of attribution and A/B testing, and the habit of turning numbers into budget advice. Ask for a sample report with private data removed. The best candidates explain what the data can’t prove as clearly as what it shows. No license is required.

qa.q: How do I test a marketing analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-limited task using a made-up campaign dataset with spend, clicks and conversions by channel. Include a few planted errors, like duplicate rows or a tracking gap. Ask for a one-page summary on where to shift budget and why. Judge accuracy, the errors they catch and how clearly they explain limits.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No US license is needed for this role. A marketing degree is common but not required. Optional certificates in analytics, email or social media tools show initiative. Weigh a portfolio of real posts, emails and event materials, and call references about deadlines met.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can schedule posts across several platforms, build and test an email, proofread copy cleanly and keep a content calendar in a spreadsheet or project tool. Ask them to read basic results like open rate, click rate and post reach and say what they’d change.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about deadlines, handoffs and checklists, not just ideas. They can explain how they worked with designers, writers and vendors to get materials out on time. They know email basics under federal CAN-SPAM rules, such as a working unsubscribe link and a postal address.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Typos or wrong names in their application, since this job is about details. Vague answers about their own role in team campaigns. No examples of an event or launch they helped run. Blaming others for every missed deadline instead of describing what they fixed.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through a campaign you kept on schedule. What slipped and how did you recover?” “What do you check before an email goes out?” “How do you prepare for an event two weeks out?” Real experience shows in specific steps and tools.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a marketing coordinator?
qa.a: Look for strong organization, clean writing and comfort with scheduling, email and project tools. A good coordinator keeps a calendar, tracks deadlines and follows up with designers and vendors. No license is required, so judge them on a portfolio, clear examples of campaigns or events they supported, and references who can speak to reliability.

qa.q: How do I test a marketing coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Hand them a draft email and three social posts with a few planted errors, plus a launch date. Ask them to fix the copy, build a simple posting schedule and list the steps to send the email. Review accuracy, how they handle the deadline and the questions they ask.

look.label: Results to verify
look.text: Ask for two or three past campaigns with the goal, budget range, channels and outcome. Look for numbers they can explain, like cost per lead or conversion rate. Confirm the results with a reference who saw the work. No US license is required for this role.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check their ability to plan a campaign from goal to launch, write a clear brief, read analytics, split a budget across channels and run simple A/B tests. Match their email, paid search, social ads and CRM experience to the channels your business actually uses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask who your customers are and what a new customer is worth before suggesting tactics. They talk openly about what failed and what they changed. They know compliance basics, such as CAN-SPAM rules for email and FTC guidance on endorsements and influencer posts.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: They claim credit for results but can’t describe their own role. They report only likes or impressions, with no link to leads or sales. They offer the same template for every business. They give vague answers about budgets they managed or how spending was tracked.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through a campaign that missed its target. What did you change?” “How did you split a limited budget?” “Which numbers did you report each week, and to whom?” Listen for specific steps, tools and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they have planned and run campaigns that brought in customers, not just posts or ads. Ask for past goals, budgets and results, and confirm them with references. Check that their channel experience fits yours. Make sure they can read data and explain decisions in plain terms. No license is required.

qa.q: How do I test a marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-limited task. Share a real goal, a sample budget and basic customer facts. Ask for a one-page campaign plan with channels, timeline, budget split and how success will be measured. Review how they set priorities and which numbers they would track. Keep it small, and don’t use their work without paying for it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Vendor certifications from marketing automation, CRM and analytics platforms are optional but show hands-on training. Check them in the vendor’s public directory, and weigh proof of real admin work over a list of badges.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Building segmented email sends with suppression lists, setting up a lead scoring model, tagging links with UTM parameters, fixing a broken sync between the email platform and the CRM, and turning raw data into a clear report. Solid spreadsheet skills matter, and basic SQL is a plus.

look.label: Compliance know-how
look.text: They should know CAN-SPAM basics: honest sender details and subject lines, a working opt-out, a valid postal address, and honoring unsubscribes within 10 business days. Ask how they track consent and handle data requests under state privacy laws, which vary by state, and the stricter consent rules for marketing texts.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They document processes and clean data before building on it. They define lead stages together with sales. They test every send and form before launch. They can walk you through a dashboard they built and name a decision it changed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Talks only about tools, never about results. Cannot explain how a lead moves from a form fill to a sales rep. Blames bad data on other teams without a fix. Has never audited tracking or run a test send before a campaign went live.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a marketing operations manager?
qa.a: Look for proven admin work in an email platform and CRM, a clear way of explaining lead scoring, and clean reporting habits. They should know CAN-SPAM basics and how state privacy laws affect consent. Strong candidates document their work, test before launch, and tie reports to business decisions, not just tool features.

qa.q: How do I test a marketing operations manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Share a sample lead export with messy fields and ask them to clean it, propose a simple lead scoring model, and outline a report for sales. Ask them to explain their choices aloud. Watch for how they handle duplicates, missing consent data and unclear stage definitions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Look for a degree in materials science, metallurgy, chemical or mechanical engineering. A Professional Engineer (PE) license is optional for most industry roles, but rules and title use vary by state. Six Sigma belts or quality training are a plus. Check them by asking for the issuer and confirming directly.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test material selection trade-offs among strength, weight, cost, corrosion and heat resistance. Also check design of experiments, statistical process control, process capability and FMEA. Ask them to read a stress-strain curve, a hardness report or a micrograph and explain what it means for the part.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates walk you through a real failure analysis from symptom to root cause to fix. They talk about scale-up from lab to production line, supplier changes and process qualification. They cite the test standards and specifications they used and explain why each mattered.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for picking materials from habit without weighing cost or manufacturability. Be wary of blaming operators for every defect, having no data behind past claims, or being vague about their own role in a team project. Skipping documentation and change control is another warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a part that failed in the field and how they found the cause. Ask how they would cut cost on a material without hurting performance. Ask what they check before releasing a new process to production and how they proved it was stable.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a materials and process engineer?
qa.a: Look for a relevant engineering degree and hands-on work with the materials and processes you use, such as metals, polymers, composites or coatings. They should show skill in failure analysis, design of experiments and statistical process control. A PE license is rarely required in industry and its rules vary by state. Clear writing of reports and specifications also matters.

qa.q: How do I test a materials and process engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short case. Share a failed part’s photos, test data and process sheet, and ask for likely causes, the next tests to run and a corrective action. You can also ask them to pick a material for a sample part and defend the choice on cost, performance and how easily it can be made.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: ASE certifications are voluntary but widely used; ask which areas they cover and whether they are current. Anyone handling vehicle AC refrigerant needs federal EPA Section 609 certification. A few states require state mechanic certification or inspection licenses, so check your state’s rules.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them diagnose a real fault using a scan tool and a multimeter. Watch how they read live data, check wiring and confirm the cause before replacing parts. For diesel work, include aftertreatment systems like DPF and DEF, injection and, if relevant, air brakes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a logical diagnostic process, check service information and technical bulletins, and verify the repair with a road test or rescan. They keep tools organized, follow torque specs and write clear notes on the repair order that a customer could understand.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for guessing and swapping parts until a problem goes away, skipping safety steps with lifts, jacks or high-voltage hybrid systems, and vague answers about past repairs. For mobile work, a candidate who cannot hold a valid driver’s license or plan a job site is a poor fit.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through their hardest intermittent electrical fault and how they found it. Ask which makes, engines and equipment they know best, what tools they own, and how they handle a comeback when a repair fails.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an automotive and diesel mechanic?
qa.a: Look for a clear diagnostic process, hands-on experience with the vehicles or equipment you service, and relevant ASE certifications. Confirm EPA Section 609 certification if they will touch AC systems. Check any state licensing rules where you operate. Good mechanics explain repairs simply, follow safety rules and document their work.

qa.q: How do I test an automotive and diesel mechanic before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid working interview on a vehicle with a known fault. Ask them to diagnose it with your scan tool and meter, explain their findings and estimate the repair. Score how methodical they are, how safely they work and whether they confirm the fault before recommending parts.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm the degree if your role requires one. A PE license is rarely needed for product design work, and many states exempt engineers working for manufacturers, but rules vary by state. Treat CAD or GD&T certifications as a plus, not proof of skill.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them model a part, build a small assembly, and make a fully dimensioned drawing with tolerances and GD&T. Check for a clean feature tree, clear design intent, and choices that suit the way the part will actually be made.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe parts that went from CAD through prototype, test and production. They know the limits of machining, molding or sheet metal, can run a tolerance stack-up, and check designs with quick hand calculations before trusting a simulation.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: A portfolio of polished renders with no drawings. No talk of materials, tolerances or cost. Blaming the shop when parts did not fit. Simulation results they cannot explain or sanity-check. Sharing a former employer’s confidential files without permission.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a part that failed in testing and what they changed. Ask how they chose a material or tolerance. Ask what a machinist or molder pushed back on. Real experience shows in specific details and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mechanical design engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid CAD skills, clean drawings with proper tolerances and GD&T, and a track record of taking parts through prototyping and testing. Strong candidates understand manufacturing processes and materials and can explain past design failures. A PE license is usually not required for product design, though rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test a mechanical design engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-limited task: model a simple part or bracket from a sketch, then produce a dimensioned drawing with tolerances. Ask them to explain material choice and how it would be made. Review redacted or personal portfolio work, since past employer designs are often confidential.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check the engineering degree. If the work needs stamped or sealed drawings, confirm a Professional Engineer (PE) license on the state board’s public lookup. Many in-house product design roles fall under an industrial exemption and need no PE, but these rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a dimensioned drawing with GD&T, a tolerance stack-up, and a quick hand calculation on stress or heat flow. Check that they work well in 3D CAD and can design for molding, machining or sheet metal, not just make nice-looking models.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about parts that shipped, test failures they fixed and how they worked with suppliers. They raise cost, assembly and service early. Their portfolio includes real drawings, and they can explain what changed between prototype and production.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: A portfolio of renderings only, with no drawings or tolerances. Vague answers about who did what on team projects. No mention of testing, thermal margins or manufacturing limits. Sharing a former employer’s confidential files as a work sample is also a warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a part that failed in testing and what they changed. Ask how they chose the material for a housing, or how they sized cooling for a hot component. Strong answers include numbers, tradeoffs and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mechanical engineer?
qa.a: Look for an engineering degree, solid 3D CAD skills, clean drawings with GD&T, and experience taking parts from prototype to production. Ask for a portfolio and specific stories about failures and fixes. A PE license matters only if your work needs stamped drawings, and that depends on your state and project.

qa.q: How do I test a mechanical engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-limited task tied to your product, such as designing a simple bracket or enclosure. Ask for a drawing with tolerances and a note on material and cooling choices. Then review it together. Ask why they made each decision and how they would change it for higher volume.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No general US license exists for mechanical technicians. Verify any associate degree or certificate in mechanical engineering technology. Also check role-specific credentials, such as EPA Section 608 certification if they will handle refrigerants, or a welding certification if the job includes welding.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them read a drawing, including tolerances, fits and GD&T callouts. Watch them measure with micrometers, calipers and dial indicators. Check that they follow torque specs and tightening sequences, align and shim parts correctly, and record test results clearly.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They check a drawing’s revision before starting. They zero and verify gauges before measuring and treat surfaces and seals with care. They explain why a part failed a test, not just that it failed. Their notes are neat enough for an engineer to use.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for guessing at tolerances or rounding measurements, skipping torque values, and forcing parts that do not fit. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a past assembly step by step, ignores lockout and safety steps, or blames tools for every rework.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a time a part did not match the drawing and what they did. Ask how they set up a pressure or leak test. Ask which measuring tools they trust for tight tolerances and how they check them.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mechanical technician?
qa.a: Look for someone who reads drawings accurately, measures with precision tools, and follows torque and assembly specs exactly. Hands-on experience with engines, valves or structures like yours matters. Check any degree or certificate, plus role-specific credentials such as EPA Section 608 for refrigerant work. Clear test records and careful handling of parts are strong signs.

qa.q: How do I test a mechanical technician before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a simple drawing and a small subassembly. Ask them to measure key features, flag anything out of tolerance, assemble it to the stated torque specs, and run a basic function or leak check. Have them write up results. Watch their tool use, safety habits and how they handle a deliberate mismatch.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check medical assistant certification such as CMA, RMA, CCMA or NCMA with the issuing body, and a current BLS card. Confirm what your state lets medical assistants do, such as injections or X-rays, and any state credential it requires.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Watch a candidate take vital signs, room a mock patient and chart it. Check injection and blood draw technique on a training arm, and test scheduling and prior authorization tasks in your system.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates are accurate under time pressure, explain each step to patients, stay within their scope and ask the provider when unsure. They keep rooms clean and protect patient privacy without being reminded.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about injections or blood draws, giving medical advice, careless talk about patients, or not knowing which tasks state law allows. Gaps in sharps and infection control habits are a serious concern.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A blood pressure reads 182/112 at intake. What do you do? What is the order of draw? A patient asks if they can stop a medicine. What do you say? How do you handle a denied prior authorization? Strong answers name each step and stay within scope.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a medical assistant?
qa.a: Look for certification or a recent accredited program, a current BLS card and solid clinical skills: vital signs, rooming, injections and blood draws where your state allows them. Check front-office skills, kindness with patients and privacy habits, and ask references from providers about accuracy and reliability.

qa.q: How do I test a medical assistant before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short paid working interview or skills check: room a mock patient, take vital signs, chart the visit, show injection technique on a training arm and handle a scheduling or prior authorization task. Watch for accuracy, how they explain steps and whether they stay within their scope.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required, but most employers want a national coding certification, such as CPC or CCS, or a billing credential. Verify active status with the certifying body’s online lookup. Specialty credentials, such as risk adjustment or surgical coding, matter for focused roles.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test ICD-10-CM, CPT and HCPCS coding from sample notes, modifier use, evaluation and management levels and bundling edits. For billers, check claim scrubbing, reading remittances, denial research, appeals and payer rules. Check speed and accuracy in your billing software and coding tools.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates code only what the note supports and query providers when documentation is unclear. They track yearly code changes, sort denials by cause and fix the root problem. They protect patient data and know compliance rules on upcoding and unbundling.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for coding from charge slips without reading notes, guessing at modifiers, or treating upcoding as normal. Be careful with lapsed certifications, weak knowledge of current code sets, or billers who resubmit denied claims without finding the cause.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a denied claim you overturned. When do you query a provider? How do you choose an evaluation and management level? How do you stay current with yearly code changes? Strong answers cite official guidelines, not habits.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a medical coder or biller?
qa.a: Look for an active national coding or billing certification, accuracy with current code sets, solid denial and appeal skills and experience in your specialty. Check compliance knowledge and privacy habits. References from coding managers or practice managers confirm accuracy and productivity.

qa.q: How do I test a medical coder or biller before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid test with de-identified sample notes to code, plus a few denied claims to research and fix. Compare their answers to an audited key. Review accuracy, modifier use, provider query choices and how clearly they explain the cause of each denial.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an MD or DO degree and an active, unrestricted license from the medical board in every state where they will practice or oversee care. Check board certification through ABMS or AOA boards, search the federal OIG exclusion list, and query the National Practitioner Data Bank if your organization is eligible.

look.label: Experience that fits your setting
look.text: A clinic or care company needs someone who has run peer review, quality programs and clinical protocols. A biotech needs trial design, Good Clinical Practice, drug safety monitoring and FDA meeting experience. Telehealth leaders should understand that licensing rules depend on the state where each patient is located.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them review a sample protocol, adverse event case or clinical policy and explain what they would change. Watch how they weigh patient safety, evidence and regulations against business pressure, and how clearly they explain medical reasoning to executives who are not clinicians.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They give concrete examples of changing a standard of care, stopping an unsafe practice or leading a team through an inspection or audit. They name trade-offs openly, credit their teams and keep their medical knowledge current through continuing education.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for lapsed or restricted licenses, vague answers about past board actions, and claims about trials or programs they cannot describe in detail. Be wary of anyone willing to sign off on work they did not review or who treats compliance as someone else’s job.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a medical director?
qa.a: Look for an MD or DO with an active, unrestricted license in each state where they will oversee care, plus board certification in a relevant specialty. Then match their experience to your setting, such as quality programs for clinics or clinical trials and FDA work for biotech. Strong candidates show sound judgment, clear communication and a record of putting patient safety first.

qa.q: How do I test a chief medical officer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case drawn from your real work, such as a draft protocol, a safety signal or a disputed clinical policy. Ask for a written or spoken recommendation and the reasoning behind it. Then have them present it to nonclinical leaders. You will see their medical judgment, their grasp of regulations and how well they lead people outside medicine.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most liaisons hold a doctoral degree such as a PharmD, PhD or MD, so verify the degree with the school. No license is required for the role, but if they claim a pharmacist, physician or nursing license, check it on the state board’s lookup. Medical affairs certifications are optional.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they critique a clinical paper, present trial data to a skeptical specialist and answer an unsolicited off-label question within company and FDA rules. Check they can gather and report field insights, support investigator studies and record interactions accurately in your system.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong liaisons speak as scientific peers, not salespeople. They know the treatment landscape and competing evidence in your therapy area, admit the limits of the data, build trust with experts over time and bring back insights that shape medical strategy and future studies.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for talk about driving prescriptions or sales targets, raising off-label uses without an unsolicited request, or overselling weak data. Be wary of anyone unfamiliar with how payments and meals given to doctors are reported under the federal Open Payments program.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A doctor asks about an unapproved use of our drug. What do you do? Walk me through a recent study in our area and its weaknesses. Tell me about an insight you brought back that changed a plan. Strong answers stay balanced and compliant.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a medical science liaison?
qa.a: Look for a doctoral-level scientific background, deep knowledge of your therapy area and the ability to discuss evidence as a peer with specialists. Check they understand the line between scientific exchange and promotion, FDA rules on off-label information and Open Payments reporting. Verify degrees and any claimed license directly.

qa.q: How do I test a medical science liaison before hiring?
qa.a: Ask for a short presentation of a recent published trial in your therapy area to a panel acting as skeptical doctors. Include an unsolicited off-label question and a hard critique of the study design. Review scientific accuracy, balance, clarity and whether every answer stays within compliance rules.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses medical writers. Voluntary certifications from professional groups exist but are optional. Verify past work instead: ask for redacted samples, confirm authorship and role with references, and check any claimed degree in life sciences, pharmacy or medicine with the school.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the documents you need, such as clinical study reports, regulatory submissions, journal manuscripts, continuing education or patient leaflets. Check accurate reading of statistics, correct citations, AMA style, plain language for patients and the ICH E3 structure for study reports.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong writers check every number against the source table, keep a reference log and know the authorship rules journals follow. They switch tone between regulators, doctors and patients, and push back when a draft claim goes beyond what the data show.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for samples with no clear source data, claims stronger than the study supports, copied text or missing citations, and no grasp of FDA rules on off-label promotion and fair balance. Be careful with anyone who shares confidential sponsor documents as samples without permission.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you handle a sponsor who wants a stronger conclusion than the data allow? How do you check that numbers in the text match the tables? Walk me through writing a plain language summary. Strong answers name concrete steps and review cycles.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a medical writer?
qa.a: Look for samples in your document type, accurate handling of data and references, and the ability to write for your audience, whether regulators, doctors or patients. Check knowledge of study report structure, journal authorship rules and promotional rules. No license is required, so verified samples and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a medical writer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your real work, such as writing a results summary from a set of mock tables, or a patient leaflet from a published paper. Review accuracy against the source, correct citations, clear structure, plain language where needed and whether claims stay within the data.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an active, independent license through the state board’s online lookup, and check for discipline. Titles vary by state, such as LPC, LMHC, LCSW, LMFT or licensed psychologist. Associates and interns may see clients only under a licensed supervisor, so ask who supervises them.

look.label: Telehealth rules to check
look.text: A therapist generally must be licensed in the state where the client is located during the session. Some interstate compacts, such as PSYPACT for psychologists, allow practice across states, but participation varies by state. Ask which states they can serve and which HIPAA-compliant video platform they use.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them walk through an intake and treatment plan for a sample anxiety case, then a crisis scenario. Listen for evidence-based methods such as CBT, clear documentation, suicide risk screening, safety planning and knowing when to refer to a psychiatrist or a higher level of care.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They set measurable goals and track progress with standard tools like the PHQ-9 or GAD-7. They explain confidentiality limits and mandated reporting plainly, keep notes current, seek consultation on hard cases and say honestly which conditions fall outside their training.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: A lapsed license or unresolved board discipline, vague answers about crisis steps, careless talk about past clients, or promises of quick cures. Be cautious with anyone who treats outside their scope, resists supervision or cannot explain how they protect records under HIPAA.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a therapist?
qa.a: Start with an active state license that fits the role, a clean disciplinary record and professional liability insurance. Then look for training in evidence-based treatments, sound crisis and risk procedures, timely documentation and comfort with telehealth if you offer it. Confirm they are licensed in every state where your clients will be located.

qa.q: How do I test a therapist before hiring?
qa.a: Use a made-up case vignette. Ask the candidate to outline an intake, the diagnoses they would consider, a treatment plan and how they would respond if the client disclosed suicidal thoughts. Have them write a sample progress note. Never use real client information, and have a licensed clinician on your team score the answers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Licensed counselors hold a state license whose title varies by state, such as LPC or LMHC. Addiction counselors usually need a state credential, and associates practice under supervision. Mental health technicians often need no license, though a few states license psychiatric technicians. Verify status on state board sites.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test intake assessment, suicide and violence risk screening, crisis de-escalation and treatment planning. Check evidence-based methods such as cognitive behavioral therapy and motivational interviewing, clear progress notes and privacy rules, including stricter federal rules for substance use records. Ward staff need safe observation and approved crisis training.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates keep firm boundaries, explain the limits of confidentiality clearly and know your state’s mandated reporting rules. They use supervision well, stay calm in crises and write notes that are timely, objective and useful to the team.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for boundary problems, such as dual relationships or oversharing about themselves, board discipline, or vague answers about risk assessment. Be careful with anyone who dismisses documentation, privacy rules or the need for clinical supervision.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you assess suicide risk. Tell me about a crisis you de-escalated. When would you break confidentiality? How do you handle a client who wants to connect on social media? Strong answers are calm and specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mental health technician or counselor?
qa.a: Look for the license or credential your state requires for the role, solid risk assessment and de-escalation skills, firm boundaries and clear notes. Check knowledge of confidentiality and mandated reporting rules. References from clinical supervisors show judgment better than a resume does.

qa.q: How do I test a mental health technician or counselor before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid role-play with a staff member acting as a client in crisis, then ask for a progress note and a safety plan. Use only made-up details. Judge risk assessment, empathy, boundaries, clear writing and whether they know when to involve a supervisor.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for clear written replies to upset merchants. The person should explain a payout delay, a fee breakdown or a listing error in plain words. They should also read an account history, find the likely cause and leave notes the next agent can follow.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Past seller, driver or business customer support is a plus. Strong candidates know terms like chargeback, dispute, refund and payout. They ask questions before answering. They escalate fraud or policy cases instead of guessing, and they treat a merchant’s lost income as urgent.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who promise refunds or exceptions they could not approve, or who blame the merchant. Be wary if they would change account details without checking identity, or if they cannot describe how they worked a ticket queue in a past job.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through a merchant whose payout never arrived.” Also ask: “What would you check before changing the bank details on an account?” And: “Tell me about a seller who threatened to leave the platform. What did you do?”

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Check past employers and references for support roles. If the job touches card or bank data, plan to train the new hire on your security rules, such as the PCI DSS steps your company follows.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a merchant support specialist?
qa.a: Look for clear writing, patience with frustrated business owners and a basic grasp of payments, payouts and chargebacks. Good candidates verify identity before changing accounts, escalate fraud instead of guessing and keep tidy ticket notes. Experience supporting sellers, restaurants or drivers helps, but strong customer support skills can carry over.

qa.q: How do I test a merchant support specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short mock ticket, such as a restaurant owner angry about a missing payout. Ask the candidate to write a reply and list the account details they would check. Then ask what they would escalate and why. Judge accuracy, tone, security steps and how clearly they explain next steps.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required in most industries, though regulated products such as insurance or securities need their own licenses. Verify sales results instead. Ask for quota and attainment by year, the deal sizes and cycle lengths they handled, and confirm them with former managers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test discovery, a demo tailored to the buyer, finding the economic buyer and building a mutual close plan. Check how they manage several stakeholders, procurement and security reviews, pricing negotiation, clean CRM records and an accurate forecast.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain deals in detail: who signed, why they bought now and what nearly killed the deal. They keep a balanced pipeline, build contacts across departments, forecast honestly and can close without leaning on heavy discounts.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for results they cannot break down, wins credited to luck or one big deal, frequent job changes before quota could be judged, and weak answers about lost deals. Be wary of anyone who blames marketing or product for every miss.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your biggest deal last year, from first call to signature. How did you find the person who controlled the budget? Tell me about a deal you lost late. Strong answers name stakeholders, steps and what they would change.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mid-market account executive?
qa.a: Look for a verified record of hitting quota on deals similar to yours in size, cycle length and buyer. They should run sharp discovery, manage several stakeholders, negotiate without heavy discounting and forecast accurately. No license is required in most industries, so references from former managers matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a mid-market account executive before hiring?
qa.a: Run a mock discovery call and demo with someone playing a buyer at a medium-sized company, using a short brief on your product. Then ask for a written close plan with stakeholders, next steps and risks. Judge their questions, listening, how they handle objections and whether the plan is realistic.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to fly spacecraft from the ground; regulators license the spacecraft and its radios, not individual operators. Ask about console certifications earned on past missions and confirm them with references. Missions flown, passes supported and anomalies handled are the best proof.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test pass planning, building and checking command sequences, reading telemetry against limits, and following contingency procedures. Check orbital basics, ground station scheduling, scripting for automation, and clear shift handover notes. For crewed or high-value missions, check experience with formal flight rules and voice loops.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates verify commands before sending, know their spacecraft’s subsystems and safe modes, and write clear logs and handovers. They stay calm during faults, follow flight rules, and push for automation or procedure fixes after each anomaly instead of repeating workarounds.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for sending commands from memory, skipping two-person checks, poor logs, and blaming the spacecraft or ground station without data. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain safe mode on a vehicle they flew or how a past anomaly was closed out.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a pass from planning to post-pass review. Tell me about a fault during a contact and what you did first. How do you verify a command before upload? Strong answers name telemetry, procedures, flight rules and clear communication with engineering.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mission operations engineer or flight controller?
qa.a: Look for real console time on satellites or spacecraft, strict command discipline, solid knowledge of subsystems and safe modes, and clear logs. Check scripting skills and calm fault handling. No license is required for operators, so console certifications from past missions, anomaly reports and references from flight directors or engineers matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a mission operations engineer or flight controller before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid simulation. Give them a sample pass plan, telemetry with one value drifting toward a limit, and a contingency procedure. Ask them to plan the pass, spot the problem and choose safe commands. Review command checks, use of procedures, timing and how clearly they report to engineering.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Cloud provider or Kubernetes certifications are optional and show baseline knowledge, but they do not replace proof. Ask for code samples, design documents or a detailed walkthrough of systems they ran in production.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Containers and Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, GPU scheduling, CI/CD for models, model serving with latency targets, and monitoring for drift and cost. Have them debug a failed training job or a slow inference endpoint instead of quizzing them on definitions.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk in numbers: GPU utilization, training time, serving latency and cloud spend. They explain tradeoffs between managed services and self-hosted tools. They have made pipelines reproducible with versioned data, code and models. They can describe an outage they caused and how they fixed it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Only notebook work with no production deployments. Cannot explain how a model gets from training to serving. Ignores cost, security or access controls. Blames data scientists for every failure. Proposes a large, complex platform when your team needs a simple, reliable pipeline.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through the last model you put into production. What broke first? How did you cut GPU costs or idle time? How do you roll back a bad model? How do you spot drift? Listen for specific details, not a list of tools.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an ML infrastructure engineer?
qa.a: Look for production experience, not just research. Strong candidates have deployed and monitored models, managed GPU or cloud resources, and automated training and release pipelines. They understand containers, Kubernetes and infrastructure as code. They track cost and latency. No license is required, so judge them on real systems they built and how clearly they explain their choices.

qa.q: How do I test an ML infrastructure engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task or a live session. Ask them to containerize a small model, deploy it as an endpoint with health checks, and add a retraining step to a pipeline. Or hand them a broken config to debug. Keep it to a few hours, use sample data rather than your own, and score it with your scorecard.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses mobile engineers, and certificates are optional. Verify published work instead. Ask for app store links, confirm their role with references, and ask exactly which screens and features they built on any team app.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the platform you ship on: Swift for iPhone, Kotlin for Android, or the cross-platform framework you use. Check networking, offline storage, push notifications, screen reader accessibility, crash reporting, and how they handle app store review rules and privacy disclosures.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have shipped and maintained apps through several OS updates, not just launched them. They talk about crash rates, app size, battery use and slow networks, test on real devices, and release with feature flags and staged rollouts.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for apps that crash on basic flows, no experience getting through app store review, passwords or tokens stored in plain text, and no automated tests. Be wary of anyone who has only built tutorial apps or cannot explain their own code.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an app rejected in review and what you changed. How do you handle a user who loses signal mid-checkout? How did you track down a crash you could not reproduce? Strong answers name real tools and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mobile engineer?
qa.a: Look for shipped apps you can download, code they can explain, and skills that match your stack, whether native or cross-platform. Check their habits on testing, accessibility, privacy and crash monitoring. No license is required in the US, so live apps and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a mobile engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your real work, such as building one screen that loads data from an API, caches it and handles errors and lost signal. Ask for the source code with tests. Run it on a real phone and review stability, accessibility and code clarity.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Federal law requires every mortgage loan originator to have a unique NMLS ID. Loan officers at nonbank lenders need a state license in each state where they originate, which means education, a national test and a background check. Bank and credit union employees register federally instead. Verify on NMLS Consumer Access.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test income calculation for salaried, hourly and self-employed borrowers, reading credit reports, debt-to-income and asset review, and matching borrowers to loan programs. Check they know federal disclosure timing, rate lock procedures and how to move a file from application through underwriting to closing.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong loan officers explain loan options in plain words, set realistic timelines, and give processors complete files the first time. They keep borrowers and agents informed through closing, track every condition, and treat every applicant the same way under fair lending rules.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for promises of approval before reviewing documents, steering borrowers toward loans that pay the officer more, or pressure to adjust income or asset figures. Be wary of a missing or lapsed license in your states and any disciplinary history on NMLS.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you calculate income for a self-employed borrower. Tell me about a loan that nearly failed before closing and how you saved it. How do you handle an appraisal that comes in low? Strong answers name documents, steps and timelines.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a mortgage loan officer?
qa.a: Look for an active state license or federal registration with a clean NMLS record in each state you lend in. Check they can calculate income accurately, explain loan programs simply and manage files to closing on time. Ask how they follow fair lending and disclosure rules, since mistakes there bring real regulatory risk.

qa.q: How do I test a mortgage loan officer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise using an anonymized borrower file with pay stubs, tax returns, bank statements and a credit report. Ask them to calculate qualifying income, pick suitable loan programs and list missing documents. Then role-play a call explaining options to the borrower. Review accuracy, fair treatment and clarity.

look.label: Reel and portfolio review
look.text: Ask for a short demo reel that opens with the best work, plus breakdowns of key projects. Each piece should state what the candidate did personally, such as design, animation, 3D or compositing, versus what the team or other artists handled.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check timing, easing and spacing, kinetic typography, and clean keyframe curves. Confirm they can export for different targets: vertical and square social formats, broadcast specs, and lightweight animation files for websites, apps or game engines.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain why they chose a timing or transition, follow brand guidelines closely, and hand over tidy project files with named layers and organized assets. They plan with storyboards or style frames before animating and sync motion well to voice and music.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for reels built mostly from purchased templates or tutorial projects, vague answers about their own role on team work, and fonts, music or footage used without proper licenses. Missed export specs and messy, unlabeled files often mean trouble on real deadlines.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through one project from brief to final render. Ask how they handle a big client change late in production, and how they set up files so another animator or editor can pick them up easily.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a motion designer?
qa.a: No state license is required for this work, so judge the reel and the process. Look for smooth timing, clear typography and work that matches your platforms, such as social video, apps or games. Ask what they personally made on each piece, and confirm they use properly licensed fonts, music and stock footage.

qa.q: How do I test a motion designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid test. Share a logo or static design and your brand guide, and ask for a 5 to 10 second animation in two sizes by a set deadline. Then give one round of feedback. Judge the timing, the organization of the project file, and how well they apply your notes.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required for network engineers. Vendor and vendor-neutral networking certifications are common, and many employers ask for them. Verify them through the issuer’s online lookup, and confirm hands-on work with references who saw their changes in production.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test routing and switching, including VLANs, OSPF and BGP, plus firewalls, VPNs, wireless, DNS and DHCP. Check troubleshooting with packet captures and logs, change planning with rollback steps, and basic automation with scripts or configuration tools.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates document networks, use change windows and rollback plans, and monitor links before users complain. They can explain an outage they caused or fixed, step by step, and design for redundancy instead of single points of failure.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for untested changes made directly in production, no documentation, default passwords left on devices, and certifications without hands-on stories. Be careful with anyone who blames other teams for every outage or cannot read a packet capture.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Users at one office cannot reach a cloud app, but others can. Walk me through your steps. Tell me about a change that caused an outage. How do you secure remote access? Strong answers go layer by layer and name real commands.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a network engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on routing, switching, firewall and wireless experience, careful change habits and clear documentation. Certifications help but are optional, and no state license is required, so verify them with the issuer and test real troubleshooting. References who saw their production work matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a network engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid lab exercise in a simulator, such as fixing a broken route, a mistyped VLAN and a firewall rule that blocks traffic. Ask them to explain each step aloud and write a short change plan with rollback. Review method, accuracy and how they confirm the fix.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for hands-on work with tokenization, transformer models, fine-tuning and evaluation. For speech roles, check audio basics too: sampling rates, feature extraction, and handling noise, accents and overlapping speakers. Strong candidates explain the tradeoffs between model size, speed, cost and accuracy.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this work. A degree in computer science, linguistics or a related field helps but is not essential. Verify claims through code samples, published papers, open-source contributions or a past project they can walk through in depth.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They pick metrics that fit the task, such as word error rate for transcription or automatic scores plus human review for translation. They build test sets from real user data, track errors by language or dialect, and know when a simple rule beats a model.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Only demos that call a hosted model with no evaluation behind them. Vague answers about where training data came from, its licensing or user privacy. No plan for latency, cost or failure cases. Claims of near-perfect accuracy without saying what data it was measured on.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they lowered word error rate on noisy calls, how they handled a language with little training data, or how they kept a chatbot from making things up. Listen for specific steps, what they measured and what they would change next time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an NLP and speech engineer?
qa.a: Look for proof they shipped language or speech features to real users, not just notebooks. They should know modern model types, choose sound evaluation metrics, clean messy text or audio data and weigh speed against accuracy. Clear writing matters, since they must explain model limits to product teams. No license applies, so judge them on their work.

qa.q: How do I test an NLP and speech engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task using data like yours, such as transcripts with errors or customer messages to sort by intent. Ask for a working baseline, an evaluation plan and a written note on where it fails. Then review it together and ask what they would try with one more week.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as a Node.js developer. Node.js certifications exist but are optional. Verify work instead: review repositories or code samples, ask which services they built and kept running, and call references from past teams.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the event loop, async and await, error handling and streams. Check the framework you use, such as Express, Fastify or NestJS, plus TypeScript, database access, input validation, authentication and tests. Ask how they keep npm dependencies patched and keep heavy work off the event loop.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have run Node.js services in production and can explain how they handled crashes, memory leaks and slow requests. They validate every input, log in a structured way, write tests and keep the dependency list short and current.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for unhandled promise rejections, callbacks and async code mixed at random, secrets in source code, and packages added for trivial tasks. Be careful with candidates who cannot say what blocks the event loop or who have only built front ends.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How would you find a memory leak in a Node.js service? What happens when CPU-heavy work runs on the main thread, and how do you avoid it? How do you handle an npm package with a security warning? Strong answers name specific tools and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Node.js developer?
qa.a: Look for back-end services they built and ran in production, with code they can explain. Check async patterns, error handling, TypeScript, databases, security habits and care with dependencies. No license is required in the US, so working code, references and clear answers about real incidents matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a Node.js developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work, such as building a small REST API endpoint with validation, a database call and tests, in JavaScript or TypeScript. Ask them to use Git and explain their choices. Review error handling, input validation, async correctness, test quality and how readable the code is.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an active RN license and an NP or APRN license in each state where patients will be. Check national board certification in their population focus, such as family or adult-gerontology. Verify their NPI number and, if they will prescribe controlled substances, DEA registration and any state controlled substance registration.

look.label: State rules to check
look.text: Practice authority varies by state. Some states allow NPs to practice fully on their own. Others require a collaborative or supervisory agreement with a physician. For video visits, the NP generally must be licensed where the patient is located. The multistate RN compact does not cover NP practice.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test clinical reasoning with a realistic case. Ask them to take a history, form a differential diagnosis, choose tests and explain a treatment plan. Check safe prescribing, clear notes in an electronic health record, and how they examine and assess patients by video.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: A strong NP explains decisions in plain words, knows when to refer or send a patient to the ER, and documents clearly. They know your state’s prescribing and supervision rules. They show calm, warm communication with patients, including on camera.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for lapsed or restricted licenses, gaps they cannot explain, or certification outside your patient population. Be cautious if they seem unsure of state scope rules, prescribe controlled substances casually, or cannot describe how they handle emergencies during a video visit.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a nurse practitioner?
qa.a: Look for active RN and NP licenses in every state they will serve, national certification matching your patients, an NPI number and DEA registration if needed. Check board actions on the state license lookup. Then look for sound clinical judgment, safe prescribing, clear documentation and good patient communication, in person and by video.

qa.q: How do I test a nurse practitioner before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case interview. Present a patient complaint and ask them to walk through history, exam, differential diagnosis, tests and treatment. Include a prescribing decision and a moment when referral is needed. For telehealth roles, run a mock video visit and review a sample note they write afterward.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an active RN or LPN/LVN license through the state board of nursing’s online lookup, and check for discipline or restrictions. Many employers also require current BLS certification. Nurse practitioners hold a separate advanced license, and their scope of practice varies by state.

look.label: Telehealth licensing rules
look.text: A nurse generally must be licensed in the state where the patient is physically located during each visit. A multistate license under the Nurse Licensure Compact covers member states only, and not every state has joined. Plan for patients who travel or are temporarily away.
