look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test medication safety and dosage math, patient assessment, clear charting and prioritizing several patients at once. For video visits, check how they assess and triage without touching the patient, and when they send someone to in-person or emergency care.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Gives concrete examples of catching a change in a patient’s condition. Coordinates smoothly with doctors, pharmacists and families. Documents promptly, follows patient privacy rules such as HIPAA, explains care in plain words and admits what they don’t know.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: A license that is inactive, restricted or issued in a different state than claimed. Vague answers about medication errors, blaming others, sharing identifiable details about past patients, or reluctance to follow protocols and speak up about safety concerns.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a nurse?
qa.a: Start with an active, unrestricted license in the right state, verified with the state board of nursing. For telehealth, make sure it covers every state where patients will be located during visits. Then look for sound clinical judgment, safe medication habits, careful charting, calm communication and a habit of escalating concerns early.

qa.q: How do I test a nurse before hiring?
qa.a: Use realistic scenarios: a patient whose vital signs are slipping, a medication order that looks wrong, or several patients needing care at once. Add a short dosage calculation and a sample chart note. For telehealth roles, run a mock video triage. Never let an unverified candidate care for real patients.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for observability work. Cloud and monitoring vendor certifications are optional. Verify with dashboards, alert rules and runbooks they built, incidents they helped resolve, and references from on-call engineers who relied on their tools.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test logs, metrics and traces, with tools such as OpenTelemetry and Prometheus. Check query languages for metrics and logs, service level objectives and error budgets, alert design, sampling, and control of label cardinality and storage cost. Confirm they can instrument code in your main languages.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates cut noisy alerts and tie each alert to user impact and a runbook. They set service level objectives with product teams, control data volume and cost, and keep passwords and personal data out of logs.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who alert on every metric, build dashboards nobody uses, or add high-cardinality labels such as user IDs to metrics. Be careful with anyone who ignores what logging costs, or logs sensitive data without thinking about who can see it.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an outage your tools caught early, or one they missed. How do you decide what deserves a page at night? How do you set a service level objective? How did you cut logging costs without losing signal? Strong answers are specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an observability engineer?
qa.a: Look for experience building logs, metrics, traces and alerts that on-call engineers actually use. Check OpenTelemetry or similar tools, service level objectives, alert design, cardinality and cost control, plus coding to instrument services. Ask about real incidents. No license is required, so built systems and references from engineers matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an observability engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your systems: instrument a small sample service with metrics and traces, write two or three alerts tied to a service level objective, and draft a runbook for one. Review signal versus noise, label choices, cost awareness and how clearly the runbook guides a tired on-call engineer.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required to work as an office manager. Check past employment and call references who saw their daily work. Some candidates hold a voluntary administrative professional certification. Treat it as a plus, not a must.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for supply tracking against a budget, vendor and repair calls, calendar and room booking, spreadsheets, and clear notices to staff. Ask them to turn a messy request into a supply order and a short building notice.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe systems they built, like reorder lists, new hire checklists, visitor sign-in and maintenance logs. They give real examples of cutting vendor costs, running events on budget, and staying calm when several problems land at once.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about what they handled versus what a boss did. No example of fixing a vendor problem. Loose habits with confidential files, keys or petty cash. Blaming or gossiping about the coworkers they supported.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through setting up a new hire’s first day.” “Tell me about a vendor who missed a deadline. What did you do?” “How did you track supplies and spending?” Strong answers include clear steps, numbers and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an office manager?
qa.a: Look for someone organized, calm and clear in writing. They should have handled supplies, vendors, visitors, events and the office space on their own. Ask for examples of systems they built and money they saved. No license is required, so rely on references and a short practical test to confirm their skills.

qa.q: How do I test an office manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task that mirrors a real day. Hand them a list of requests, like a broken printer, a low supply order, a visitor arriving and a team lunch, and ask them to rank and plan each one. Add a small budget spreadsheet. Keep it brief, or pay for longer work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most oil and gas engineers need no license, though a state PE license is needed to seal some designs. Pipeline workers on covered tasks need federal operator qualification. Offshore staff in federal waters need required well control training. Verify safety orientation, hydrogen sulfide training and site access cards.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Match the test to the role. Reservoir engineers should analyze decline curves and pressure data. Drilling engineers should design casing and plan well control. Facilities and pipeline engineers should read P&IDs, size lines and run hydraulic or process models. All should know process safety basics.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain the economics behind their technical choices, have field time on rigs or plants, and use stop-work authority without hesitation. They know the federal and state rules for their work, such as pipeline integrity or air emissions, and keep management of change records.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for casual talk about bypassing safety systems, skipping permits or lockout, or hiding spills and leaks. Be careful with candidates who know only simulation software and cannot explain the physics, or who blame crews for every incident without looking at design.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a time you used stop-work authority. How did you handle a well kick or a pressure upset? Walk me through a hazard review you led. How did you improve production or cut downtime on an asset you managed? Strong answers include data, not just stories.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an oil and gas engineer?
qa.a: Look for the specialty you need, field experience, process safety habits and any required training, such as pipeline operator qualification or offshore well control. Check PE status if they must seal designs. Strong candidates tie engineering choices to safety and cost, and their references confirm real field results.

qa.q: How do I test an oil and gas engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case study from your field, such as a decline curve to forecast, a casing design to check or a P&ID with a hidden hazard to find. Ask them to explain their assumptions aloud. Review technical accuracy, safety thinking and how clearly they present a recommendation.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them work in a real spreadsheet. They should clean a messy export, build a pivot table, use lookups and spot an outlier. For analyst roles, add a basic SQL query. Watch whether they check the data before trusting it, not just how fast they write formulas.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Lean Six Sigma belts and similar process certificates are optional. Many different bodies issue them, with no single standard, so treat them as a plus, not proof. Verify past roles and results through references.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a process they changed with a clear before and after, such as hours saved, errors cut or backlogs cleared. They write step-by-step instructions others can follow. They can explain a chart to someone who doesn’t work with numbers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague claims like “improved efficiency” with no numbers or method. Complex automations nobody else can maintain. Blaming coworkers for every broken process. No habit of documenting work. Picking a tool before asking how the work is actually done today.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through a report you built that changed a decision.” “Tell me about a process you automated. What broke afterward?” “How do you know your numbers are right?” Strong answers name data sources, checks and the people involved.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an operations analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong spreadsheet skills, clean data habits and a track record of fixing real processes. Good candidates show results with numbers, document what they build and explain findings in plain words. Optional certificates can help, but no license is required, so judge them mainly on past work and a practical test.

qa.q: How do I test an operations analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give them an anonymized dataset from a real process, such as orders or support tickets. Ask them to find the main bottleneck, suggest one fix or automation, and write a short summary for a manager. Keep the task to a few hours. Paying for longer tasks is good practice.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can read a profit and loss statement, build a staff schedule, map a messy process into clear steps and compare supplier quotes. Ask them to spot where money or time is leaking in a short sample of your real numbers.

look.label: Credentials worth checking
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Project management or Lean Six Sigma certifications can show training but are optional. Verify past job titles, the size of teams they ran and the budgets they managed by calling references directly.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk in results they can measure, such as lower overtime, fewer stockouts or faster order turnaround. They explain how they tracked the change, who they worked with and what they would do differently next time.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague claims like “improved efficiency” with no example or number. Blaming past staff or bosses for every problem. No experience with hard conversations, such as coaching a weak performer or pushing back on a supplier. Avoiding questions about mistakes.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Tell me about a supplier that let you down. What did you do?” “Walk me through how you set a monthly budget.” “Describe a process you changed and how you got staff to follow it.” Listen for concrete steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an operations manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has run people, processes, suppliers and costs at a business like yours. They should read financial reports, build schedules and fix broken workflows. Strong candidates give specific, measured results and explain how they got them. No license is required, so verify experience through references.

qa.q: How do I test an operations manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-limited task using sample data from your business. For example, ask them to find cost savings in a supplier list, fix a weekly staff schedule or outline a plan for a recurring problem. Then have them walk you through their choices and trade-offs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles call for a degree in optics, physics or electrical engineering. Verify degrees directly with the school. No state license is usually needed. A Professional Engineer license is rare in optics, and its rules vary by state. For laser work, a laser safety officer certification exists but is optional.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give a short spec with focal length, field of view and wavelength band. Watch how they set up ray tracing and read spot diagrams and MTF curves. See whether they add tolerances so a shop can actually build the part.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They show designs that were built and measured, not just simulated. They bring up stray light, thermal shifts, coatings and alignment without prompting. They can explain trade-offs to mechanical and electrical teams in plain words.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Their portfolio is only software output with no lab or test data. They ignore tolerances, cost or manufacturability. They treat laser safety casually or cannot describe basic controls like interlocks, protective eyewear and beam enclosures.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Tell me about a design that failed in test. What did you measure, and what did you change?” Ask how they split an error budget across a system. Strong answers include real steps, data and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an optical engineer?
qa.a: Look for a degree in optics, physics or a related field, and designs that were built and tested, not just modeled. Check that they handle tolerancing, stray light and thermal effects. Good candidates explain trade-offs clearly and take laser safety seriously. A state license is usually not required.

qa.q: How do I test an optical engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small paid design task with a clear spec, such as a simple lens for a set wavelength and field of view. Ask for ray-tracing results, a tolerance check and a short write-up of trade-offs. Then have them walk you through test data from a past project and explain what they would change.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for organizational development work. Coaching and assessment certifications are optional. Anyone using the title psychologist generally needs a state license, and rules vary by state. Verify through case studies with measured outcomes and references from leaders they worked with.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test organization design, change management, leadership program design, performance review and calibration processes, and career path frameworks. Check survey design and analysis, facilitation, and knowledge that assessments used for promotion must be job-related and fair under federal equal employment rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates start from the business problem, involve managers and employees, and measure results such as retention, promotion readiness or engagement. They adapt frameworks to your size and culture, explain tradeoffs clearly and follow through after the workshop ends.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for one framework applied to every problem, programs judged only by attendance or satisfaction, and personality tests used for promotion without validation. Be wary of anyone who cannot show results or who redesigns structures without involving the people affected.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a reorganization you designed and how you measured success. How did you fix a performance review process managers disliked? How do you decide whether a leadership program worked? Strong answers show diagnosis, stakeholder work and measured results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an organizational development specialist?
qa.a: Look for case studies tied to business problems, with measured results in retention, performance or leadership readiness. Check skills in organization design, change management, survey analysis and facilitation, and fair, job-related use of assessments. No license is required, though each state regulates the psychologist title. References from leaders matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an organizational development specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case: anonymized engagement survey results and a description of a team with high turnover. Ask for a diagnosis, a few interventions and how they would measure success. Then have them facilitate a short mock session. Review analysis, practicality, measurement and facilitation.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for most OT or product security work. Industrial security training and certifications based on ISA/IEC 62443 show relevant knowledge but are optional. A state engineering license matters only for sealed designs, and rules vary by state. Check references from plants or product teams.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test knowledge of industrial protocols such as Modbus and DNP3, segmentation between IT and plant networks, and safe asset discovery that will not disrupt controllers. For products, check threat modeling, secure boot, firmware updates and vulnerability handling. Ask how they work within downtime limits.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates put safety and uptime first and work closely with operators and engineers. They know a controller may wait months for a patch, so they use compensating controls. They know sector rules that apply to you, such as NERC CIP for power or FDA expectations for medical devices.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who want to run active scans on live control networks without a plan, apply office IT rules unchanged to plants, or ignore safety systems. Be careful with anyone who has never worked beside operators or cannot explain how a controller works.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How would you find all devices on a plant network without disrupting production? A controller cannot be patched until next year; what do you do? How do you threat model a connected product? Strong answers stress safety, uptime and layered controls.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an OT and product security engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with industrial control systems or embedded devices, knowledge of industrial protocols and standards such as ISA/IEC 62443, and a safety-first mindset. Check they work well with plant operators or product engineers. No license is usually required, so references and past projects matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test an OT and product security engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task, such as reviewing a simple plant network diagram and proposing segmentation, or threat modeling a connected device from a short spec. Ask them to rank risks and fixes with downtime in mind. Review safety awareness, practical controls and clear writing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for packaging engineers, and the Certified Packaging Professional credential is optional. For chip packaging, verify work on packages that reached production. Check knowledge of rules your products face, such as hazardous materials shipping, food contact, and packaging laws that vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: For shipping packaging, test material and structure choice, cushion design and transit testing such as drop, vibration and compression. For chip packaging, test substrates, wire bond or flip chip, thermal and warpage analysis, and reliability testing. Check CAD drawings and clear specifications for suppliers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates balance protection, cost, line speed and recyclability, and prove designs with tests rather than guesses. They work closely with suppliers and production, track damage claims or yield data, and can show a design that cut damage, material or failures.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for designs never tested in transit or reliability conditions, no grasp of supplier tolerances, and environmental claims they cannot back up. Be wary of anyone who ignores state packaging laws or who cannot explain a past failure and its fix.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a package you designed from brief to production. Tell me about a test failure and what you changed. How do you trade protection against cost and recyclability? For chip roles, what drove warpage in your last package? Strong answers cite data.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a packaging engineer?
qa.a: Look for designs that reached production, test data that proves them, and experience with your packaging type, from shipping boxes to semiconductor packages. Check knowledge of materials, suppliers and the rules your products face, which may vary by state. No license is required, so portfolios, test reports and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a packaging engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise, such as designing packaging for one of your products with protection and material targets, plus a test plan. For chip roles, share package data with a reliability failure and ask for causes and fixes. Review test thinking, tradeoffs, drawings and clear writing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most states do not license paralegals, so certification is usually voluntary. Some states have their own voluntary certification programs. California sets education or experience rules for anyone using the paralegal title. Confirm any certificate, degree or certification the candidate lists, and check references from attorneys who supervised their work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test drafting from a template, proofreading and legal citation format. Check how they calculate and calendar deadlines under court rules, which vary by state and court. Ask about e-filing, document management and contract tracking tools, and how they keep records organized for quick retrieval.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong paralegals double-check every deadline against the source document and keep a backup calendar. They know the practice area’s common documents, protect client confidentiality, and flag possible conflicts early. They write clear file notes, so any lawyer can pick up a matter and see what happened.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for anyone comfortable giving clients legal advice or setting fees, since only lawyers may do that. Other warning signs are vague answers about tools they claim to know, careless talk about past clients’ matters, typos in their own application, and no system for tracking deadlines.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through calendaring a deadline from a court order. Ask about a time they caught an error before a filing went out. Ask which case management and e-filing systems they used, and what they would do if a lawyer was unreachable near a deadline.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a paralegal?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, deadline discipline and experience in your practice area. Check any degree or certificate they list, though most states do not require one. Make sure they understand they cannot give legal advice and must work under a lawyer’s supervision. References from attorneys they worked for are the best proof of reliable, confidential work.

qa.q: How do I test a paralegal before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or clearly limited task using made-up facts. Ask them to draft a simple document from a template, proofread a page with planted errors, and list the deadlines from a sample court order or contract. Review accuracy, formatting and how they explain their deadline math.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Verify partner results instead. Ask for joint business plans, partner programs they built and revenue they sourced or influenced through partners, and call partner contacts as references. Vendor partner certifications are optional but show familiarity with a platform.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they pick partners, write a joint business plan, run deal registration and settle channel conflict with direct sales. Check partner enablement, co-marketing, tracking partner-sourced versus influenced revenue and reading the key terms of a partner agreement.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates focus on a few partners who truly sell, not a long list of logos. They train partner teams, share leads fairly, earn trust from your own sales reps and can show revenue that clearly came through partners.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for big partner counts with little revenue, credit claimed for deals sales closed alone, and no plan for channel conflict. Be wary of anyone who signs partners without enablement or cannot explain how partner deals were tracked.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you decide which partners deserve your time? Tell me about a conflict between a partner and your direct sales team. How do you measure partner-influenced revenue? Strong answers name criteria, processes and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a partner manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of growing revenue through resellers, integrations or agencies, strong relationships on both sides and fair handling of channel conflict. They should build joint plans, enable partner teams and track sourced and influenced deals. No license is required, so partner references and verified results matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a partner manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: describe your product and a few possible partners, and ask them to choose one, explain why and outline a joint business plan for the first two quarters. Include a channel conflict scenario. Judge their choice, the plan’s realism and how they protect both relationships.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to sketch a joint campaign with a reseller: shared goals, who funds what, lead handoff rules and how results get reported. Strong candidates think about both companies’ incentives, not just their own brand’s reach.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can explain how they tied partner programs to pipeline or revenue, not just impressions. They know co-marketing funds, deal registration, partner portals and marketplace listings, and they talk comfortably about working with sales and channel teams.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a partner relationship that stalled and how they revived it. Ask how they decided which partners got marketing funds or attention. Ask how they split credit for leads that both companies touched.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague claims about “managing partners” with no numbers, programs or examples. Treating partners like a pure ad channel. No sense of brand approval steps, contract limits or how to resolve disputes over lead ownership.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for this work in the US. Some vendors offer partner program or marketplace certifications, which can help. Check references from past partner contacts or channel sales leaders to confirm the results they describe.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a partner marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they have run joint campaigns with partners, resellers or marketplaces and measured the results in pipeline or revenue. They should handle co-marketing funds, shared lead rules and brand approvals on both sides. Strong people listen to partners’ goals, keep clear plans and work closely with your sales and channel teams.

qa.q: How do I test a partner marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task: pick a sample partner and ask for a one-page joint campaign plan. It should cover target buyers, each company’s role and budget share, lead handoff, timeline and how success is measured. Then discuss it live, and ask how they would handle a partner who misses commitments.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check the state nurse aide registry for nursing assistant certification, any national PCT, phlebotomy or EKG certificates, and a current BLS card. For dialysis roles, confirm certification or a plan to certify within 18 months of hire.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have candidates take vital signs, place leads for a 12-lead EKG on a manikin, show blood draw technique on a training arm and do a safe transfer. Ask them to chart the results correctly.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates report changes to the nurse at once, stay within their scope, work steadily on a busy unit and treat patients with patience. They know fall and pressure injury prevention and infection control.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for willingness to give medications, careless identification before a blood draw, sitting on abnormal readings, poor hand hygiene and rough handling of patients. Gaps in BLS or certification need explaining.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A glucose reads 52. What do you do? Where does V1 go? A nurse asks you to give pills. What do you say? How do you care for a patient on contact precautions? Strong answers bring in the nurse at once.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a patient care technician?
qa.a: Look for nursing assistant or PCT certification, current BLS, and real skill in vital signs, blood draws and EKGs. Check that they report changes quickly and know their scope. References from nurses who worked with them are the best guide to how they handle a busy unit.

qa.q: How do I test a patient care technician before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short skills station: vital signs, EKG lead placement on a manikin, venipuncture on a training arm, a safe transfer and charting. Add two scenarios, a low blood sugar and a patient who refuses care, and score safety, speed and how they involve the nurse.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for payments engineers. Instead, confirm past work on systems in scope for PCI DSS, the card industry security standard. PCI auditor training is optional and not required for the role. Call references about payment systems they shipped, ran and supported after launch.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Storing money as integers in minor units or exact decimals, never floating point. Using idempotency keys so a retried charge never bills twice. Designing a double-entry ledger where every transaction balances. Handling webhooks that arrive late, twice or out of order.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They bring up reconciliation early, matching your ledger against processor and bank settlement reports. They have handled refunds, chargebacks, partial captures and ACH returns. They can explain authorization, capture and settlement timing, and they have been on call for money incidents.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Uses floats for amounts. Wants to store full card numbers or security codes in your own database. Retries a timed-out charge without an idempotency key. Edits ledger rows in place instead of posting reversing entries. Stays vague about incidents they caused.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “A customer was charged twice. How do you find the cause and fix the ledger?” “How do you handle currencies with different decimal places?” “What changes when you add ACH, where returns can arrive days after the payment?”

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a payments engineer?
qa.a: Look for someone who has built and run payment flows in production, not just called a checkout API. They should understand idempotency, double-entry ledgers, reconciliation and reducing PCI DSS scope through tokenization. No license is required, so weigh references, shipped systems and how they handled past money incidents.

qa.q: How do I test a payments engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task or pairing session: build a small ledger that records a charge, a partial refund and a duplicate webhook, with balances correct to the cent. Review it together. Ask how they would reconcile it against a settlement report and what happens when the processor times out mid-request.

look.label: Credentials worth checking
look.text: No US state licenses payroll specialists. Some candidates hold the Certified Payroll Professional (CPP) or Fundamental Payroll Certification (FPC). These are voluntary, so treat them as a plus, not a requirement. Verify any credential with the issuing body, and confirm hands-on experience with payroll software like yours.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to run gross-to-net pay for a sample employee. Include overtime under federal FLSA rules, a pre-tax benefit deduction and a wage garnishment. Check that they apply federal, state and local withholding correctly and can explain each step in plain words.

look.label: Knowledge that matters
look.text: Strong candidates know Form W-4, quarterly Form 941, year-end W-2s and how to reconcile payroll to the general ledger. They know pay frequency, final paycheck deadlines and some overtime rules vary by state, and they check the rules for every state where you have employees.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They double-check before submitting, keep clear records and can describe a payroll error they caught and fixed. They meet hard deadlines calmly and guard salary and bank details. Good ones ask early about your pay schedule, benefits and the states you operate in.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful if they guess at tax rules instead of looking them up, treat every state the same, or call a missed tax deposit minor. Sharing a past employer’s salary details during the interview is a warning sign about how they handle confidential data.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a payroll specialist?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, solid knowledge of federal and state withholding and overtime rules, and experience with payroll software similar to yours. Check that they can reconcile payroll and prepare quarterly and year-end forms. A CPP or FPC credential is a plus but not required. Strict confidentiality with pay and bank data is essential.

qa.q: How do I test a payroll specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short exercise with made-up employee data. Include hourly and salaried staff, overtime, a pre-tax deduction and a garnishment. Ask them to calculate net pay and find a planted error in a sample payroll register. Watch how they check their work and how clearly they explain their reasoning.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to design circuit boards. Industry designer certifications, such as Certified Interconnect Designer, are optional but verifiable. Ask for board screenshots, fabrication outputs and bring-up notes where confidentiality allows, and check with references which boards the candidate laid out personally.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test stack-up planning, impedance-controlled and high-speed routing, power delivery, grounding, thermal relief and design for manufacturing and assembly. Check clean schematics, footprints, fabrication and assembly outputs, and bench bring-up of first boards with a multimeter, oscilloscope and power supply.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk to the fab and assembly house early, review stack-ups and footprints carefully, and keep design rules in the tool. They bring up boards methodically, log every rework and can show a board revision that fixed a real noise or assembly problem.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for autorouted boards with no constraints, footprints copied without checking datasheets, missing test points and fiducials, and no habit of design review. Be wary of anyone who has never handled a board after it came back from the fab.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through the stack-up of your most complex board and why you chose it. Tell me about a first board that did not power up and what you checked first. How do you route a high-speed differential pair? Strong answers name specific rules and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a PCB design engineer?
qa.a: Look for complex boards that went into production, clean schematics and layouts, and strong design for manufacturing habits. Check high-speed and power integrity skills if your product needs them, and real bring-up experience on the bench. No license is required, so board samples, revision history and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a PCB design engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work, such as placing and routing a small board section from a schematic with a given stack-up, or reviewing a layout with planted errors. Ask for notes on their choices. Review routing quality, footprints, return paths, manufacturability and whether they caught the planted mistakes.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: There is no single national license for penetration testers. Certifications earned through a hands-on practical exam, such as OSCP, say more about skill than knowledge-only tests. Confirm any certification directly with the issuer, and ask for sample reports with client details removed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give a scoped lab target and watch how they work. Look for recon, finding a web or network flaw, proving impact without causing damage, and writing it up. Check that they can explain a finding to a manager and to a developer in different words.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask about scope, written permission and rules of engagement before touching anything. They talk about false positives, retesting fixes and ranking risk by business impact, not just tool output. Their reports give clear steps to reproduce each issue and practical fixes.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Bragging about breaking into systems without permission, which can be a federal crime under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Reports that are raw scanner output. Vague answers about protecting client data, or little interest in staying inside agreed scope.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a finding they’re proud of, from first clue to fix. Ask what they do when they spot something outside scope, or when a system starts to fail during testing. Real testers answer with specific steps, not buzzwords.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a penetration tester?
qa.a: Look for proven hands-on skill, sound judgment about scope and permission, and clear writing. Review redacted sample reports, verify certifications with the issuer, and check references from past clients or teams. A strong tester finds real issues, explains business risk plainly and never steps outside written authorization.

qa.q: How do I test a penetration tester before hiring?
qa.a: Set up an isolated practice environment or a deliberately vulnerable lab app you own. Give written scope and a time limit, then ask for a short report. Judge how they found issues, whether they avoided damage, and how clearly they explained risk and fixes. Never let a candidate test your live systems.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses this role. Optional national HR certifications exist and show study of employment law and practice. Confirm any claimed certification with the issuing body. Also verify hands-on experience with an HR information system and a payroll platform, since most of the job runs through them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they know Form I-9 timing: the employee completes Section 1 by the first day of work, and the employer completes Section 2 within three business days. Test spreadsheet accuracy, clean HR data entry, and clear onboarding and offboarding checklists.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They keep employee records confidential. They log every pay, title or status change with dates and approvals. They ask which states your staff work in, because final pay deadlines, leave rules and required notices vary by state. They know when to bring in payroll, benefits or legal counsel.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who would tell new hires which I-9 documents to bring, since employees choose from the acceptable list. Other warning signs are guessing at state rules, sharing personnel details casually, skipping written records of changes, or treating offboarding as just collecting a laptop.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: An employee resigns and their last day is Friday. What happens, and by when? Ask about a data error they found in an HR system and how they fixed the cause. Ask how they handle a manager who wants to change someone’s pay without approval.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a people operations specialist?
qa.a: Look for accuracy with employee data, sound knowledge of onboarding steps like Form I-9, and awareness that final pay and leave rules vary by state. Strong candidates keep records confidential, document every change, and know when to escalate. HR certifications are optional, so weigh real experience with HR systems and payroll just as heavily.

qa.q: How do I test a people operations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short practical task. Ask them to build an onboarding checklist for a new hire, then find planted errors in a sample employee data spreadsheet. Add an offboarding scenario and ask what must happen and by when. Use fictional data only, and look for accuracy, clear steps and good questions about state rules.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for performance marketing. Ad platform certifications show basic platform knowledge only. Verify real results instead: ask for anonymized account screenshots or case studies showing spend, cost per acquisition and return, and call references who saw the numbers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test campaign structure, bidding, audience targeting, creative testing and conversion tracking on search, social and other ad channels. Check analytics, attribution limits, budget pacing and landing page testing. Ask them to explain how privacy changes affect tracking and measurement.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates focus on profit and new customers, not clicks. They test one change at a time, check results with holdout or incrementality tests, and cut spend that does not work. They know advertising and consumer protection rules, and privacy laws, which vary by state.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who quote cheap clicks or high returns with no proof of conversion tracking, take credit for sales other channels drove, or ignore incrementality. Be careful with anyone who suggests misleading ads or collecting data without proper consent.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you know a campaign drove sales that would not have happened anyway? How do you scale spend without raising costs too fast? How do you set up conversion tracking? Strong answers mention tests, attribution limits and specific steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a performance marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for proven results on the ad channels you use, with clear tracking from ad to sale. Check they understand bidding, creative testing, attribution limits and privacy rules, which vary by state. No license is required, and platform certifications show only basics, so real account results and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a performance marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task using an anonymized export from one of your ad accounts. Ask them to find wasted spend, propose tests and explain how they would measure true impact. Review their reasoning, attention to tracking and whether their plan focuses on profit, not clicks.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: New pharmacists need a doctor of pharmacy degree, a passing score on the national licensure exam, usually a state law exam, and a license in each state where they practice. Verify licenses on state board sites. Check immunization training if they give vaccines, since rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test prescription verification, dosing checks such as kidney adjustments, drug interaction screening and patient counseling. Check controlled substance law, compounding standards if you compound, insurance claim handling and inventory. Hospital roles need order review, sterile product checks and clinical rounding skills.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates catch errors calmly and call prescribers with clear, polite questions. They counsel patients in plain language, keep controlled substance records exact and support their technicians. They stay current on new drugs, guidelines and state pharmacy rules.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for board discipline, careless controlled substance practices, or a habit of overriding interaction alerts without review. Be careful with anyone who rushes verification to hit volume targets, dismisses technician concerns or cannot explain recent rule changes in your state.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a prescription you refused or clarified, and why. How do you spot a forged controlled substance prescription? How do you counsel a patient starting a blood thinner? What do you do once you find a dispensing error? Strong answers put patient safety first.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a pharmacist?
qa.a: Look for an active license in your state, solid verification and counseling skills, and sound judgment with controlled substances. Check experience in your setting, such as retail, hospital, specialty or long-term care. Immunization, compounding or sterile training matters if the role needs it. References confirm accuracy.

qa.q: How do I test a pharmacist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid verification exercise with mock prescriptions that contain planted errors, interactions and dosing problems. Add a short counseling role-play with a staff member. Review what they catch, how they would contact the prescriber and how clearly they explain risks to a patient.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most states require pharmacy technicians to register, be licensed or be certified, and rules vary by state. Some states require national certification, and many employers prefer it. Verify status on the state board site. Sterile compounding roles need documented training and competency checks.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test prescription data entry, counting and labeling accuracy, days supply math and insurance claim handling, such as rejections and prior authorizations. Check inventory and controlled substance counts. Hospital roles need sterile compounding technique, unit dose packaging and automated dispensing cabinet restocking.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates work fast without losing accuracy, double-check every label and ask the pharmacist when unsure. They stay patient with upset customers, protect privacy and know which questions only a pharmacist may answer. They keep work areas clean and organized.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for lapsed registration, careless counting, or offering clinical advice that only a pharmacist may give. Be careful with anyone casual about controlled substance counts or patient privacy, or who cannot explain how to handle an insurance rejection.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A claim rejects as a refill too soon. What do you do? How do you calculate days supply for an inhaler or insulin? What do you do when a count is off? How do you answer a patient who asks about side effects? Strong answers stay within technician scope.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a pharmacy technician?
qa.a: Look for active state registration or license, national certification where required or preferred, and accurate data entry, counting and claim handling. Check patient service and privacy habits. Hospital roles need sterile compounding training. References from pharmacists confirm accuracy and reliability.

qa.q: How do I test a pharmacy technician before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid test with mock prescriptions to enter, count and label, plus days supply math and an insurance rejection to resolve. For hospital roles, include an observed aseptic technique check. Review accuracy, speed, awareness of scope and how they ask for help.

look.label: Research record to check
look.text: Read their papers, preprints, thesis topic and public code. Ask which parts they did themselves on coauthored work. A short call with their advisor or a coauthor can confirm their role and how independently they work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the core skill for your project. For AI roles, that may be implementing a method from a paper, designing a fair experiment and reading results critically. For science or engineering roles, it may be simulation, data analysis or a specific lab method.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain their research clearly to a non-expert. They talk openly about experiments that failed and what they learned. They can scope a goal that fits the internship length, and their code or lab notes are organized enough for others to reproduce.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about their own contribution. Results described without baselines or error bars. Overclaiming what a model or method can do. Little interest in your problem beyond their thesis. Pushback on reasonable discussion of publication, data access and intellectual property terms.

look.label: Paperwork to plan early
look.text: No license exists for this work. Confirm the dates fit their academic calendar and advisor’s plans. Ask every candidate the same question: are they authorized to work in the US, and will they need sponsorship. Some students need school approval, such as CPT, before starting.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a PhD intern?
qa.a: Look for research that matches your problem, clear ownership of their published work and the ability to explain it simply. Strong candidates scope a realistic project for the internship length, write reproducible code or keep clean lab records, and are honest about failed results. Agree early on publication rights, data access and intellectual property.

qa.q: How do I test a PhD intern before hiring?
qa.a: Ask them to present one of their own projects and probe the choices behind it. Then give a short task close to your work, such as critiquing a paper, proposing an experiment or fixing a small piece of research code. Judge their reasoning, assumptions and how they handle uncertainty, not just the final answer.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most states require security officers to hold a state guard license or registration, and the rules vary by state. Armed posts usually need a separate armed permit and firearms training. Check that the license is current through your state’s licensing agency.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for clear written incident reports, calm verbal de-escalation and steady attention on long shifts. For control room roles, check that they can watch several camera feeds, spot unusual activity, and log alarms and calls accurately.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a real incident they handled, who they called and what they wrote in the report. Ask how they would handle a guest who refuses to leave, or a door alarm in the middle of the night.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They know the limits of their authority and when to observe and report rather than step in. They follow post orders, speak clearly on the radio, keep detailed logs and arrive on time. Current CPR and first aid training is a plus.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Eager talk about using force or making arrests, vague or sloppy sample reports, unclear answers about license status, or a record of sleeping on post or leaving early. Be wary of anyone who treats confidential site information lightly.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a security officer?
qa.a: Start with a valid state guard license or registration where your state requires one, plus an armed permit for armed posts. Then look for calm judgment, clear report writing, reliable attendance and a solid grasp of what an officer may and may not do. For control rooms, add strong focus and accurate logging.

qa.q: How do I test a security officer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short written scenario and ask for an incident report. Role-play a tense moment, such as a visitor who won’t leave, and watch how they calm it down. For control room work, show a short video clip and ask them to note anything unusual. A paid trial shift can confirm reliability.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm an active, unrestricted medical license from the board in each state where they will practice. Check the MD or DO degree, residency completion, board certification if your role requires it, an individual DEA registration for prescribing controlled substances, and any state controlled substance registration your state requires.

look.label: Background checks to run
look.text: Search the federal OIG exclusion list and your state’s Medicaid exclusion list. Review public discipline records on each state medical board website. Hospitals and other eligible entities query the National Practitioner Data Bank for malpractice payments and adverse actions. Verify everything with the original source.

look.label: Telehealth licensing rules
look.text: For online care, the doctor generally needs a license in the state where the patient is located, not where the doctor sits. Rules and exceptions vary by state. Some states belong to the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact, which can speed up extra licenses. Online prescribing of controlled substances has added federal and state rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Clear, patient-friendly explanations, careful and timely notes, and comfort with electronic health records. Strong candidates explain when they refer or escalate, how they track test results so nothing is missed, and how they work with nurses, medical assistants and front desk staff.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Dates on the CV that do not match verified records, license restrictions or probation they did not disclose, vague answers about past malpractice claims, or references who will not confirm their role. Also watch for dismissive talk about patients or impatience with support staff.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a physician?
qa.a: Start with an active, unrestricted license in your state, a verified MD or DO degree, completed residency, and board certification if the role needs it. Check DEA registration if they will prescribe controlled substances. Then look for clear communication, solid clinical judgment, good documentation habits, and a clean record on exclusion lists and state board sites.

qa.q: How do I test a physician before hiring?
qa.a: Use case-based interviews where they talk through a realistic patient, from history to plan and follow-up. Have a physician on your team review their reasoning. Ask them to write a short sample note. Add peer and staff interviews and call references directly. In hospitals, new doctors usually go through a focused review period after they start.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: PAs need a state license and usually hold national certification, shown by the PA-C title. Verify both online, plus DEA registration and any state controlled substance registration if they prescribe. Check board actions and malpractice history during credentialing. Supervision or collaboration rules vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test history taking, physical exam, differential diagnosis and ordering and reading labs and imaging in your specialty. Check procedures the role needs, such as suturing, joint injections or splinting. Review clear, billable notes in your health record system and safe prescribing, including controlled substances.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know their scope and escalate to the physician at the right time. They explain diagnoses in plain language, follow up on results without reminders and keep notes complete and timely. References from supervising physicians praise their judgment, not just their speed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for board discipline, unexplained limits on hospital privileges, or vague reasons for leaving past jobs. Be careful with candidates who prescribe loosely, rarely consult physicians, or cannot explain recent guideline changes in the specialty they claim.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a patient you escalated and why. Walk me through your workup for chest pain in clinic. How do you handle a patient asking for opioids you do not think are needed? How do you track pending results? Strong answers show safe, reasoned judgment.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a physician assistant?
qa.a: Look for an active state license, national certification, prescribing registrations and experience in your specialty. Check clinical judgment, knowing when to escalate, clear documentation and patient communication. Your credentialing process should confirm board history. References from supervising physicians matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a physician assistant before hiring?
qa.a: Use case-based interviews with de-identified scenarios from your specialty, asking for a differential diagnosis, workup and plan. Add a short documentation exercise. Once credentialing allows, a paid shadow shift with a physician shows real patient interaction. Judge reasoning, safety and clear communication.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for platform engineering. Cloud provider and Kubernetes certifications exist and show study, but they are optional. Verify past work instead. Ask for references from teams that used their tools, and review code samples or design docs they are allowed to share.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test infrastructure as code, container orchestration, CI/CD pipeline design and scripting in a language your team uses. Have them read a broken deployment config and explain the fault. Check how they handle secrets, access control and rollback, not just whether the build passes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They treat other engineers as customers. Strong candidates talk about developer experience, adoption and self-service. They can name a tool they built that teams chose to use. They measure results, such as faster deploys or fewer incidents, and write clear docs others can follow.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who only lists tools without explaining tradeoffs, blames users when a platform goes unused, or has never been on call for what they built. Also be wary of plans to rebuild everything from scratch before learning how your teams work today.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a platform change that broke other teams and how they recovered. Ask how they got engineers to adopt a new internal tool. Ask when they would buy a managed service instead of building one. Listen for specifics, numbers and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a platform engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on depth in cloud infrastructure, containers, infrastructure as code and CI/CD, plus a product mindset toward internal users. The best candidates can show tools other teams adopted, explain build versus buy tradeoffs, and have run production systems on call. No license is required, so weigh real work and references over certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a platform engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-boxed task that mirrors your stack. For example, ask them to write a pipeline that builds, tests and deploys a small service, or to debug a failing infrastructure config. Follow with a design talk on how they would roll it out to many teams safely. Score clarity, security and rollback plans.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most states license plumbers at apprentice, journeyman and master levels, though some leave licensing to cities or counties. Gas fitting, backflow testing and medical gas work may need separate credentials. Pipefitters on pressure piping often need welding qualifications to code. Check licenses on state or local sites.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading plans and isometric drawings, drain sizing, venting and slope under your local plumbing code, and pressure testing. Check soldering, brazing, threading, PEX and press fittings. For pipefitters, check welding, steam and process piping, valve work and rigging heavy pipe safely.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates pull permits, pass inspections and leave neat, supported, labeled pipe runs. They explain why code rules exist, not just what they say. They protect finished spaces, test their work before walls are closed and communicate clearly with customers and other trades.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for work done without permits, unlicensed work in places that require a license, or advice to skip pressure tests. Be careful with candidates who cannot explain venting or backflow, mix incompatible pipe materials, or are vague about checking gas lines for leaks.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you size a drain line for a new bathroom group? How do you test a gas line before turning it on? Tell me about a hard leak you found. For pipefitters: how do you prepare and fit up a pipe joint before welding? Strong answers cite code and testing.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a plumber or pipefitter?
qa.a: Look for the right license level for your state or city, plus any gas, backflow or welding credentials the work needs. Check code knowledge, neat work and testing habits. Photos of past jobs, inspection records and references from contractors or customers show real quality.

qa.q: How do I test a plumber or pipefitter before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid, supervised practical test, such as building a small drain, waste and vent assembly or soldering and pressure testing a copper manifold. For pipefitters, include a fit-up or weld test to the code you use. Judge accuracy, neatness, safety and whether the work passes the test.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm state peace officer certification for lateral hires, or eligibility for your academy. Check the state certification board for any decertification, and run the full background investigation your state and agency require.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Use scenario tests for judgment, de-escalation and decisions about force, a report-writing exercise and the physical fitness test. Ride-along feedback or field training records show how a lateral officer works.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates stay calm, listen before acting, explain the law clearly, write precise reports and treat people with respect. They admit mistakes and show a record of honest, steady conduct.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for dishonesty anywhere in the application, a pattern of complaints or use-of-force problems at past agencies, a resignation while under investigation, and enthusiasm for force or contempt for the public.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What is the difference between reasonable suspicion and probable cause? Your partner uses too much force: what do you do? Walk me through a domestic call. When must you give Miranda warnings? Strong answers cite both the law and department policy.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a police officer?
qa.a: Look for integrity first, then sound judgment, calm communication and respect for the public. Check certification and decertification records, past agencies’ files and the full background. Scenario tests, report writing and the fitness test show skills; references from supervisors and the community show character.

qa.q: How do I check a lateral police officer’s record?
qa.a: Get written consent and request the officer’s personnel, internal affairs and training files from every prior agency, check the state certification board for decertification and search the national decertification index where your state uses it. Interview past supervisors, and ask why the officer is leaving.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work in policy. Confirm claimed degrees, past employers and job titles. Federal lobbying reports and many state lobbying registrations are public, so you can check the issues and agencies a candidate says they worked on.

look.label: Compliance to plan for
look.text: If the hire will lobby federal officials and meets the Lobbying Disclosure Act thresholds, your organization registers, files the reports and lists them as a lobbyist. State and local lobbying rules vary by state. Some require the individual to register too. Former government staff may face post-employment limits.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: The candidate should be able to read a bill or proposed rule and explain its impact on your business in plain words. They should also be able to draft a clear comment letter or position paper. Ask for a writing sample they wrote mostly on their own.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They name specific laws or rules they tracked, the agencies involved and what changed because of their work. They understand how notice and comment rulemaking works. They know when to bring in legal counsel. They keep working relationships with officials across parties.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for promises of guaranteed outcomes or special access, or vague claims about who they know. Be wary of anyone who shares confidential details from past employers. Another warning sign is not knowing the gift and ethics rules that limit what you can offer public officials.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a policy manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who can track new laws and rules, explain them simply and represent your company honestly with regulators. Check past work you can verify, such as public comment letters or lobbying filings. They should know lobbying registration and ethics rules, which vary by state, and should never promise guaranteed results.

qa.q: How do I test a policy manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a recent proposed rule or bill that affects your industry. Ask for a one page memo on what it means for your business and what you should do next. Then run a short role play where they brief a regulator or a company leader and answer tough follow-up questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a policy analyst. If the role includes contacting officials to influence laws or rules, lobbying registration may be required under federal law and state laws, which vary by state. Verify skills through writing samples, comment letters and references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading statutes, bills and proposed rules accurately, tracking rulemaking stages and comment deadlines, and turning complex issues into short briefs. Check their use of evidence, their estimates of costs and impacts, and a clear company position that answers the strongest counterarguments.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong analysts separate facts from advocacy, cite sources, and present opposing views fairly before making the case. They know how agencies and legislatures actually work, track deadlines carefully, and write for busy executives and regulators in plain words.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for writing that is all opinion, misread bill status or rule stages, and claims without sources. Be wary of anyone who does not understand lobbying disclosure and gift rules, or who cannot explain an issue from the other side’s point of view.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a comment letter you wrote and how the agency responded. How do you track a bill through committees? Tell me about an argument you dropped because the evidence was weak. Strong answers show process, sources and judgment.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a policy analyst?
qa.a: Look for accurate reading of laws and rules, clear writing for executives and regulators, and evidence-based arguments that address the other side. Check they understand rulemaking and legislative stages and the lobbying disclosure rules that apply to your work, which vary by state. Writing samples and comment letters matter more than credentials.

qa.q: How do I test a policy analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise using a real or mock proposed rule. Ask for a two-page brief summarizing what it does, how it affects your business and a recommended position, plus one paragraph of draft comments. Review accuracy, sourcing, fairness to opposing views and plain writing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Depending on the firm and its clients, they may need to register as an investment adviser representative, which usually means passing a qualifying securities exam; rules vary by state. Check registration and any disciplinary history on the SEC’s public adviser search. The CFA charter is respected but optional.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test portfolio construction, position sizing, risk limits and how they follow an investment mandate or policy statement. Check research and valuation methods, performance attribution, trading and liquidity awareness, and how they explain results and risks to investors in plain words.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have a documented, repeatable process and a track record they can explain, including losses. They respect risk and compliance limits, put clients first as fiduciaries and talk honestly with investors in good and bad periods.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a track record that is cherry-picked, cannot be documented or ignores fees, and for disciplinary history. Be wary of style drift, hidden leverage, dismissing compliance, or any hint of trading on inside information or favoring some accounts over others.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a position from idea to exit. Tell me about your worst loss and what you changed. How do you size positions and set limits? How was your track record calculated? Strong answers are specific, consistent and honest.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a portfolio manager?
qa.a: Look for a clear, repeatable investment process, a documented track record you can verify, disciplined risk management and a clean regulatory history. Check whether the role requires investment adviser representative registration, which varies by state and client type. A CFA charter helps but is optional. Honest communication with investors matters too.

qa.q: How do I test a portfolio manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case: a sample mandate with goals, limits and a starting portfolio. Ask them to propose changes, size the positions, describe the main risks and write a short investor update. Ask how their past returns were calculated. Judge process, risk discipline, fit with the mandate and clarity.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to design power electronics for products. A Professional Engineer license, which varies by state, matters mainly for utility or building power work. Verify past designs instead: shipped products, test reports, patents and references who can confirm what the candidate designed personally.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test converter topologies such as buck, boost, flyback and resonant designs, magnetics, silicon carbide and gallium nitride switches, gate drives, control loops and thermal design. Check low-noise layout, EMI testing, safety spacing and insulation rules, and derating for harsh or space use.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain losses, efficiency and heating with data from their own bench tests. They read waveforms with care, measure loop stability, design for safety certification and EMI from the start, and can describe a failure they traced to a root cause.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for designs proven only in simulation, unsafe habits around high voltage or stored energy, and no experience passing EMI or safety testing. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain why a switch failed or who ignores layout, parasitics and thermal limits.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a converter you designed and its loss budget. Tell me about a board that failed EMI testing and how you fixed it. How do you probe a fast switching node safely and accurately? Strong answers name measurements, tradeoffs and safety steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a power electronics engineer?
qa.a: Look for shipped converter or motor drive designs, strong bench skills, and a clear grasp of magnetics, switching losses, control loops and thermal limits. Check experience passing safety and EMI testing for your market. No license is usually required, so design reviews, test reports and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a power electronics engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid design exercise, such as choosing a topology and parts for a converter with stated input, output and efficiency targets, with a loss estimate and a control approach. Add a bench waveform with ringing and ask what causes it. Review reasoning, safety awareness, tradeoffs and clear documentation.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Nuclear control room operators need an NRC reactor operator license tied to one plant. Transmission and grid control room operators need NERC system operator certification. Some states and cities license boiler operators or stationary engineers. Elsewhere, verify plant qualification records and references from shift supervisors.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading one-line diagrams and P&IDs, switching orders, lockout and tagout, startup and shutdown steps and alarm response. Check control system and SCADA skills, rounds and readings, water chemistry basics and your plant type, such as gas turbines, steam, hydro or solar.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates follow procedures to the letter, keep precise logs and give clear shift turnovers. They stay calm during trips and explain what they checked first. They report near misses, question unclear orders and know the limits of their qualifications.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for shortcuts in switching or lockout, vague logs, or stories of running equipment past limits to avoid a shutdown. Be careful with anyone who blames others for every trip or cannot explain the plant systems they claim to have operated.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your actions during your last unit trip. How do you verify isolation before work begins? What do you check on rounds for a steam turbine or transformer? How do you handle a switching order that looks wrong? Strong answers follow procedure step by step.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a power plant operator?
qa.a: Look for experience on your plant type, strict procedure use, clean logs and safe switching and lockout habits. Check any required license or certification, such as an NRC operator license for nuclear plants or NERC certification for grid operators. References from shift supervisors confirm reliability on rotating shifts.

qa.q: How do I test a power plant operator before hiring?
qa.a: Use a paid, supervised exercise where they trace a system on a P&ID and identify isolation points, or run a simulator or tabletop scenario of a unit trip. Ask them to write a log entry and a shift turnover. Judge procedure use, calm thinking and safety awareness.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: For senior roles, check for a Professional Engineer license, often earned through the NCEES Electrical and Computer: Power exam. Verify it on the state board’s website. Only a licensed PE may seal drawings, and licensing and comity rules vary by state. Junior hires may hold an Engineer in Training or Engineer Intern certificate.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test load flow, short-circuit, and protection coordination studies, plus arc flash analysis under IEEE 1584 and NFPA 70E. Check grounding design and equipment sizing. Confirm they know when the National Electrical Code applies on premises and when the National Electrical Safety Code applies on the utility side.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates walk you through a study from data gathering to final settings. They hand check software results and can explain why. They have worked with utilities on interconnection requests and know the steps. Field time in commissioning or relay testing is a clear plus.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about their own role on team projects. Be wary if they trust software output without sanity checks, cannot say who sealed their drawings, or mix up NEC and NESC. For bulk grid work, unfamiliarity with NERC reliability standards is a warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to describe a protection coordination problem they solved and what changed. Ask how they collected utility fault data for a short-circuit study. Ask about a project where an interconnection study raised costs or delays, and how they handled it with the client.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a power systems engineer?
qa.a: Look for proven experience with load flow, short-circuit, protection, and arc flash studies. Confirm a PE license for anyone who will seal drawings, and verify it with the state board, since rules vary by state.
