Check that they know which codes apply to your work and can explain results clearly to non-engineers.

qa.q: How do I test a power systems engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small one-line diagram with utility fault data and transformer sizes. Ask them to estimate fault currents, pick breaker ratings, and outline a protection scheme. Then have them explain their assumptions and how they would check software results. Review their reasoning, not only the final numbers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: In the US, event contracts trade on exchanges regulated by the CFTC, and exchange staff usually need no personal license, though roles at a futures broker may need registration and an exam. States contest some sports contracts, so check current rules. Verify past roles with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test contract design, including clear outcome definitions, settlement sources and edge cases, plus probability pricing and market surveillance for insider trading and manipulation. Check knowledge of exchange core principles, customer identity checks, market maker programs and fair handling of disputed outcomes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write contract terms so precise that any reader would settle them the same way. They think about who could know the outcome early, document every resolution decision, understand how probabilities relate to prices and explain markets plainly to customers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague settlement rules, treating the business like a sportsbook without exchange rules, or trading personally on markets they could influence or oversee. Be wary of anyone unaware of CFTC oversight or of how state gambling laws may apply.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How would you write the settlement rule for a contract on tomorrow’s rainfall? A data source changes after a market closes. What do you do? How would you detect insider trading on an event? Strong answers are precise and cite rules.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a prediction markets specialist?
qa.a: Look for precise contract writing, strong probability and pricing skills, and knowledge of surveillance, customer identity rules and CFTC oversight of event contracts. Check how they handle disputed outcomes and conflicts of interest. Most staff need no personal license, so references and scenario answers reveal more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a prediction markets specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid task: ask them to draft terms for two event contracts, such as a weather market and an economic data market, including settlement sources and edge cases. Add a mock dispute after an unclear result. Review precision, fairness, surveillance thinking and awareness of regulatory limits.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Check that the candidate meets your state’s licensing rules for the role, such as a CDA, an early childhood degree or a teaching license for public pre-K. Run the background checks with fingerprints that child care licensing requires before they start.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Watch the candidate lead circle time or a small group activity in a real classroom, and ask them to plan a short lesson for your age group. Ask how they would observe and record a child’s progress.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates get down to children’s level, use calm and positive guidance, keep constant headcounts and talk warmly with families. Their lesson ideas use play and fit the children’s ages.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for harsh discipline, losing track of children, worksheet-heavy plans for preschoolers, unclear answers about reporting abuse and speaking badly about past families or coworkers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A child bites another child. What do you do? How do you build early reading skills? What would you do if you suspected abuse? How do you bring up a behavior concern with a family? Strong answers keep children safe and families informed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a preschool teacher?
qa.a: Look for the education and training your state requires, a clean background check and real warmth with children. Watch a classroom activity, check that their plans use play, and listen for safe supervision, positive guidance and respect for families. References from directors and families help.

qa.q: How do I test a preschool teacher before hiring?
qa.a: Invite them for a paid classroom visit to lead a story or small group activity and help with a transition, with your lead teacher watching. Ask them to write a short weekly plan and to talk through a biting incident and a family conversation about behavior.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a pricing analyst. Confirm degrees or coursework in economics, finance, statistics or math, and check past roles with references. Some analysts hold optional industry pricing certifications. Treat them as a plus, not a requirement.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for advanced spreadsheet work, SQL queries and price elasticity analysis. Ask them to build a margin waterfall or estimate how sales volume shifts after a price change. Strong work has clear assumptions and a short summary a sales lead can follow.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They tie pricing to margin, not just revenue. They talk about testing changes with control groups or A/B tests, and they spot discount leakage. They can name a past price change, explain why they made it and show what happened after.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for casual talk about sharing price plans with competitors, which can break federal antitrust law. Also be wary of models never checked against real results, or no awareness that price gouging rules during emergencies vary by state.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through a price increase you recommended. What data did you use, how did customers react, and what would you change?” Strong answers mention customer segments, churn or volume, and how they tracked results after launch.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a pricing analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong spreadsheet and SQL skills, a solid grasp of elasticity and margins, and past price changes they can explain with real results. No license is required. Good analysts work well with sales and finance and know the basic antitrust rules against sharing prices with competitors.

qa.q: How do I test a pricing analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short take-home case with sample sales data, costs and discounts. Ask them to recommend a price change, estimate its effect on volume and margin, and list their assumptions. Then have them present it in about 15 minutes. Judge their logic, how they clean the data and how clearly they explain tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Confirm active bar admission and good standing through the state bar’s public lookup. In-house lawyers working in a state where they aren’t admitted may need to register there, and those rules vary by state. Privacy certifications such as CIPP/US are useful but optional.

look.label: Laws they should know
look.text: They should know federal sector laws such as HIPAA, COPPA, GLBA and FCRA. They should also know the growing set of state consumer privacy laws, starting with California’s, plus state breach notification laws, which differ by state. GDPR matters if you handle data on people in Europe.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test whether they can map how data flows through your business. They should be able to draft a clear privacy notice, negotiate vendor data terms and run a privacy impact assessment. They must also turn legal rules into plain steps a product or marketing team can follow.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They give practical advice ranked by risk instead of a flat no. They have worked with engineers and marketers on consent, cookies, tracking pixels and data retention. They can describe a breach response or regulator inquiry they handled without revealing client confidences.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who assume one law covers every state or who can’t apply the law to your business model. Be wary of anyone who shares confidential client details. Another warning sign is offering template policies without first asking how your data is actually collected and used.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a privacy counsel?
qa.a: Look for an active law license in good standing and hands-on work with the privacy laws that fit your industry and the states where your customers live. Look for practical judgment as well. The best candidates explain risk in plain words, work well with technical teams and know how to respond to a data breach.

qa.q: How do I test a privacy counsel before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise using a made-up product. Ask them to spot the privacy risks in a sample data flow and mark up a draft privacy notice or vendor clause. Then ask for a one-page memo to executives. Judge their accuracy, their prioritization and how clearly they write.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for process development scientists. Verify degrees with the school and ask for redacted tech transfer documents, reports or patents. Confirm with references which steps they scaled personally. For drug work, experience under FDA current good manufacturing practice rules matters most.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test design of experiments, scale-up factors such as mixing and heat transfer, and the unit operations you use, from reactions and crystallization to cell culture, chromatography and filtration. Check they can define critical process parameters, write batch records and run process safety studies.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates think about scale, cost and safety from the first bench experiment. They use statistics rather than changing one factor at a time, document control strategies clearly and work smoothly with manufacturing, quality and analytical teams during tech transfer.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for bench-only experience presented as scale-up, ignoring impurities or thermal hazards, weak documentation, or blaming manufacturing for every failed batch. Be wary of anyone unfamiliar with deviation reports, change control or what regulatory filings require.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a process that worked in the lab but failed at scale and what you changed. How did you choose your operating ranges? How do you hand a process to a manufacturing site? Strong answers include data, risks and specific fixes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a process development scientist?
qa.a: Look for real scale-up and tech transfer experience with your type of product, solid design of experiments and statistics, and knowledge of good manufacturing practice. Check they consider cost, safety and quality early. No license is required, so verified project records, patents and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a process development scientist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case study: share bench data for a reaction or cell culture step and ask how they would scale it up, which parameters are critical, what experiments they would run and what could go wrong. Review statistical thinking, safety awareness and how practical their plan is.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Lean Six Sigma belts, such as Green Belt and Black Belt, are common, but no single official body issues them, so standards differ. Ask what project the belt required, verify it with the issuer, and check references about measured results.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test process mapping, value stream maps, root cause tools and basic statistics, such as control charts and simple hypothesis tests. Check they follow a structured method like DMAIC, collect real data, and run pilots before rolling a new process out widely.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates go and see the work where it happens, talk with the people doing it, and measure before and after. They make small, tested changes, hold gains with standard work and controls, and give credit to frontline teams.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who quote belt levels but cannot show measured results, push complex statistics where a simple fix would do, or redesign processes without talking to workers. Be careful with claimed savings that finance never confirmed.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a project from problem statement to control plan. How did you measure the baseline? How did the gains last after you left? Strong answers name data, tools, the people involved and results confirmed by others.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a process improvement specialist?
qa.a: Look for completed projects with measured before and after results, skill in process mapping and root cause analysis, and the ability to work with frontline staff. Lean Six Sigma belts are common but not standardized, and no license is required, so confirmed results and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a process improvement specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case: a simple process description with step times and error data. Ask them to map the process, find the main sources of waste or delay, and propose a pilot with measures. Review their use of data, practical ideas and how they would involve the people doing the work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for procurement roles. Supply management certifications exist and are optional. Government buying follows federal or state procurement rules, which vary. Verify past savings and contracts with references, and ask how much spend and which categories they managed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test requests for proposals, supplier evaluation, negotiation, contract basics such as payment terms, warranties and liability, and total cost of ownership. Check purchase order processes, matching invoices to orders and receipts, spend analysis in spreadsheets and supplier risk review.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates prepare before negotiating, compare suppliers on total cost and risk rather than price alone, and keep a clear paper trail. They describe savings along with how they were measured, and both suppliers and internal teams respect them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for savings claims with no baseline, accepting gifts or favors from suppliers, single-sourcing without a reason, and skipping competitive bids. Be careful with anyone who hides conflicts of interest or treats contracts as paperwork.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a negotiation where the supplier would not move on price. What did you change instead? How do you handle an urgent purchase that skips the process? How do you check a new supplier? Strong answers include specific terms and controls.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a procurement specialist?
qa.a: Look for strong negotiation, clear supplier evaluation, contract knowledge and disciplined purchasing controls. Good candidates measure savings against a baseline and follow ethics rules on gifts and conflicts. No license is required, so verified results, references and a realistic negotiation exercise matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a procurement specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: compare three sample supplier quotes with different prices, terms and delivery risks, and recommend one with a negotiation plan. Add a role-play with a supplier who refuses a discount. Review total cost reasoning, contract awareness, preparation and professionalism.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for procurement operations work. Optional certifications include Certified Professional in Supply Management, and Certified Professional Public Buyer for government roles; verify them with the issuing body. Weigh proven experience with your procurement or ERP system and references from finance and requesters.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test turning a messy request into a clean purchase order, routing approvals by policy, vendor setup with tax forms, and three-way matching of order, receipt and invoice. Check reporting on open orders and spend, and comfort with your procurement or ERP system.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates keep the queue moving while holding the line on policy. They write clear guides for requesters, fix catalog and vendor data at the source, spot split orders and duplicate vendors, and can show a process change that cut cycle time or errors.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for comfort with after-the-fact purchase orders, approvals skipped to save time, unverified vendor bank detail changes, and no grasp of segregation of duties. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain how invoices get matched or why a payment was held.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you handle a request that arrives after the invoice? What checks do you run before changing a vendor’s bank details? How would you find orders split to avoid approval limits? Strong answers show controls, clear steps and good relations with requesters.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a procurement operations specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience running requests, approvals and purchase orders in a system like yours, strong control habits and clear communication with requesters and finance. Check they understand three-way matching and fraud warning signs. No license is required, and certifications are optional, so references and process examples matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a procurement operations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise with a sample queue: a few requests, a policy with approval levels, a vendor bank change email and a mismatched invoice. Ask them to process each and explain decisions. Review policy accuracy, fraud awareness, data quality and how clearly they write back to requesters.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Turning a scope into a schedule, finding the critical path, and cutting features, scenes or segments when time runs short. Have them turn a short brief into milestones and a rough budget, then show what they would drop if the deadline moved up two weeks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They name projects they shipped, their exact role, and what slipped and why. They talk calmly about trade-offs with creative leads, track risks in writing, and know the kinds of tools your team uses, such as task trackers, budget sheets or review workflows.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a key person leaving mid-project, a client changing scope late, or a budget overrun. Strong answers say who they told, what they changed in the plan, and how the project finally turned out.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a producer in the US. Check shipped credits and call references from directors, leads or clients. A project management certification such as the PMP can be a plus but is optional.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague credits where they cannot explain their own part, blaming the team for every delay, no habit of written schedules or budgets, or promising a timeline before asking about scope, team size and who signs off.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a producer?
qa.a: Look for proof they shipped work like yours, whether games, video, podcasts or shows. Check credits and references. Strong producers keep clear written schedules and budgets, flag risks early, and can explain hard trade-offs they made. The medium matters, since game and video producers often use different workflows, vendors and approval steps.

qa.q: How do I test a producer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task: a one-page project brief with a fixed deadline and budget. Ask for a milestone schedule, a rough budget, the top risks, and a plan for what to cut if time drops. Then talk it through live and change one constraint to see how they adjust.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can write SQL to pull and join event data, build funnels and retention cohorts, and read A/B test results correctly. Ask them to explain statistical significance and sample size in plain words. Comfort with a spreadsheet and one charting or dashboard tool is expected.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Some candidates hold vendor or online certificates in analytics tools or SQL. Treat these as a bonus, not proof. Verify past roles through references and look closely at real work samples or a portfolio.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They start with the product question before touching data. They define metrics clearly, question odd numbers, and check how events are tracked. They turn findings into a short, clear recommendation the product team can act on, and they say how confident they are.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for dashboards with no conclusions, claims that correlation proves cause, or stopping tests early because results look good. Be wary if they can’t explain how a metric is calculated, blame bad data without fixing it, or never mention user privacy rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a change they recommended that shipped and what happened after. Ask how they handled a test that showed no effect. Ask how they would find why sign-ups dropped last week. Strong answers name specific metrics, checks and trade-offs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a product analyst?
qa.a: Look for solid SQL, experience with funnels, retention and A/B tests, and the ability to explain findings simply. The best candidates ask what decision the data should support. They check data quality before trusting it and give clear recommendations. No license is needed, so judge them on work samples, references and how they reason through a real product problem.

qa.q: How do I test a product analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short take-home or live task using a small sample dataset with made-up user events. Ask them to find where users drop off, suggest one change, and outline an A/B test to check it. Review their queries, their logic and a one-page summary. Then have them present it to someone on your product team.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for product designers, and design certificates are optional. Verify work through a portfolio of case studies, live products you can try, and references from engineers and product managers who built their designs.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test user flows, wireframes, interaction design, visual design, design systems and prototyping in your design tool. Check accessibility basics such as color contrast, focus states and screen reader labels, and their ability to run simple user tests.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show the problem, research, rejected options and results, not only polished final screens. They design for errors and empty states, hand off clear specs to engineers, and can point to changes that improved real user behavior.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for portfolios with only attractive mockups and no reasoning, no mention of users or results, ignored accessibility, and designs that never shipped. Be careful with anyone who cannot say which parts of team work were theirs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a design that tested badly and what you changed. How do you handle an engineer saying a design is too hard to build? How do you design an error state? Strong answers include real tradeoffs and outcomes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a product designer?
qa.a: Look for case studies that show the problem, research, options and measured results, not just polished screens. Check interaction design, visual craft, accessibility and how well they work with engineers. No license is required, so the portfolio, a short exercise and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a product designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise close to your product, such as redesigning one confusing flow with notes on tradeoffs. Ask for a clickable prototype that includes error and empty states. Review clarity, accessibility, reasoning and how they respond to feedback in a follow-up conversation.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for full-stack ability across front end, back end and data. A product engineer should ship a small feature end to end, write clear tests, and explain tradeoffs between speed and quality. Ask them to scope a vague request into a plan before writing code.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about users and outcomes, not just code. They describe features they shipped, how they measured results, what they changed after launch, and how they worked with design and support. They cut scope to ship sooner and say no with reasons.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a feature they owned from idea to release. What problem did it solve? How did they learn what users needed? What metric moved? What would they do differently? Vague answers or credit given only to others can mean limited ownership.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who only want detailed specs handed to them, dismiss user feedback, or cannot explain why a feature mattered. Other warning signs are no interest in analytics, blaming teammates for every delay, and resumes listing many tools but no shipped work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for software engineering. Degrees and cloud or vendor certifications are optional. Verify past roles through references, and review shipped products, public code or portfolio links. Confirm work authorization through the standard I-9 process after an offer, as required for every hire.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a product engineer?
qa.a: Look for a software engineer who cares about users as much as code. They should build across the stack, turn unclear ideas into a shippable plan, and measure results after release. Ask for examples of features they owned end to end, how they gathered feedback, and what changed because of their work.

qa.q: How do I test a product engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-boxed task with a loose brief, like adding a small feature to a sample app. Judge how they ask questions, cut scope, write tests and explain tradeoffs. Follow with a review call where they walk through choices and say what they would build next.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a product manager, and no state regulates the title. Optional certifications in agile or product ownership exist, but they show training, not results. Verify past roles, shipped products and references from engineers or designers who worked with the candidate.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they turn messy user feedback and business goals into a clear, ranked plan. Look for sharp problem statements, simple success metrics, honest tradeoffs, and written specs an engineer could build from without a long meeting.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about outcomes, not just features shipped. They name a metric that moved, explain what they learned from users, and describe a time they said no to a request and why. They credit the team and admit what did not work.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who only list features, cannot explain why something was built, or blame engineering for every delay. Vague answers about metrics, no contact with real users, and a habit of saying yes to every stakeholder suggest weak judgment.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a feature they decided not to build. Ask how they measured whether their last launch worked. Ask about a time data and a senior leader disagreed. Good answers include specifics, not slogans.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a product manager?
qa.a: Look for clear thinking about users and business goals, strong writing, and the ability to rank work by impact. A good product manager explains tradeoffs simply, works well with engineers and designers, and measures results. No license is required in the US, so check past products and references instead of credentials.

qa.q: How do I test a product manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-limited case. Share a product problem, some user feedback and a business goal, then ask for a one-page plan with priorities, a success metric and what they would cut. Have them present it to an engineer and a designer, and watch how they handle questions and pushback.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short positioning statement for a product they know. Look for a clear target customer, the problem solved, the main alternative, and a reason to believe. Strong candidates write plainly and cut jargon without being told.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about customer interviews, win and loss reviews, and time spent with sales. They can name a launch they ran, the goal they set, and what changed afterward. They admit what did not work and what they learned.

look.label: Work samples to request
look.text: Ask for examples such as a launch plan, a battlecard, a sales one pager, or a messaging framework. Have them walk you through one, including who used it and how. Expect some details to be removed for confidentiality.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague claims about driving growth with no clear role or results. Be cautious if they cannot explain how product marketing differs from demand generation or brand work, or if they never mention talking to customers or sales.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Some candidates hold voluntary product marketing or general marketing certificates, which are optional. Verify past employers and titles through references, and ask former sales or product partners how the candidate worked with them.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a product marketing manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who can explain who a product is for and why it beats the alternatives in plain words. They should show past launches, sales materials they built, and evidence they learned from customers and sales teams. Clear writing, sound judgment about the market, and a record of working well with product and sales matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a product marketing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time limited exercise. Share a brief product description and ask for a positioning statement, three key messages for one buyer, and an outline of a launch plan. Then have them present it and answer questions as if you were the sales team. Judge clarity, customer focus, and how they handle pushback.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for product operations. Verify past work instead: ask for launch checklists, process documents or feedback reports they built, with private details removed, and call product managers who worked with them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test launch planning, sorting customer and support feedback into themes, running product tools, writing release notes and tracking simple metrics. Check they can run a cross-team meeting with clear owners and dates, and write processes people actually follow.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates remove friction rather than add meetings. They can show a launch that went smoothly because of their checklist, a feedback system that changed the roadmap, or tool cleanup that saved teams real time.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for process for its own sake, heavy templates nobody uses, no way to measure whether their work helped, and feedback passed along without sorting or summary. Be careful with anyone who cannot name a process they retired.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a launch that went wrong and what you changed afterward. How do you turn hundreds of support tickets into something a product manager can use? Which process did you remove? Strong answers include specific tools and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a product operations manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has run launches, organized customer feedback into clear themes and improved product tools, with proof such as checklists and reports. Good candidates measure results and cut needless process. No license is required, so work samples and references from product managers matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a product operations manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task, such as turning a set of sample support tickets into a feedback summary with top themes, or drafting a launch plan for a small feature. Review structure, clarity, task owners, dates and whether the output would help a busy product team decide.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to be a product owner. Scrum product owner certifications show basic training but are optional and quick to earn. Verify real work instead: ask for sample backlogs and user stories, and call references from developers and stakeholders on teams they served.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test writing user stories with clear acceptance criteria, ordering a backlog by value and risk, and splitting large features into small pieces. Check they can run sprint reviews, say no to stakeholders politely, and accept or reject finished work against agreed criteria.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates are available to the team every day, answer questions quickly and keep the backlog clean. They know the users and the business goals, and explain why items rank where they do. Developers trust their stories because they are clear and testable.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for stories with no acceptance criteria, backlogs ranked by whoever shouts loudest, or accepting unfinished work to hit a date. Be careful with candidates who cannot explain the value of items they ranked or who micromanage how developers do the work.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Show me a user story you wrote and its acceptance criteria. How do you handle two stakeholders who both want their item first? Tell me about work you rejected at a sprint review. Strong answers show clear priorities and respect for the team.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a product owner?
qa.a: Look for clear user stories with testable acceptance criteria, a backlog ordered by value, and strong ties with both users and developers. Check they can say no and explain why. No license is required and certifications are optional, so sample backlogs and references from development teams matter more.

qa.q: How do I test a product owner before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: a feature request and some user feedback. Ask them to split it into user stories with acceptance criteria and order them for the next sprints. Review whether the stories are small, testable and valuable, and how they explain their priorities.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No federal or state license is required to work as a production planner. Some hold a voluntary certification such as CPIM (Certified in Planning and Inventory Management). Treat it as a plus, not a must. Check past roles, the ERP or MRP systems they used, and the type of plant with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Reading a bill of materials, running MRP logic by hand, and setting lead times and safety stock. Balancing a schedule against real machine and labor capacity. Building a clear schedule in a spreadsheet. Spotting a material shortage weeks before it stops a line.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk in numbers like on-time delivery, schedule adherence and inventory levels. They describe working closely with purchasing, sales and shop floor leads. They can explain how they handled a rush order, a late supplier or a machine breakdown without losing the week.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Blaming other departments for every missed date. Knowing which buttons to click in one system but not the logic behind it. Vague answers about past results. Little interest in walking the floor to see how jobs actually run.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they rebuilt a schedule after a key part arrived late. Ask how they choose what runs first when two orders need the same line. Ask how they set safety stock for a part with unsteady demand, and what they changed when it did not work.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a production planner?
qa.a: Look for someone who understands MRP, bills of materials, lead times and real capacity limits. Strong planners keep schedules realistic, catch shortages early and talk easily with purchasing and the shop floor. Experience in a plant like yours helps. A certification such as CPIM is a plus but not required by law.

qa.q: How do I test a production planner before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid exercise. Share a simple bill of materials, current inventory, open orders and line capacity. Ask them to build a two week schedule, list parts to order and explain what they would do if a supplier ships late. Judge the logic and clarity, not just the final numbers.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for production supervisors or plant managers. Lean or Six Sigma belts and OSHA outreach training cards are optional but useful. Plant managers may answer for environmental permits and OSHA compliance. Verify results with references on safety, quality, output and team retention.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading production, scrap and downtime data, planning labor and shifts, running daily tier meetings, and leading root cause work. Check knowledge of OSHA rules, including lockout and tagout and injury recordkeeping, your quality system such as ISO 9001, and any union contract your plant has.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates walk the floor daily, know the bottleneck and keep standard work current. They put safety first, treat near misses as lessons, coach supervisors and operators, and can show a line or plant they improved with numbers they can explain.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for pushing output over safety, discouraging injury reports, blaming operators for system problems, and running the plant from the office. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain their scrap or downtime drivers or who had high turnover among their supervisors.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a shift that fell behind and what you changed. How do you decide whether an injury is recordable? Tell me about a quality escape and the root cause you found. Strong answers name data, specific actions and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a production supervisor or plant manager?
qa.a: Look for a safety record they can explain, steady gains in quality and output, and supervisors they developed. Check knowledge of OSHA rules, lean methods and your quality system. No license is required, so references from plant leaders, operators and quality teams show more than certificates or titles.

qa.q: How do I test a production supervisor or plant manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case using sample shift data with downtime, scrap and a safety near miss. Ask them to set priorities, plan a tier meeting and outline root cause steps. For plant managers, add a budget and a staffing gap. Review safety judgment, use of data and clear, practical actions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for most production work. If the job includes driving a forklift, OSHA requires you to train and evaluate them on your own trucks and site, even if they were certified elsewhere. Check any certificates your process needs, such as soldering workmanship, and call past supervisors.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test following written work instructions, reading simple drawings, and measuring parts with calipers or go and no-go gauges. Check safe machine habits, such as using guards and following lockout and tagout, plus basic setup, changeovers and keeping the work area clean and organized.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates follow the instruction every time, check their own work, and speak up early when parts or machines look wrong. They learn new stations quickly, keep their area clean, respect guards and lockout rules, and can describe machines they ran and how they checked quality.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for bypassing guards or sensors to go faster, skipping quality checks, guessing instead of asking, and vague answers about past machines or tasks. Be wary of anyone who treats safety rules as optional or cannot read a simple measurement.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What machines have you run, and how did you check your parts? What do you do if a machine starts making bad parts? Tell me about a safety rule you followed when it slowed you down. Strong answers name real steps and checks.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a production worker or machine operator?
qa.a: Look for steady work habits, care with safety rules, and the ability to follow written instructions and check their own work. Experience with similar machines or assembly helps, but training can fill gaps. No license is required for most roles, so references from past supervisors and a hands-on trial matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a production worker or machine operator before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid hands-on trial. Ask them to follow a written work instruction to assemble or inspect a few sample parts, measure them with calipers and record results. Watch safety habits, accuracy, pace and whether they ask when something is unclear. Keep the test the same for every candidate.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for this work. Many software vendors offer platform certifications, and most let you confirm them online by name or credential ID. Treat them as a plus, not proof. References from past implementation clients or project managers tell you more.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for product configuration, data mapping and migration, and basic work with APIs and integrations. Also test scoping, written documentation and running a client call. A good consultant turns vague customer wishes into clear requirements and a realistic plan.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask about the customer’s goals before talking about features. They explain technical choices in plain language, handle change requests through a clear process, and leave behind documentation so the customer can run the setup without them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who blame every delay on clients, promise custom builds without checking limits, or cannot describe a project that went wrong and what they learned. Weak note taking and no habit of confirming scope in writing also cause trouble later.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through one implementation from kickoff to go-live. Ask how they handled scope creep, a messy data import, or a customer who rejected the result. Listen for specific steps, timelines and trade-offs, not general claims.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a professional services consultant?
qa.a: Look for proven implementations from kickoff to go-live, solid configuration and integration skills, and calm client handling. Strong candidates scope carefully, document their work and manage change requests in writing. Vendor certifications help but are optional. Check references from past clients or project managers.

qa.q: How do I test a professional services consultant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case: a sample customer brief and messy data. Ask them to write a scope with open questions, map the data to your product, and outline the go-live plan. Then role-play a client call where you push for extra features. Judge their clarity, accuracy and how they protect the scope.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to teach at a college. Verify the highest degree with the school that granted it, and check that it meets your accreditor’s faculty qualification rules, usually a graduate degree in the subject. In clinical or professional fields, also check any required professional license.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a teaching demonstration with real students or a faculty panel, plus a sample syllabus, assignments and grading rubric. For research roles, review the publication record, grant history, research plan and how they mentor students. Check accessible course design and online teaching if needed.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show evidence of student learning, not just good evaluations. They revise courses based on results, explain complex ideas clearly, have a funded or fundable research agenda where required, and describe concrete mentoring of students and junior colleagues.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for no teaching evidence for a teaching role, publications they cannot discuss in depth, or dismissive talk about students. Check for retracted papers or research misconduct findings, and be wary of anyone unaware of student privacy rules or campus reporting duties.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you change a course after students struggled? Describe your research plan and how you will fund it. How do you support a student who is falling behind? How do you protect student records? Strong answers include specific examples and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a professor or lecturer?
qa.a: Look for a qualifying degree in the subject, proven teaching ability and, for research roles, a strong publication and funding record. Check fit with your mission, course needs and accreditor rules. No state license is needed for most college teaching, so verified degrees, teaching evidence and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a professor or lecturer before hiring?
qa.a: Ask for a teaching demonstration on a topic from your curriculum, a sample syllabus and graded work, and a research talk for research roles. Review clarity, student engagement, assessment design and whether the research plan is realistic. Keep every candidate’s format and questions the same for fairness.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for program coordinators, and project management certificates are optional. If the program serves children or vulnerable adults, many states require background checks, and the rules vary by state. Verify past programs through references and samples of schedules, reports or trackers they built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test scheduling and logistics, spreadsheet or database tracking, clear email and meeting notes, and simple budget tracking against a grant or plan. For grant-funded work, check they understand funder reporting, allowable costs and record keeping, including federal Uniform Guidance rules when federal money is involved.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates keep one reliable tracker, flag deadlines before they slip, and keep participants, staff and partners informed. They know which records a funder or auditor will ask for, file paperwork correctly the first time, and can show a program they kept running smoothly.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for missed deadlines blamed on others, no system for tracking participants or documents, loose handling of personal data, and confusion about what costs a grant allows. Be wary of anyone who cannot name the outcomes a past program was supposed to report.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your tracker for a past program. Tell me about a deadline you nearly missed and what you changed. How do you handle sign-in sheets and personal data? What did the funder ask for at reporting time? Strong answers show systems, not heroics.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a program coordinator?
qa.a: Look for strong organization, a clear system for tracking schedules, participants and documents, and calm communication with staff, partners and participants. For grant-funded programs, check they understand funder reporting and allowable costs. No license is required, so references and samples of trackers, schedules or reports matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a program coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise based on your program, such as building a schedule for a training series from a list of rooms, trainers and dates, then drafting a short progress report for the funder. Review accuracy, attention to deadlines, privacy of participant data and how clearly they write.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required to manage projects. Some candidates hold the PMP or PgMP certification, which you can confirm in the issuing body’s public online registry. Treat it as a plus, not proof of skill. Agile and Scrum credentials vary a lot in rigor.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can break a goal into tasks, map dependencies between teams, find the critical path and build a realistic schedule. They should keep a risk list, track budget against plan, manage scope changes and write short status updates that leaders can act on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain their own role clearly, not just the team’s. They describe a project that slipped, how they spotted it early and what they traded off to recover. They speak in dates, milestones and outcomes, and they stay calm when teams disagree.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers that say “we” for everything, blame on other teams, or talk only about software tools. Be wary if they cannot explain how they handled a scope change, a missed deadline or a stakeholder who pushed back.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through your largest multi-team project. How many teams, what was the timeline, and what went wrong?” Then ask how they set priorities when two teams needed the same people, and how they reported bad news to leadership.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a program and project manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they have run work across several teams. They should plan schedules with dependencies, track risks and budgets, and handle scope changes. Clear writing and calm handling of conflict matter as much as tools. A PMP or similar certification is a plus but is not legally required, so weigh real results more heavily.

qa.q: How do I test a program and project manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Describe a project with three teams, a fixed deadline and one delayed dependency. Ask for a simple plan, the top risks and a one-page status update for leadership. Then change a requirement and see how they adjust the plan and explain the tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to work as a programmer in the US. Degrees and vendor certifications are optional, not proof of skill. Check past roles with references. Ask for code samples, a portfolio or shipped projects they are allowed to share.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Match the test to your work. Game roles often need C++ or C# and engine experience. Machine tool roles need G-code, CAM software and blueprint reading. Older companies may need COBOL, RPG or SQL on legacy systems. Test debugging, not just writing new code.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Reads existing code before changing it. Uses version control and writes tests. Explains tradeoffs in plain words and asks about requirements first. For CNC work, talks about dry runs, checking tool paths and inspecting first parts before a full run.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Cannot explain code in their own portfolio. Pastes generated code they cannot walk through. Skips version control or testing. Blames teammates for every bug. For machine tool work, treats crashes, broken tools or scrapped parts as normal.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a bug that took days to find. How did you change code nobody understood? What do you check before running a new program on a machine? Strong candidates give specific, detailed stories instead of buzzwords.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a programmer?
qa.a: Look for proven skill in your exact languages and tools, such as C++ for games, G-code for machine tools or COBOL for legacy systems. Check that they use version control, test their work and can explain their code clearly. No US license is required, so rely on samples, references and a practical test.

qa.q: How do I test a programmer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task close to the real job. Ask them to fix a bug in existing code, add a small feature or, for CNC roles, write or correct a simple part program. Then have them walk you through their choices. Keep it brief, use the same task for every candidate and do not use the work in production.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for project coordinators. An entry-level project management certificate shows basic knowledge but is optional. Check references from project managers they supported, and ask for samples of trackers, meeting notes or status reports, with private details removed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test scheduling, task tracking in spreadsheets or project software, meeting notes with clear action items, and short status updates. Check attention to detail, follow-up on late tasks, and how they keep a shared plan current when dates change.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates follow up before deadlines slip, keep notes and trackers accurate, and flag risks early to the project manager. They write short, clear messages, handle many small tasks without dropping any, and stay polite when chasing busy people.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for careless errors in their own application, vague answers about tools, or sample trackers that were never kept current. Be careful with candidates who wait to be told everything, avoid following up with senior people, or let issues pile up without telling the project manager.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you track many tasks across several people each week? Tell me about a deadline you saw slipping and what you did. How do you write meeting notes so people act on them? Strong answers name tools and daily habits.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a project coordinator?
qa.a: Look for strong organization, attention to detail and clear, polite follow-up. Check they know the tools you use for schedules and task tracking, and can write short status updates and meeting notes. No license is required, so references from project managers and work samples matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a project coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: messy meeting notes and a simple project plan. Ask them to write action items with owners and dates, update the plan and draft a reminder to a late task owner. Review accuracy, clarity, tone and how quickly they spot conflicts.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a general license to work as a project manager. Many candidates hold the PMP, CAPM or a Scrum credential. You can confirm a PMP in the issuer’s public online registry. Treat any certificate as a plus, not proof of delivered projects. Construction roles may need extra credentials that vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can break work into tasks, set dependencies and find the critical path. They should track a budget against actual spend, keep a risk log and write a short status report a busy executive can read in two minutes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe past projects with numbers: the starting scope, budget and deadline, and how each actually ended. They explain the tradeoffs they made, own their misses, and choose a method, such as agile or waterfall, to fit the project rather than out of habit.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who talks only about software tools and never about results. Other warnings are no example of a project that went off track, blaming the team for every delay, and a vague “we” whenever you ask what they personally decided.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Tell me about a project that ran late. When did you first see it, who did you tell, and what changed?” Also ask how they handled a scope change request in the middle of a project and who approved it.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a project manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they have delivered projects close to their time and budget, and can explain what happened when they did not. Strong candidates plan clearly, flag risks early and report status in plain language. Certifications like the PMP help, but no general state license exists, so weigh real results most.

qa.q: How do I test a project manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid exercise. Share a simple project brief with a deadline, budget and a few constraints. Ask for a task schedule with dependencies, a list of top risks, and a one-page status update after you introduce a surprise delay. Judge how clearly they reason, prioritize and communicate the tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many states require a real estate broker or property management license to lease units or collect rent for owners, while some exempt on-site employees. Rules vary by state, so check yours and verify the license on the state lookup. Certified Property Manager and similar credentials are optional.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test lease and rent roll basics, collections and late notices, move-in and move-out inspections, work order handling and budget variance reports. Check knowledge of fair housing law, security deposit rules and eviction steps, which vary by state and city, and the property management software you use.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates keep collections current, turn vacant units quickly, and explain each line of an operating budget. They document everything, hold owner and tenant money in the separate accounts state rules require, answer tenants promptly and can show owner reports they prepared.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for mixing owner or tenant funds with their own, steering applicants toward or away from certain buildings, skipping written notices, or vague answers about deposit deductions. Be wary of anyone who handles repairs without bids or records, or who treats eviction as the first tool.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you handle a tenant who is two months behind. How do you decide what to deduct from a deposit? How do you screen applicants consistently? Tell me about an owner budget that went over and what you did.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a property manager?
qa.a: Look for the license your state requires for managing property for others, strong knowledge of fair housing and landlord-tenant law, and clean handling of rent and deposits. Check experience with your property type, whether apartments or offices. Owner references and sample reports show how they manage budgets, repairs and tenant problems.

qa.q: How do I test a property manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case using a sample rent roll, a few late accounts, a repair request and a budget variance. Ask them to plan collection steps under your state’s rules, prioritize the repair and draft a short owner update. Review accuracy, fair and consistent treatment of tenants, and clear writing.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them build a compliance matrix from a sample solicitation. They should map every instruction and evaluation criterion to an outline. Check that page limits, font rules, required forms and submission steps are tracked, and that nothing is missed.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state or federal license is required for this work. Industry certifications in proposal management exist at several levels and show formal training, but they are optional. Some government bids need a security clearance; require one only when the contract truly calls for it.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about bid or no-bid decisions, customer research before the solicitation is released, win themes and discriminators, and staged color team reviews. They can explain how they kept writers, pricing staff and subject experts on schedule and delivered every proposal on time.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treating proposals as pure writing with no capture plan. Vague answers about their own role or results on past bids. No clear method for tracking compliance. A pattern of late submissions is serious, since late federal proposals are usually not considered.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a bid they lost and what they changed afterward. Ask how they handled an amendment that arrived days before the due date. Ask how they got busy experts to deliver their sections on time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a proposal and capture manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who handles the whole cycle, from early customer research and bid or no-bid decisions to a compliant, on-time submission. They should read solicitations closely, build compliance matrices, write clear win themes and run review cycles. Certifications are optional, so weigh real results and process more heavily.

qa.q: How do I test a proposal and capture manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short sample solicitation and ask for a compliance matrix, a proposal outline and a schedule working back from the due date. Add a draft section to edit. Review how complete, organized and persuasive their work is, and ask them to explain their choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles call for a degree in aerospace or mechanical engineering. A Professional Engineer (PE) license exists but is rarely required in aerospace, since many states exempt engineers working for manufacturers. Rules vary by state. Confirm any degree or license the candidate lists.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for working command of thermodynamics, fluid flow, combustion and heat transfer. Check hands-on use of CAD, analysis or CFD tools, and test data review. Ask them to size a nozzle or explain a performance drop from real numbers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can walk you through an engine or component they helped design, build or test. They explain trade-offs between weight, cost and reliability. They respect hazardous propellant and test stand safety and write clear test plans and reports.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful if they can’t say what they personally did on a team project. Watch for shrugging off safety steps, blaming others for failed tests, or quoting software results they can’t check by hand.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a test that went wrong and how they found the root cause. Ask how they chose materials for hot sections. Ask what instruments they placed on a test article and why.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a propulsion engineer?
qa.a: Look for an aerospace or mechanical engineering degree, solid grounding in thermodynamics and combustion, and real design or test work on engines or components. Good candidates explain trade-offs clearly, take test safety seriously and can show what they personally contributed. A PE license is rarely required in this field, and rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test a propulsion engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short technical task tied to your work, such as reviewing a set of test data and spotting an anomaly, or doing a rough sizing of a nozzle or pump. Ask them to talk through their assumptions. Follow with a review of a past project where they explain their own design and test choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most public administration roles need no license. Verify degrees and past public service through references. Some jobs require specific credentials, such as in budgeting, procurement or emergency management, and civil service rules like exams and veterans’ preference vary by government and state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test program management, budgeting within appropriations, grant compliance, procurement rules and performance measurement. Check knowledge of public records and open meetings laws, which vary by state, plus clear writing for elected officials, residents and staff, and comfort presenting at public meetings.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates measure program results, not just activity, and explain them in plain words. They follow procurement and ethics rules carefully, work well across departments, and handle public scrutiny calmly. They can show a service they improved and how residents benefited.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for disregard of procurement, public records or open meetings rules, and for undisclosed conflicts of interest. Be wary of candidates who cannot explain how a program was funded or measured, or who blame elected officials for every setback.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a program you ran, its funding source and how you measured results. How do you handle a public records request on a sensitive topic? Describe a time you had to say no to an official. Strong answers show rules followed and outcomes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a public administrator?
qa.a: Look for program and budget experience, careful respect for procurement, ethics and public records rules, and clear communication with officials and residents. Check results they measured, not just duties they held. Civil service and veterans’ preference rules vary by government, so follow your own hiring rules when you assess candidates.

qa.q: How do I test a public administrator before hiring?
qa.a: Use a structured, job-related exercise that fits your civil service rules, such as a written case on a struggling program with budget and service data. Ask for a short memo with problems, options and a recommendation, then a brief presentation. Score every candidate on the same rubric for analysis, rule awareness and clarity.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for epidemiologists or health economists. Verify degrees such as an MPH or PhD with the school, and review published papers, reports or models they built. Voluntary public health certifications exist. Credit only the work they can explain in detail.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test study design, biostatistics and the software you use, such as R, SAS or Stata. For economics roles, check cost-effectiveness and budget impact models, quality-adjusted life years and sensitivity analysis. For population health roles, check surveillance data, confounding, bias and clear writing for policymakers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates state assumptions plainly, show which inputs move the result most, and share code or model files others can rerun. They know claims, survey and health record data and their limits, and explain findings to non-experts without overstating them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for confusing correlation with causation, models no one else can follow, results tuned to a sponsor’s wishes, or no plan for missing data. Be wary of casual handling of patient-level data, which federal privacy rules and data use agreements restrict.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Which input changed your last model’s result the most, and how did you test it? How did you handle confounding in an observational study? Tell me about a finding that disappointed a client or agency. Strong answers name methods, data and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a public health specialist or health economist?
qa.a: Look for solid methods in study design, statistics or economic modeling, matched to your work, plus clear writing for policymakers, payers or the public. Check published work, reports or models they can walk through in detail. No license is required, so verified degrees, work samples and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a public health specialist or health economist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a public or mock dataset, such as estimating the effect of a program while handling confounding, or building a simple cost-effectiveness model with a sensitivity analysis. Ask for code, a short write-up and a summary for non-experts. Review assumptions, accuracy and clarity.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work in public relations. Some specialists hold the voluntary Accreditation in Public Relations (APR), which shows tested knowledge and ethics. Verify any claimed credential with the issuing body, and confirm past roles and media results with former employers or clients.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test writing first: a clean press release, a short pitch email and a holding statement for bad news. Check news style, accuracy and speed. Then test judgment, such as which reporters fit a story, what to say on the record and when to stay quiet.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show real coverage they earned and explain how they got it. They know the outlets and reporters in your field, respect deadlines, and never promise guaranteed placements. They stay calm under pressure and push for facts before speaking to the press.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for guarantees of coverage, vague claims like “I know everyone,” clips they cannot explain, or sloppy writing. Be wary of anyone who suggests misleading reporters, hiding facts, or paying for editorial coverage without clear disclosure. Those habits can damage your reputation fast.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a pitch that landed and one that failed. Ask how they handled a hostile reporter or a crisis, who approved statements, and what they would do differently. Specific names of outlets, timelines and outcomes signal real experience.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a public relations specialist?
qa.a: Look for strong writing, real media relationships in your industry and calm judgment during bad news. Ask for coverage they personally secured and have them explain how. No license is required in the US, though some hold the voluntary APR. Avoid anyone who guarantees placements or suggests misleading the press.

qa.q: How do I test a public relations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task based on your business. Ask for a press release on a real or sample announcement, a pitch email to a named type of reporter and a brief statement responding to a negative story. Judge accuracy, clarity, news sense and how quickly they ask the right questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No sales license is required, but some states and cities require lobbyist registration for some selling to government, and rules vary. Confirm any security clearance they claim is active. Former government staff may face post-employment rules that limit contact with their old agency.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they read a request for proposal, plan a response and use cooperative contracts, schedules and resellers. Check knowledge of procurement rules, budget and fiscal year timing, compliance needs such as accessibility and security, and long sales cycles.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know how public buyers really decide: budgets, procurement officers, evaluation scoring and board approvals. They build relationships the right way, follow gift and ethics rules strictly and can show contracts won through formal bids.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for anyone who suggests gifts, meals or favors for officials, contact with evaluators during a no-contact period, or shaping a bid improperly. Be wary of claimed clearances they cannot document and wins they cannot name at the agency level.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a bid you won, from first meeting to contract award. How do you learn a buyer’s budget cycle? What ethics rules have you followed when meeting officials? Strong answers name steps, rules and timelines.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a public sector sales rep?
qa.a: Look for wins with governments, schools or agencies through formal bids, strong knowledge of procurement and contract vehicles, and spotless ethics. They should plan around budget cycles and long sales timelines. No sales license is required, but lobbying, ethics and clearance rules may apply and vary by state and agency.

qa.q: How do I test a public sector sales rep before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task using a sample request for proposal. Ask for a bid or no-bid decision, a response outline, questions for the buyer through the official process and a timeline to award. Judge whether they read requirements carefully, respect the rules and spot compliance risks.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for Python developers, and certificates are optional. Verify real work instead: a portfolio, public code repositories, shipped projects and references from past managers or clients. Confirm the work shown is theirs by asking them to walk through it.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test core Python, data structures, error handling and writing tests with pytest. Check Git, SQL and virtual environments. Then test your stack: Django, Flask or FastAPI for web backends, pandas for data pipelines, or the AI libraries and APIs you actually use.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates write readable code that follows common Python style, add tests without being asked and explain tradeoffs clearly. They log errors, keep secrets out of code, pin dependencies and can describe how they found and fixed a hard bug.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who cannot explain their own code, paste AI-generated code they do not understand, skip tests, hard-code passwords or API keys, or have never used version control. Vague answers about past projects are another warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they sped up a slow script, how they handle a pipeline job that fails halfway, how they manage package versions across projects, and what broke in production once and how they fixed it.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Python developer?
qa.a: Look for solid Python fundamentals, experience with your specific frameworks, and habits like writing tests, using Git and handling errors well. No license is required, so judge real work: code samples, past projects and references. A good developer explains decisions in plain language and can read and improve code written by others.

qa.q: How do I test a Python developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your real work, such as a small API endpoint, a data cleaning script or an automation job. Ask for tests and a brief readme. Then review the code together and ask them to explain choices and handle a small change live. This shows skill and understanding, not just a finished file.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No state license is required to work as a QA engineer in the US. Optional software testing certifications exist, but they show study, not skill. Give more weight to real test plans, bug reports and automation code they can walk you through.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them write test cases for a simple feature, find bugs in a small app, and automate one check in the tool or language your team uses. Watch how they cover edge cases, bad input, and different browsers or devices.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Their bug reports are clear, with steps to reproduce, expected results and actual results. They ask about users and risk before they start testing. They know when a manual check beats automation and keep tests stable, fast and easy to maintain.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: They only test the happy path. Their bug reports are vague. They can’t explain tests they wrote on past projects. They blame developers instead of working with them. Their automated tests rely on fixed waits and break with small page changes.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a serious bug they caught before release and how they found it. Ask how they decide what to test when time is short. Ask how they dealt with flaky automated tests in a build pipeline.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a QA engineer?
qa.a: Look for someone who thinks like a user and a skeptic at once. They should write clear bug reports, plan tests around risk, and know both manual testing and automation. Check that they can work with the tools your team uses and explain their past test work in plain terms.

qa.q: How do I test a QA engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-boxed task. Share a small app or feature with a few planted bugs. Ask them to write test cases, report the bugs they find, and automate one or two checks. Then review how complete, clear and maintainable their work is.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is needed for most quality engineering roles. Voluntary credentials such as a Certified Quality Engineer exam or a Six Sigma belt show study, but belt standards vary by issuer. Check the issuer and the date, and weigh hands-on results more.

look.label: Skills to test
