look.text: Test root cause methods such as 5 Whys, fishbone diagrams and 8D reports. Also check reading drawings with GD&T, statistical process control, gage R&R studies, FMEA and control plans. Ask them to work through a real defect from your line.

look.label: Standards they should know
look.text: Match their background to your industry. ISO 9001 is common across manufacturing. Automotive work often uses IATF 16949 and PPAP. Aerospace uses AS9100. Medical devices follow FDA quality system rules and ISO 13485. Ask which audits they have faced.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a defect they traced to its true cause, the fix they put in place and how they proved it stayed fixed. They talk about data, not blame. They work well with operators, suppliers and design engineers on the floor.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who only adds more inspection instead of fixing the process. Other warnings are vague stories with no numbers, no follow-up after a corrective action, or treating paperwork as the goal rather than a better product.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a quality engineer?
qa.a: Look for proven root cause skills, comfort with measurement and statistics, and the ability to read drawings and tolerances. Experience with the quality standard your industry uses, such as ISO 9001, IATF 16949, AS9100 or ISO 13485, saves time. Strong candidates explain past fixes with data and show how they kept problems from coming back.

qa.q: How do I test a quality engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a real or sample defect case with a drawing, some measurement data and a short complaint. Ask them to find likely causes, choose a containment step, propose a lasting fix and say how they would verify it. You can also ask them to review a control plan or interpret an SPC chart.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No general license is required, and the Certified Quality Inspector credential is optional. Nondestructive testing staff are usually certified by the employer under a written practice. Industrial radiography with radioactive sources requires radiographer certification under federal or state rules. Weld inspection often calls for Certified Welding Inspector status.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test reading drawings and geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, and accurate use of calipers, micrometers, height gauges, and coordinate measuring machines or scanners. Check sampling plans, first article inspection, calibration status checks, clear nonconformance reports and basic statistical process control charts.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates measure the same way every time, check gauge calibration before use and record results clearly. They stop bad parts calmly even under schedule pressure, explain the reason with data, and help production find the cause instead of just rejecting parts.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for rounding or guessing measurements, using out-of-calibration gauges, passing parts to keep the line moving, and records filled in after the fact. Be wary of anyone who cannot read a feature control frame or explain how they handle a borderline part.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you measure the true position of a hole? What do you do when a part is right at the tolerance limit? Tell me about a time you held parts despite pressure from production. Strong answers show method, data and integrity.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a quality inspector?
qa.a: Look for accurate measurement skills, strong blueprint and tolerance reading, careful records and the integrity to stop bad parts. Check experience with your gauges and methods, from hand tools to scanners or X-ray. Certifications are optional for most inspection but required for some nondestructive testing and radiography, so verify what your work needs.

qa.q: How do I test a quality inspector before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid bench test. Give them a drawing and a few sample parts, including one out of tolerance, with the gauges you use. Ask them to measure, record results and write a short nonconformance report. Review accuracy, repeatability, gauge handling and whether they caught the bad part.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test probability, statistics, linear algebra and time series analysis. Check coding in Python, C++ or the language your team uses. Give messy market data with gaps, splits and bad ticks, and watch how they clean it before modeling.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates bring up look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, overfitting and transaction costs without being asked. They test out of sample, question their own results and can explain clearly why an idea failed, not just why one worked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for backtests with very high returns and no costs or slippage. Be wary if they cannot explain their assumptions. Walk away if they offer code, signals or data from a former employer, which can expose you to trade secret claims.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most research roles need no license. If the person will trade or supervise trading at a broker-dealer, FINRA registration such as the Series 57 may apply, so check with compliance. Verify degrees, published papers and code samples, and call references.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a strategy they built, from data to live results. Ask how they chose the test period, how they modeled costs, and what happened when live performance differed from the backtest.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a quantitative researcher?
qa.a: Look for solid math and statistics, clean code, and a careful habit of attacking their own results. Good researchers know common backtest traps like overfitting and look-ahead bias. They explain ideas simply. Confirm they respect confidentiality and will not bring a former employer’s code or data.

qa.q: How do I test a quantitative researcher before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short take-home or live task using a public or synthetic dataset. Ask them to build and backtest a simple signal, include costs, and report out-of-sample results. Then review it together. Focus on how they handle data issues, check for bias and explain limits, not on the return number.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for quantum engineers. Most roles call for a graduate degree in physics, electrical engineering, computer science or a related field, though strong hands-on work can count. Verify listed degrees, publications and patents, and confirm that shared code repositories are the candidate’s own work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Match the test to the track. Hardware candidates should explain qubit coherence, gate fidelity, cryogenic or vacuum setups, and microwave or laser control. Software candidates should write and debug a small circuit in Python with an open-source quantum toolkit. They should also explain noise, error mitigation, and how simulator results differ from real hardware.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They speak honestly about what current machines can and cannot do. They describe a specific experiment or algorithm they built, what went wrong, and how they measured improvement. They follow recent research and connect theory to working code or lab results.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Big claims of quantum speedup with no benchmark against a classical method. Buzzwords with no hands-on circuits, calibrations or measurements. No plain-language explanation of decoherence or error correction. Vague answers about their own role in team papers or projects.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Walk me through calibrating a two-qubit gate,” or “How would you check whether this algorithm beats a classical solver?” Ask which noise sources limited their last project and what they did about them. Strong answers include numbers, tradeoffs and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a quantum engineer?
qa.a: First decide whether you need hardware or software skills. Then look for a relevant graduate degree or equal experience, hands-on work with real qubits or quantum toolkits, and clear talk about the limits of today’s machines. No license is required. Check publications, code and references to confirm what the candidate personally did.

qa.q: How do I test a quantum engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-boxed task tied to your actual work. Software candidates can implement a small algorithm, run it on a simulator, and explain how noise would change the results. Hardware candidates can analyze sample lab data, such as a qubit decay curve, and suggest fixes. Judge their reasoning, not just the final answer.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as a React developer, and there is no official React certification employers commonly require. Course certificates are optional. Review live apps and code instead, and ask which parts the candidate built personally.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test components, props, state and hooks, especially useEffect and when not to use it. Check TypeScript, data fetching, forms, routing, state management and testing with tools such as React Testing Library. Look for accessible markup, responsive layouts and awareness of rendering performance.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates build small, reusable components with clear props, keep state close to where it is used and can explain why a component rerenders. They test behavior rather than internals, use semantic HTML and keyboard support, and work well with a design system.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for useEffect used for everything, giant components, copied state that drifts out of sync, and clickable divs instead of buttons. Be careful with candidates who cannot explain keys in lists, ignore loading and error states, or show only tutorial apps.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a slow React screen you sped up and how you measured it. When do you avoid useEffect? How do you decide where state lives? How do you make a custom dropdown accessible? Strong answers name tools and specific tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a React developer?
qa.a: Look for live apps and code they can explain, built with modern React and hooks. Check TypeScript, state management, data fetching, testing, accessibility and performance habits. Make sure they can work from your designs and with your back end. No license is required in the US, so real work matters more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a React developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your product, such as building a searchable list from a mockup and a sample API, with loading, empty and error states. Ask them to use Git and add a few tests. Review component structure, state handling, accessibility, keyboard use and how it behaves on a phone.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most states do not require a real estate license for an employee handling only their own company’s property, but rules vary by state. Some candidates hold a license or voluntary industry designations. Confirm any license with the state’s real estate commission, and verify degrees and past titles.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for lease vs. buy analysis, net present value modeling, reading and abstracting leases, and knowing how ASC 842 puts leases on the balance sheet. They should also know site selection, zoning checks, Phase I environmental reviews and working with outside brokers and lawyers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can walk you through a full deal they led, from finding sites to signing. They talk about cost per square foot, renewal options, exit rights and how the space served the business plan. For factories or data centers, they mention power, water, fiber and labor supply.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague claims like “managed a big portfolio” with no deal sizes or results. Be careful if they can’t explain a lease clause they negotiated, blame brokers for every bad outcome, or have never worked with finance, legal or facilities teams.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Tell me about a lease you renegotiated. What did you give up and what did you win?” Or: “How did you pick between two sites for a new facility?” Strong answers include numbers, tradeoffs and who signed off.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a corporate real estate manager?
qa.a: Look for a track record of closed leases and purchases you can check, strong financial modeling, and solid knowledge of lease terms and lease accounting. They should explain how real estate choices supported business goals. A license is usually not needed for in-house work, but rules vary by state, so confirm with your state.

qa.q: How do I test a corporate real estate manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a sample lease and ask for a one-page summary of key terms, costs and risks. Then hand them two site options with rent, buildout and moving costs, and ask for a lease vs. buy or site recommendation with a simple cost model. Have them present it to you as they would to leadership.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Every state requires a real estate license to help others buy, sell or lease property for pay, and agents must work under a licensed broker. Check the license on the state licensing agency’s online lookup. Rules for leasing staff vary, and some states exempt an owner’s on-site employees.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test pricing a property from comparable sales, writing a clear listing, showing homes or offices well and explaining offers, contingencies and disclosure forms. Check they know fair housing law, local rental rules and how to keep a deal on track to closing.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know the local market street by street, return calls quickly and keep clients informed at every step. They have a record of closed deals or signed leases, repeat clients and referrals, and no disciplinary actions on their license.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for an expired or inactive license, past discipline, pressure on clients, or steering buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on protected traits, which fair housing law bans. Be wary of anyone vague about required disclosures.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your last closing, from listing to keys. How do you price a home with few comparable sales? How do you handle a lowball offer or a failed inspection? Strong answers include specific steps, forms and timelines.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a real estate agent?
qa.a: Look for an active state license under a supervising broker, a clean disciplinary record and a history of closed sales or leases in your market. They should price well, communicate fast and know fair housing and disclosure rules. Licensing details vary by state, so check the state agency’s online lookup.

qa.q: How do I test a real estate agent before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short role-play and a market task. Ask them to price a sample property from recent comparable sales, then present it to you as a seller and handle objections. Add a renter or buyer question touching fair housing. Judge local knowledge, accuracy, honesty and how clearly they explain next steps.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a receptionist. In clinics, prior training on patient privacy under HIPAA is a plus, and in hotels, experience with front desk systems helps. Verify reliability and customer service through references from past supervisors.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test handling a multi-line phone, scheduling software, visitor check-in and sign-in procedures, message taking and clear, polite email. Check typing accuracy, basic spreadsheet use, and how they handle an upset caller and a waiting visitor at the same time.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong receptionists greet every visitor warmly, keep calm under pressure, and pass on messages accurately and promptly. They follow security and privacy steps every time, know the office well enough to route questions, and keep the front desk tidy and organized.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for poor phone manner, inaccurate messages, or a habit of discussing visitors and patients within earshot of others. Be wary of anyone who skips visitor sign-in rules or gives vague answers about how they handled busy, stressful shifts.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a time the phones rang while a visitor needed help. How do you handle a caller who is angry? What do you do when someone without an appointment insists on seeing a manager? Strong answers show calm priorities, courtesy and clear steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a receptionist?
qa.a: Look for a warm, professional manner, calm under pressure and accurate message taking. Check skills with phones, scheduling and check-in systems, plus respect for privacy and security rules, such as HIPAA in clinics. No license is required, so references from past supervisors and a short role-play tell you the most.

qa.q: How do I test a receptionist before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role-play with mock calls and a visitor arriving at the same time, then a brief task such as booking an appointment in sample software or writing up a phone message. Review courtesy, priorities, accuracy of details and whether they follow privacy and sign-in steps. Pay for any task longer than a normal interview.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask the candidate to write a Boolean search string for a hard-to-fill role and draft a short outreach message. Watch how they read a job description, pick out must-have skills and screen a sample resume fairly and quickly.

look.label: Fair hiring knowledge
look.text: A good recruiter knows which interview questions break federal and state anti-discrimination laws. They should know that rules on pay transparency, salary history and criminal history questions vary by state and city. They should also know when to check with HR or legal.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most in-house recruiters need no license. Some states regulate employment agencies or staffing firms, so check your state’s rules if the person will run one. HR certifications are optional. Confirm past roles, hires made and tools used with former managers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can name roles they filled, where they found people and why candidates accepted. They track every step in an applicant tracking system, follow up fast and keep hiring managers and candidates informed without being asked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about results, blaming hiring managers for every lost hire, or treating ghosting candidates as normal. Also watch for anyone who suggests screening people by age, family plans or other traits the law protects.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a recruiter?
qa.a: Look for proof they have filled roles like yours, strong sourcing skills and clear writing. They should know fair hiring rules, use an applicant tracking system well and respond quickly. Ask former managers how many hires they made and how candidates felt about the process.

qa.q: How do I test a recruiter before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a real job description and ask for a sourcing plan, a Boolean search string and an outreach message. Then role-play a phone screen with a mock candidate and a tough talk with a hiring manager. Judge their accuracy, tone and follow-up.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this job. Optional HR certifications exist but are not needed. Verify past work instead. Ask references how many open roles and interviews the person handled each week, and which applicant tracking system and calendar tools they used daily.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test calendar juggling across time zones, clear written messages to candidates, and careful data entry in an applicant tracking system. Check they know the basics of hiring paperwork, such as the standalone background check disclosure and Form I-9 timing. Rules on salary history and criminal record questions vary by state and city.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They confirm details in writing, send reminders without being asked, and give every candidate a clear next step, even a rejection. They keep candidate data private. They flag a stalled offer or a missing signature before the hiring manager has to ask.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Typos or wrong names in their own emails to you, slow replies while scheduling their own interview, and vague answers about how much volume they handled. Also watch for comfort with ghosting candidates or casual sharing of other applicants’ details.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “A panel interviewer cancels one hour before the interview. What do you do?” and “How did you track ten open roles at once?” Strong answers name specific steps, tools and messages, not general promises to stay organized.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a recruiting coordinator?
qa.a: Look for tight organization, clear and friendly writing, and calm handling of last-minute changes. They should know an applicant tracking system and shared calendars, keep candidate data private, and understand hiring paperwork basics. No license is needed, so check references on the volume they handled and how accurate their work was.

qa.q: How do I test a recruiting coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid or brief task. Ask them to schedule three interviews for one candidate across two time zones with conflicting calendars, then write the confirmation email and a polite rejection to another candidate. Grade accuracy, tone and speed. Also notice how they handle scheduling their own interview with you.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Optional HR certifications exist and can show grounding in employment law, but they are not mandatory. Check references and ask which applicant tracking systems they actually administered, not just used.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for hands-on applicant tracking system setup, clean data habits and strong spreadsheet skills. They should build funnel reports on time to fill, pass-through rates and source of hire. They should also write clear posting templates and career page content.

look.label: Compliance know-how
look.text: They should understand FCRA disclosure and adverse action steps for background checks and hiring record retention. They should know to keep voluntary self-identification data apart from hiring decisions. Pay transparency and ban-the-box rules vary by state and city. Federal contractors carry extra duties.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a process they fixed with before and after numbers. They document workflows so recruiters can follow them. They train hiring managers on the tools. They tie employer brand work to real results, such as better applicant quality or fewer drop-offs.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: They can’t explain how their past reports were built or where the data came from. They blame the tools for every problem. They are casual about sharing candidate data. They describe employer branding as polish with no honest detail about the job.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a recruiting operations specialist?
qa.a: Look for someone who has administered an applicant tracking system, keeps data clean and builds reliable hiring reports. They should know background check and record-keeping rules, and they should know that pay transparency laws vary by state and city. Strong candidates show a process they improved, with numbers, and can write honest employer brand content.

qa.q: How do I test a recruiting operations specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a messy sample export of fake candidate data. Ask them to clean it, build a simple funnel report and suggest one process fix. Add a short job posting to review for clarity and for the pay disclosure rules in your location. Never share real candidate data. Pay for any task that takes more than an hour or two.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required in most industries, though teams selling insurance, securities or real estate need licensed staff and may need a licensed supervisor. Verify results instead: revenue against target each year, team size and turnover, and references from managers and former reps.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test forecasting, territory and quota design, hiring and coaching front-line managers, and running pipeline reviews. Check how they read a regional sales report, spot a weak team early, work with marketing and finance, and decide where to add headcount.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates hit target across several years and teams, not once. They grow managers who get promoted, keep good reps, forecast close to actual results and can explain exactly what changed when a team turned around under them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for results that rest on one large account, high rep turnover they cannot explain, forecasts that often missed, and a habit of selling deals themselves instead of coaching. Be wary of vague answers about how they handled underperformers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you build last year’s regional forecast, and how close was it? Tell me about a manager you coached out of a slump. How do you set territories and quotas? Strong answers include specific numbers, decisions and lessons.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a regional sales director?
qa.a: Look for years of hitting regional targets, managers they hired and developed, and accurate forecasting. They should design fair territories and quotas, run disciplined pipeline reviews and keep good reps. No license is required in most industries, so verified results and references from former managers and reps matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a regional sales director before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case using a sample regional report with a few struggling teams. Ask for a diagnosis, a ninety-day plan, a forecasting approach and how they would coach each manager. Have them present it to your sales leaders. Judge their reasoning, priorities and use of data.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. The Regulatory Affairs Certification (RAC) is a respected voluntary credential. Most hires hold a degree in life sciences, engineering, chemistry or a related field. Confirm the submissions, approvals and audits they list by checking with past employers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test whether they can read a new rule or agency guidance and explain what it changes for your products. Check clear, accurate technical writing, organized document control and deadline tracking. They should know the approval pathways for your field, such as 510(k), De Novo or PMA for medical devices.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a submission they owned from start to finish. Ask how they answered an agency deficiency letter or inspection finding. Ask how they learn about proposed rules early and how they explained a costly new requirement to leadership.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates cite the specific regulations behind their answers, such as the relevant parts of the Code of Federal Regulations. They admit when they would need to check guidance. They describe working closely with quality, research, legal and marketing teams, and they keep careful records.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of anyone who is vague about their own part in past submissions or promises a guaranteed approval. Walk away if they suggest leaving out unfavorable data, delaying required reports or bending marketing claims beyond what was cleared or approved.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a regulatory affairs specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with the agencies that oversee your products, such as the FDA, EPA or FCC. They should have real submissions and audits behind them. Look for precise writing and comfort reading dense regulations. The voluntary RAC credential is a plus. Integrity matters most, because they speak for your company to regulators.

qa.q: How do I test a regulatory affairs specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short, real agency guidance document or proposed rule. Ask for a one-page summary of what it means for your products and what actions to take. You can also ask them to draft a reply to a sample deficiency question. Judge their accuracy, clarity and whether they cite sources correctly.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Physical therapists, occupational therapists and their assistants need a state license or other state credential, and rules vary by state. Verify status on state board sites, and check compact privileges if they will practice across state lines. Many employers also require current CPR certification.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test evaluation, goal setting and treatment planning for your patient group, such as orthopedic, neurological, pediatric or older adults. Check manual therapy, therapeutic exercise, gait or daily living skills training, and equipment use. Review documentation that shows medical necessity and progress for insurers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates set measurable goals, progress patients safely and adjust plans based on results. They teach home programs clearly, work well with doctors, nurses and assistants and follow your state’s supervision rules for assistants. Their notes are timely and specific.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for copy-and-paste notes, billing for time not spent, or vague goals that never change. Be careful with license discipline, poor safety with transfers or fall risk, or anyone who cannot explain why they chose an intervention.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you progress a patient after a knee replacement? Tell me about a patient who stopped improving and what you changed. How do you decide a patient is ready for discharge? How do you supervise an assistant? Strong answers tie choices to measurable goals.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a physical or occupational therapist?
qa.a: Look for an active state license, experience with your patient population and sound clinical reasoning. Check documentation that supports medical necessity, safe patient handling and clear patient teaching. References from supervisors or rehab managers confirm results. Check compact privileges if they will treat patients in more than one state.

qa.q: How do I test a physical or occupational therapist before hiring?
qa.a: Use case-based interviews with de-identified patient scenarios, asking for an evaluation plan, goals and first sessions. Add a documentation exercise and a hands-on skills check with a staff member acting as the patient. Judge clinical reasoning, safety and clear explanations.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or state certification exists for this work. Verify what can be checked instead: published papers, public code, and references from past research leads. Confirm the candidate’s actual role on any listed paper or project, since team credit is often shared.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test policy gradient methods such as PPO, reward modeling, and preference-based tuning like RLHF or DPO. Check their skill at debugging unstable training runs, designing fair evaluations, and writing clean, reproducible experiment code in a common deep learning framework.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain failed experiments as clearly as successful ones. They run baselines and ablations, track compute costs, and read model outputs instead of trusting a rising reward curve. They can describe reward hacking they caught and how they fixed it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for experience limited to toy tutorial environments, claims of gains with no baseline, and no way to reproduce results. Be wary if they cannot explain why a run diverged or never checked whether the model gamed the reward.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a reward model your policy exploited. How did you notice? How do you choose the KL penalty or similar constraint? Walk me through a run that collapsed and the steps you took to find the cause.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a reinforcement learning researcher?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work training models with reward signals, not just coursework. Good candidates know PPO, reward modeling and preference tuning, debug unstable runs, and design honest evaluations. Ask for code or papers, confirm their role, and check that they read real model outputs to catch reward hacking. No license applies, so references and work samples carry the most weight.

qa.q: How do I test a reinforcement learning researcher before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short take-home or live task. Share logs from a training run where reward rose but output quality fell, and ask them to diagnose it and propose fixes. Or have them design an evaluation for a tuned model. Judge their reasoning, use of baselines, and how clearly they explain tradeoffs, not just the final answer.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test forecasting and pipeline discipline. Ask how they track contracts 90 to 120 days out, flag risk early, and report expected renewal rates. Strong managers know their numbers, use the CRM daily, and can explain how they handle price increases without losing accounts.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for someone who can name specific accounts they saved and explain why they were at risk. Good renewals managers work closely with customer success, read usage data, and know when an upsell fits and when pushing it would cost the renewal.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What renewal rate did you own, and how was it measured? Walk me through a renewal that nearly churned. How do you negotiate when a customer asks for a discount or a shorter term? Vague answers or no metrics suggest limited ownership.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of candidates who treat renewals as paperwork, wait for customers to reach out, or rely mainly on discounts to close. Also watch for people who cannot separate gross retention from net retention, or who blame churn entirely on product or support.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license or certification is required for this work in the US. Check references from past managers about retention results, forecast accuracy and how they handled tough negotiations. Familiarity with your contract terms and billing tools is a plus but can be learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a renewals manager?
qa.a: Look for proven ownership of a renewal book with clear retention numbers, steady forecasting habits, and calm negotiation skills. The best candidates spot risk early using usage data and customer signals, work well with customer success and finance, and add upsells only when they truly help the customer.

qa.q: How do I test a renewals manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short list of sample accounts with contract dates, usage trends and support history. Ask them to rank risk, plan outreach timing, and role-play a renewal call where the customer pushes back on a price increase. Watch how they ask questions, protect value and close.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to work as a reporting analyst. A CPA license, issued by each state, matters mainly when reports involve accounting judgment. Business intelligence tool certifications are optional. Verify with sample reports, reconciliations they built and references who relied on their figures.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test SQL, spreadsheet skills such as lookups and pivot tables, and the business intelligence tool you use. Check how they reconcile report totals to source systems, document definitions and automate recurring reports. For regulated reports, confirm they follow the regulator’s instructions and filing deadlines.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates tie every figure back to a source, keep a clear record of changes and catch errors before readers do. They ask what decision a report supports, define each metric in writing and flag when the data cannot support a number.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for manual copy and paste with no checks, numbers that change between runs without explanation, and no written definitions. Be careful with anyone who adjusts figures to match expectations or cannot explain internal controls over financial reporting.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an error in a published report and how you found and fixed it. How do you reconcile a report to the general ledger or source system? How do you handle a late change to a metric definition? Strong answers name specific checks.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a reporting analyst?
qa.a: Look for accuracy, strong SQL and spreadsheet skills, and a habit of reconciling figures to their source. Check experience with your business intelligence tool and, for regulated reports, with the rules that apply in your industry. No license is required, so sample reports, documented processes and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a reporting analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work: share sample data with a planted error, and ask them to build a recurring report, reconcile it to a control total and document the definitions. Review whether they find the error, how they check figures and how clearly they explain the method.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: If the analyst will write equity research reports for a FINRA member broker-dealer, they generally must pass the Series 86 and 87 exams plus the SIE. You can confirm registration on FINRA BrokerCheck. For in-house market, company or crypto research, no license is required; a CFA charter is optional proof of skill.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can read income statements, balance sheets and cash flow statements, build a clean spreadsheet model, and pull data with SQL or Python if the role needs it. For crypto work, test whether they can read on-chain data, token supply schedules and protocol documentation.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong analysts state their assumptions, cite every source, and separate facts from opinion. They show a range of outcomes instead of one confident number. Their writing samples lead with the conclusion, use short charts that make one point each, and say plainly what the data cannot show.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for bold price calls with no model behind them, numbers without sources, and charts that start the axis to exaggerate a trend. Be wary if they cannot rebuild their own model step by step, or if they will not disclose personal holdings in stocks or tokens they would cover.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a call they got wrong and what they missed. Ask where the data in a past report came from and how they checked it. Ask how they would size a market when no clean data exists.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a research analyst?
qa.a: Look for someone who reads financial statements or on-chain data fluently, builds models you can follow, and writes clear conclusions backed by sources. Ask for writing samples. If they will publish equity research at a broker-dealer, confirm Series 86 and 87 registration. Otherwise judge them on skill, honesty about uncertainty, and disclosure of their own holdings.

qa.q: How do I test a research analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task using public data, such as a company’s recent filings or a protocol’s documentation. Ask for a one-page summary with a simple model and listed sources. Then have them walk you through it live. Check whether their numbers tie out, their assumptions are stated, and they can defend or revise them under questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for research program managers. Project management and research administration certifications exist but are optional. Verify past programs with references from scientists and funders, and ask which budgets, grants and partner agreements they managed personally rather than supported.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test planning milestones and budgets, tracking spend against grants, and drafting partner documents such as collaboration or material transfer agreements. For federal funding, check they know the Uniform Guidance cost rules. Also check risk tracking, equipment purchasing and work with review boards, biosafety and export control.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong managers understand the science well enough to spot risks early, keep scientists focused on research rather than paperwork, and give funders honest progress reports. They plan for failed experiments, recommend stopping weak projects and keep partners aligned on intellectual property and timelines.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for treating research like a fixed construction schedule, no grasp of grant rules, or reports that hide bad news. Be wary of anyone who cannot describe a project they helped stop or a budget they had to cut.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a program that slipped and what you changed. How do you handle a funder asking for results that are not ready? How did you settle an intellectual property dispute with a partner? Strong answers name real tradeoffs and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a research program manager?
qa.a: Look for experience running research programs end to end, including budgets, grant compliance, partners and equipment, plus enough scientific understanding to earn researchers’ trust. Check honest reporting and judgment about when to stop work. No license is required, so references from scientists and funders matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a research program manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case: share a mock program with a slipping timeline, an overspent budget line and a partner dispute, and ask for a recovery plan and a one-page update for funders. Review realism, grant compliance, clear priorities and how honestly they report the problems.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license exists for research scientists. A PhD is common but not always required. Read their publications, preprints and code yourself, and ask co-authors or references exactly what the candidate contributed to multi-author papers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test experiment design with strong baselines and ablations, the math behind their methods, and coding in Python with a deep learning framework. Check they can reproduce a published result, read papers critically and explain findings simply.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain why an idea should work before testing it, report negative results honestly and keep experiments reproducible with fixed seeds and logged settings. They can show methods that were published, open sourced or shipped in a product.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for results without baselines, cherry-picked benchmarks, test data leaking into training, and code nobody else can run. Be careful with anyone who cannot explain their own role on a paper or the main weakness of their best result.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What is the weakest part of your best paper? Tell me about an experiment that failed and what you learned. How would you check whether a result is real or just noise? Strong answers show rigor and honest doubt.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a research scientist?
qa.a: Look for rigorous experiments with strong baselines, reproducible code and honest reporting of limits. Read their publications and code yourself, and confirm their role on team papers. A PhD is common but no license is required, so research quality, code and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a research scientist before hiring?
qa.a: Ask for a research talk on their own work, then a short, paid task such as reproducing a small published result or proposing experiments for a problem you share. Review experimental design, baselines, ablations, code quality and how well they handle hard questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most retail jobs need no license in the US. If your store sells alcohol, tobacco or prepared food, your state, county or city may require seller or food handler training. Rules vary by state, so check locally and verify any card the candidate already holds.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Greeting and helping a customer, counting a cash drawer, making change without the register’s help and handling a return. Have them find an item in the stockroom, then restock and face a shelf. Watch their pace, accuracy and care with the merchandise.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They approach shoppers without hovering, suggest an add-on when it fits, and stay calm when the line grows. They tidy the floor between rushes. Good openers and closers follow the checklist, count the drawer carefully and report a shortage right away.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about cash handling, blaming past customers or coworkers, or no interest in what you sell. Be wary of anyone who treats opening and closing steps as optional, or who brushes off questions about following store policy on returns and discounts.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a return without a receipt, what they did when their drawer came up short, and how they opened or closed a store. Strong candidates give concrete steps and real examples, not general claims about loving people.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a retail worker?
qa.a: Look for friendly but not pushy customer service, accurate cash handling and steady work on the floor. Ask about returns, drawer counts and opening or closing duties. If you sell alcohol, tobacco or food, check whether your state or city requires seller or food handler training.

qa.q: How do I test a retail worker before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role play: you act as a shopper with a question, then a customer making a return. Have them count a sample drawer and make change by hand. If you hold a trial shift, pay for the time worked, as federal and state wage laws require.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask the candidate to ring up a short sale, count back change from cash and handle a return. Watch whether they confirm prices, stay accurate while you talk to them and explain the receipt clearly to the customer.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They greet people first, ask what the shopper needs before pointing, and suggest a matching item without pushing. They notice a messy shelf or a missing price tag and fix it on their own. Prior cashier, food service or hospitality work often transfers well.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who talks over customers, guesses at answers instead of offering to check, or seems careless with cash and receipts. Vague reasons for short past jobs and complaints about every former manager deserve follow-up questions, not instant rejection.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled an upset customer who wanted a refund outside the policy. Ask what they do when the line is long and someone needs help on the floor. Ask how they balanced their drawer at the end of a shift.

look.label: Rules to check by state
look.text: No general license is required for retail sales work. If the job sells alcohol or tobacco, some states or cities require responsible seller training, and rules vary by state. Background checks must follow federal consumer reporting law and any state or local fair chance rules.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a retail sales associate?
qa.a: Look for friendly, steady communication with strangers, accuracy with cash and the register, and a habit of keeping the floor tidy without being told. Ask about real situations, like an angry customer or a busy rush. Reliability matters a lot, so confirm they can work the schedule you need, including weekends and holidays if the store requires them.

qa.q: How do I test a retail sales associate before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role play. Play a shopper looking for a gift and see how they ask questions and suggest items. Then have them ring up a mock sale, make change and process a return on a practice register or on paper. If you hold a working trial shift, pay for the time and follow your state’s wage rules.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most revenue accountant roles do not require a CPA license. If a candidate claims one, check it with the state board of accountancy that issued it, since rules vary by state. Verify degrees with the school or a degree-verification service, with written FCRA authorization if a background check company does it.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them apply the five-step ASC 606 model to a sample contract: identify the contract, find performance obligations, set the transaction price, allocate it, and time recognition. Watch how they handle variable consideration, contract modifications and principal versus agent questions.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain judgment calls in plain words and back them with written memos. They reconcile deferred revenue and contract assets to the general ledger. They know billing is not revenue. For public companies, experience with SOX controls over revenue is a plus.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treating invoices or cash received as revenue. No clear way to support standalone selling prices. Vague answers about who made the key judgments in past work. Impatience with documentation or auditor questions. Talk of timing revenue to hit targets rather than following the contract terms.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a contract modification they accounted for. Ask how they supported a standalone selling price when none was observable. Ask what auditors questioned in their revenue memos and how they responded.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a revenue accountant?
qa.a: Look for hands-on ASC 606 work: finding performance obligations, allocating price and timing revenue contract by contract. Strong candidates write clear memos, reconcile deferred revenue to the ledger and explain judgments simply. A CPA license helps but is usually not required. If one is claimed, confirm it with the issuing state board, since rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test a revenue accountant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a made-up contract that bundles a product, setup, support and a discount. Ask the candidate to list performance obligations, allocate the price, build a recognition schedule and write a short memo explaining their choices. Then ask how the answer changes if the contract is modified midway. Never use real customer contracts or confidential data.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most RF design work needs no license. A degree in electrical engineering or physics is common. A Professional Engineer license is optional, and its rules vary by state. It matters mainly when the engineer must sign off on public or structural work, such as towers. Confirm any security clearance only if the role truly requires one.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can build a link budget, match an impedance on a Smith chart, and read S-parameters. Ask how they use a vector network analyzer and a spectrum analyzer. Look for hands-on use of electromagnetic simulation tools and some knowledge of FCC equipment authorization rules.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain why a simulation and a lab measurement disagreed and how they found the cause. They talk about grounding, layout, cable losses, and test fixtures. They have taken a design through prototype, tuning, and compliance testing, not just simulation.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with someone who only describes simulations and never touched hardware. Watch for vague answers about noise figure, antenna gain, or interference. Another warning sign is ignoring regulatory limits on power and emissions, or blaming every failed test on the lab.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a design that failed emissions or range testing and what they changed. Ask how they would pick an antenna for a small battery device. Ask how they budget margin in a satellite or long-range link.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an RF and wireless engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on lab work with network and spectrum analyzers, solid simulation skills, and a clear grasp of link budgets and impedance matching. Experience taking products through FCC equipment authorization is a plus. A Professional Engineer license is rarely required, and its rules vary by state. Ask for specific projects they carried from design to working hardware.

qa.q: How do I test an RF and wireless engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task, such as building a link budget for a stated range and frequency, or designing a matching network from given S-parameter data. Ask them to explain their assumptions and margins. If you have a lab, let them measure a sample board and talk through what they see on the instrument.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most risk manager roles need no US state license. Common voluntary credentials include the Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Professional Risk Manager (PRM) designations, plus the Associate in Risk Management (ARM) for insurance work. Confirm any claimed credential directly with the issuing body.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a quick read of a sample exposure report. Look for sound use of limits, stress scenarios and value at risk, solid spreadsheet or SQL work, and the ability to explain a breach and its fix in plain words.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a limit or control they built, the data behind it and what changed afterward. They know the rules in your field, such as banking, insurance or public company reporting. They challenge the business without blocking it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Talking only in model names or jargon, with no example of a loss prevented or a gap found. Blaming other teams for past incidents. Vague answers about handling an override, a missed limit or pressure to soften a finding.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a limit breach they escalated and what happened next. Ask how they sized a risk with little data, and which control they retired because it stopped working. Real answers include numbers, owners and timelines.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a risk manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they found and reduced real exposures, not just wrote policies. Check experience with the rules in your field, comfort with data and spreadsheets, and the backbone to escalate bad news. Credentials like the FRM or PRM help but are optional, since most roles need no state license.

qa.q: How do I test a risk manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case with a sample portfolio or process, a few recent incidents and some limits. Ask them to rank the top risks, propose controls and write a one-page memo for executives. Judge the logic, the clarity and whether they flag missing data. Keep the task to a few hours.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for steady, repeatable control of a robot by joystick, VR headset or leader arm. A good operator can do the same task many times in a row the same way, follow a written task script, and reset the scene correctly between takes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong operators notice bad data on their own, like a blocked camera, a slipped grip or a dropped frame, and flag it. They label each take honestly, stay patient with repetitive work, and handle basic computer and software problems without stopping the whole session.

look.label: Safety habits to check
look.text: Ask how they would stop a robot that moves the wrong way. They should know where the emergency stop is, keep clear of the robot’s reach while it runs, check the work area before starting, and report near misses instead of shrugging them off.

look.label: Credentials to know about
look.text: No US license is required to operate robots for data collection. Industrial robot safety training or a robot maker’s operator certificate can be a plus, but most skills are learned on the job. Judge candidates on what they can show you, not on paperwork alone.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who rush takes to hit a count, hide or relabel failed attempts, skip scene resets, or ignore the task script. Also be careful with anyone who treats the robot like a game and takes needless risks with equipment or people nearby.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a robot operator?
qa.a: Look for steady, consistent control, patience with repetitive tasks and strong attention to detail. The best operators follow task scripts exactly, label data honestly and catch problems like blocked cameras early. They should also have solid safety habits, such as knowing the emergency stop and keeping clear of a moving robot. No US license is required for this work.

qa.q: How do I test a robot operator before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid trial on your setup. Give a written task, such as picking and placing an object, and ask for ten takes with resets and labels. Check how consistent the takes are, how many fail, whether failures are reported honestly, and whether they use the emergency stop and safety steps correctly.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for working code, not just résumé terms. Check C++ or Python, ROS or ROS 2, kinematics, control loops and sensor fusion. Have them debug a robot that drifts or overshoots and explain each fix they make.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most robotics roles in the US need no license. A Professional Engineer license exists, and its rules vary by state, but it matters mainly when someone must sign off on engineering plans. Verify degrees and review public code, papers or demo videos.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They have moved code from simulation onto real hardware and can describe what broke. They know safety standards such as ISO 10218 for industrial robots or ISO 26262 for vehicles. They log, test and document their work.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Only simulation or class projects with no hardware time. Vague answers about their own part in a team robot. Treating emergency stops, safety zones or testing near people as an afterthought.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a robot that failed in the field and how they found the cause. Ask how they tuned a controller. Ask what they do when a sensor sends bad or missing data.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a robotics engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with real hardware, strong C++ or Python, and comfort with ROS, control and perception. Ask what they personally built and how they tested it. Check that they take safety seriously around moving machines and people. A degree helps, but robots they actually shipped and clear code count more.

qa.q: How do I test a robotics engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task that matches your work, such as tuning a PID controller in simulation, fusing noisy sensor data, or planning a path around obstacles. Then review the code together. Ask them to explain their choices, the edge cases, and how they would test it safely on real hardware.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses Ruby or Rails developers, and no certification is commonly required by employers. Verify experience instead. Review live apps, code samples or open-source contributions, and call references who can confirm which features and fixes the candidate built personally.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test Ruby itself and core Rails: Active Record models and associations, migrations, validations, background jobs and caching. Check they write tests with RSpec or Minitest, spot N+1 queries, use strong parameters and keep Rails security defaults such as protection against cross-site request forgery.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have upgraded a Rails app across major versions and can explain what broke. They keep controllers thin, write useful tests, read logs to find slow queries and follow Rails conventions unless there is a clear reason not to.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for apps with no tests, SQL built by pasting in user input, and outdated gems nobody updates. Be careful with candidates who blame Rails for every slowdown, cannot explain callbacks they wrote, or have only built tutorial apps.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a Rails upgrade you led and what broke. How do you find and fix an N+1 query? When would you move work into a background job? How do you keep a migration safe on a large production table? Strong answers name specific steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Ruby on Rails developer?
qa.a: Look for production Rails apps they built or maintained, with code and tests they can explain. Check Active Record, database design, background jobs, upgrades and security habits. Many Rails roles involve older codebases, so steady debugging and upgrade experience matter. No license exists, so real work and references count more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a Ruby on Rails developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task in a small Rails app: add a feature with a model, migration, controller and tests, or fix a slow page caused by N+1 queries. Ask them to work in Git and explain their choices. Review test coverage, query efficiency, security and whether the code follows Rails conventions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or standard certification exists for Rust work, so judge real code instead. Ask for public repositories, published crates or work samples, and confirm the candidate wrote them. For trading or finance roles, follow your firm’s compliance policies and applicable federal and state law on background checks.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ownership, borrowing and lifetimes without fighting the compiler. Error handling with Result and the ? operator. Traits and generics. Async code on an async runtime. Safe concurrency using Send, Sync, channels and locks. Profiling and benchmarking to prove the code is actually fast.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Explains why code is safe, not just that it compiles. Keeps unsafe blocks small and documents the reasons. Writes tests and runs clippy and rustfmt by habit. Checks dependencies for upkeep and security. Can read flame graphs when speed matters.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Cloning data or wrapping everything in Rc<RefCell> just to silence the borrow checker. Heavy unwrap and expect in production paths. Unsafe code with no explanation. Claims of years of Rust work with no code to show. Quoting benchmarks run in debug mode.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask when they would choose Box, Rc or Arc. Ask how they found and fixed a deadlock or a slow hot path. Ask why they once reached for unsafe and how they proved it sound. For trading or blockchain roles, ask how they handled latency and determinism.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Rust developer?
qa.a: Look for real Rust code you can read, such as public repositories or published crates. A strong developer understands ownership and lifetimes, handles errors cleanly, writes tests, and uses unsafe code rarely and with clear reasons. For your domain, check matching experience, such as low latency for trading or determinism for blockchains. No license is required, so code review matters most.

qa.q: How do I test a Rust developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your real work, such as a small concurrent service or a parser with tests. Review whether it compiles cleanly, passes clippy, avoids needless clones and unwraps, and handles errors. Then ask the candidate to walk through the code and explain one design choice. That conversation shows real understanding better than a quiz.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Accurate pricing math covering discounts, multi-year ramps, proration and co-terming add-on orders. Fluency with spreadsheets and a CRM or quoting tool. The ability to spot non-standard terms in an order form or contract and route them to the right approver.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Confirm past titles, the tools they used and typical deal sizes with references. A certification in a CRM or quoting platform can help but is optional. Legal review of contracts should stay with your attorneys.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain why a discount needs approval, not just how to apply it. They keep a clean audit trail. They understand at a basic level how order terms affect billing and revenue recognition. They push back politely when a rep’s deal breaks policy.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treats quote errors as minor. Cannot describe an approval workflow they followed. Blames sales or finance for every delay. Admits to booking orders or changing signed terms without required approvals. Stays vague about the tools and deal sizes they actually handled.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Walk me through a deal that needed an exception approval. How do you prorate an add-on bought mid-term? What do you check before an order is booked? Tell me about a quote error you caught and what you changed afterward.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a deal desk analyst?
qa.a: Look for precise pricing math, comfort with CRM and quoting tools, and a firm grasp of approval rules. Strong analysts read order forms closely, flag non-standard terms and explain their reasoning clearly to sales and finance. No license is required, so verify experience through references and a practical test.

qa.q: How do I test a deal desk analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short exercise built on a sample quote request: a multi-year deal with a discount, an add-on mid-term and one non-standard term. Ask them to build the pricing, find errors in a draft order form and say which items need approval and from whom. Judge accuracy and how clearly they explain their choices.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short cold email to a real type of buyer you sell to. Then run a five minute mock call where you raise common objections. Watch how fast they research, how clearly they write, and whether they ask for the meeting.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know their past numbers, such as calls per day and meetings booked, and can explain how they improved them. They take feedback well, stay upbeat after rejection, ask curious questions about your buyers, and keep tidy notes in a CRM.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “How do you research an account before reaching out?” and “Tell me about a sequence that stopped working and what you changed.” Real experience shows in specific steps, tools and results, not general talk about loving people.

look.label: Rules they should know
look.text: Most SDR roles need no license. Good candidates know the basics of CAN-SPAM for email and the national Do Not Call list for calls. Call recording consent rules vary by state. In regulated fields like insurance or securities, unlicensed staff may be limited in what they discuss.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about results, blaming bad leads or territory for every miss, and reading scripts word for word. Be careful with anyone who dismisses outreach rules or who never follows up after the interview, since follow-up is the job.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sales development representative?
qa.a: Look for resilience, clear writing, curiosity about buyers and comfort on the phone. Prior sales experience helps but is not required for this entry-level role. Ask for past activity and meeting numbers, check how they take coaching, and confirm they understand basic outreach rules such as CAN-SPAM and the Do Not Call list.

qa.q: How do I test a sales development representative before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short research task on a sample prospect, then ask for a cold email and a voicemail script. Follow with a mock call where you push back with common objections. Give one piece of feedback and have them try again. Score research quality, clarity, tone and how well they apply your coaching.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work. Some private training groups offer sales enablement certificates, but treat them as a bonus, not proof. Instead, verify past roles and ask references, ideally a sales leader and a rep they trained, what changed after the programs launched.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for clear writing, confident training delivery and the ability to turn dense product details into a simple playbook or pitch. They should also know your CRM and content tools well enough to track which materials reps actually use and which deals they help close.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates tie their work to sales results like ramp time for new hires, win rates or deal size. They sit in on sales calls, ask reps what is missing and work smoothly with marketing, product and sales leaders to keep content current.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through an onboarding program they built from scratch. Ask how they decided what to retire from an old content library, how they got busy reps to show up for training and how they measured whether a playbook worked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful if they only count decks and trainings produced, with no link to sales outcomes. Other warning signs include never joining live sales calls, vague answers about rep adoption, or blaming reps when a program failed instead of explaining what they changed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sales enablement manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who understands how your reps sell and can build training, playbooks and pitch materials they will actually use. Strong candidates measure results such as ramp time and win rates, work well with marketing and product teams, and can show real examples of programs they created and improved.

qa.q: How do I test a sales enablement manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short product summary and ask for a one page playbook or a brief training outline for new reps. Then have them present a short piece of it to a small panel. Judge clarity, focus on what reps need, and how they plan to measure whether it worked.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for sales engineers. Product and cloud certifications are optional but can help in technical sales. Verify experience through references from account executives and customers, and ask about deals they supported and proofs of concept they ran.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test a live demo tailored to a sample customer, discovery questions, handling hard technical objections, and planning a proof of concept with success criteria. Check they can answer security questionnaires, explain integrations and APIs, and write clear follow-up notes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates ask about the customer’s problem before showing features, tailor demos to the buyer, set clear success criteria for trials and say they will find out instead of guessing. Sales and product teams both trust their notes.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for feature tours that ignore the buyer’s needs, promises of features that do not exist, shaky technical depth under follow-up questions, and blaming the product for every lost deal. Be careful with anyone who cannot describe a lost deal and why.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a proof of concept that failed and what you learned. How do you answer a question you cannot answer in front of a customer? How do you decide a deal is not a fit? Strong answers are specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sales engineer?
qa.a: Look for real technical depth, demos built around the customer’s problem, and honesty when they do not know an answer. Check they can run proofs of concept, handle security questions and work well with account executives. No license is required, so references and a mock demo matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a sales engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid mock demo: share a short brief about a fictional customer and ask them to run a discovery call and a tailored demo of a product they know or your own. Add one hard technical objection. Review their questions, clarity, accuracy and how they plan the next step.

look.label: Proof of team results
look.text: Ask for numbers they can explain: team quota attainment, win rates, sales cycle length and forecast accuracy over several quarters. Strong candidates separate their own deals from the team’s results and can say what they changed to move each figure.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test coaching, forecasting and hiring judgment. Have them review a recorded or written sales call and give feedback, build a simple quarterly forecast from a pipeline sample, and explain how they would set targets for reps with different territories or experience.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about reps they developed and promoted, not only deals they closed. They know their CRM well, run regular pipeline reviews, hold people to clear standards, and can describe a hire that failed and what they learned from it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about team numbers, blaming every miss on the market or the reps, and forecasts built on gut feel. Be careful with a top individual seller who has never managed people and cannot describe a coaching routine.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you handle a rep who missed quota two quarters in a row? How do you decide which deals go in the commit forecast? Walk me through how you hired and onboarded your last salesperson.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sales manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of leading a team to target, not just personal sales. Check forecast accuracy, how they coach and hire reps, and how they run pipeline reviews. No license is needed for most sales managers, though some fields, such as insurance or securities, require licenses that vary by product and state. Confirm results with past employers.

qa.q: How do I test a sales manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic task. Share a sample pipeline and ask for a quarterly forecast with reasons. Play a call recording or script and ask for coaching notes. Then role-play a one-on-one with an underperforming rep. Judge clarity, fairness, use of data and whether their plan would actually change behavior.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Strong spreadsheet work with lookups, pivot tables and clean formulas. CRM reporting and dashboard building. Basic data cleanup, such as merging duplicate accounts. The ability to calculate a commission payout by hand from a comp plan and explain each step.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this role. Some CRM vendors offer administrator certifications, and many can be checked on the vendor’s public verification page. Treat them as a plus, not a must. References from sales leaders or finance partners tell you more.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a specific process they fixed, like pipeline stage rules or territory balancing, and what changed afterward. They talk about working with reps, managers and finance. They document their work so others can follow it.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a commission dispute with a rep. Ask how they built or rebalanced territories and what data they used. Ask how they judged whether a forecast was accurate and what they did when it missed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Only builds reports and has never owned a process. Can’t explain where forecast numbers come from. Blames reps for bad data without a plan to fix it. Talks loosely about past employers’ pay or customer data, which signals weak handling of confidential information.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sales operations analyst?
qa.a: Look for solid spreadsheet and CRM reporting skills, a clear grasp of how forecasts and commissions are calculated, and examples of processes they improved. Good analysts work well with reps and finance, keep data clean, and handle pay and customer information with care. No license is required, so focus on proven work and references.

qa.q: How do I test a sales operations analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short take-home task with sample data. Ask them to clean a messy pipeline export, build a simple forecast by stage, and calculate payouts from a sample comp plan. Then have them walk you through their choices. Watch how they explain assumptions and flag data problems.

look.label: Licenses for some products
look.text: Most sales roles need no license. Selling insurance or real estate requires a state license, and rules vary by state. Selling securities requires FINRA registration and often a state exam. If your product falls in one of these areas, verify the license or registration with the state agency or FINRA’s public lookup.

look.label: Skills to test
