look.text: Run a short role play where the candidate sells you a simple product. Watch whether they ask about your needs before pitching, handle an objection calmly and ask for the sale or a clear next step. For phone or online roles, hold the role play by phone or video.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They give specific results from past jobs, such as quota reached or deals closed, and explain how they got there. They ask smart questions about your product, customers and pricing. They follow up promptly after the interview and describe a clear habit for tracking leads.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague claims of being a top seller with no details to back them up. Blaming every lost deal on the product or territory. Talking over you instead of listening. Promising features the product lacks, or shrugging off rules like do-not-call lists and consent for calls and texts.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a deal they lost and what they changed afterward. Ask how they plan a day and track leads. Ask about the hardest objection they hear and how they answer it. Strong answers include clear steps, tools and real customer situations.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sales representative?
qa.a: Look for proof of results, such as targets met or deals closed, with a clear story of how they did it. Good reps listen first, ask questions and handle objections without pressure. Check that they follow up and stay organized. If you sell insurance, real estate or securities, confirm the required license or registration, which varies by product and state.

qa.q: How do I test a sales representative before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short brief on a simple product, then run a ten-minute role play as a hesitant customer. Raise one or two common objections. Score how well they uncover your needs, explain value, stay honest and ask for a next step. For phone sales, do it by phone. You can also ask for a written follow-up email afterward.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Salesforce issues its own certifications, such as Administrator, Platform App Builder and Platform Developer. No state license applies to this work. Confirm any claimed certification on Salesforce’s public credential verification page. Certifications require periodic maintenance and can lapse, so check that they are current.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them work in a sandbox. Ask them to add a custom field, a validation rule, a record-triggered Flow, a report and a dashboard. Check how they use profiles, permission sets and sharing settings so users see only the records they should. Watch how they import data and handle duplicates.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask how your sales team works before changing settings. They test in a sandbox first and document what they build. They can explain when to use point-and-click tools and when code is needed, in plain words. They bring up data quality and user training without prompting.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Making changes straight in the live system with no testing. Giving everyone admin rights to save time. Writing custom code for jobs a Flow or a standard feature already handles. Vague answers about past projects, or no specific problem they can say they solved.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to describe a cluttered Salesforce setup they cleaned up and what they changed first. Ask how they move changes from sandbox to production. Ask how they decide who can see which records. Ask how they moved older automation to Flow. Look for concrete steps and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Salesforce specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with setups like yours and current Salesforce certifications you can verify online. Check that they understand security settings, automation with Flow, reports and data imports. Strong candidates ask about your sales process first, test changes in a sandbox, and write down what they build so others can maintain it.

qa.q: How do I test a Salesforce specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short task in a free developer org or a sandbox, never your live system. Ask them to build a simple Flow, a validation rule and a report, then set access for two user types. Have them walk you through their choices. Clear reasoning and tidy, documented work matter more than speed.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for SAP consulting. SAP offers its own certifications by module and release, and candidates can share a digital badge you can check. Weigh full projects they completed, their exact module and version, and references from past implementations more heavily.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the module you need, such as finance, controlling, sales and distribution, or materials management, in S/4HANA or ECC. Check configuration, master data, integration with other modules, testing and cutover steps. Ask them to explain how a document flows through your process from order to posting.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong consultants map your process before configuring, and explain where standard SAP fits and where it does not. They write clear functional specs, plan testing with business users, and know how a change in one module affects others, such as purchasing affecting finance.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who list many modules with only shallow work in each, push custom code for problems standard configuration solves, or cannot describe a go-live they supported. Be careful with vague answers about which project phases they actually worked on.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a go-live you supported and what broke in the first week. How do you handle a requirement standard SAP does not meet? How do you test a change across modules? Strong answers name transactions, data issues and fixes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an SAP consultant?
qa.a: Look for deep experience in the exact module and version you run, at least one full implementation from design to go-live, and strong communication with business users. SAP certifications show training but are optional, and no license is required. References from past projects and clear examples of fixes matter most.

qa.q: How do I test an SAP consultant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid scenario from your process, such as setting up a new company code or fixing an invoice that will not post. Ask them to walk through configuration steps, data checks and testing. Review accuracy, whether they consider other modules, and how clearly they explain it to a business user.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license exists for this work. Common voluntary certifications include Certified ScrumMaster (CSM) and Professional Scrum Master (PSM). Check any you are shown in the issuer’s public online registry. A short course proves less than years of running real sprints.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for skill in running sprint planning and retrospectives, splitting a large story into smaller ones, reading a burndown or flow chart, and spotting blockers early. Ask them to run a short mock standup and watch whether it stays on time and on topic.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about team outcomes, not personal heroics. They give concrete examples of a blocker they removed, a release they got out the door, or a process they dropped because it didn’t help. They know Kanban as well as Scrum and adapt to how your team works.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who treats Scrum as a rulebook or acts like the team’s boss and assigns tasks. Other warning signs are not being able to explain why a sprint failed, judging success only by velocity, or blaming developers for every missed release.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about a sprint that went badly and what you changed afterward.” Or ask, “How did you handle a stakeholder pushing new work mid-sprint?” Strong answers name specific steps and the people involved. They also say what changed at the next retrospective.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a scrum master?
qa.a: Look for proof they have run real sprints and shipped releases, not just a certificate. Good candidates guide the team rather than command it, remove blockers quickly, and use data like cycle time to improve. Certifications such as CSM or PSM are voluntary. Verify them in the issuer’s registry and weigh them below hands-on experience.

qa.q: How do I test a scrum master before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short exercise during the interview. Give them a messy backlog to prioritize with a product owner, a mock retrospective to run, or a release that is blocked the day before launch. Watch how they ask questions, involve the team, and turn the discussion into clear next steps with owners.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Degrees in computer science, statistics or information retrieval are common but optional. Verify with systems they built and can explain, published papers or open-source work, and references who confirm the ranking changes and results they owned.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test indexing, text analysis, keyword ranking such as BM25, and vector search with embeddings. Check learning-to-rank models, recommendation methods such as collaborative filtering, and offline metrics like NDCG, precision and recall. Confirm they can design an A/B test and serve results quickly at scale.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates tie ranking changes to user outcomes and know when offline metrics disagree with live tests. They read real queries and results by hand, handle new items and new users with little data, and watch for feedback loops that bury good content.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who chase a single metric, never look at actual results, or trust offline gains without a live test. Be careful with anyone who ignores latency, spam and manipulation, or fairness problems in what gets shown first.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a ranking change that won offline but lost in an A/B test. How do you handle a new item with no clicks? How do you tell if position bias skews your training data? How do you keep latency low? Strong answers are specific.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a search and recommendations engineer?
qa.a: Look for search or recommendation systems they built and improved, with results they can explain through offline metrics and live tests. Check indexing, ranking models, embeddings, experiment design and latency. Good judgment about what users should see first matters. No license is required, so real systems, papers and references count most.

qa.q: How do I test a search and recommendations engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task on a sample dataset: build or improve a simple ranking for a set of queries, measure it with a metric such as NDCG, and describe how they would test it live. Review their evaluation, their analysis of bad results and how clearly they explain tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No general US license is required for security analysts. Industry certifications are common, and Defense Department contracts can require specific ones for some roles. Verify certifications through the issuer’s online lookup, and confirm real incident work with references who saw them handle alerts.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test alert triage, log analysis in a security monitoring tool, phishing email review, endpoint and network evidence, and the incident response cycle from detection to recovery. Check they preserve evidence, write clear timelines and know every state has its own breach notification law.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain how they decide an alert is real, keep careful notes, contain an attack without destroying evidence and escalate early. They write incident reports managers can follow and tune detections to cut false alarms.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for closing alerts without investigating, wiping machines before collecting evidence, no notes or timelines, and blaming users instead of fixing gaps. Be careful with anyone who boasts about breaking into systems without permission.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a real alert you investigated, from first signal to closure. What would you do first if an employee’s account started sending phishing emails? How do you tell a false positive from an attack? Strong answers follow a clear, ordered process.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a security analyst?
qa.a: Look for hands-on triage and investigation experience, careful evidence handling, clear writing and calm escalation. Certifications are common and some government contracts require them, but no general license exists, so verify them and test real skills. References from past incident work matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a security analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise with sample logs and a suspicious email, and ask them to decide what happened, what to contain first and who to notify. Ask for a short timeline and incident summary. Review accuracy, order of steps, evidence handling and clarity of writing.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license is required for this role. Common certifications include CISSP, its architecture concentration ISSAP, CCSP for cloud security, and SABSA or TOGAF for enterprise architecture. Confirm them through the issuing body’s online lookup. Treat certifications as a baseline, not proof of design skill.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Threat modeling, zero trust network design, identity and access management, encryption and key management, and secure cloud account structure. Check that they can map controls to frameworks like NIST CSF, ISO 27001 or PCI DSS. Ask them to diagram a system and explain the trade-offs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Explains choices in terms of business risk and cost, not just tools. Has written reference architectures or design standards that engineers actually followed. Can describe a design they changed after a review or incident. Speaks clearly to developers, auditors and executives alike.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Answers every problem with a product name. Cannot draw a data flow or point out trust boundaries. Shares a past employer’s confidential diagrams or vulnerability details. Has only run scans or worked tickets and never owned a design decision from start to finish.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through an architecture they designed and what they would change today. Ask how they got a team to adopt a control it resisted. Ask how they would give contractors access to one sensitive app. Listen for specifics and trade-offs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a security architect?
qa.a: Look for someone who has owned security designs across networks, identities, data and cloud, not just run tools. They should explain decisions in business risk terms and know frameworks like NIST CSF or ISO 27001. Certifications such as CISSP or CCSP help, but no state license is required. Strong communication with engineers and leaders matters as much as technical depth.

qa.q: How do I test a security architect before hiring?
qa.a: Give a design exercise based on a fictional company. Describe its apps, users and cloud setup, then ask for a diagram, the main threats, the controls they would add and what they would do first. Review it together and probe the trade-offs. Keep it short, use made-up systems, and pay for any longer take-home work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for GRC work. Useful certifications include CISA, CRISC, CISSP and ISO 27001 Lead Auditor or Lead Implementer. Check them through the issuing body’s online lookup. Only a licensed CPA firm can issue a SOC 2 report, so the analyst prepares the company and works with the auditor.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Mapping controls to the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, ISO 27001 and NIST frameworks. Writing clear policies people actually follow. Collecting evidence an auditor will accept. Answering customer security questionnaires. Running access reviews and vendor risk assessments.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can walk through a full SOC 2 Type II cycle, from scoping and readiness to the observation period and fixing exceptions. They explain controls to engineers in plain words. They keep a steady evidence schedule instead of rushing the week before fieldwork.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Calls SOC 2 a certification instead of an attestation report. Can’t explain the difference between Type I and Type II. Treats compliance as paperwork only. Is vague about what they did versus what their team or an outside consultant did.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an audit exception you handled. How did you decide which systems were in scope? How do you get engineers to hand over evidence on time? Listen for specific steps, tradeoffs and lessons, not general theory.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a GRC analyst?
qa.a: Look for hands-on audit experience, ideally a full SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 cycle. They should map controls to frameworks, write clear policies, gather solid evidence and answer customer questionnaires. Certifications like CISA or CRISC help but are optional. Strong candidates explain risk in plain words and work well with engineers.

qa.q: How do I test a GRC analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task using made-up data. Share a sample control, a few pieces of messy evidence and a customer security questionnaire. Ask them to say whether the evidence would satisfy an auditor, list gaps, and draft answers to several questions. Then discuss their reasoning. Keep it brief, or pay for longer work.

look.label: Credentials worth checking
look.text: No US state license exists for security engineers. Certifications such as CISSP, OSCP or CompTIA Security+ show focused study, and you can verify them with the issuing body. Weigh them below real work. Some defense contractor roles require specific certifications or a security clearance, so state that in the posting.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Threat modeling a new feature, reading code for flaws like injection or broken access control, tightening cloud permissions, setting up logging and alerts, and explaining a fix to developers in plain terms. Ask them to walk through each one using a stack like yours.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about risk in business terms, rank fixes by impact, and build automated checks into the release pipeline instead of blocking every release. They can describe an incident they handled, what went wrong, and what they changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Bragging about breaking into systems without permission, sharing confidential details from a past employer, relying only on scanner output, or calling every finding critical. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a vulnerability without heavy jargon.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “How would you secure a new public API?” “Tell me about a vulnerability you found and how you got it fixed.” “How do you handle secrets like keys and passwords?” Listen for concrete steps, sensible tools and honest tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a security engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work securing real systems, not just certificates. A strong candidate can threat model a design, spot common code and cloud flaws, automate checks, and explain risk to developers and managers. Check certifications with the issuing body if listed. Value clear judgment about which fixes matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a security engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short exercise on a sample app or design you own with planted flaws. Ask them to find the issues, rank them and propose fixes. Never ask a candidate to probe live systems without written authorization, since unauthorized access can break federal and state computer crime laws. Pay for longer tasks.

look.label: Process skills to test
look.text: Check that they can read SPC control charts, set up a design of experiments, and work through a yield excursion with data. Ask them to walk through how they would find the root cause of a sudden drop in wafer yield on one tool.

look.label: Tool and module experience
look.text: Match their background to your module, such as lithography, etch, thin film deposition, CMP, implant, diffusion or metrology. Ask which tools they ran, which wafer sizes, and how much they owned recipes versus only monitoring them.

look.label: Credentials worth noting
look.text: Most hires hold a degree in electrical, chemical or materials engineering, or physics. No state license is needed for fab process work. Six Sigma belts are private certificates, not required, but they can show training in statistics and structured problem solving.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a specific problem they solved, with numbers, and explain the tradeoffs they weighed. They talk about working with technicians and other engineers, using change control for recipe changes, and following clean room and hazardous chemical and gas safety rules.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers that blur their own work with the team’s, talk of changing recipes without data or approval, casual views on gowning or chemical safety, and no clear grasp of basic statistics like variation and process capability.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a semiconductor fab engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience in your process module, strong statistics skills such as SPC and design of experiments, and a record of solving yield or tool problems with data. Good candidates respect clean room protocol and safety rules, document every change, and work well with technicians on shift.

qa.q: How do I test a semiconductor fab engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short case with sample control chart or yield data and ask them to spot the problem, suggest likely causes, and plan an experiment to confirm it. Then ask how they would roll out the fix through change control. Their reasoning matters more than one right answer.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: A CPA license is not required for most company accounting roles but is common at senior level. Each state board of accountancy licenses CPAs and sets its own rules, so verify status on the state lookup. Check past close and audit work with references.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test journal entries, accruals, account reconciliations, fixed assets and the month-end close. Check knowledge of GAAP, including revenue recognition and lease accounting, plus ERP and spreadsheet skills, audit support schedules and, for public companies, internal control work.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates close on time with few auditor adjustments, explain how each balance was built and improve the close process. They write clear memos on tricky accounting issues and train junior staff.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for reconciliations that only tie totals without explaining items, unsupported manual entries and weak GAAP answers. Be wary of anyone who cannot describe their own role in an audit or has a habit of plugging differences to close.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through your month-end close and your part in it. Tell me about an audit adjustment and what caused it. How would you account for a multi-year software contract? Strong answers cite the right rules and clear steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a senior accountant?
qa.a: Look for a clean record of month-end closes, well-supported reconciliations and solid GAAP knowledge, including revenue and leases. They should support audits, write clear memos and help train staff. A CPA license is common but not always required. CPA rules vary by state, so verify any license on the state board’s lookup.

qa.q: How do I test a senior accountant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with a sample trial balance and supporting data. Ask them to prepare a few adjusting entries, reconcile an account with planted differences and write a brief memo on a revenue question. Judge accuracy, support for each number, GAAP reasoning and clarity.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is needed for most software engineering roles, and certifications are optional. Verify past roles and titles with references. If you use a background check service, federal law requires written notice and the candidate’s consent first. Some states and cities also limit when you can ask about criminal history.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test system design on a problem close to your product, such as scaling a busy endpoint. Ask them to review a real pull request and debug a failing service. Watch how they weigh tradeoffs in cost, speed and reliability, not just whether the code runs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe features they owned from planning through launch, monitoring and cleanup. They explain why they chose one approach over another. They talk about helping junior engineers through reviews and pairing, and they write clear design notes others can follow.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a launch that went wrong and what they changed afterward. Ask how they split a large feature into smaller releases. Ask how they gave hard feedback on a teammate’s code. Experienced engineers answer with specific details, the metrics they tracked and the lessons they learned.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about their own role on team projects. Blaming others for every failure. Pushing a favorite tool for every problem. Dismissing tests, code review or documentation as a waste of time. Little interest in mentoring, since helping less experienced colleagues is a core part of this job.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a senior software engineer?
qa.a: Look for proof they have owned large features end to end, from design to launch and support. They should explain tradeoffs clearly, review code well and debug calmly under pressure. Strong senior engineers also lift the team by mentoring others. Check references for how they handled scope, deadlines and production incidents.

qa.q: How do I test a senior software engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short, time-limited exercise tied to your real work. Good options are a system design discussion, a review of an existing pull request and a live debugging session. Talk through their choices afterward to see how they reason. Avoid long unpaid take-home projects, since strong candidates often decline them.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for SEO work. Free certifications from search ad and analytics platforms show basic knowledge, but they are optional. Verify real results instead. Ask for dated screenshots or read-only access showing traffic, rankings and conversions before and after their work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test keyword research, page titles and descriptions, and technical fixes such as slow pages, broken links and indexing errors. Check how they read analytics. For search ads, test bid strategy, ad copy, negative keywords and how they keep spending inside a set budget.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about leads and sales, not just rankings. They explain why a past change worked and admit what failed. They set realistic timelines, since organic results often take months. They follow search engine guidelines and keep up with algorithm updates.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for promises of a guaranteed first place ranking, bulk link buying or secret methods. Other warnings are no before and after data, reports that show traffic with no link to revenue, and tactics like keyword stuffing or copied content that can trigger penalties.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a site that lost traffic and how they found the cause. Ask how they would split a small budget between content and ads. Ask what they check first on a new site and why.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an SEO manager?
qa.a: Look for proof of results tied to business goals, such as leads or sales, not just rankings. Strong candidates handle keyword research, technical fixes, content and analytics, and can manage search ads if you run them. They set realistic timelines and avoid shortcuts that break search engine guidelines.

qa.q: How do I test an SEO manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Share your site or a sample site and ask for a brief audit: the top three technical issues, five keyword opportunities and one page rewrite. If you run ads, add a sample campaign plan. Judge their reasoning, priorities and clarity, not the length.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a small model built in the method your work uses, such as finite element analysis, computational fluid dynamics, multibody dynamics or a real-time virtual world. Check the setup, boundary conditions, mesh or time step choices, and whether results make physical sense.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about verification and validation without being asked. They run mesh or time step convergence checks, compare results with hand calculations or test data, state their assumptions, and explain how much to trust a result before anyone builds hardware.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles ask for an engineering, physics or computer science degree. A Professional Engineer license exists but is rarely required for this work. Rules for who must hold one vary by state, so verify it only when the person will sign off on regulated designs.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of candidates who show colorful plots but cannot explain units, material properties or loads. Other warnings are never checking results against reality, blaming the software for odd answers, or sharing confidential models from a past employer as portfolio work.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a simulation that disagreed with a physical test and what they changed. Ask how they chose between model detail and run time. Real experience shows in specifics: what they simplified, what they checked, and what the team decided based on the result.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a simulation engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid physics and math, hands-on skill in the modeling method your products need, and the habit of checking results against hand calculations or test data. Good engineers also script repetitive work, document assumptions clearly, and explain results to designers who are not simulation experts. A degree matters less than proof they have validated real models.

qa.q: How do I test a simulation engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work, such as modeling a simple bracket under load or flow through a basic duct, using made-up data. Ask for the model, a convergence check and a one-page summary of assumptions and limits. Then have them walk you through it and explain what they would do with more time.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state license exists for site reliability engineers. Cloud platform and container orchestration certifications are optional. They show baseline knowledge, so confirm them through the issuer’s online lookup. Weigh real on-call and production experience far more heavily than any certificate.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test Linux troubleshooting and networking basics like DNS, load balancing and TLS. Check scripting or coding to automate repetitive work, and monitoring and alerting design. Ask them to set a service level objective and error budget for a sample service and defend their choices.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through an outage they handled. Cover how they spotted it, what they checked first, how they kept others informed, and what changed afterward. Strong answers name specific metrics, tradeoffs they weighed and lasting fixes, not just a quick restart.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They write blameless postmortems and automate a fix instead of repeating it by hand. They trim noisy alerts so real problems stand out, and they plan capacity and roll out changes in small, reversible steps. They also explain complex failures plainly to people outside engineering.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for blaming individuals for outages, or restarting things without looking for root cause. Be wary of anyone who has never kept runbooks or worked on call. Another warning sign is pushing risky production changes with no review, testing or rollback plan.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a site reliability engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on production experience, including on-call duty and real incidents they helped resolve. They should know Linux, networking, monitoring and at least one scripting or programming language. Good candidates think in service level objectives, automate repeat work and write clear postmortems. Calm communication during an outage matters as much as technical depth.

qa.q: How do I test a site reliability engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short incident simulation in a test environment, never your live systems. Break something, give them dashboards and logs, and watch how they find and fix the cause while explaining their steps. Add a design discussion on monitoring or scaling a sample service. Keep take-home work brief, and consider paying for longer assignments.

look.label: Proof of past work
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this job, so verify real work instead. Ask for deployed contract addresses, public code repositories and any audit reports that cover their code. Then have them walk you through that code to confirm they wrote it.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test fluency in Solidity or the language your chain uses, gas-aware design and strong testing habits such as unit, fuzz and invariant tests. Check that they know common attacks like reentrancy, broken access control, oracle manipulation and front-running.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They treat every external call as hostile and keep contracts small and simple. They test heavily before any deployment and plan upgrades, pauses and admin roles on purpose. They welcome outside audits and can explain trade-offs in plain words to non-engineers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for rushing to mainnet without tests or an audit, copying code they cannot explain, or calling audits a waste of time. Also be wary of careless handling of private keys, claims that their code has no bugs, and vague answers about past incidents.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a bug they found or shipped and how they handled it. Ask how they would secure admin keys, for example with a multisig wallet. Ask how they decide whether a contract should be upgradeable and what risks that adds.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a smart contract engineer?
qa.a: Look for deployed contracts and public code you can review, deep knowledge of common attacks, and serious testing habits. There is no US license for this work, so judge them on proof. Strong candidates keep code simple, plan for audits and key security, and can explain risks clearly, because mistakes on a blockchain cannot be undone.

qa.q: How do I test a smart contract engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short contract with hidden flaws and ask them to find and fix the issues, then write tests that prove the fixes work. Run it on a test network, never with real funds. Afterward, have them explain their reasoning. How they spot reentrancy, access control gaps and edge cases tells you more than a résumé.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for fast discovery, clear short demos, handling price objections and asking for the close. SMB reps juggle many deals at once, so test how they qualify a lead in a few minutes and how they keep notes and next steps in a CRM.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know their numbers without hesitating. They can explain quota, attainment, average deal size, sales cycle length and how many deals they closed a month. They talk about owner and founder buyers with empathy and show steady follow-up habits.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a deal they closed in under two weeks. Ask how they handle a busy owner who goes silent, how they build a daily call and email plan, and what they do when a prospect says the price is too high.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about results, only long enterprise cycles with no high-volume work, blaming leads or marketing for missed targets, and weak follow-up. Pushy closing that ignores what a small business needs often leads to churn and refunds.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most SMB sales roles need no license. If the job sells insurance or securities, a state insurance license or FINRA registration may be required, and insurance rules vary by state. Confirm past results through references and prior employers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an SMB account executive?
qa.a: Look for someone who thrives on volume and speed. They should qualify leads quickly, run short focused demos, handle objections calmly and close without long cycles. Ask for specific numbers on quota, deal size and monthly closes. Good reps also keep a clean CRM and follow up with busy owners until they get a clear yes or no.

qa.q: How do I test an SMB account executive before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short role play. Give them a simple product sheet and a buyer profile, such as a busy shop owner or startup founder. Have them do a quick discovery call, a five-minute pitch and a close. Add a price objection. Then ask them to write the follow-up email and the next steps they would log.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state or federal license exists for SOC analysts. Certifications in security basics, incident handling or threat detection show study, so check them on the issuer’s public lookup. If you hold defense contracts, DoD 8140 rules may require approved certifications for some roles.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Reading raw logs, triaging an alert in a SIEM, and telling a false positive from a real intrusion. Also basic networking such as TCP/IP and DNS, and spotting phishing in email headers. They should write a short, clear ticket the next shift can act on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Walks through an alert step by step and says what they would check next and why. Knows when to escalate and keeps careful notes. Home labs, capture-the-flag practice or past help desk work often show real curiosity and hands-on habits.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Lists many tools but can’t explain one real investigation. Closes alerts without evidence or blames everything on noise. Would wipe a machine before saving evidence. Shares a past employer’s confidential details in interview stories.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Tell me about an alert you escalated and what happened next.” “How would you check if a login from a new country is real?” “What do you do when you’re unsure on a night shift?” Listen for logs, evidence and clean handoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a SOC analyst?
qa.a: Look for someone who can read logs, triage alerts calmly and explain their reasoning. No license is required, but certifications show study and are easy to verify. Strong candidates take clear notes, know when to escalate and protect evidence. Confirm they can work the shifts you need, since SOCs often run around the clock.

qa.q: How do I test a SOC analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, timed exercise with a few sample alerts and log extracts, using made-up data, never real customer records. Ask them to sort real threats from false positives, decide what to escalate and write a ticket for the next shift. Judge their reasoning and clarity more than speed or tool names.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is needed for this work. Platform-issued ad and analytics certifications show training, but they matter less than proof. Ask for live examples, before-and-after results they can explain, and references from past employers or clients.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can write short posts in your brand voice, plan a content calendar, read analytics to explain what worked, and answer an angry comment calmly. If they will manage creators, see how they write a brief and track deliverables.

look.label: Creator and disclosure know-how
look.text: Strong candidates know the FTC Endorsement Guides require creators to clearly disclose paid, gifted or other material connections. They should explain how they put disclosure terms, content usage rights, deadlines and approval steps in writing before a creator posts.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for bragging about follower counts with no engagement or sales results, any history of buying followers, no plan for a crisis or a posting mistake, and vague answers about who owned and controlled the accounts they ran.

look.label: What not to ask
look.text: Do not ask for passwords or login access to a candidate’s personal social accounts. Many states ban this. Judge public work samples only on skill, and keep the interview on the job, not their private life.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a social media manager?
qa.a: Look for clear writing, a steady brand voice, and the ability to explain results with real numbers, not just follower counts. They should plan content ahead, handle negative comments calmly, and know that the FTC requires creators to disclose paid or gifted posts. Ask for live work samples and references.

qa.q: How do I test a social media manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task tied to your brand. Ask for a week of draft posts for one platform, replies to two sample negative comments, and a brief summary of a sample analytics report. If they will work with creators, add a one-page creator brief. Keep it short or pay for the time.

look.label: Credentials to weigh
look.text: No US state license exists for software architects. Cloud and enterprise architecture certifications are optional and show study, not judgment. Give more weight to systems they have shipped, design documents they have written, and references from engineering leaders who worked with them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test system design under real constraints. Can they split a system into services or modules, define interfaces between teams, choose data stores, and plan for scale, failure and security? Ask them to sketch a design and explain the options they rejected and why.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They write clear decision records and talk about trade-offs rather than favorite tools. They can name a design they got wrong and how they fixed it. Engineers who worked with them say decisions were explained and discussed, not simply imposed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Diagrams with no thought for cost, operations, monitoring or migration from the current system. Pushing one technology for every problem. Years without reading or writing real code. Blaming teams for failures that came from their own designs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they got several teams to agree on a shared interface, how they replaced a legacy system without long outages, and what they measured to know an architecture was working. Listen for specific numbers, names of decisions and lessons, not buzzwords.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a software architect?
qa.a: Look for someone who has designed systems that several teams built and ran in production. They should explain trade-offs in plain words, write clear design documents, and still understand code well. Check references from engineers and managers who lived with their decisions. Certifications are optional, and no state license applies to this work.

qa.q: How do I test a software architect before hiring?
qa.a: Give a design exercise based on a realistic problem, such as splitting a growing application so separate teams can own parts. Ask for a diagram, an interface outline and a short decision record. Then discuss it live, add a new constraint like higher traffic or a failed component, and watch how they adapt. Pay for take-home work that runs more than a few hours.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the skills the job actually uses. Have candidates read unfamiliar code, fix a real bug, write a small feature with tests, and explain their choices. Debugging and code reading often matter more day to day than solving puzzles from memory.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong engineers ask clarifying questions before coding, explain tradeoffs in plain words, and write code others can follow. They talk about testing, code review, and what happens after release, not just about getting something to work once.

look.label: Work to review
look.text: Ask for work samples you can discuss: public code, a portfolio project, or a walkthrough of a past system with confidential details left out. Have them explain what they built themselves versus what the team did, and what they would change now.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about their own role, blaming past teammates for every problem, no interest in testing or code review, and an inability to explain code they submitted. Be cautious if a take-home solution looks polished but they cannot walk through it.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a production bug they tracked down, a design decision they would reverse, and how they handled a deadline that forced a shortcut. Specific details about logs, rollbacks, and follow-up fixes usually show real hands-on experience.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a software engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid problem solving, clean and readable code, and the habit of testing their work. Check experience with the languages and tools your product uses, but weigh the ability to learn just as much. Good communication matters, since engineers work through code reviews, tickets, and teammates. No license is required for most software jobs in the US.

qa.q: How do I test a software engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short, realistic task tied to your work, such as fixing a bug or adding a small feature to sample code. Keep take-home tasks to a few hours, or pay for longer ones. Then hold a live review where the candidate explains choices, handles a change request, and discusses how they would test it.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Rules vary by state. Some states require an electrical license for solar wiring, and some have a solar contractor license. Check your state licensing board. NABCEP certification is voluntary but widely respected. Ask for OSHA 10 or 30 safety cards for field roles.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to read a single-line diagram and size a string for cold temperatures. Ask how they apply NEC Article 690 rules, including rapid shutdown and grounding. For designers, check shade analysis and design software skills. For installers, check roof attachment and flashing.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe past projects clearly, with system size, type (rooftop, ground-mount or utility-scale), equipment and inspection results. They understand local permitting and utility interconnection. They talk about fall protection and lockout steps without being asked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about fall protection or working near energized circuits. Be wary of anyone who treats permits and inspections as optional or claims certifications they cannot show. A candidate who cannot explain why voltage rises in cold weather may lack design depth.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a failed inspection and how they fixed it. Ask how they seal roof penetrations to prevent leaks. Ask how they troubleshoot a string producing less than expected. Real experience shows in specific, step-by-step answers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a solar energy specialist?
qa.a: Look for proven project experience, strong safety habits and working knowledge of NEC Article 690. Confirm any license your state requires, since solar and electrical licensing rules vary by state. NABCEP certification is a good sign but is voluntary. Check references from past installs or designs, and ask about inspection results.

qa.q: How do I test a solar energy specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short practical task that matches the role. Designers can lay out a small rooftop array, size strings and draw a single-line diagram. Installers can explain mounting, flashing and wiring steps on a mock-up or photo set. Ask them to point out code or safety problems in sample plans. Pay for longer tasks.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work. Many candidates hold vendor cloud or platform architect certifications. These are earned by exam and usually expire unless renewed, so check the current status on the issuer’s public verification page. Treat them as proof of baseline knowledge, not of skill with customers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for the ability to map a customer’s current systems, find where your product connects, and draw a clear integration plan. They should cover APIs, data flows, security, identity and scale. They must also explain tradeoffs in plain words to a buyer who is not technical.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates ask about the customer’s business goal before naming a tool. They can describe a deal they helped win and the handoff they made to the delivery team. They admit what the product cannot do and suggest honest workarounds instead of overpromising.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of anyone who jumps to a design without asking questions. Other warnings are heavy jargon with no clear explanation, blaming sales or customers for failed projects, and no examples of work after the contract was signed. Also watch for designs that ignore security or ongoing cost.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a design a customer rejected and what they changed. Ask how they handled a demo that failed live. Ask how they documented a solution so the implementation team could build it without calling them every day.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a solutions architect?
qa.a: Look for solid technical depth in integrations, cloud and security, plus strong communication with buyers. They should work well with sales before the deal and with delivery teams after it. Check that any certifications they list are current. Ask for real examples of designs they built and the results customers saw.

qa.q: How do I test a solutions architect before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short written scenario about a sample customer’s systems and goals. Ask them to sketch an integration design, list risks and open questions, and present it in a 20 to 30 minute mock customer meeting. Have a team member play a skeptical buyer. Judge clarity, honesty about limits and the quality of their questions.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for someone who can run a live demo, answer technical questions on the spot and connect features to a buyer’s real problem. Check their grasp of APIs, integrations, data flows and basic scripting, since many deals hinge on how the product fits existing systems.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates ask about the customer before showing anything. They tailor demos to the use case and explain complex ideas in plain words. They also describe how they partnered with account executives to move deals forward, and how they handed off clean notes to implementation teams.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for this work in any state. Cloud or vendor certifications can show real platform knowledge, so confirm any they list through the issuer’s verification page. Weigh hands-on experience with similar products and buyers more heavily than certificates.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for feature dumping without asking questions, bluffing when they do not know an answer, or overpromising what the product can do. Also be wary of anyone who cannot name a deal they lost and what they learned, or who talks down to nontechnical buyers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a proof of concept they ran from scoping to close. Ask how they handled a technical objection that threatened a deal. Ask how they decide when a request belongs with sales, support or product, and how they push back on unrealistic timelines.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a solutions engineer?
qa.a: Look for a mix of technical depth and sales sense. They should run clear demos, understand integrations and APIs, and ask good discovery questions before pitching. Strong communication with both engineers and executives matters. Ask for examples of proofs of concept they led, deals they helped close and how they worked with account executives.

qa.q: How do I test a solutions engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short brief on a fictional customer and a sandbox or overview of your product. Ask them to run a 20 to 30 minute demo for your team acting as buyers. Throw in a tough technical question and an objection. Score how well they discover needs, stay honest and explain the setup steps.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for sourcing. Recruiting and sourcing certificates are optional. Verify results instead: ask for anonymized pipelines, outreach messages and search strings, and ask references how many sourced candidates were hired and how hiring managers rated them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test Boolean and advanced web search, talent mapping of target teams, and personalized outreach that earns replies from people who are not looking. Check use of the applicant tracking system or recruiting CRM, careful notes, and respect for privacy rules and site terms when collecting candidate data.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong sourcers understand the role deeply, ask hiring managers sharp questions and adjust searches when results miss. Their messages are short and specific to each person. They track reply and conversion rates, widen reach fairly and judge candidates only on job-related criteria.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for mass, generic messages, inflated pipeline counts, or any idea of filtering candidates by age, sex, race or another protected trait. Be wary of anyone who scrapes data against site rules or misrepresents the job to get replies.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Show me a search string you used for a hard role and how you refined it. Walk me through a message that got a passive candidate to reply. How do you report your results? Strong answers show method, measured outcomes and fair, job-related criteria.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sourcer?
qa.a: Look for strong search skills, personalized outreach that gets replies and a track record of sourced candidates who were hired. Check careful notes in your recruiting systems and fair, job-related screening. No license is required, so sample searches, messages and references from recruiters and hiring managers matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a sourcer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise: share a real job description and ask for search strings, a map of target companies, a short list of anonymized profiles and two outreach messages. Review how well the profiles fit, the quality of the messages and whether their criteria are job-related and fair.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for procurement or spend analysis work. Supply management certifications are optional. Verify skills through work samples instead, such as a cleaned spend dataset, a category analysis or a savings report, and ask references how the candidate’s savings were measured.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test cleaning and grouping messy supplier data, building a spend cube by category, supplier and business unit, and finding savings levers such as volume consolidation, contract compliance and payment terms. Check spreadsheet, SQL or BI tool skills and total cost of ownership analysis.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong analysts separate hard savings from cost avoidance and always use a clear baseline. They link findings to contracts and invoices, explain results to buyers and finance in plain words, and suggest practical next steps such as a bid event or a renegotiation.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for savings claims with no baseline, charts without source data, or analysis that ignores quality, delivery and supplier risk. Be wary of candidates who cannot explain how they merged duplicate supplier names or classified unclear invoice lines.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you build a spend taxonomy from raw accounts payable data? Tell me about a savings opportunity you found and whether it was realized. How do you report cost avoidance? Strong answers describe data sources, cleaning steps and how finance agreed the numbers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a spend analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong data skills, from cleaning supplier records to building a spend cube, and real savings work with clear baselines. Check they understand contracts, total cost of ownership and supplier risk, not just price. No license is required, so work samples and references from finance or procurement leaders matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a spend analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise with an anonymized accounts payable extract containing duplicate suppliers and unclear descriptions. Ask them to clean and categorize the data, identify the top savings opportunities and present them on one page. Review data accuracy, the savings logic and whether the recommendations are practical.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to manage sponsorships. Verify past deals instead. Ask for proposals, contracts with figures removed and fulfillment reports, and call references on both the buying and selling side. If they work with college athletes, check they know NIL rules, which vary by state and school.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they value an asset, such as signage, naming rights or an athlete’s social posts, and write a proposal around the partner’s goals. Check contract terms like exclusivity, category rights and make-goods, plus activation planning and post-event reporting.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates sell or buy around goals, not logos. They track every promised benefit, deliver proof such as photos and audience data, and renew partners year after year. They plan activation, not just placement, and know when to walk away.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for deals justified only by vague exposure, no records of fulfillment, and promised benefits that never made it into contracts. Be wary of anyone unaware of ambush marketing risks, trademark limits or disclosure rules for sponsored social posts.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you put a value on a sponsorship package? Tell me about a partner who felt shortchanged and what you did. What do you report after an event? Strong answers mention measurement, make-goods and specific activation ideas.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sponsorships manager?
qa.a: Look for a record of closing and renewing deals, sound valuation of assets, and careful tracking of what each side was promised. They should know contract terms like exclusivity and make-goods, plan activation and report results. No license is required, so proposals, fulfillment reports and references from partners matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a sponsorships manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: describe an event or team and a target partner, and ask for a one-page proposal with benefits, activation ideas, key contract terms and how success will be measured. Judge whether the package fits the partner’s goals and whether every promise can be delivered and proven.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Run a background check and confirm CPR, first aid and concussion training. Check SafeSport training where it applies, any coaching certificates your state association or league requires, and the sport’s own coaching licenses.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have candidates run a short practice with your athletes while you watch. Ask for a written practice plan and a season plan, and ask how they would handle an injury and a parent complaint.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates teach clearly, keep every athlete moving, correct with specific cues, put safety before winning and talk respectfully with players and parents. Former players and assistants speak well of them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for yelling or shaming players, playing hurt athletes, ignoring concussion or heat rules, private one-on-one messages with minors, and a history of leaving programs suddenly.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A player takes a hit to the head and says they are fine. What do you do? How do you plan a practice? How do you handle a playing time complaint? What does SafeSport training cover? Strong answers put athlete safety ahead of the score.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a sports coach?
qa.a: Look for safety training, a clean background check, real knowledge of the sport and the ability to teach it. Watch them run a practice, check how they handle injuries and parents, and talk with former players, assistants and athletic directors about their conduct and how they develop athletes.

qa.q: How do I check a coach’s background?
qa.a: Run a criminal background check, check the U.S. Center for SafeSport’s disciplinary records where the sport is covered, and call past schools or clubs directly, not only the references the candidate gives. Ask about conduct with athletes and why the coach left each program.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as a SQL developer. Database vendor certifications are optional but can show knowledge of a specific platform. Verify skill with real queries, stored procedures or reports they wrote, and references who rely on their work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test joins, grouping, subqueries, common table expressions and window functions. Check indexing, reading execution plans, transactions and locking, stored procedures and data types. Confirm they know your database platform and use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates think in sets, not row-by-row loops, and check results against known totals before sharing them. They read execution plans to fix slow queries, document their logic and ask what a business term means before writing a query.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for SELECT star in production code, cursors where a set-based query works, queries built by pasting user input into strings, and joins that silently duplicate rows. Be careful with candidates who cannot explain NULL behavior or why a query is slow.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you find out why a query got slow? When would you use a window function instead of GROUP BY? How do you check that a report total is right? Tell me about a deadlock you resolved. Strong answers name specific steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a SQL developer?
qa.a: Look for strong command of joins, window functions, indexing and execution plans on your database platform, plus careful checking of results. Ask for queries or procedures they wrote and can explain. No license is required in the US, so real work, clear reasoning and references matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a SQL developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task on a sample database close to yours: write queries that answer real business questions, including one with a window function, then speed up a slow query you provide. Review correctness, handling of NULLs and duplicates, use of indexes and how clearly they explain the logic.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No single US license covers this role. Check past work on live token or stablecoin projects, code repositories and audit reports. If they will act for a broker-dealer, FINRA registration may apply. Money transmitter licenses are held by companies and vary by state.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for smart contract skill in Solidity, token standards such as ERC-20, and permissioned tokens that limit transfers to approved wallets. They should understand mint and redeem flows, reserve reporting, custody, oracles and how onchain records match offchain books.

look.label: Regulatory awareness
look.text: A strong candidate knows that tokenized bonds and fund shares are usually still securities under federal law. They follow the federal payment stablecoin law passed in 2025 as its rules take shape. They also know Bank Secrecy Act duties and that state money transmitter rules differ.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about failure cases without being asked: a frozen wallet, a lost key, a depeg, a failed redemption, a bad oracle price. They explain tradeoffs between public and private chains clearly to nontechnical staff and lawyers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Promises of guaranteed yield or a token that is not a security because it sits on a blockchain. No security audits on past code. Vague claims about launches they cannot show. Dismissing KYC, sanctions screening or reserve audits as optional.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a stablecoin and tokenization specialist?
qa.a: Look for shipped work: token contracts, mint and redeem systems or tokenized fund projects you can review. They should combine smart contract security skills with a working grasp of securities law, stablecoin rules and anti-money laundering duties. Clear thinking about custody, reserves and failure cases matters more than buzzwords.

qa.q: How do I test a stablecoin and tokenization specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid task. Ask them to review a sample token contract with transfer limits and find flaws, or to design a mint and redeem flow for a tokenized fund. Have them explain how they would handle a lost key, a sanctions hit and a reserve shortfall. Judge the reasoning, not just the code.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for staff or principal engineers, and titles mean different things at different employers. Verify scope instead: ask for design documents they wrote, and ask references which systems they led, how many teams were involved and what changed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test system design at your scale, technical writing, tradeoff analysis and depth in code review. Check they can break a large migration into safe steps, set standards others follow, and mentor senior engineers without managing them.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates show work that spanned several teams, such as a platform migration or reliability program, and can explain the business reason. They write clearly, change their minds with evidence, make other engineers better and still write code when it matters.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for heroics with no lasting systems, rewrites pushed for taste rather than need, dismissive treatment of junior engineers, and vague claims about leading work others did. Be careful with anyone who cannot name a technical decision they got wrong.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a technical direction you set that other teams adopted. How did you get agreement? Describe a decision you reversed. How do you choose what not to build? Strong answers include written proposals, tradeoffs and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a staff or principal engineer?
qa.a: Look for proof of impact across several teams, clear technical writing, sound system design and the ability to lead without authority. Check how they mentor others and handle disagreement. Titles vary by employer and no license is required, so design documents and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a staff or principal engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Run a system design session on a real problem from your company with sensitive details removed, then ask for a short, paid written proposal with options and tradeoffs. Add a code review of a sample change. Review judgment, clarity of writing and how they handle pushback.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to work as a statistician. Many roles call for a master’s or doctoral degree in statistics or biostatistics, and a voluntary professional accreditation from a national statistics society exists. Verify degrees, published work and references, plus experience with any rules your field follows.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test study and survey design, sampling, power analysis, regression, mixed models and survival analysis. Check handling of missing data, multiple comparisons and causal inference. Confirm skill in R, SAS or Python, reproducible code and clear writing for people who are not statisticians.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates ask how the data was collected before running any model. They state assumptions, report effect sizes with confidence intervals rather than only p-values, and say plainly what the data cannot show. They write analysis plans before seeing results.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for p-hacking, such as running many tests until one looks significant, confusing correlation with causation, and ignoring missing data or sampling bias. Be careful with anyone who cannot explain a method’s assumptions or who promises the answer a sponsor wants.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a study you designed and how you chose the sample size. How do you handle data that is not missing at random? When would you use a mixed model? Tell me about telling a client the data could not answer their question.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a statistician?
qa.a: Look for sound study design, honest handling of uncertainty and clear writing for non-experts. Check methods that match your field, such as clinical trials, surveys or experiments, and skill in R, SAS or Python. No state license is required. Graduate degrees, published work and references are the usual proof.

qa.q: How do I test a statistician before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your work: share a sample dataset and a question, and ask for an analysis plan, the analysis with code and a one-page summary for a manager. Review whether they check assumptions and data quality, report uncertainty honestly and state what the data cannot prove.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required to work as a storage engineer in the US. Vendor certifications for storage arrays, backup software and cloud platforms are common, and most issuers let you check them online. Treat them as a plus, not proof of skill.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: SAN and NAS design, RAID levels, snapshots and replication, iSCSI and Fibre Channel, NFS and SMB shares, object storage, backup and restore tools, and scripting to automate routine work. Ask them to size storage for a real workload and explain the tradeoffs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about restores, not just backups. They mention recovery point and recovery time targets, capacity planning, monitoring alerts and change windows. They can describe a past outage, what failed, and what they changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Treating RAID or replication as a backup. No story of an actual restore test. Vague answers about access permissions, encryption or data retention. Blaming hardware for every problem. Making risky production changes without a rollback plan.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through the last full restore they ran. Ask how they moved data with little downtime. Ask what they check first when a volume fills fast overnight. Listen for clear steps, measured results and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a storage engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with SAN, NAS and cloud storage, plus backup and restore experience. Strong candidates plan for capacity, set recovery targets and test restores on a schedule. They script repetitive tasks and document their changes. Certifications help, but past outages they handled and fixed tell you more.

qa.q: How do I test a storage engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short scenario in a lab or on paper, never on your live systems. Describe a workload, its growth and its recovery targets, then ask for a storage and backup design. Add a troubleshooting case, such as a slow file share. Judge their reasoning, tradeoffs and how they would prove the restore works.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to build a weekly schedule within a labor-hour budget, read a sales report and spot the weak day, and explain how they run an inventory count. A strong manager links staffing, stock and sales instead of treating them as separate jobs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They speak in numbers: sales against target, shrink, labor cost and staff turnover. They can name people they trained who became shift leads, and they describe handling a busy weekend or a short-staffed day calmly and in order.

look.label: Rules they should know
look.text: A good manager understands overtime, breaks and meal periods, which vary by state, plus predictive scheduling laws in some states and cities. In food retail, many states and localities require a certified food protection manager on staff, so check your local rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you handle an employee who kept arriving late? Walk me through a month you missed your sales target. How do you find out why inventory counts do not match the system? Listen for real steps, documentation and follow-up.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Blaming past staff or bosses for every problem, vague answers about sales or shrink figures, no experience with coaching or written warnings, and loose habits around cash handling, deposits or key control. Also watch for someone who only works the floor and avoids planning.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a store manager?
qa.a: Look for proven experience leading a team, building schedules within a labor budget and hitting sales targets. Strong candidates know their past numbers, can explain how they control inventory and shrink, and show they have trained staff who grew into leads. Check that they understand wage and hour rules, which vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test a store manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or clearly limited exercise. Hand them a sample sales report and a labor budget, then ask for a weekly schedule and three ideas to lift a slow day. Add a role play where they coach an underperforming employee. Judge their reasoning, priorities and tone, not polish.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this role. Optional certifications such as CPSM or CSCP show formal supply management training, so confirm them with the issuing body. A degree in supply chain, business or engineering is common but not essential if the track record is strong.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check spend analysis in spreadsheets, total cost of ownership modeling, and building a clear RFP or RFQ. Ask them to plan a negotiation and to explain contract terms like price escalators, service levels, payment terms, liability limits and exit clauses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain how savings were measured, not just the total. They talk about supplier risk, backup sources and performance reviews. They work closely with finance, legal and operations, and they know the markets for the categories they managed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who only talks about squeezing price, cannot show how savings were tracked, or is vague about contract details. Also be wary of casual answers about supplier gifts, conflicts of interest or bending company buying rules.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through one sourcing project from spend data to contract award. Ask about a supplier that failed and what they changed afterward. Ask how they handled a key supplier that held most of the leverage.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a strategic sourcing manager?
qa.a: Look for proof of results with a clear method behind them. Strong candidates can explain spend analysis, supplier selection, contract terms and how they measured savings. They should manage supplier risk, work well with legal and finance, and hold firm ethics on gifts and conflicts. Certifications like CPSM or CSCP help but are optional.

qa.q: How do I test a strategic sourcing manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Share sample spend data and a few supplier quotes with different prices, terms and delivery records. Ask them to pick a supplier, explain total cost, list risks and outline negotiation goals and must-have contract terms. Then role-play a brief negotiation to see how they handle pushback.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: To seal building designs, a structural engineer needs a state Professional Engineer license, and some states require a separate Structural Engineer license for some or all structural work.
