Rules vary by state, so verify on the state board site. Aerospace and product roles usually need no license.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test load paths, hand calculations that check software output, and design to the codes you use, such as ASCE 7, the building code, and steel, concrete or wood standards. For aerospace or machines, test finite element analysis, fatigue, buckling and margins of safety tied to test data.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates check finite element results against hand calculations, document assumptions clearly, and know when a connection or detail drives the design. They coordinate well with architects or design teams, respond to site or test findings quickly and own their mistakes.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for trusting software output without checks, unclear load assumptions, ignored connections, and no experience with code updates or local amendments. Be wary of anyone offering to seal drawings they did not prepare or supervise, which state engineering boards forbid.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through the load path of a building or part you designed. Tell me about a time a model gave a wrong answer and how you caught it. How do you handle a field change or test failure? Strong answers show checks, judgment and clear notes.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a structural engineer?
qa.a: Look for a state Professional Engineer license if they will seal building work, and a Structural Engineer license where your state requires it. Check experience with your structure type and codes, or with analysis and testing for aerospace hardware. Hand calculation habits, clear documentation and references from project managers matter as much as software skill.

qa.q: How do I test a structural engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise such as sizing a beam, column or bracket for given loads, with hand calculations and a short memo of assumptions. For senior roles, ask them to review a sample calculation package with planted errors. Review correct load paths, code use, clarity and whether they flag what needs checking.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the one or two skills the internship really needs. That might be writing a clear email, cleaning up a spreadsheet, basic coding or researching a topic. Use a short, made up task, not real company work, and judge the result against the same standard for every candidate.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Look for class projects, campus clubs, volunteer roles or part time jobs where they finished something. Strong candidates explain what they personally did, ask good questions about the team and meet every deadline in your hiring process.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a project they are proud of and name the part that was theirs. Ask about a group project that went wrong and what they did next. Ask what they want to learn this summer.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for a candidate who cannot explain their own role in group work, misses interviews without notice or shows no interest in what your company does. Also be wary of polished answers that fall apart when you ask one follow up question.

look.label: Dates to confirm
look.text: Confirm they can work the full ten to twelve weeks you plan. School calendars differ, and some schools finish later in spring than others. Agree on start and end dates and weekly hours before you make the offer.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a summer intern?
qa.a: Look for curiosity, reliability and proof they can finish work, such as class projects, club roles or part time jobs. Check that they can explain their own part in group work. Make sure their available dates fit your ten to twelve week plan, and think about whether they could grow into a full time hire.

qa.q: How do I test a summer intern before hiring?
qa.a: Give every finalist the same short task tied to the role, such as a sample email, a small data exercise or a quick research summary. Keep it to an hour or two. Use made up or sample material, and never use what candidates produce in your business, since using their work can create a duty to pay them.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Many superintendents hold an OSHA 30-hour Construction card, and some states and cities require it on certain jobs. Ask for first aid and CPR training, and competent person training if your work involves excavation, scaffolds or fall protection. Rules for site supervisor licenses vary by state and city, so check yours.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them read a drawing set and spot conflicts between trades. Ask them to build a three-week look-ahead from a master schedule. Check that they can write a clear daily report, run a short coordination meeting and plan inspections in the right order.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about past projects with specifics: building type, size, number of subcontractors and how they pulled a slipping schedule back. They keep daily logs and photos. Their references include project managers and subcontractors who would work with them again.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who blames every delay on subcontractors or the owner. Be wary if they are vague about safety, treat it as paperwork, keep no written records or cannot explain how they fixed a failed inspection or a quality problem.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: “Walk me through a failed inspection and what you did next.” “What do you do when a sub falls behind and blocks other trades?” “How do you run a safety meeting?” “Which parts of a job like ours need the most coordination?”

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a construction superintendent?
qa.a: Look for experience running projects like yours in type and size. Verify safety training such as an OSHA 30-hour card, and check local rules, which vary by state and city. A strong superintendent schedules well, reads drawings closely, keeps clear daily records and handles subcontractors firmly but fairly. Call references from both project managers and subcontractors.

qa.q: How do I test a construction superintendent before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short scenario from a real job: a drawing set, a master schedule and a problem such as a late subcontractor or a failed inspection. Ask them to build a three-week look-ahead, list the conflicts they see and explain their fix. Have them write a sample daily report. Pay attention to how clearly they explain their choices.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most supervisor roles need no state license. Check what your industry requires, such as a food protection manager certificate, which many states and cities require in food service, or OSHA outreach training cards on job sites. Verify past supervisory roles with references who saw them lead a shift.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they assign work by skill and priority, check quality, and adjust when someone calls out or a machine goes down. Check they can coach and correct fairly, document issues, run a clear shift handoff, and know the safety and break rules for your state.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates spend time on the floor, know each person’s strengths, and give feedback early and privately. They keep records, follow up on safety near misses, and can name a time they turned around a weak shift or helped a team member improve.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for blaming the team for every miss, avoiding hard conversations, playing favorites, or bending safety and wage rules to hit a target. Be wary of anyone who cannot describe how they would handle a harassment complaint or a safety concern raised by a worker.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a shift where two people called out. What did you change? How did you handle a worker who kept making the same mistake? What do you do when an employee reports harassment? Strong answers show fairness, documentation and follow-up.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a supervisor?
qa.a: Look for real experience leading a shift or small team, fair and steady communication, and a habit of checking work and safety. Confirm any certificate your industry requires, such as food protection or forklift training. References from former managers and team members show how they handle pressure, conflict and complaints.

qa.q: How do I test a supervisor before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid scenario exercise. Give them a shift plan, a staff list with skills, a sudden absence and a quality problem. Ask how they would reassign work, talk to the people involved and record what happened. Review their fairness, safety awareness and how clearly they explain decisions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No state license is required for this work. Useful credentials include a Certified Quality Engineer or Certified Quality Auditor certification, ISO 9001 or IATF 16949 lead auditor training, and Six Sigma belts. Ask for proof of each credential and check whether it is current, since some must be renewed.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Hand them a real PPAP package or first article inspection report with a few planted errors and ask what they would reject. Check that they can read a drawing with GD&T, judge a Gage R&R result, and spot an out-of-control SPC chart.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe a supplier problem they closed with an 8D or similar root cause method, name the containment step, and show data proving the fix held. They talk about building the supplier’s process capability, not only issuing corrective action requests.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Blames suppliers for every problem, cannot explain the difference between a process audit and a product audit, or closes corrective actions on paperwork alone. Be wary if they cannot name the standards or customer-specific requirements that applied in past roles.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a supplier you put on containment. What did your on-site audit find that the paperwork missed? How did you decide the supplier was ready to exit? Also confirm they can travel as often as the job requires.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a supplier quality and development engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience auditing suppliers in your industry, fluency in PPAP, APQP, FMEA and control plans, and proof they have closed corrective actions with data. Strong candidates also coach suppliers, communicate firmly but fairly, and can travel. Certifications help, but they do not replace a record of real supplier fixes.

qa.q: How do I test a supplier quality and development engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case with a defect report, a drawing, a control plan and some measurement data from a supplier. Ask them to plan containment, choose a root cause method, and list what they would check on a site visit. Score how they use the data and how clearly they write the corrective action request.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No state license is required for this work. Some planners hold voluntary industry certifications such as CPIM, CSCP or CLTD. Treat these as a plus, not a must, and confirm them with the issuing body if the candidate lists them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for strong spreadsheet work: lookups, pivot tables and clean formulas. They should explain demand forecasting, safety stock, reorder points, lead times and MRP logic. Ask which ERP or planning systems they have used and what they did in them day to day.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong planners talk in numbers they tracked, such as forecast accuracy, fill rate, inventory turns or on-time delivery. They describe working with buyers, production and sales to balance stock levels against cost, and they flag problems early instead of waiting for a shortage.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of someone who blames suppliers for every late order, cannot explain how a forecast was built, or only says they ‘managed inventory’ without results. Also watch for weak follow-up habits, since missed supplier check-ins often cause stockouts.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a time a key part was going to run out. What did they see first, who did they call, and what changed afterward? Ask how they set safety stock for a slow item versus a fast one.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a supply chain planner?
qa.a: Look for solid spreadsheet skills, hands-on time in an ERP or planning system, and a clear grasp of forecasting, lead times and safety stock. Good candidates share results they tracked, like fill rate or inventory turns. A certification such as CPIM or CSCP is helpful but optional, since no license is required.

qa.q: How do I test a supply chain planner before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case with twelve months of demand, current stock, open orders and supplier lead times for a few items. Ask them to build a reorder plan in a spreadsheet and explain their safety stock choices. Then add a surprise, like a supplier delay, and see how they adjust and who they would contact.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for supply chain planners. Degrees and optional supply chain certifications show study of planning methods. Verify past work instead: ask how forecast accuracy, service levels or inventory changed under their plans, and confirm with references in operations or sales.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test demand forecasting, material requirements planning, safety stock setting and capacity planning. Check skill with your ERP planning module and advanced spreadsheets. Ask them to measure forecast error and bias, and to plan around supplier lead times and minimum order quantities.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates run sales and operations planning meetings with clear data, explain tradeoffs between cost, inventory and service, and flag shortages early. They work well with buyers, production and sales, and they fix master data instead of planning around bad numbers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for blaming the forecast for every miss, planning only from gut feel, or hiding shortages until it is too late. Be careful with anyone who cannot explain how safety stock is set or who overrides system plans without recording why.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How did you set safety stock for a volatile item? Tell me about a shortage you saw coming and what you did. How do you measure forecast bias? How do you handle a sales team that keeps changing the forecast? Strong answers show data and method.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a supply chain planner?
qa.a: Look for forecasting, MRP and safety stock skills, strong spreadsheet and ERP use, and clear communication across sales, buying and production. Ask for results they can explain, such as better service or leaner stock. No license is required, so tests and references count most.

qa.q: How do I test a supply chain planner before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case with sample demand history, lead times and stock levels. Ask for a forecast, a reorder plan and a short note on risks. Review their method, spreadsheet accuracy, how they handle outliers and whether they explain choices clearly to a manager.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give them a real log file and a short customer complaint. Watch how they search for errors, line up timestamps and form a theory. Check comfort with the command line, basic SQL, API requests and the networking basics like DNS, ports and certificates that your product depends on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask clarifying questions before touching anything. They change one thing at a time, write down each step, and can turn a vague report into exact reproduction steps. They explain the cause in plain words to a customer and in technical detail to engineers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a fault they reproduced that others could not. Ask what they checked first, what they ruled out and how they knew. Ask how they decide when to escalate and what they include in the ticket they hand to engineering.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Guessing at fixes without looking at evidence. Blaming customers or other teams. Vague stories with no specific error, tool or outcome. Careless habits with passwords or customer data. Escalation notes that would leave an engineer starting from zero.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Vendor or industry certifications can show study but are optional. Verify past roles and talk to references about ticket quality. Background checks need written consent under federal law, and state and local rules on timing vary.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technical support engineer?
qa.a: Look for someone who works from evidence. They should read logs, reproduce faults step by step and explain findings clearly to both customers and developers. Check that they know your stack’s basics, such as networking, APIs or databases. Good judgment about when to escalate, and clean written notes, matter as much as raw technical skill.

qa.q: How do I test a technical support engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Set up a short paid or time-boxed exercise. Give a sample customer ticket, a matching log file and access to a test environment with a planted fault. Ask them to find the cause, write a reply to the customer and draft an escalation ticket. Score their reasoning, accuracy and clarity, not just whether they found the bug.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to build a weekly schedule from a sample ticket volume chart. Have them review three real or mock tickets and score them for accuracy, tone and policy. Strong managers explain staffing trade-offs and give feedback an agent could act on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about first response time, resolution time and customer satisfaction with context, not just numbers. They have coached agents who improved, written or updated help articles, and pushed product teams to fix the root causes of repeat tickets.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a sudden spike in tickets, how they turned around an underperforming agent, and how they set up a quality review process. Listen for specific steps, tools they used and what they would do differently.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who blames agents for every problem, measures only speed, or cannot describe how they hired or trained anyone. Vague answers about escalations, or no experience with a help desk or ticketing system, also deserve a closer look.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Optional customer service or help desk certifications exist, but proven team results matter more. Check references from former agents and managers, and confirm past titles and team sizes with prior employers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a customer support manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who has led a team of agents, not just answered tickets. They should handle scheduling, quality reviews, coaching and hiring. Good candidates know the key metrics and explain what drives them. They also show calm judgment with upset customers and clear communication with other teams.

qa.q: How do I test a customer support manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short practical task. Share sample ticket volumes and ask for a staffing plan. Provide a few tickets to grade and ask for written feedback to an agent. Then role-play a coaching conversation or an escalation. Score each candidate with the same rubric.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses system administrators. Certifications are optional but useful. Check that any certificate a candidate lists is current, since many expire or need renewal, and confirm it through the issuer’s online lookup. Weigh hands-on history with systems like yours more than paper.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to set up a user with the right group permissions, restore a file from backup, read a log to find why a service failed, and write a short script for a routine task. Watch whether they check their work before calling it done.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They bring up least privilege, removing access the day someone leaves, tested backups and regular patching. They document changes, keep a rollback plan, and can explain a past outage in plain words: what broke, how they found it and what they changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Sharing admin passwords, using one account for everything, or never testing a restore. Be wary of anyone who blames users for every problem, can’t describe a mistake they made, or wants broad access with no logging. Vague answers about security updates are also a warning.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How would you offboard an employee who had access to ten systems? Tell me about a backup you restored under pressure. How do you decide who gets admin rights? Real experience shows in concrete steps, tools described by type and lessons learned.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a system administrator?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with the systems you run, a habit of granting only the access people need, and proof they test backups. Good candidates document their work, plan for rollback and explain technical issues clearly to non-technical staff. Certifications help but are optional, since no US state licenses this role.

qa.q: How do I test a system administrator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, clearly limited task in a sandbox, never your live systems. For example, ask them to create accounts with set permissions, fix a broken service using its logs, and write notes another admin could follow. Never share real passwords during a test. Judge accuracy, caution and the quality of their documentation.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most systems engineers in industry need no license. A state Professional Engineer license is mainly required to offer engineering services to the public or sign certain documents, and rules vary by state. Systems engineering certifications are optional. Defense work may require a security clearance.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test requirements writing, interface definitions, trade studies, risk analysis, and verification and validation planning. Check traceability from each requirement to a test, model-based tools such as SysML if you use them, and enough hardware and software depth to spot integration problems.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have taken a product from concept through integration testing and delivery. They write requirements that can be tested, manage interfaces between teams, keep a risk list current and can explain a failure found late and the process change that followed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for requirements that cannot be measured, no integration testing experience, treating documents as paperwork rather than design tools, and deep knowledge of one discipline with no feel for the others. Be careful with vague claims about owning the whole system.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about an integration problem between two subsystems and how you traced it. How do you write a requirement that can be verified? How do you handle a change request late in a program? Strong answers name specific documents, tests and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a systems engineer?
qa.a: Look for experience taking complex products through requirements, integration and testing, with clear, testable requirements and good traceability. Check they understand hardware and software well enough to manage interfaces. Most roles need no license, though a state Professional Engineer license or a security clearance may apply to some work.

qa.q: How do I test a systems engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task, such as writing testable requirements and an interface list for a simple product, then planning how each requirement will be verified. Add a scenario with a late design change. Review clarity, traceability, risk thinking and how they weigh cost, schedule and performance.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test low-level languages such as C, C++ or Rust, plus memory management, concurrency and debugging. Ask them to find a race condition or memory leak in a small program. Have them explain how they would use a debugger, profiler or sanitizer to track it down.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license or required certification exists for this work. Check what they actually built instead: open-source commits, kernel or driver patches, design docs or code samples. Confirm past roles with references who saw their work on storage, networking, operating system or compiler code.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain tradeoffs clearly, such as latency versus throughput or safety versus speed. They measure before they optimize, write tests for edge cases and read hardware or OS documentation. They can walk you through a hard bug they chased down, step by step.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about past systems and a habit of blaming the compiler or hardware first. Other warning signs are no benchmarking habit and code that skips error handling or failure cases. Be wary of claims of deep systems work backed only by high-level framework experience.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask what happens, step by step, when a program reads a file or opens a network connection. Ask how they would find out why a database query slowed down after a release. Ask about a production crash they debugged and what they changed afterward.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a systems software engineer?
qa.a: Look for strong skills in C, C++ or Rust and a solid grasp of memory, concurrency and operating system internals. Ask for proof of real work, such as code samples or open-source contributions. Strong candidates measure before they optimize and explain tradeoffs in plain terms. No license is required, so focus on verified past work and references.

qa.q: How do I test a systems software engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, time-boxed task tied to your own stack. For example, ask them to fix a memory leak, find a race condition or speed up a slow function and prove it with a benchmark. Then have them walk you through their reasoning. Watch how they use debuggers and profilers and how they handle edge cases and errors.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: A CPA license is common but not always required for analyst roles. CPA licenses are issued by state boards of accountancy, and requirements vary by state, so confirm status with the issuing board. An enrolled agent credential, issued by the IRS, also shows tested federal tax knowledge.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have them prepare a short book-to-tax reconciliation and explain each adjustment. Check their comfort with income tax provision work under ASC 740, state apportionment, sales and use tax, and spreadsheets. If your company operates abroad, also probe VAT or GST, transfer pricing and tax treaties.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They cite the code section or guidance behind an answer. They keep a clear calendar of filing and payment deadlines. Their workpapers are documented so a reviewer can follow every number. They raise questions early instead of guessing on gray areas.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers on which returns they prepared versus only reviewed. Only individual return experience when you need corporate work. Mixing up temporary and permanent differences. Treating a missed estimated payment or extension deadline as no big deal.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through the last business return they worked on, from trial balance to filing. Ask how they handled a state nexus question or a tax notice. Listen for specific steps, sources they checked and who signed off.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a tax analyst?
qa.a: Look for hands-on business tax experience that matches your filings, such as federal and state income tax, sales and use tax, or international work if you operate abroad. Verify any CPA license with the state board. Favor candidates who research carefully, document their workpapers and meet deadlines without reminders.

qa.q: How do I test a tax analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, clearly limited exercise using made-up numbers. For example, provide a simple trial balance and ask for the book-to-tax adjustments and estimated federal taxable income, with a note on each item. Then ask them to explain their choices. Judge accuracy, clarity and how they flag uncertain points.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test both halves of the job. Have them review a real pull request and explain what they would flag and why. Then ask them to break a vague feature into tasks a small team could ship, with risks and order of work.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about outcomes their team shipped, not just code they wrote. They describe how they kept reviews fast, wrote clear tickets and still took hands-on coding work. They can explain a tradeoff they made and what they would do differently.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they unblocked an engineer who was stuck for days. Ask about a design decision the team disagreed on and how it was settled. Ask how they balance their own coding time against reviews, planning and meetings.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who rewrites others’ code instead of coaching, blames past teammates for every miss, or cannot name a time they cut scope. Vague answers about team size, their exact role, or results usually mean they did not lead.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to be a tech lead. Cloud or vendor certifications can show knowledge but do not prove leadership. Check references from engineers they led and managers they reported to, and review public code or design docs if available.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a tech lead?
qa.a: Look for someone who still codes well and also makes the team faster. They should plan work into clear tasks, give useful code reviews, and remove blockers quickly. Strong candidates explain tradeoffs plainly, own mistakes, and can point to projects their team delivered, not just their own commits.

qa.q: How do I test a tech lead before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short, paid or time-boxed exercise. Ask them to review a sample pull request with real flaws, then plan a small feature for a team of three or four. Follow with a talk-through where they explain priorities, risks, and how they would split the work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for technical account managers. Product and cloud certifications are optional. Verify experience through references from customers or former teammates, and ask how they handled accounts through upgrades, outages and renewals.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test troubleshooting from logs and error messages, explaining APIs and integrations, planning an upgrade or migration, and writing clear incident updates for customers. Check they track open issues, escalate to engineering with good detail and run review meetings.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates know each customer’s setup in detail, spot risks before tickets arrive and keep promises realistic. They can show account plans, upgrade plans or incident summaries, and engineering teams trust their bug reports.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for people who only forward tickets, promise roadmap features they cannot guarantee, avoid giving bad news, or lack the technical depth to reproduce a problem. Be careful with anyone who cannot describe a customer they nearly lost.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a major outage for a key customer and how you handled communication. How do you plan a risky upgrade? What do you include in a bug report to engineering? Strong answers name steps, timelines and owners.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technical account manager?
qa.a: Look for real technical depth, calm communication under pressure and a habit of planning ahead for customers. Check troubleshooting, upgrade planning and how well they work with engineering and sales. No license is required, so references from customers and a realistic role-play matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a technical account manager before hiring?
qa.a: Run a short, paid role-play: a fictional customer reports an outage after an upgrade. Ask them to gather facts, write a customer update and draft an escalation to engineering. Review accuracy, tone, the technical questions they ask and whether next steps have clear owners and times.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check that they can read an API spec, sketch a system diagram and explain tradeoffs like latency versus cost or build versus buy. They should be able to write a clear requirements doc that engineers can estimate from without a long round of follow-up questions.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates talk about developers as customers. They mention docs, onboarding time, error messages, versioning and deprecation plans. They can name the metrics they tracked, such as adoption or uptime, and explain how those numbers changed a roadmap decision.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they handled a breaking API change, how they said no to an internal team’s request, or how they prioritized tech debt against new features. Listen for concrete steps, who they consulted and what they would do differently next time.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Product or agile certificates exist but are optional and vary in rigor. Verify past titles and dates with references, and ask a former engineering lead how the candidate worked with their team.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers that hide behind buzzwords, no examples of shipping to technical users, or blaming engineers for missed dates. Be cautious if they cannot explain a technical concept simply, or if they treat documentation and developer feedback as afterthoughts.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technical product manager?
qa.a: Look for someone who understands how platforms and APIs are built and used, writes clear specs, and earns trust from engineers. They should prioritize with data, plan for versioning and deprecation, and treat developer experience as part of the product. Ask for specific shipped examples and talk to engineering references.

qa.q: How do I test a technical product manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid or time-boxed exercise. Share a sample API or platform problem and ask for a one-page spec with goals, users, success metrics, risks and a rollout plan. Then have an engineer review it with them live to see how they handle questions and tradeoffs.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Certifications such as the PMP or agile and Scrum credentials are optional. If a candidate lists one, confirm it in the issuer’s public registry. Weigh real programs shipped across several teams more heavily than any certificate.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test whether they can map dependencies, build a realistic schedule, and keep a live risk list with owners. Check their technical depth. They should follow system design trade-offs with engineers. They should also write a clear one-page status update for executives.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates describe specific programs that spanned many teams. They explain their own role, not just the team’s. They talk about scope they cut, risks they raised early, and how they got teams outside their reporting line to commit.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be cautious if they talk only about tools, tickets and meetings. Watch for someone who cannot explain the architecture of a past project, or who blames other teams for every slip. Status reports that stayed green until launch week are another warning sign.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about a date that slipped. When did you first know, and who did you tell?” Ask, “How did you handle a dependency on a team that had other priorities?” Listen for timing, trade-offs and clear escalation.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technical program manager?
qa.a: Look for proof they have run engineering work across several teams. They should handle dependencies, risks and dates. They need enough technical depth to question estimates and design choices. They should write clear updates for leaders. Certifications are optional, so focus on concrete examples of programs they delivered and problems they caught early.

qa.q: How do I test a technical program manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short case. Describe a feature that needs work from three teams, with one team overloaded and a fixed launch date. Ask for a dependency map, a top-five risk list with owners, and a brief status note for an executive. Then have an engineer probe their technical reasoning in a follow-up conversation.

look.label: Technical knowledge to test
look.text: A good technical recruiter is not an engineer but can talk like one. They should explain how backend, frontend, data and DevOps roles differ. They should also know common languages and tools, and separate must-have skills from nice-to-haves in a job description.

look.label: Sourcing skills to test
look.text: Ask them to build a Boolean search string for one of your open roles and draft a short first message to a passive engineer. Strong recruiters find people beyond job boards, in developer communities and public code. They write outreach that feels personal, not copied.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They know their own numbers, such as reply rate, time to fill and offer acceptance. Hiring managers trust their shortlists. They can tell you why they turned down a candidate who looked good on paper. Engineers they placed would happily take their call again.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for pure keyword matching, mass generic messages and overselling roles to close a deal. Be wary if they cannot explain a technical requirement they recruited for. Any suggestion to screen on age, family plans or other protected traits is a serious warning sign.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to recruit in-house. Some states license employment agencies, so agency recruiters may need one depending on the state. Industry certifications exist but are optional. Check references from hiring managers and confirm they know fair hiring and pay transparency rules, which vary by state.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technical recruiter?
qa.a: Look for someone who understands engineering roles well enough to judge fit, not just match keywords. They should source passive candidates, write strong outreach and work closely with hiring managers. Ask about their metrics and past placements. Make sure they follow fair hiring laws and treat candidates honestly, since your employer brand rides on every message they send.

qa.q: How do I test a technical recruiter before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a real job description for an engineering role. Ask them to list the must-have skills, write a search string, draft an outreach message and outline screening questions. Then have one of your engineers review their work. Follow up by asking them to explain how they would tell a strong candidate from a weak one.

look.label: Credentials to check
look.text: No US state or federal license exists for technical writers. Some hold optional certificates from professional groups or colleges. Treat these as a plus, not a requirement. Judge candidates mainly on their writing samples and how clearly they explain real products.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for three to five samples, such as a user manual, help article, tutorial or API reference. Check for clear structure, plain language, consistent terms and numbered steps. Ask what they wrote versus edited. Accept redacted or rewritten samples when the originals are confidential.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for the ability to interview engineers and turn rough notes into accurate steps for a defined reader. For API work, check that they can read code samples, explain REST requests and JSON, and use tools like Markdown and Git. Test with the tools your team actually uses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask who the reader is before writing. They run through the steps themselves and flag product gaps. They follow or build a style guide, plan for updates between versions, and think about search, screenshots and accessibility for readers who use screen readers.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for samples full of jargon, missing prerequisites or steps that skip actions. Be careful if every sample is marketing copy, if they cannot explain their choices, or if they blame engineers for gaps instead of describing how they got the answers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technical writer?
qa.a: Look for clear, accurate samples that match your needs, such as help articles, manuals or API guides. Strong writers ask about the audience, interview experts well and test steps themselves. Check they know your tools, like Markdown, Git or a help authoring tool. No license is required, so samples and a short test matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a technical writer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task based on a real feature. Share a brief spec or demo and offer a short call with an engineer. Ask for a how-to article or one API endpoint reference. Judge accuracy, structure, plain language and the questions they asked. Keep it brief, and pay for anything longer than a few hours.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Requirements depend on the trade and often vary by state or city. Electrical, plumbing and HVAC work commonly needs a state or local license. Servicing stationary refrigeration or AC equipment requires EPA Section 608 certification; motor vehicle AC work requires Section 609. Confirm any license with the issuing agency.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Have candidates find a real fault on equipment like yours, read a wiring diagram or service manual, and use a multimeter and hand tools correctly. Watch whether they follow a logical order instead of swapping parts until something works.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain what they checked and why, keep clear notes on each job, and follow lockout/tagout and other safety steps without reminders. Good technicians ask about the equipment’s history before they touch it.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Skipping power isolation or protective gear, vague answers about past repairs, blaming every failure on bad parts, and no record of work done. Be cautious with anyone who claims a license or certification you cannot confirm.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through the hardest repair they solved, which tools they used, and what they would do differently. Ask what they do when a job is outside their training or license.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technician?
qa.a: Look for hands-on experience with equipment like yours, any license or certification your trade and state require, and safe work habits. Strong technicians troubleshoot step by step, explain their reasoning in plain words, and document their work. Check references from past supervisors about reliability and repair quality.

qa.q: How do I test a technician before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, supervised practical task on equipment similar to yours, with a planted fault to find. Watch how they isolate power, use tools and meters, and narrow down the cause. Ask them to explain the fix and write a brief service note. Use the same task for every candidate.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a technology consultant. Vendor or industry certifications in cloud platforms, networking, security or project management can show real study. Confirm them through the issuer’s online verification tool, and check that they match the systems you actually use.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for clear needs assessment, honest comparison of options, and plain explanations for nontechnical staff. Test how they scope a project, estimate cost and time, plan data migration and training, and spot security or compliance risks before recommending a system.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong consultants ask about your goals, budget and current tools before naming any product. They can describe past projects with measurable results, admit what went wrong, and leave behind written documentation so your team is not dependent on them.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of anyone who pushes one vendor in every answer without disclosing partner commissions. Watch for jargon used to avoid direct answers, vague timelines, no references, or reluctance to put scope, deliverables and data handling in writing.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a system they chose and set up, start to finish. Ask how they handled user resistance, a failed integration, or a project running over budget. Ask what they would do differently now.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a technology consultant?
qa.a: Look for someone who listens first, explains options in plain language and recommends based on your needs, not a favorite vendor. Check references from similar projects, verify any certifications with the issuer, and ask whether they earn referral fees from products they suggest. Good consultants also document their work and train your staff.

qa.q: How do I test a technology consultant before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic scenario, such as choosing a scheduling or accounting system for a small team with a set budget. Ask for a brief written recommendation with options, risks, rollout steps and training plan. Then have them present it to a nontechnical staff member and see how well they answer questions.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most telecom engineering roles need no license. A state Professional Engineer license, with rules that vary by state, matters only if they will seal designs. For field work, confirm tower climbing and RF safety training. Check vendor certifications on your equipment and call references from past network projects.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test RF planning and link budgets, IP routing and MPLS, and the mobile core and radio access network for LTE and 5G. Check they can read drive test or performance data, find the cause of dropped calls or slow data, and document changes safely.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates have taken sites or network changes from design to live traffic. They plan maintenance windows with rollback steps, read alarms and counters calmly, and explain coverage or capacity tradeoffs to managers. They know the FCC rules that apply to the work, such as RF exposure limits.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for engineers who have only used planning tools without field results, cannot explain a link budget, or make live network changes without a written procedure and rollback plan. Be careful with vague answers about which part of a large rollout they personally did.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a site or link you designed and how it performed after launch. How did you track down a rise in dropped calls? How do you plan a core network change at night? Strong answers name tools, counters and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a telecommunications engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work in your network type, whether radio access, microwave links, fiber or the mobile core. Check they read performance data, follow change control and work safely around towers and RF. Most roles need no license, so project results and references matter most. A PE license, which varies by state, matters only for sealed designs.

qa.q: How do I test a telecommunications engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your real work, such as a link budget for a microwave hop, or a set of network counters showing a fault to diagnose. Ask them to explain each step. Review accuracy, their safety and rollback thinking, and how clearly they write it up.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most territory roles need no license. If the job means daily driving, confirm a valid driver’s license and check the driving record only with written consent, following FCRA and state rules. Selling insurance needs a state producer license, and selling securities needs FINRA registration plus any state requirements.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test prospecting new accounts in an unfamiliar area, planning a week of visits that limits wasted driving, and running a discovery conversation that uncovers real needs. Also check that they log activity in a CRM and can build a forecast they will stand behind.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates give clear numbers: quota attainment by year, accounts opened, revenue grown in existing accounts. They explain how they ranked accounts, which few drove most results, and how they rebuilt a weak stretch of territory without being asked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about past targets, results credited only to the team, or no clear routine for a week in the field. Be wary of anyone who blames the territory or the product for every miss, or who speaks badly of former customers.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they split time between new and existing accounts. Ask them to walk through a deal they lost and what they changed. Ask whether a non-compete or non-solicitation agreement limits their work, since enforceability varies by state.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a territory sales manager?
qa.a: Look for a track record of hitting targets that the candidate can explain with real numbers. They should prospect on their own, plan efficient field routes, keep a CRM current and forecast honestly. If the role involves driving, confirm a valid driver’s license. Check for any non-compete or non-solicitation agreement that could limit their work.

qa.q: How do I test a territory sales manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short list of sample accounts in a real or mock territory. Ask them to rank the accounts, plan a week of visits and explain why. Then run a role play of a first meeting with a skeptical buyer. Judge their questions, their listening and the next step they secure.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most roles need no state license. A PE license matters only if the person must sign or seal engineering work, and those rules vary by state. A Certified Reliability Engineer credential is optional but shows grounding in failure data and life testing.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short test plan for a real part, covering thermal cycling limits, vibration profile, sensor placement, sample size and pass criteria. Check that they can set up data acquisition, script analysis in Python or similar tools, and apply standards such as MIL-STD-810 or IEC 60068.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They talk about failures they found, not just tests they ran. They explain root cause, fixture design and how they kept test data traceable. They question vague requirements and can explain how an accelerated life test differs from a simple burn-in.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: They list equipment names without results. They cannot explain why a test profile was chosen or how many units were needed. They treat one passed test as proof with no margin. They blame design teams instead of documenting failures clearly.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask, “Tell me about a failure that showed up late in testing. How did you find it?” Or, “How did you keep a fixture from adding its own resonance?” Real answers include numbers, tools and what changed in the design afterward.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a test and validation engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on work with thermal chambers, vibration shakers and data acquisition, plus clear test plans and reports. Strong candidates tie each test to a requirement, find root causes and know the standards used in your industry. A state license is rarely needed unless they sign engineering documents, and those rules vary by state.

qa.q: How do I test a test and validation engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task. Share a part drawing and spec, and ask for a test plan with environmental profiles, sensor placement, sample size and pass or fail criteria. Then share a messy data set and ask them to find the anomaly and explain the likely cause. Review their reasoning together in a follow-up call.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: A bachelor’s in mechanical or a related engineering field is typical. If the role involves sealing designs for clients or the public, confirm a Professional Engineer license with the state board. Rules and industry exemptions vary by state. The PE mechanical exam offers a thermal and fluid systems option.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask them to size a pump or fan from a system curve, estimate the heat load on a component, and pick a cooling approach. Check that they can work it out by hand first, then explain when CFD or thermal simulation is worth the time.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They check simulation results against test data and simple hand estimates. They talk clearly about pressure drop, flow rates, temperature margins and real tolerances. They can describe a design that failed in testing and explain what they changed.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Trusting colorful simulation plots without checking the mesh, boundary conditions or units. Vague answers about which parts of a project were truly theirs. No awareness of cavitation, condensation, or how fouling and wear change performance over time.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: "Walk me through a cooling or flow problem you solved, from requirements to test." "How did you validate your model?" "What would you check first if a system ran hotter than predicted?" Listen for real numbers, instruments and tradeoffs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a thermal and fluids engineer?
qa.a: Look for solid heat transfer and fluid mechanics basics, hands-on test experience, and the habit of checking models against measurements. A mechanical engineering degree is typical. A Professional Engineer license matters if they will seal designs, and those rules vary by state. Strong candidates explain tradeoffs between cost, size, noise and cooling performance in plain terms.

qa.q: How do I test a thermal and fluids engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, realistic problem, such as cooling an enclosure with a known heat load or sizing a pump for a simple piping loop. Ask for hand calculations, stated assumptions and a recommended design. Then discuss how they would confirm it with simulation or a bench test. Pay for any task that takes more than an hour or two.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses threat intelligence analysts. Certifications in cyber threat intelligence or security analysis can show study, but they are optional. Confirm any listed certification with the body that issued it. Give more weight to past reports, briefings and investigation work they can describe without sharing a former employer’s secrets.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: See if they can track an attacker from a few clues, such as a suspicious domain, IP address or file hash. Look for careful sourcing, mapping behavior to known attacker techniques, separating fact from guess, and turning findings into steps your team can act on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They write short, plain briefings for leaders and detailed notes for defenders. They state confidence levels, cite sources, and tie threats to your industry and systems instead of repeating every headline. They keep up with new scams and malware and can explain why each one matters to you.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Reports that copy outside feeds with no analysis. Claims stated as certain with no sources. No idea how findings reach the people who block attacks. Boasting about breaking into systems or criminal spaces in ways that may break the law or your policies.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a threat you warned about before it hit. How did you decide which threats mattered most? How do you handle leaked data you find? What would you watch first here? Good answers show judgment, ethics and real results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a threat intelligence analyst?
qa.a: Look for someone who can follow attacker groups, scams and malware, then explain what it means for your company. Strong analysts cite sources, give confidence levels and suggest clear defensive steps. No state license exists, so focus on writing samples, investigation skills, sound ethics and how they share findings with security and business teams.

qa.q: How do I test a threat intelligence analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a small, safe exercise. Share a few clues, such as a phishing email, a domain and a file hash, using public or made-up data. Ask for a one-page briefing within a set time. Judge their sourcing, logic, confidence levels and practical advice, and how well a busy manager could understand it.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give them a part drawing and ask what would make it hard to mold or stamp. Listen for draft angles, uneven wall thickness, undercuts that need slides or lifters, gate and parting line placement, shrink allowance and GD&T tolerances they would question.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most tooling roles need no US license. A Professional Engineer license exists, with rules that vary by state, but it is rarely required for this work. Verify the degree or toolmaking background, past tool designs they can share, and any simulation training they list.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can follow a tool from quote to production: design review, steel choice, cooling layout, venting, tryout and fixes. They explain how they solved short shots, flash, sink or warp, and they weigh cycle time, tool life and maintenance cost.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: They have only modeled parts and never stood at a press during tryout. They cannot explain why a part warped. They blame the toolmaker for every problem, or stay vague about which parts of a past design were their own work.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a tool that failed its first tryout and what they changed. Ask when they choose a hot runner over a cold runner. Ask how they locate a part in a fixture so it repeats every time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a tooling and molding engineer?
qa.a: Look for hands-on time with real tools, not just CAD models. A strong engineer knows design for manufacturing, gating, cooling, venting, steel selection and fixture locating. They can read GD&T, explain how they fixed defects during tryout, and talk about cycle time and tool life. Ask to see past designs and have them describe their own role in each.

qa.q: How do I test a tooling and molding engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Share a simple part model or drawing and ask for a short design review. Have them mark draft, wall thickness, undercuts, gate location and parting line, then sketch a basic tool or fixture concept. Follow up with a defect photo, such as warp or flash, and ask for likely causes and fixes. Keep the task short and paid if it takes hours.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Needs depend on the role and firm type. Traders at a broker-dealer generally need FINRA registration, often the SIE plus the Series 57. Futures roles usually need the Series 3 through the NFA. Check the candidate’s record on FINRA BrokerCheck or NFA BASIC.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test quick, accurate math under time pressure, order types and execution, and position sizing. Check that they know the asset class you trade and its market hours, liquidity and costs. Ask them to use a trading platform or a spreadsheet to model risk on a sample position.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong traders explain losing trades as clearly as winning ones. They respect risk limits without being told, keep a trade journal, and can explain best execution and why rules against market manipulation matter. They stay calm and precise when a market moves fast.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who talks only about big wins, blames the market for every loss, or is vague about how they sized positions. Be careful with anyone who brushes off compliance, has broken risk limits before, or has unexplained disclosures on their regulatory record.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through their worst trade and what they changed afterward. Ask how they set a stop or a loss limit before entering a position. Ask how they handle a client order that conflicts with their own market view.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a trader?
qa.a: Look for the registrations your role requires, such as the SIE and Series 57 at a broker-dealer or the Series 3 for futures. Then look for disciplined risk management, honest review of losses, strong math under pressure, and respect for compliance. Check BrokerCheck or NFA BASIC for any disciplinary history.

qa.q: How do I test a trader before hiring?
qa.a: Use a short simulated session with a sample market and a set risk limit. Ask the candidate to plan entries, exits and position size, then change the conditions midway. Score how they protect capital, follow the limit, and explain each decision. Add a timed mental math check and a review of a past losing trade.

look.label: Registration to check
look.text: There is no general license for this work. At a FINRA member broker-dealer, people mainly responsible for designing or significantly changing algorithmic trading strategies may need to register as Securities Traders. That requires passing the SIE and Series 57 exams. Confirm with your compliance team.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for modern C++ or Java tuned for low latency, lock-free data structures, cache-aware memory layout, Linux networking and profiling. Check knowledge of FIX and binary exchange protocols, market data feed handling and order book design. They should measure tail latency, not just averages.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe latency in concrete numbers they measured and explain how. They weigh speed against safety and bring up pre-trade risk checks, kill switches and replay testing unprompted. They have handled production incidents and can explain what they changed afterward.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Chasing speed while dismissing risk controls or testing. Claims like “made it faster” with no measurement method. No experience with replay testing or market data gaps. Offering to share code or trade secrets from a past employer, which signals a confidentiality problem.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask how they would track down a rare latency spike in production. Ask how an order book handles cancels and amends at high message rates. Ask what their system does when a feed drops packets or an exchange session disconnects.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a trading systems engineer?
qa.a: Look for deep low-latency skill in C++ or Java, Linux networking, and exchange protocols such as FIX. Strong candidates measure performance carefully and treat risk controls as part of the design. If you are a FINRA member firm, check whether the role requires Securities Trader registration. Ask about real incidents they handled and what they learned.

qa.q: How do I test a trading systems engineer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task. For example, build a simple limit order book with price-time priority, plus tests and a benchmark. Then review it together. Ask how they would cut latency, handle bad input and add a risk check. Never use your proprietary code in the test, and never ask for code from their past employer.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a trainer. Certifications in training or instructional design are optional. If the role includes teaching the OSHA 10- or 30-hour Outreach courses and issuing their cards, confirm current OSHA Outreach trainer authorization. Product certifications matter only if your courses cover that product.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask for a short live teaching sample. Watch pacing, clear steps, checks for understanding and how they handle questions. Then test course building: an outline with learning goals, a hands-on activity and a short quiz or skills check tied to real job tasks.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They first ask what learners must do differently after training. They can show course materials they built, explain how they measured results, and describe changing a course after feedback. They adapt easily to new hires, experienced staff and customers, in person and online.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Slides packed with text, reading straight from notes, or no way to check if learners understood. Vague answers about results, no samples of their own work, or blaming learners when training did not stick. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain a topic simply.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a course they built from scratch. Ask how they handled a disengaged or difficult group. Ask which tools they used for online courses and how they kept remote learners involved and on track.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a trainer?
qa.a: Look for someone who explains things clearly, builds courses around real job tasks, and can show proof of results. Ask for course samples and a live teaching demo. No license is required in general, but check any authorization tied to specific courses they will teach, such as OSHA Outreach cards.

qa.q: How do I test a trainer before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short topic from your business and ask for a 10 to 15 minute teaching session with a few of your staff as learners. Then ask for a one-page course outline with goals and a skills check. Judge clarity, engagement and whether learners can actually do the task afterward.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to coordinate business travel in-house. Agencies that sell travel to the public must register in some states, and those rules vary by state. Optional travel industry certifications exist. Weigh references from travelers they supported and proof of the booking tools they used.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test booking in your travel tool or a global distribution system, applying a travel policy, comparing fares and fare rules, and building a complete itinerary. Check they know passport and visa basics, research entry rules from official government sources, and keep traveler data private.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates think ahead about connections, time zones and cancellation rules, and keep travelers informed without being asked. They track unused tickets and credits, rebook fast during disruptions, and keep clear records for expense reports and for knowing where travelers are.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for booking without checking policy or fare rules, guessing at visa or entry requirements, careless handling of passport details and payment cards, and no plan for after-hours problems. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain how they fixed a booking mistake.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: A flight cancels at midnight with a traveler stuck abroad. What do you do? How do you check visa needs for a new destination? How do you handle an executive who wants a booking outside policy? Strong answers show calm, specific steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a travel coordinator?
qa.a: Look for accurate booking skills, a strong grip on fare rules and travel policy, and calm problem solving when plans fall apart. Check they research passport and visa rules from official sources and protect traveler data. No license is required for in-house roles, so references from travelers and managers matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a travel coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise such as planning a multi-city trip with set dates, your travel policy and one international stop. Then add a disruption, like a canceled flight, and ask for a rebooking plan. Review accuracy, policy compliance, entry requirement research and how clearly they update the traveler.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for corporate treasury roles. Professional treasury and investment certifications exist, are optional and can be verified with the issuer. Call references about the accuracy of their cash forecasts, the banks they managed and the payment controls they ran.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test cash forecasting, bank account and payment management, liquidity planning and basic currency and interest rate hedging. Check spreadsheet modeling, how wires and ACH payments move, fraud controls such as dual approval and positive pay, and their grasp of debt covenants.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates compare forecasts against actual cash and explain the gaps, spread deposits across banks with insurance limits in mind, and treat hedging as risk reduction, not betting. They can describe a payment fraud attempt they stopped.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for weak payment controls, changing vendor bank details from an email without a callback, speculating with hedges, and no tracking of forecast errors. Be careful with anyone who cannot explain how a hedge affected the company’s results or covenants.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you build and check a short-term cash forecast? A vendor emails new bank details. What do you do? How would you protect against a currency swing on a large foreign contract? Strong answers include specific controls and steps.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a treasury manager?
qa.a: Look for accurate cash forecasting, strong payment and fraud controls, solid bank relationships and a careful approach to currency and interest rate risk. No license is required for corporate treasury roles, so verify optional certifications with the issuer and ask references about forecasts and controls.

qa.q: How do I test a treasury manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task with sample bank balances, payables and receivables, and ask for a short-term cash forecast that names key risks. Add a scenario about a suspicious change to a vendor’s bank details. Review accuracy, assumptions, controls and how clearly they explain the plan.

look.label: Knowledge to check
look.text: No US license exists for this work. Check working knowledge of the laws it touches: Section 230, DMCA takedown and counter-notice steps, and the federal duty for platforms to report apparent child sexual abuse material. Privacy and online safety laws vary by state, so ask what they know for your users.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Applying a written policy to gray-area cases the same way every time. Writing clear rules with examples. Explaining a decision in plain words for an appeal. Spotting coordinated abuse such as spam rings, fake accounts or ban evasion. Comfort with review queues, tagging tools and simple spreadsheets.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They cite the exact policy line behind each call. They flag unclear rules instead of guessing. They track accuracy and how often appeals overturn their decisions. They can describe a clear escalation path for threats of violence or child safety and know when to bring in legal.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Judging cases by personal taste rather than written policy. Little interest in appeals or second looks. Thin or sloppy case notes. Casual talk about sharing user data. Treating speed as the only goal. Ignoring context such as satire, news value or reclaimed slang.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a borderline case they handled and why. Ask how they changed a rule after seeing edge cases. Ask what work practices help them stay focused when reviewing disturbing material, without asking about their health history.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a trust and safety specialist?
qa.a: Look for steady judgment tied to written policy, clear writing for rules and appeal replies, and an eye for patterns of abuse. No license is required, but they should know Section 230, DMCA basics and the federal duty to report child sexual abuse material. Strong candidates escalate threats quickly and keep careful case notes.

qa.q: How do I test a trust and safety specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short copy of your policy and ten to fifteen made-up reports, mostly gray-area cases. Use no real user data and no graphic material. Ask them to decide each case, cite the rule, flag anything to escalate, and draft one appeal reply. Then discuss where they hesitated and why.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: No US license or certification is required for UI design, so the portfolio does the work. Look for real shipped screens, not only polished concept shots. Ask to see early sketches, rejected versions and the final file so you can judge process, not just taste.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check type hierarchy, spacing on a consistent grid, and color use that meets WCAG contrast guidance, such as 4.5:1 for normal body text. See if they design every state: hover, focus, disabled, loading, empty and error. Confirm they can build reusable components in your design tool.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain each choice with a reason tied to users or the brand. They work inside a design system or can start one. They know iOS and Android platform conventions, name layers clearly and prepare handoff specs developers can build without guessing.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of portfolios full of pretty shots with no context or outcome. Other warning signs: light gray text that is hard to read, no error or empty states, messy unnamed files, and defensiveness when you give feedback. Copying popular trends without fitting your product is another concern.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: ’Walk me through a screen you redesigned and what changed after launch.’ ’How do you hand files off to developers?’ ’Tell me about a design a developer couldn’t build as drawn and what you did.’ Detailed, specific answers show real project experience.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a UI and visual designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio with shipped work and a clear process behind it. Check typography, spacing, color contrast and complete component states. Good designers explain their choices, organize files cleanly and hand off specs developers can build. There is no state license for this work, so judge skill directly through the portfolio and a short test.

qa.q: How do I test a UI and visual designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small, paid task based on a real screen from your product, such as a sign-up form or settings page. Ask for default, error and empty states plus a short note on their choices. Review readability, contrast, consistency and how easily a developer could build it. Then discuss the work together to see how they take feedback.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Most underwriters do not need a state license. Agents and loan originators usually do. Check designations the candidate claims, such as CPCU for property and casualty or FHA Direct Endorsement underwriter authority for mortgage work. Confirm past signing authority limits with former employers.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Give a real but anonymized file. See if they can read financial statements, loss runs, credit reports or medical summaries for your line. Watch how they spot missing items, apply your guidelines, set terms or price, and write a clear decision note another reviewer could follow.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They explain why they declined or changed a risk in plain terms. They know their line’s rules, including fair lending or unfair discrimination limits. They ask for documents before deciding, track their own loss or default results, and know when to send a file up for approval.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who brags about approval volume but cannot discuss later losses or defaults. Be wary of anyone who approved files above their authority or bent guidelines to please sales. Vague answers about why a file was declined also suggest weak judgment.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a file they declined that sales pushed for, and how they handled it. Ask what their authority limit was and what made them escalate. Ask which documents they request first on a new file, and why.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring an underwriter?
qa.a: Look for experience in your exact line, such as commercial property, life or mortgage. Check that they can read the documents your files use and apply written guidelines. Verify any designations and past authority limits. Strong underwriters explain decisions clearly, escalate when needed and hold firm under sales pressure.

qa.q: How do I test an underwriter before hiring?
