qa.a: Hand them two or three anonymized sample files from your business with your guidelines. Ask them to approve, decline or change terms and write a short reason for each. Then talk through their calls. Check whether they found gaps, asked for missing documents and stayed within the rules.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required to work as a recruiter. Verify past employers, job titles, and the size of the intern and graduate classes they actually hired. HR certifications are voluntary. Treat them as a plus, not a requirement.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for skill in building ties with campus career centers and faculty, planning career fairs and info sessions, and screening many applicants who have little work history. They should use an applicant tracking system well and track offer acceptance and intern-to-hire conversion.

look.label: Rules they should know
look.text: A strong candidate understands the basics. Unpaid internships at for-profit employers must pass the federal primary beneficiary test, and some states add their own rules. They know how CPT and OPT affect F-1 students and screen every applicant the same fair way.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They can walk you through a full yearly cycle, from fall recruiting to intern start dates and return offers. They cite real results, keep students informed at every step, and speak with ease to large groups, in person and on video.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for vague answers about numbers, no clear reason for choosing target schools, and candidates left without replies. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain how they kept an intern program organized, or who screens on traits unrelated to the job.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a university recruiter?
qa.a: Look for proven campus relationships, experience running internship and graduate programs, and measurable results such as offer acceptance and intern return rates. They should handle high applicant volume, speak well to groups, and know the basics of intern pay rules and student work authorization. No license is required, so check references and past results.

qa.q: How do I test a university recruiter before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short task. Ask them to plan a semester campus strategy for one role, with target schools, events, timeline and success measures. Then have them screen a few sample student resumes and explain their choices. Finish with a mock info session pitch to see how they present to students.

look.label: Portfolio with real process
look.text: Look for case studies that show the problem, the research, early sketches, wireframes, testing and what changed after users tried it. Polished final screens alone say little. Ask what the candidate personally did versus the team, and what the outcome was.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test how they map a user flow, turn it into wireframes, and plan a short usability test. Check that they can explain choices in plain words, handle accessibility basics such as contrast and keyboard use, and work in the design tool your team uses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong UX designers ask who the users are before drawing anything. They talk about tradeoffs, constraints from engineering and business goals, and findings that proved them wrong. They can show a design that improved after testing with real users.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with portfolios full of visual mockups but no research or testing, vague answers about their own role, or claims that users always loved every design. A candidate who dismisses developer or stakeholder feedback may struggle on a real team.

look.label: Credentials to note
look.text: No US license is required to work as a UX designer. Certificates and bootcamp diplomas exist but vary widely in depth, so treat them as a bonus. The portfolio and a work sample tell you far more than any certificate.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a UX designer?
qa.a: Look for a portfolio that shows process, not just pretty screens. Good case studies explain the user problem, research methods, wireframes, testing and what changed as a result. Check that they can explain decisions clearly, work with developers and product owners, and apply accessibility basics. Clear ownership of their part of each project matters more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a UX designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid or time-boxed task, such as improving a sign-up or checkout flow. Ask for a simple user flow, rough wireframes and a plan to test it with a few users. Then have them walk you through their thinking. Judge their questions, reasoning and tradeoffs more than visual polish.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US state licenses UX or market researchers. Some associations and training providers offer certificates, but they are optional. Verify skill through a portfolio of case studies that show the research question, method, who took part, key findings and what the team changed because of them.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for someone who can write a discussion guide without leading questions and pick the right method, such as interviews, usability tests or surveys. They should recruit the right participants, take clean notes, turn raw data into clear themes and present findings stakeholders can act on.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong researchers talk about what people did, not just what they said. They explain why they chose a method and admit its limits. They can tell you how a finding changed a product decision, and they stay curious and quiet during sessions instead of steering the participant.

look.label: Consent and data care
look.text: A good researcher gets informed consent, explains how recordings will be used and stores personal data securely. Recording consent rules vary by state, and some states require every party to agree. Ask how they handle consent forms, incentives and deleting data after a study ends.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of portfolios full of polished slides with no outcome, findings based on a handful of friendly coworkers, or surveys with obvious sample bias. Leading questions, defending a design during a test and treating opinions as proof are also warning signs.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a UX and market researcher?
qa.a: Look for case studies that show the full process, from research question to method, participants, findings and the product change that followed. Check that they write neutral questions, choose methods that fit the goal and handle consent and personal data with care. No license is required, so their portfolio and a practical task matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a UX and market researcher before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short brief about a real product problem and ask for a research plan with goals, method, participant criteria and a few interview questions. Then have them run a brief mock usability session with a colleague and summarize what they learned. Watch for neutral questions, careful listening and clear, actionable findings.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. The same title is used in construction and manufacturing, where value engineering certifications cover a different discipline. Verify past deal support through references from sales leaders or customer success managers, and ask for redacted business cases they built.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test whether they can turn discovery notes into a clear ROI or total cost of ownership model. Look for clean spreadsheet logic, stated assumptions, payback period, net present value, sensitivity ranges and a one-page summary a finance executive can read in minutes.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates build on the customer’s own data, not generic benchmarks. They use conservative assumptions, tie value to metrics a CFO already tracks, and follow up after the sale to measure realized value that supports renewals and expansions.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for inflated savings that no buyer would believe, assumptions they cannot explain, and reliance on a canned calculator. Be wary if they cannot describe a deal they lost or a model a customer’s finance team challenged.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk through a business case a CFO pushed back on and what they changed. Ask how they gathered baseline data, how they handled missing numbers, and how they proved value at renewal time.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a value engineer and business value consultant?
qa.a: Look for solid financial modeling skills, comfort with ROI, payback and net present value, and the ability to explain numbers to executives in plain language. Good candidates use conservative, customer-based assumptions and can show how their work helped close or renew deals. No license is required, so rely on work samples and references.

qa.q: How do I test a value engineer and business value consultant before hiring?
qa.a: Give them a short case with sample discovery notes and cost data. Ask them to build a simple ROI model, list their assumptions, and present a one-page summary. Then play a skeptical CFO and challenge the numbers. Judge how they defend, adjust and explain the model, not just the final figure.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is needed to shoot or edit video. If the job includes paid drone footage, the pilot needs an FAA Part 107 remote pilot certificate, so ask to see it. Software certifications exist but are optional. A strong reel and references matter more.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check story structure and pacing, clean audio mixing, color correction, and graphics or captions. Confirm they can export correctly for vertical social clips and long-form video. If they will shoot, test camera settings, lighting, and recording clear sound on location.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: A reel with varied work, plus a clear account of their role on each piece. They keep media organized, back up footage in more than one place, handle feedback rounds calmly, and understand music licensing and when to get on-camera releases.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Popular songs used without a license, vague answers about who shot or cut team projects, no backup habit, and missed deadlines on past jobs. Be wary if they share a past client’s private or unreleased footage without permission.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through one project from raw footage to final delivery. Ask how they handle changes after the cut is locked, how they choose and clear music, and what they do when audio from a shoot is unusable.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a video editor and producer?
qa.a: Look for a reel that matches your kind of work, from short social clips to longer stories. Ask what they personally shot, cut and finished. Check audio quality, pacing and color. Confirm they back up files, meet deadlines and use licensed music. If they fly drones for you, they need an FAA Part 107 certificate.

qa.q: How do I test a video editor before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short paid test. Hand over raw clips, a script or brief, and a time limit, and ask for a one-minute edit in your target format. Review the story, sound, color and captions. Then send one round of notes to see how they take feedback and how quickly they deliver changes.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for a reel plus two or three complete projects, not just highlights. Have them explain their exact role on each piece: what they animated, edited or designed themselves, and what came from teammates, templates or stock libraries.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for smooth timing and easing, clear typography, and text that stays readable on a phone. Check that they can sync motion to voice and music, add accurate captions, and export clean files in the vertical, square and wide sizes your channels need.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this work. Software vendor certifications in animation or editing exist but are optional. References from past clients and real delivered work tell you more. If you also need filming, check it separately, since camera work is a distinct skill.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They ask about audience, platform and goal before designing. They keep tidy, well named project files and follow brand guidelines. They know that stock music, footage and fonts need proper licenses for commercial use and can show how they track them.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask “Walk me through a project that changed late,” “How do you handle feedback rounds?” and “How do you license music and fonts?” Then put ownership of the final work and any editable source files in a written contract, since a freelancer usually keeps copyright without one.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a motion designer?
qa.a: Look for a reel and full projects that match your use, whether ads, training or social clips. Strong candidates combine animation, editing, typography and sound sync, and can explain their own role in each piece. If you also need someone to shoot footage, treat that as a separate skill and ask for camera samples. Check references and how they handle feedback.

qa.q: How do I test a motion designer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a small paid task, such as animating your logo or a 15 second social clip from a short script and your brand assets. Set a deadline and allow one round of notes. Judge timing, readability on a phone, caption accuracy, export settings and how well they apply feedback. Agree in writing who owns the test work.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: If the role covers securities at a broker-dealer, the firm usually must sponsor FINRA registrations such as Series 7, and most states also require Series 63. Check FINRA BrokerCheck for status and disclosures. Bank and crypto exchange roles may need no personal license, so ask for proof of AML and KYC training instead.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Ask the candidate to explain fee tiers, margin calls, settlement timing and API access to a fund client in plain words. Have them write a short message telling a large trader about an outage. Check that they can read account activity and spot a client at risk of leaving.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates can describe accounts they kept through market stress or service problems. They know where their authority ends and bring in trading, operations, legal and compliance at the right time. They talk about client needs, not only volume, and they document every promise in writing.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be wary of anyone who promises special pricing or exceptions without approval, hints at sharing client or market information, or guarantees returns. Plans to bring a former employer’s client list may break their agreements. Vague answers about which accounts they personally managed also deserve follow up.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a top client who threatened to leave and what you did. How do you handle a client asking for a fee waiver you cannot approve? Walk me through onboarding an institutional account, from due diligence to first trade.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a VIP and institutional relationship manager?
qa.a: Look for proven work with funds, firms or high volume traders, solid knowledge of your products, and a clear sense of compliance limits. Verify any FINRA registrations on BrokerCheck if the role covers securities. Strong candidates show calm judgment under pressure, clear writing, and a record of keeping and growing large accounts.

qa.q: How do I test a VIP and institutional relationship manager before hiring?
qa.a: Run a role play where you act as an unhappy fund client after a trading outage or a fee dispute. Then ask for a short written follow up email and an account plan for a sample client. Score how well they listen, explain, stay within approved terms and involve the right internal teams.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for visual merchandisers. Ask for a portfolio with before and after photos of displays, windows and floor sets, plus planograms they built. Confirm with references which work was theirs, and ask what happened to sales after each change.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test planogram reading and building, fixture layouts, color, lighting and signage, and carrying out brand guidelines across many stores. For assortment roles, check sell-through and inventory data. Check they keep aisles, exits and fire equipment clear and accessible routes open for customers with disabilities.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong merchandisers connect every display to sales data, refresh layouts on a clear calendar and write instructions stores can follow without them. They balance creativity with budget, safety and stock levels, and adjust quickly when a product sells faster or slower than planned.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for beautiful displays with no link to sales, layouts that block aisles, exits or sprinklers, ignored brand standards, or overspending on props. Be wary of anyone who cannot explain why a display failed or how they measured results.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a display that did not sell and what you changed. How do you roll out a floor set to many stores? How do you choose which products get the best spots? Strong answers mention data, timing and store teams.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a visual merchandiser?
qa.a: Look for a strong portfolio of real store work, the ability to read sales and inventory data, and skill with planograms, fixtures and brand guidelines. Check they plan safe, accessible layouts and work well with store teams. No license is required, so portfolios and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a visual merchandiser before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid task: share photos and a sales report for one store section, and ask for a new layout or planogram, a display concept and simple setup instructions for staff. Review the link to sales data, brand fit, safety, cost and how clear the instructions are.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They have led managers, not only engineers. They can explain how team structure, hiring, delivery speed and quality changed under their lead. They talk about tradeoffs in business terms and give credit to the teams that did the work.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Organization design, headcount and budget planning, and turning company goals into an engineering roadmap. Also test technical judgment on architecture and build-or-buy choices, how they run incidents, and how they coach a struggling manager.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask about a reorganization they led and what they would do differently. Ask about a manager they had to coach or let go, a project they stopped, and how they handled a missed deadline with executives.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Every story is about their own code, not their teams. They blame past teams or leaders, cannot name the measures they used, have never hired a manager, or push one fixed process no matter the company size.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No US license is required for this role. Verify titles, team sizes and dates through references, including former direct reports and peers. Third-party background checks need written consent under federal law, and rules on criminal history questions vary by state and city.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a director or VP of engineering?
qa.a: Look for proof they have led managers and several teams, not just engineers. Strong candidates explain how they shaped team structure, hiring and delivery, and tie technical choices to business goals. Check that former reports and peers describe them as fair, clear and good at growing other leaders.

qa.q: How do I test a VP of engineering before hiring?
qa.a: Give a realistic case based on your situation, with sensitive details removed. Ask for a short first-90-days plan covering team structure, priorities and risks, then have them present it to a panel of executives, managers and engineers. Watch how they ask questions, handle pushback and admit what they do not yet know.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required to lead sales, unless you sell regulated products such as securities, insurance or real estate. Verify quota attainment, team size and results through references from former managers and reps. Many states and cities ban asking about salary history, so ask about results, not past pay.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test forecasting accuracy, pipeline reviews, territory and quota planning, and compensation plan design. Check how they hire, coach and manage underperforming reps, and how well they use your CRM and sales data. Match their experience to your deal size, sales cycle and buyers.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong sales leaders forecast within a narrow range, explain exactly how deals were won and lost, and build teams where many reps hit quota, not just a few stars. They work well with marketing, product and finance and keep the reps they develop.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for numbers they cannot explain or verify, blaming product or marketing for every miss, high team turnover, or heavy discounting to close deals. Be wary of leaders whose success came only from a market or product that sold itself.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through how you build your forecast and how accurate it was last year. Tell me about a rep you turned around and one you let go. How did you set quotas? Strong answers include specific methods, numbers and lessons.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a VP of sales?
qa.a: Look for a verified record of hitting revenue targets in a similar market, deal size and sales cycle, plus accurate forecasting and the ability to hire and develop reps. Check how they work with marketing and finance. No license is required for most roles, so references from managers and reps matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a VP of sales before hiring?
qa.a: Give a paid case using your anonymized pipeline data: ask for a forecast, the deals they would focus on and a ninety-day plan for the team. Include a mock deal review with a rep. Review rigor, coaching style, realism and how they handle questions from the CEO and finance.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required for vulnerability management. Security certifications covering core concepts, defense or penetration testing show training but are optional. Verify them with the issuing body, and ask references whether the candidate actually reduced open findings and met patch deadlines.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test scanner setup and tuning, reading CVE details and CVSS scores, and ranking findings by real risk, such as known exploitation and internet exposure. Check they can track fixes with system owners, handle exceptions and report progress against remediation deadlines.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates rank by exploitability and business impact, not just severity scores. They check sources such as the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, build good working ties with IT teams, verify fixes with rescans, and keep an accurate asset inventory.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who forward raw scan reports with thousands of findings, treat every high score as equal, or never confirm patches with a rescan. Be careful with anyone who ignores assets missing from scans or approves exceptions with no end date.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: You have many critical findings and one maintenance window; how do you choose? How do you handle a team that will not patch? How do you find systems the scanner misses? Strong answers mention exploit data, owners, deadlines and rescans.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a vulnerability management specialist?
qa.a: Look for hands-on scanner experience, the ability to rank findings by real risk, and a record of getting teams to patch on time. Check they know CVE and CVSS basics and verify fixes. No license is required, so certifications are a bonus; references and reduced backlogs matter more.

qa.q: How do I test a vulnerability management specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task: a sample scan export with a mix of findings and asset details. Ask them to pick the items to fix first, explain why, and draft a note to a system owner. Review their risk reasoning, use of exploit data and how clearly they write.

look.label: Equipment credentials to verify
look.text: If the job includes forklifts or other powered industrial trucks, OSHA requires you to train and evaluate each operator on your own equipment and site. A card from a past employer shows experience but does not replace your evaluation. Ask which truck types they have run, such as sit-down, reach or order picker.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check accuracy before speed. Can they read a pick list, match SKUs and lot numbers, count units correctly and spot a wrong label? Ask about handheld RF scanners and any warehouse management system they have used. Also ask how they pack fragile or mixed items.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong associates talk about pick accuracy, not only rate. They mention double-checking counts, reporting damage at receiving, keeping aisles clear and putting stock back in the right location. Steady attendance in past roles and comfort with your shift schedule and peak seasons are good signs.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for someone who brags about speed but cannot explain how they avoid mispicks. Other warning signs are shrugging off safety rules or describing equipment they were never trained on. Vague answers about handling a short shipment or a damaged pallet suggest thin experience.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: What do you do when the bin count does not match the system? How do you build a stable pallet? Walk me through receiving a delivery with missing cartons. Describe the job’s lifting and standing demands and ask if they can do them with or without reasonable accommodation.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a warehouse associate?
qa.a: Look for accuracy with counts, SKUs and labels, comfort with RF scanners, and safe work habits. Ask about receiving, picking, packing and shipping tasks they have done. If the role uses forklifts, prior experience helps, but OSHA still requires you to train and evaluate them on your own equipment. Steady attendance and clear answers about fixing errors matter too.

qa.q: How do I test a warehouse associate before hiring?
qa.a: Use non-productive exercises. Give a mock pick list with sample items, ask them to count and match SKUs, scan practice labels and pack a test box. If you want them to work real orders, pay them for that time, since federal law generally requires pay for productive work. Never let an untrained candidate drive a forklift.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Anyone giving investment advice for pay usually must register as an investment adviser representative, often after passing a securities exam, and selling securities requires broker registration. Selling insurance needs a state license. Rules vary by state. Check SEC and FINRA public disclosure records for complaints or discipline.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test portfolio construction and rebalancing, tax-aware investing, retirement income planning, and estate basics such as trusts, beneficiary designations and gifting. Check they can read a client’s tax return and trust summary, and know when to bring in the client’s attorney or CPA.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong candidates explain fiduciary duty and conflicts of interest clearly, including how they are paid. They write plans clients understand, coordinate with tax and legal advisers, and keep thorough records of advice given. Planning designations add weight but never replace a clean record.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for disclosed complaints or regulatory actions, promises of returns, pressure toward high-commission products, or vague answers about compensation. Be wary of anyone who drafts trusts or gives legal opinions without a law license, or who offers to bring client lists in breach of a prior agreement.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Walk me through a plan you built for a client with a business, a trust and concentrated stock. How do you handle a client who wants to sell everything in a downturn? How are you paid? Strong answers show process, tax awareness and candor.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a wealth manager?
qa.a: Look for proper registration for the advice they give, a clean public disclosure record and clear answers on how they are paid. Check depth in investments, tax-aware planning and estate basics, and how they work with clients’ attorneys and CPAs. Rules vary by state, so confirm registrations where your clients live.

qa.q: How do I test a wealth manager before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid case study: an anonymized household with income, holdings, a trust and stated goals. Ask for a one-page plan covering investments, tax moves and estate next steps, plus a plain-language summary for the client. Review accuracy, disclosure of conflicts and whether they flag issues for an attorney or CPA.

look.label: Portfolio to review
look.text: Ask for links to live sites and code samples, such as a shared repository. Open the sites on a phone and a laptop. Ask which parts the candidate built personally and which came from a team, a theme or a template.

look.label: Credentials to know
look.text: No US state requires a license to work as a web developer. Degrees, bootcamp certificates and vendor certifications are optional. Treat them as a bonus and weigh real, working sites and clear explanations of code more heavily.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Check HTML, CSS and JavaScript, plus the back-end language or content management system your site uses. Look for Git version control, responsive layouts, basic accessibility, page speed, and safe handling of forms, logins and updates.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for candidates who cannot explain their own code, show only lightly edited templates, skip mobile testing, or ignore backups and security updates. Be careful with anyone vague about handing over code, passwords and hosting access when work ends.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: Tell me about a site that broke after launch and how you found the cause. How do you make a contact form accessible? How do you keep a client’s site updated and backed up? Strong answers name specific steps and tools.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a web developer?
qa.a: Look for live sites they built, code they can explain line by line, and skills that match your setup, whether that’s custom code or a content management system. Check mobile layouts, accessibility and security habits. No license is required in the US, so real work and clear communication matter more than certificates.

qa.q: How do I test a web developer before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task close to your real work, such as building a responsive page from a mockup or fixing a bug in sample code. Ask them to use Git and explain their choices. Review whether it works on a phone, loads quickly, is accessible, and whether the code is clean and readable.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Ask for current welder qualification records tied to the code your work follows, such as AWS D1.1 for structural steel, ASME Section IX for pressure piping, or API 1104 for pipelines. Check the process, position, and material covered, and confirm continuity logs are up to date. Some states and cities require a welder license or card, so check local rules.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test the exact process and position your job needs, such as stick, MIG, flux core, or TIG, in flat, vertical, overhead, or 6G pipe. Watch fit-up, tack placement, heat control, and cleaning between passes. Ask them to read a drawing with weld symbols and follow a written welding procedure.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong welders inspect their own work and can name defects like porosity, undercut, cold lap, and lack of fusion. They explain why they pick a rod, wire, gas, or amperage setting. They wear proper protection, set up ventilation, and use a fire watch when needed without being told.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Be careful with expired or vague qualifications, papers that do not match the process they claim, or a candidate who cannot explain a procedure spec. Rushing a test plate, skipping grinding or cleaning, or careless handling of gas cylinders and hot work areas are warning signs.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask which materials and thicknesses they weld most, which positions give them trouble, and how they fixed a weld that failed inspection. Ask how they control distortion on thin metal and how they prepare stainless or aluminum. Real experience shows in specific, practical answers.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a welder?
qa.a: Look for current qualifications that match your process, position, and code, plus proof of continuity. Check that they can read blueprints and weld symbols, follow a written procedure, and spot defects in their own welds. Safe habits with protective gear, ventilation, and hot work matter as much as bead quality. Confirm any license your state or city requires.

qa.q: How do I test a welder before hiring?
qa.a: Run a paid weld test on coupons that match your real work, in the same process, material, thickness, and position. Inspect the weld visually, then use a bend test, cut and etch, or a third party inspector if your code requires it. Also watch their setup, fit-up, safety, and cleanup during the test.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: Workday certifications are issued through Workday’s own training, mainly for partner consultants and customer staff, by area such as HCM, Payroll, Financials or Integrations. Ask which areas, when they were earned and whether they are still active, since many require ongoing update training. Request proof rather than taking a résumé line on trust.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Look for hands-on work with business process configuration, security groups, condition rules, calculated fields and custom reports. For data work, check experience with EIB loads. For integrations, ask about Core Connectors or Workday Studio. A strong specialist also knows how to plan for and test Workday’s twice-yearly feature releases.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask them to walk you through a business process they changed, how they tested it and who signed off. Ask about a calculated field or report they built and the problem it solved. Ask what broke during a release update and how they found it. Real answers include specific steps and tradeoffs.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They test changes in a sandbox tenant before moving them to production. They document what they changed and why. They understand the HR, payroll or finance rules behind the setup, not just the clicks. They treat employee pay and personal data with care and limit access to what each role needs.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Experience only as an end user who entered time or approved requests. Vague answers about which modules or tenants they worked in. Comfort making changes directly in production without testing. Trouble explaining how security groups control access. Claiming certifications they cannot show proof of or that have lapsed.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a Workday specialist?
qa.a: Match their experience to your modules, such as HCM, Payroll, Financials or Integrations. Verify any Workday certification and whether it is still active. Look for hands-on configuration of business processes, security, calculated fields and reports, plus a habit of testing in a sandbox before production. Good specialists also understand the HR or finance rules behind the system and explain changes clearly to non-technical staff.

qa.q: How do I test a Workday specialist before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short written scenario, such as a new approval step for a business process or a report your managers need. Ask how they would configure it, which security groups it touches and how they would test it. If you share a sandbox tenant, use only fake or masked data. Then have them explain their approach to someone outside IT.

look.label: Credentials to verify
look.text: No license is required. Industry workforce management certifications are optional. Verify skills through work samples, such as a forecast model or schedule they built, and ask references how accurate their forecasts were and which planning tools they used daily.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Test interval forecasting from historical volume, staffing math such as Erlang C, shrinkage and occupancy planning, and schedules that meet service level goals. Check spreadsheet and workforce software skills, intraday adjustments, and awareness of predictive scheduling laws in the cities and states that have them.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: Strong analysts measure forecast accuracy and explain misses. They balance service, cost and agent workload, build fair schedules and communicate clearly with team leads. They adjust quickly when volume spikes and document assumptions so others can follow their models.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Watch for forecasts never compared with actuals, ignored shrinkage, or staffing models nobody else can understand. Be wary of anyone who blames every miss on volume, overlooks break and labor rules, or builds schedules without input from team leads.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: How do you forecast volume for a holiday or a product launch? Tell me about a day when volume beat the forecast and what you changed intraday. How do you set shrinkage? Strong answers name data, methods and measured results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a workforce management analyst?
qa.a: Look for strong forecasting and staffing math, schedules that meet service goals, and the habit of measuring accuracy. Check skills with spreadsheets and workforce software, and awareness of scheduling and break laws, which vary by state and city. No license is required, so work samples and references matter most.

qa.q: How do I test a workforce management analyst before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid exercise with several weeks of interval volume and handle time data. Ask them to forecast next week, calculate staffing needs with shrinkage and draft a simple schedule. Review the method, accuracy checks, clearly stated assumptions and how they would adjust if volume ran above forecast.

look.label: Credentials worth checking
look.text: No state license is required for this role. A current first aid, CPR and AED certification is a real plus, so ask for the card and its date. Facilities management certificates exist but are optional, so weigh proven experience more.

look.label: Skills to test
look.text: Planning a small office move, tracking supply spending against a budget, running a visitor sign-in process and writing a clear notice to staff. Have them work in the spreadsheet, calendar and ticketing tools your office already uses.

look.label: Signs of a strong candidate
look.text: They describe vendor work as a process: getting quotes, checking certificates of insurance and following up on work orders. They know where exits, extinguishers and first aid kits belong, and they keep records without being asked.

look.label: Red flags
look.text: Vague answers about what they actually managed or who they reported to. Treating fire drills, incident reports or blocked exits as minor. Blaming vendors for every problem. No examples of tracking costs, keys, badges or inventory.

look.label: Questions that reveal experience
look.text: Ask: ’Walk me through the last office move or desk change you ran.’ ’A visitor arrives and no one expects them. What do you do?’ ’How did you decide when to reorder supplies?’ Listen for steps, dates and results.

qa.q: What should I look for when hiring a workplace coordinator?
qa.a: Look for someone organized who has handled vendors, supplies, visitors and office moves. They should know basic safety practices, such as clear exits and stocked first aid kits, and keep good records. No license is required, but a current first aid and CPR card helps. Ask for specific examples with steps and results.

qa.q: How do I test a workplace coordinator before hiring?
qa.a: Give a short, paid task. Ask them to plan a move of ten desks over a weekend, list the vendors and steps, set a simple budget and draft the email to staff. Review how they order the work, flag risks and communicate. Clear, realistic plans matter more than polish.
